Sequitur: « Et principalem, et super principalem divini Patris claritatem, quae angelorum nobis in figuratis symbolis manifestat beatissimas hierarchias, immaterialibus, et non trementibus mentis oculis respicientes, iterum ex ipsa in simplum illius restituimur radium. » Hic manifeste edocet quibus gradibus divinae illuminationis processio fiat usque ad nos; et rursum quibus progressionibus mens nostra reducatur ad summae claritatis contemplationem. Divinum enim lumen primum in angelicam naturam 942Adescendit, et ab ipsa revelationibus, et demonstrationibus divinis, et mystica sacri eloquii narratione ad nostram usque intelligentiam, participationemque se transfundit. Mens vero humana eisdem rursum gradibus ad superna conscendens, sacra divini eloquii inspectione coelestia secreta, et eam, quae in angelis est, divinae claritatis illuminationem perpendit: ex qua paulatim in invisibilium agnitionem succrescens ad ipsum tandem summi luminis splendorem contemplandum convalescit; et fit, quod in principio dictum est, quia unum lumen et ad multa illuminanda se dividit, ut illuminata omnia ad unius claritatis aspectum similitudinemque reformet. Propterea cognita ex sacris divini eloquii traditionibus coelestium spirituum claritate, qualiter hanc cognitionem 942Bsummi luminis contemplatio subsequatur, ostendit, dicens: « Et principalem, et superprincipalem divini Patris claritatem, quae angelorum nobis in figuratis symbolis manifestat beatissimas hierarchias, immaterialibus, et non trementibus mentis oculis respicientes, iterum ex ipsa in simplum illius restituimur radium. » Ordo verborum est: Nos respicientes claritatem divini Patris principalem, et superprincipalem oculis mentis immaterialibus et non trementibus: quae claritas manifestat nobis beatissimas hierarchias angelorum in symbolis figuratis. iterum ex ipsa in simplum illius restituimur radium. Respicientes enim claritatem Patris restituimur, id est reformamur iterum, hoc est reductive conversi ad illud, unde venimus, in simplum ejus radium, 942Cut in uno lumine unum simus, qui lucemus ex lumine uno, et non sit discrepantia lucentium, sicut diversitas luminum non est ulla. Claritas autem Patris principalis et superprincipalis dicitur, quia non solum dignitate vel causa lucentibus omnibus superior est, sed etiam excelsior natura. Et haec claritas, quia non corporalis, sed spiritualis est, et spiritualiter lucet: idcirco nonnisi immaterialibus tantum, id est incorporalibus oculis videri potest. Quos oculos etiam non trementes, id est sanos, et perspicaces, et irreverberatos esse necesse est, ne lippienti acie tantum lumen intuentes, tenebras sibi ex ipsa claritate inducant. Merito autem post claritatem angelorum per sacra eloquia contemplatam, 942Dad divini Patris claritatem illuminamur; quia et ipsa nobis angelorum claritas a claritate Patris per eos in nos descendente ex sacri eloquii revelatione manifestatur. Hoc est, quod ait: « Quae angelorum nobis in figuratis symbolis, » id est signis et conformationibus secundum species visibiles figuratis, manifestat beatissimas hierarchias, id est principatus, dignitates et potestates. Angelorum ordines, et potestates, et divinae eorum operationes omnino invisibiles sunt: et nisi visibilibus signis, et similitudinibus ex visibilibus sumptis demonstrentur, intelligi ab iis qui visibilia tantum noverunt nequaquam possunt. Propterea Patris claritas ad principale lumen suum nos reparare volens, primum illuminationibus sacri eloquii ad contemplandam angelorum 943Aclaritatem nos excitat, et ex ea claritate illuminatos tandem ad suae claritatis agnitionem lumenque reformat, ut unum simus in illa, qui unum accepimus ab illa. Haec vero claritas Patris unius simplicis radii emissione et illuminatione per cuncta se diffundit, et penetrat cuncta, quoniam unam sapientiam Pater genuit, per quam cuncta opera sua fecit. Verbum quippe Patris lumen de lumine est; unum Verbum, et radius unus, et ipsum Verbum sapientia est, et ipsa sapientia lumen est procedens, a quo nota est: una de uno, et propterea radius unus a claritate una, a quo illuminantur, qui ad ipsum reformantur, ut luceant ex ipso, et lux sint cum ipso, sicut ille lux est. Et cum sint multa lumina illuminata, et varie dissimiliterque lucentia, unum tamen 943Blumen est illuminans in omnibus illuminatis.

Hoc est, quod sequitur: « Etenim neque ipse usquam, neque unquam radius a propria singulari unitate deseritur. » Sapientia enim Dei quamvis se varie dissimiliterque mentibus spiritualiter illuminandis secundum suscipientium capacitatem ac possibilitatem infundat, in se tamen una permanet et simplex. Nec major sibi in iis qui abundant ex ipsa, nec minor in iis qui secundum inferiorem participationis gratiam uniri accipiunt in ipsa; sed tota in toto, et in singulis tota, summa transcendens, et infimis condescendens, numerose se participandam praebens, et in se una permanens. Propterea sese in plura participantia dividit, sed ex sui participatione plura participantia ad unitatem restituit. Nos enim 943Ccolligi possumus in ipsa; sed ipsa dividi non potest in nobis. Etenim ipse radius, id est ipsa sapientia illuminans a principali lumine Patre exiens, et usque ad illuminanda omnia procedens, a sua unitate propria non deseritur unquam, quoniam semper cum illo est; neque usquam, quoniam ubique in illo est. Nam et cum per diversa tempora mentibus illuminandis dissimiliter se praebet, eadem ac indissimilis est. Et cum diversis locis, diversisque participationis consortibus simul praesentem se exhibet, multiplex non est.

Sequitur: « Ad anagogicam vero, et unificam eorum, quae provisa sunt, contemperantiam optime et pulchre multiplicatur et provenit: manetque intra 943Dse munite in incommutabili naturae similitudine uniformiter fixus: et in se, quantum fas est, respicientes proportionaliter eis extendit, et unificat secundum simplicem sui unitatem. » Ac si diceret: Divinae claritatis radius, qui spiritualiter lucentes illuminat, quamvis in se unus permaneat, participatione tamen et distributione donorum varie multiplicatur, quoniam multis diversisque modis distribuitur et multiplicatur. Haec vero multiplicatio et variatio universorum est pulchritudo; quoniam, nisi dissimiliter pulchra essent singula, summe pulchra non essent simul universa. Non enim unum aliquod ex universis diversis capere potuit, quod erat pulchritudinis totum: et idcirco summa pulchritudo varia participatione distributa est in singulis, ut 944Aperfecta esse posset simul in universis. Ipsa vero distributio multiplicatur optime et pulchre: optime in universis, et pulchre in singulis, vel, optime secundum participantium dispositionem. Optime enim multiplicatur, ut majus sit bonum, quod a multis percipitur; et pulchre multiplicatur, ut major sit decor universitatis, quod participantibus singulis varie diversisque modis infunditur, ut ex multitudine numerosa in participantibus boni fiat consummatio, ex distributione dissimili participantium pulchritudo. Sive simplicis radii, quo nos illuminamur multiplicatio convenienter intelligi potest secundum multas ac diversas divinorum eloquiorum figuras ac similitudines: quibus secundum nos sumptis divina 944Bsapientia, quae in sua puritate, ac simplicitate omnino incomprehensibilis est, mentibus humanis varie multipliciterque, cum ipsa una eademque semper sit, declaratur. Multiplicatur ergo, quoniam multis modis declaratur: optime quidem quantum ad se, et pulchre quantum ad nos. Optime multiplicatur, quoniam ex ipsa multiplicatione declarationum perfectius agnoscitur; pulchre declaratur, quoniam pulchra ac decenti se declarantium formarum specie ac dissimilitudine manifestatur. Et ipsa multiplicatio fit ad contemperantiam eorum, quae provisa sunt, hoc est electorum et provisorum ad vitam, ut contemperentur et participationis concordia uniantur quasi multa membra in uno corpore, ut ipsa diversitas donorum unitatis et pacis 944Csocietatem ad invicem confirmet: quatenus unumquodque membrum se a totius corporis compage dividere non praesumat, cum boni plenitudinem, quam in se minus habet, in aliorum societate possideat. Quia enim unumquodque habet, quod aliud non habet: propterea unumquodque in alio habet quod in se non habet, vel in alio plus habet quod in se minus habet. Et idcirco singula invicem tendunt ad se et concordiam ac pacem servant inter se: et ipsa concordia et pax contemperantia est, qua sibi consentiunt, ut stent in unum et reformentur ad unum. Propter hoc ergo ipsam contemperantia provisorum anagogicam dicit et unificam. Unificam quidem, ut stent in unum; anagogicam, ut reformentur 944Dad unum. Unificam, quia dispersos in unum colligit; anagogicam, quia dejectos ad superiora reducit. Unificam, per dilectionem proximi; anagogicam, per dilectionem Dei. Propterea pulchra est in congregatione, optima in elevatione. Ipse ergo radius divinae illustrationis multiplicatus sive per distributionem donorum spiritualium, qua intrinsecus participatur; sive per varietatem mysticarum demonstrationum, qua extrinsecus in sacro eloquio declaratur, provenit, hoc est procedit in corda illuminanda, sive ab intus per aspirationem ea replens, sive a foris per sacri verbi eruditionem se ipsis infundens: et tamen manet intra se munite, ut cum se mentibus illuminandis varie ac multipliciter participandum praestat, extra suae tamen simplicitatem 945Aunitatis non effluat. Ipsa enim ejus unitas propterea semper intra se manet, quoniam illam munit atque custodit coessentialis incommutabilitas, ut licet ad illius communicationem accedat participantium pluralitas, ad divisionem tamen illius non praevaleat participationis diversitas. Manet ergo intra se munite, ut semper idem sit, neque exeat ab eo quod est, in id quod non est: sed incommutabili similitudine sua uniformiter fixus, ut videlicet a seipso non discrepet, quasi sibi dissimilis effectus. Neque solum ipse unus manet, sed etiam respicientes in se, et conversos ad se, quantum fas est, hoc est licitum et possibile illis, extendit se eis, hoc est porrigit ut ad eos etiam veniat qui longe sunt, et a se tamen non recedat. Extendit videlicet proportionaliter, 945Bhoc est ut alii plus, alii miuus accipiant secundum dispensationem distributionis munerum, vel possibilitatem capacitatis participantium. Qui enim proximi sunt, abundantius ex illo accipiunt: et sic deinde singuli quo magis accedunt, magis accipiunt; et quo magis recedunt, minus recipiunt. Omnes tamen accipiunt; unusquisque pro parte sua. Hoc est, quod ait: « Proportionaliter se extendit, quia tamen ad omnes se extendit, et omnibus se infundit, omnes illuminat, et lumina esse facit ex lumine suo, ac per hoc unum esse facit, sicut ipse unus est. Et hoc est, quod dicit: « Unificat eos secundum simplicem sui unitatem. » Una enim illuminatio omnium, una est similitudo, et una forma, in qua unum sunt omnes ex illa, qui 945Cilluminantur ab illa, et unum cum illa, quoniam illuminati lumina sunt, sicut ipsa est lumen. Illi tamen, qui ex ipsa unum sunt, unificatione unum sunt non unitate, quia quod unum sunt ex multis, unum sunt in uno. Ipsi enim multi sunt, et propterea unum non sunt in eo quod sunt; sed, quia multi in uno sunt, ex uno multi unum sunt, et unificatione unum sunt, non unitate. Ipse vero non unificatione, sed unitate unus est, quia unus est ex eo quod est, quod unum est. Et propterea simplicem dixit unitatem, quia ex uno unus est, et idem unum a quo est, ipse est. Idcirco unitas in uno simplex est; unificatio vero multiplex in uno, quia illi ex uno unum, et unum in uno: hic autem 945Dex multis unum, quia multi in uno, et unum in multis. Deinde subjungit causam quare divinus radius, id est, sapientia divina, quae a Patre una est, et apud Patrem simplex est, varie multiplicatur per similitudines et formas demonstrationum in sacro eloquio, quoniam videlicet aliter nobis innotescere non potuit invisibilis Dei sapientia, nisi se iis quae novimus visibilium rerum formis ad similitudinem conformaret, et per eas nobis sua invisibilia quae non novimus significando exprimeret. Propterea divinus radius, qui in se unus est, et simplex, ad nos veniens, significationum et demonstrationum varietate multiplicatur, quia eum in sua puritate ac simplicitate capere non valet

946A« Etenim neque possibile est aliter nobis lucere divinum radium, nisi varietate sacrorum vel animum anagogice circumvelatum, et iis, quae secundum nos sunt, providentia paterna connaturaliter, et proprie praeparatum. » Sacra velamina, in quibus nobis radius divinus lucet, sunt mysticae in sacro eloquio descriptiones, quae visibiles adducunt formas et similitudines invisibilium ad declarationem. Quibus videlicet velaminibus ipse radius divinus anagogice circumvelatur. Anagoge enim, sicut dictum est, ascensio mentis, sive elevatio vocatur in contemplationem supernorum. Anagogice igitur circumvelatur, quia ad hoc velatur ut amplius clarescat; ob hoc tegitur ut magis appareat. Ejus igitur obumbratio nostri est illuminatio; et ejus circumvelatio; 946Bnostri elevatio. Quemadmodum infirmi oculi solem nube tectum libere conspiciunt, qui coruscum ejus lumen intueri non possunt: sic et divinum radium lippientibus mentis oculis lucere impossibile est, nisi varietate sacrorum velaminum circumvelatum et praeparatum providentia paterna connaturaliter et proprie iis, quae secundum nos sunt. Nisi enim providentia paterna nobis ineffabili bonitate in hoc providisset, oculis nostris lumen ipsius omnino lucere non posset: et idcirco paterne et pie providit nobis, ut ipsum lumen praepararet nobis et coaptaret iis, quae secundum nos sunt, rebus, et similitudinibus, et formis: et sic connaturaliter et proprie, hoc est secundum naturam nostram, et proprietatem eorum, quae naturae nostrae sunt, praeparatum 946Cet coaptatum ostenderet nobis. Conformat se nostris, ut per nostra innotescat nobis, ut ea, quae connaturalia sunt et propria nobis, in demonstrationem proposita facilius intelligantur a nobis.

Sequitur: « Propter quod et sanctissimam nostram hierarchiam perfectissima sacrorum dispositio coelestium hierarchiarum supermundana imitatione dignam judicans, et dictas immateriales hierarchias materialibus figuris, et formalibus compositionibus varificans tradidit. » Ac si diceret: Quia per visibilia convenienter invisibilia demonstrantur, idcirco divina Sapientia, quae omnia disponit ad similitudinem angelicae hierarchiae, quae invisibiliter 946Dordinata erat in coelis, humanam hierarchiam visibiliter formavit in terris, ut essent in hominibus quoque sicut in angelis potestates et principatus sacri, quibus humana conversatio temporaliter incedens gubernetur, ut ex visibili dispositione hominum, invisibilis innotescat dispositio angelorum. Hoc est enim quod ait: Propter quod perfectissima sacrorum, hoc est summa hierarchia ipsa ineffabilis Trinitas, a qua, et secundum quam sacra omnia, id est sacrae ordinationes omnes disponuntur, judicans sanctissimam nostram hierarchiam, id est humanam, dignam supermundana, id est spirituali vel intellectuali imitatione coelestium hierarchiarum, ut eas spiritualiter imitetur, et secundum illas disponatur. Et idcirco varificans id est varie ac multipliciter 947Adeclarans ipsas scilicet jam dictas immateriales, id est spirituales et angelicas hierarchias materialibus, id est corporalibus et visibilibus, vel secundum visibilia sumptis figuris et compositionibus formalibus, hoc est aptis et competenter secundum rationem formationum expressis, tradit, hoc est instituit ipsam videlicet sanctissimam nostram hierarchiam, ut in hoc quoque ratio servaretur visibilium demonstrationum ad invisibilem veritatem, ut nos ascendamus ab ipsis sacratissimis formationibus, quae foris ad demonstrationem proponuntur, ad altitudines et similitudines non figuratas, hoc est simplices et spirituales. Ascendamus dico proportionaliter nobis ipsis, hoc est, secundum proportionem et mensuram spiritualium donorum illuminati 947Bper ea, quae foris sunt, in invisibilium agnitionem, et ad sublimem, et simplicem, et eamdem semper consistentem veritatem. Altitudines enim, et similitudines ipsae sunt invisibiles potestates. Altitudines quidem dignitate, similitudines incommutabilitate, non figuratae simplicitate. Ad quarum cognitionem secundum differentiam progressionum, et incrementa illuminationum proportionaliter nobis ipsis ascendimus per gradus spiritualium profectuum in nobis, per differentiam donorum inter nos. Secundum namque illam proportionem, qua nunc dona gratiarum differenter percipimus, merito postea vel hic per mentis contemplationem, vel illic per retributionem in numerum angelorum transimus. Sic enim proportionaliter nobis ipsis ascendimus, quando secundum 947Choc, quod in praesenti per dona gratiarum, et gradus dignitatum differenter disponimur, ad invisibilis veritatis participationem secreta et invisibili promotione sublevamur. Ipsa autem veritas in nobis quidem per officia spiritualium dignitatum, et gradus, et distributiones ordinum figuraliter et materialiter figuratur, atque formatur secundum habitus, et actiones, et signa visibilia, quae in nostra sicut hierarchia ad declarationem opposita, quae omnia coelesti atque angelica hierarchia secundum simplicem veritatem sublimi, et nostrae naturae superexcellenti modo absque signis et figuris pure et uniformiter constant: secundum quam excellentiam ipsos angelicos ordines altitudines theologia vocat 947Det similitudines, vel quia per nullam mutabilitatem a semetipsis discrepant, vel quia ea in ipsis secundum simplicem veritatem sunt, quasi quaedam similitudines et exemplaria esse videntur eorum, quae per figuras et imagines consistunt. Nisi enim inter haec et illa aliqua similitudo esset, per haec ad illa nulla declaratio esset. Nunc autem, quoniam haec, quae visibilia sunt ad invisibilium aemulationem divina sapientia in prima conditione formavit, in secunda dispositione ex eisdem quoque rationali animo ad invisibilium agnitionem conscendenti signa et exempla demonstrationum constituit.

Hoc est enim, quod sequitur: « Quoniam neque possibile est nostro animo ad non materialem illam ascendere coelestium hierarchiarum imitationem, et 948Acontemplationem, nisi ea, » quae secundum ipsum est materiali manuductione utatur. Non materialem spiritualem imitationem, vel contemplationem dicit et incorporalem; quoniam omne, quod corporale est, ex materia est. Spiritualis autem natura merito immaterialis dicitur, quoniam, neque ex materia est, ut sit de alio, neque materia esse potest, ut de ipsa sit aliud. Materialem autem manuductionem corporalia signa intelligit, quorum quasi manuductione mens humana utitur, ut ex visibilibus ad invisibilium imitationem et contemplationem dirigatur. Ad imitationem quidem per exercitium virtutis; ad contemplationem vero per cognitionem veritatis. Nota autem novam compositionem et similitudinem novam in eo quod ait manuductio. Mens 948Betenim hominis tenebris ignorantiae suae obvoluta ad lumen veritatis exire non potest, nisi dirigatur, et quasi caecus manuductione utens, quo non videt, incedat. Ipsae autem manuductiones et directiones, quibus mens ad invisibilia tendens utitur, a visibilibus sumuntur signis, et demonstrationibus secundum visibilia formatis. Et hoc totum disposuit, et ordinavit perfectissima sacrorum dispositio, quae Graece hierothesia vocatur, hoc est sacrorum positio, summa videlicet Trinitas, a qua et secundum quam omnia sacra disponuntur et ordinantur in coelo, et in terra, et alio nomine teletarche, id est principium purgationis dicitur, quoniam ab ipsa omnis emundatio est et principium purgationis non solum ut bona fiant, quae mala sunt; sed et illustrationis 948Cet deificationis, ut meliora efficiantur, quae bona fuerunt. Ipsum ergo summum sacerdotium, vel summa paternitas omnia emundans, et sanctificans, et illustrans, hoc instituit et ordinavit, ut primo loco secundum ipsam angelica natura invisibiliter formetur, et secundo loco humana natura ad eamdem imaginem per visibilia excitata reformetur; quia non potest humanus animus ad invisibilium cognitionem vel imitationem reduci, nisi per visibiles demonstrationes eruditus, quoniam et ipsa visibilia a Deo sic facta sunt, ut secundum illam similitudinem et aemulationem, quam ad ipsa invisibilia acceperunt, eadem convenienter declarare possunt, ut noster animus horum ductione utens ad illa dirigatur 948Dsecundum ista, pro similitudine demonstrationis illa aestimans et perpendens.

Quemadmodum sequitur: « Visibiles quidem formas invisibilis pulchritudinis imaginationes, sive imagines arbitrans, » videlicet ipse noster animus; « et sensibiles suavitates figuras invisibilis distributionis, » subauditur, arbitrans ipse noster animus; « et immaterialis luculentiae imaginem materialia lumina, » ut iterum subaudiatur, arbitrans ipse noster animus; « secundum intellectum contemplativae plenitudinis discursas sacras disciplinas, » hic plus subaudiendum est, arbitrans noster animus imagines esse; « et adunati ad divina, et ordinati habitus earum, quae hic sunt, dispositionum ordines, » iterum subaudi, arbitrans noster animus imagines 949Aesse; « Jesu participationis ipsam divinissimae Eucharistiae assumptionem, » iterum subintellige, arbitrans noster animus imaginem esse. Summa igitur totius capituli haec est: Quoniam non potest noster animus ad invisibilium imitationem et contemplationem ascendere, nisi per visibilia dirigatur, ita videlicet, ut ex ipsis visibilibus invisibilia arbitrari, et aestimare sciat, secundum quod ipsa ad illa similitudinem habent, et significationem faciunt. Quas vero visibilium similitudines ad invisibilia ipse noster animus arbitrari debeat et existimare, quaedam distincta subjiciens exempla ostendit, ac si diceret: Ideo per visibilia invisibilium veritas demonstrata est; quia non potest noster animus ad invisibilium ipsorum veritatem ascendere, nisi per 949Bvisibilium considerationem eruditus, ita videlicet, ut arbitretur visibiles formas esse imaginationes invisibilis pulchritudinis. Quia enim in formis rerum visibilium pulchritudo earumdem consistit, congrue ex formis visibilibus invisibilem pulchritudinem demonstrari dicit, quoniam visibilis pulchritudo invisibilis pulchritudinis imago est. Quia tamen in rebus visibilibus aliud est forma, et aliud est essentia, idcirco quaecunque visibilia sunt mutabiliter pulchra sunt, quoniam quaecunque numero diversa sunt, et natura mutabilia inseparabiliter simul non consistunt. Invisibilia autem quibus aliud non est forma, et aliud essentia, quia omne quod est, unum est et simplex, et idem esse: pulchra sunt ex eo quod sunt, et non est pulchritudo illorum compacta ex 949Cmultis concurrentibus in unum, sicut visibilis natura videtur, cujus forma secundum spatia locorum explicatur, et per figuras ex multis coaptatas disponitur. Idcirco alia est pulchritudo visibilis, et alia invisibilis naturae, quoniam illa simplex, et uniformis est; ista autem multiplex et varia proportione conducta. Est tamen aliqua similitudo visibilis pulchritudinis ad invisibilem pulchritudinem, secundum aemulationem, quam invisibilis artifex ad utramque constituit, in qua quasi speculamina quaedam diverversorum proportionum unam imaginem effingunt. Secundum hoc ergo a pulchritudine visibili ad invisibilem pulchritudinem mens humana convenienter excitata ascendit; quasi de simili ad similia conducta 949Dfacile in semetipsa invisibiliter intelligens quae sit eorum, quae foris visibiliter comprehendit, ad invisibilia cognatio. Nam secundum invisibilem lucem insitam sibi noster animus ad invisibilia respiciens, facile arbitratur visibiles formas invisibilis pulchritudinis imagines esse, illi, quod invisibile intus ipse habet, amica quadam similitudine respondentes, eas secundum approbationem et affectum inveniens. Quod enim in animo est, invisibile est, sicut ipse animus invisibilis est; et concipit tamen ipse, qui invisibilis est ex iis quae visibilia sunt, gaudium, et amorem, et affectum; et diligit ex his quaedam quasi similia, et amica, et cognata et praestat se illis voluntarie, et exsultat in ipsis. Alia autem aspernatur, et odit, et refugit, et longe 950Ase facit ab illis, amore, et dilectione; et judicat peregrina a se, et disconvenientia, et nullam secum habentia similitudinem. Atque in hunc modum noster animus ex propria natura docetur quod visibilia ad invisibilia cognationem habent et similitudinem: et quod ipsa visibilia imagines sunt et simulacra eorum, quae visibiliter videri non possunt, quoniam ex his intelliguntur ea, quae non videntur; et quia secundum aliquid totum illic in incommutabili natura invisibiliter consistit, quod hic visibiliter et sensibiliter natura mutabilis accepit, ut ad invisibilia conducat. Est enim hic species et forma, quae delectat visum; est et melodiae jucunditas, quae demulcet auditum; est suavitas odoris, quae reficit olfactum; est dulcedo saporis, quae infundit 950Bgustum; et lenitas corporum, quae fovet et blande excipit tactum. Illic autem species est virtus, et forma justitia, dulcedo amor, et odor desiderium; cantus vero gaudium et exsultatio; contactus autem amati, et desiderati, et quaesiti boni inventio. Haec enim omnia ibi sunt, et vera ibi sunt, et habent ad haec, quae non vera sunt, aliquod simile secundum quod intelliguntur a nobis. Ex his enim noster animus ad illorum cognitionem et imitationem ascendit, arbitrans visibiles formas, quas vel natura secundum primam conditionem inditas ostendit, vel sacrum eloquium dispensatorie ad declarationem faciendam in significationem proponit, invisibilis pulchritudinis imagines esse et sensibiles suavitates, id est dulcedines sensibiles, figuras esse et similitudines 950Cinvisibilis distributionis, hoc est dulcedinis, quae invisibiliter distribuitur, id est diversis modis tribuitur: ut videlicet alius plus, alius minus accipiat secundum mensuram, et dona gratiae largitoris. Et similiter immaterialis luculentiae, hoc est spiritualis lucis imaginem esse materialia, id est corporalia lumina; et rursum sacras disciplinas, id est investigatas et perscrutatas ingenio, imagines esse contemplativae plenitudinis, id est plenae ac perfectae contemplationis, quae secundum intellectum, id est intellectualiter solum et invisibiliter et percipitur, et ministratur. Omnis enim illa cognitio, quam modo per sacrum eloquium studio lectionis vel meditationis discimus, quasi imago tantum est illius plenae 950Dac perfectae cognitionis, quam postmodum ex praesenti contemplatione hauriemus. Unde et Apostolus ait: « Videmus nunc per speculum in aenigmate; tunc autem facie ad faciem (I Cor. XIII). » Quid ergo mirum est, si ea, quae foris apparent sensibilia, invisibilium imagines esse dicuntur, cum ipsa nostra scientia, quae ad horum comparationem spiritualis et invisibilis creditur, imaginis et similitudinis loca ad illa existimetur?

Sequitur: « Et adunati ad divina, et ordinati habitus earum, quae hic sunt, dispositionum ordines. » Iterum subaudi, arbitrans noster animus ordines dispositionum: « quae dispositiones hic, » hoc est exterius sunt, esse imagines habitus adunati ad divina. Est enim quidam habitus mentis bonae adunatae 951Aad divina, et quasi collectae in unum a variis desideriorum scissuris, et ordinatae, ut recte incedat. Adunatae videlicet per dilectionem, et ordinatae per discretionem. Adunatae ad unum, et ordinatae in uno. Cujus videlicet habitus invisibiliter ordinati, et subsistentis imagines sunt ordines dispositionum, quae extrinsecus in gradibus, et officiis, et ministeriis in Ecclesia sancta dispensantur. Sicut enim in una Ecclesia diversi ordines, et dispositiones unam in universitate pacem et concordiam subministrando, et cooperando efficiunt, sic in una anima multae virtutes cooperando, et subministrando sibi unam perfectionis formam componunt. Sed et in unoquoque nostrum exterioris hominis dispositio, et ordo vivendi, atque agendi modus interioris hominis formam 951Bhabitumque demonstrat.

Sequitur: « Et Jesu participationis ipsam divinissimae eucharistiae assumptionem. » Rursum subintellige, quod supra, arbitrans noster animus ipsam assumptionem divinissimae eucharistiae imaginem esse participationis Jesu. Ipsa enim assumptio divinissimae Eucharistiae, id est sanctissimae perceptionis corporis et sanguinis Jesu Christi, quam nunc sacramentaliter et visibiliter in altari tractamus, imago est et forma illius participationis Jesu, qua vel nunc ei in spiritu per dilectionem conjungimur, vel postmodum in eadem forma gloriae apparentes plena similitudine uniemur. Sane hic notandum quod quidam ex hoc loco munimentum erroris sui dicere putaverunt, dicentes in sacramento altaris veritatem 951Ccorporis et sanguinis Christi non esse, sed imaginem illius tantum et figuram: propterea quia Scriptura dicit, id quod in eucharistia altaris sumitur, imaginem esse illius quod in participatione Jesu percipietur. Qui profecto in hunc erroris laqueum non inciderent, si vel sacramenta Dei recta, et humili fide susciperent, vel Scripturas sacras convenienti intelligentia tractarent. Nunc autem, quia in sacramentis Dei sensum suum fidei praeferunt, et in Scripturis sacris sanam interpretationis formam tenere contemnunt, fit ut ipse sermo veritatis amplius eos caligare faciat, dum non recte intellectus errorem pro veritate ministrat. Quod tamen Scripturae vitium non est, sed legentium et non intelligentium 951Dcaecitas; neque sacramentorum Dei confusio, sed praesumentium pravitas. Hic autem periculose erraverunt tot manifestis sententiis et assertionibus non dubiis unum ambiguum praeferentes, et in ipso magis mendacium, quam veritatem eligentes, non quia hoc ibi magis dicebatur, sed quia hoc ab illis magis credebatur. Quid enim? nunquid ideo sacramentum altaris veritas non est, quia figura est? Ergo nec mors Christi veritas est, quia figura est; et resurrectio Christi veritas non est, quia figura est. Nam et mortem Christi, et resurrectionem figuram esse, et imaginem esse, et similitudinem, et sacramentum, et exemplum Apostolus manifeste declarat, dicens: « Christus mortuus est pro delictis nostris, et resurrexit propter justificationem 952Anostram: ut peccatis mortui justitiae vivamus (I Cor. XV). » Et apostolus Petrus dixit: « Christus est passus pro nobis; vobis relinquens exemplum, ut sequamini vestigia ejus (I Petr. II). » Ergo mors Christi exemplum fuit ut peccato moriamur, et resurrectio ejus exemplum fuit ut justitiae vivamus. Nunquid ideo veritas non fuit? ergo Christus vere mortuus non est, et vere non surrexit, si mors ejus, vel resurrectio vera non fuit. Absit! Nam de ipso scriptum est: « Vere languores nostros ipse tulit, et dolores nostros ipse portavit » (Isa. LIII). Ergo mors Christi vera fuit, et tamen exemplum fuit; et resurrectio Christi vera fuit, et tamen exemplum fuit. Quare ergo sacramentum altaris similitudo esse non potest, et veritas? In alio quidem 952Bsimilitudo, et in alio veritas. Nam, cum unum sit sacramentum, tria ibi discreta proponuntur, species scilicet visibilis, et veritas corporis, et virtus gratiae spiritualis. Aliud est enim visibilis species, quae visibiliter cernitur. Aliud est veritas corporis et sanguinis, quae sub visibili specie invisibiliter creditur. Atque aliud gratia spiritualis, quae cum corpore et sanguine invisibiliter et spiritualiter percipitur. Quod enim videmus, species est panis et vini; quod autem sub specie illa credimus, verum corpus est, et verus sanguis Christi Jesu, quod pependit in cruce, et qui fluxit de latere. Nec per panem et vinum corpus et sanguinem tantum significari; sed sub specie panis et vini verum corpus et verum sanguinem consecrari. Et speciem quidem 952Cvisibilem sacramentum esse veri corporis et veri: sanguinis; corpus autem et sanguinem sacramentum esse gratiae spiritualis. Et sicut species illic cernitur, cujus res vel substantia ibi esse non creditur, sic res ibi esse veraciter et substantialiter praesens creditur, cujus species non cernitur. Videtur enim species panis et vini, et substantia panis et vini non creditur. Creditur autem substantia corporis et sanguinis Christi, et tamen illius species non cernitur.

Quod ergo videtur secundum speciem sacramentum est, et imago illius quod creditur secundum corporis veritatem, et quod creditur secundum corporis veritatem, sacramentum est illius, quod percipitur secundum gratiam spiritualem. Sacramentum ergo 952Daltaris et eucharistia divina in vero corpore et sanguine Domini nostri Jesu Christi, et imago est secundum speciem panis et vini, in qua cernitur, et res est secundum substantiae suae veritatem, in qua creditur illic atque percipitur. Et rursum, quod nunc visibiliter secundum speciem sacramenti, et corporaliter secundum carnis et sanguinis veritatem, Christum in altari sumimus, sacramentum est et imago, quod ipsum eumdem invisibiliter et spiritualiter secundum gratiae infusionem, et spiritus sui participationem in corde sumere debemus. Ergo divinissima eucharistia, quae in altari et secundum speciem panis et vini, et secundum corporis et sanguinis Christi veritatem visibiliter et corporaliter tractatur, sacramentum est, et signum, et imago 953Ainvisibilis, et spiritualis participationis Jesu, quae intus in corde per fidem et dilectionem perficitur. Voluit enim sapientia Dei, quae se per visibile manifestat, ostendere, quod ipsa animorum cibus et refectio est, et propterea carnem assumptam in edulium proposuit, ut per cibum carnis ad gustum invitaret Divinitatis. Sed, ne rursum humana infirmitas contactum carnis in assumptione horreret, consueti et principalis edulii specie illam velavit, et sic sumendam proposuit, ut sensus in uno foveretur, et fides in altero aedificaretur. Sensus enim fovetur in uno, dum solita tantum et consueta percipit; aedificatur autem fides in altero, dum in eo quod videt, quale sit illud quod non videt agnoscit. Proponitur igitur species panis et vini, ut doceatur 953Bplena et perfecta refectio esse in sumptione corporis et sanguinis Christi ex divinitate Christi. Plena autem refectio cibus et potus est; cibi autem et potus, panis et vinum principalis substantia est. Et proponitur species ex principali substantia refectionis, ut in ea sumatur, et per eum significetur veritas corporis et sanguinis, sicut ipse testatur, dicens: « Caro mea vere est cibus, et sanguis meus vere est potus (Joan. VI). » Quae tamen corporis et sanguinis sumptio, quod sola sine spirituali effectu salutem non conferat, ipse idem Salvator manifesstat, dicens: « Caro nihil prodest; spiritus est, qui vivificat (ibid.). » Virtus ergo et plenitudo spiritualis refectionis, quae in corpore et sanguine Christi est, per speciem quidem panis et vini significatur; 953Cin perceptione autem gratiae, et infusione internae et aeternae refectionis perficitur. Et sic quidem, cum tria in uno ibi sint, in primo quidem signum invenitur secundi; in secundo autem causa tertii; in tertio vero virtus secundi, et veritas primi. Et haec tria in uno sunt, et unum sacramentum. Claret itaque quod divinissimae eucharistiae assumptio sacramentum est, et imago participationis Jesu; quia hoc, quod ejus sacramentum visibiliter percipimus signum est, quod ei spiritualiter et invisibiliter uniri debemus. Ipsa autem eucharistia, id est bona gratia, ipsa scilicet hostia sacra divinissima vocatur, quoniam divinos facit et participes Divinitatis eos qui se participant. Et quia ipsa signum est, et 953Dveritas in qua vera caro Christi sub specie panis sumitur, et in carne ejus digne sumpta ipsius etiam Divinitatis susceptio, et participatio, et consortium condonatur. Propterea dignissima est, et sanctissima, et sanctificans sanctificantia omnia, et sancta.

Sequitur: « Et quaecunque alia coelestibus quidem essentiis supermundane, nobis vero symbolice tradita sunt. » Postquam quaedam, exempli gratia, ad ostendendam visibilium ad invisibilia similitudinem proposuit, nunc generaliter de toto concludit, dicens: « Et quaecunque alia coelestibus quidem essentiis supermundane, nobis vero symbolice tradita sunt, » ac si diceret: Haec quae superius memorata sunt, visibilia, arbitrari debet noster animus 954Asecundum exempla proposita ad invisibilia similitudinem habere: et non sola haec, sed quaecunque alia, quae nobis symbolice tradita sunt, vel quae coelestibus essentiis supermundane. Non enim sola haec, quae posita sunt, visibilia, id est formae suavitates, lumina disciplinae, ordines, eucharistia sacra, invisibilium habent, etsi multitudinem, et demonstrationem; sed et alia omnia visibilia quaecunque nobis, visibiliter erudiendis symbolice, id est figurative tradita, sunt proposita ad invisibilium significationem et declarationem. Et non sola haec visibilia, quae nobis symbolice tradita sunt, invisibilium demonstrationem habent; sed illa quoque, quae coelestibus essentiis, id est angelicis spiritibus, supermundane, id est invisibiliter et spiritualiter, et non 954Bsecundum hujus mundi species tradita sunt, signa sunt invisibilium, et imagines eorum, quae in excellenti et incomprehensibili Divinitatis natura supra omnem intelligentiam subsistunt, et sensum. Hoc est enim, quod dicit, quod non sola ea invisibilium signa sunt, quae nobis tradita sunt symbolice; sed illa quoque, quae caelestibus essentiis tradita sunt supermundane. Habent namque et ipsi angelici spiritus signa sua, et demonstrationes, per quas de invisibilibus Dei, et valde occultis, et secretis absconditis intus immaterialiter, et invisibiliter, et simpliciter erudiuntur. Quae quidem signa quantum ad nos, et ea quae apud nos sunt visibilia, invisibilia omnino existimantur; quantum vero ad illam multum invisibilem, et inaccessibilem lucem, et incomprehensibilem 954CDeitatis, quasi foris sunt et procedunt abintus in demonstrationem. Propter quod et ipsa signa, quae superveniunt mentibus, sive animis divinitus illuminatis, theophaniae, id est divinae apparitiones vocantur; quia in eis ad manifestationem venientibus id, quod omnino occultum Dei est demonstratur. Haec ergo sunt, quae coelestibus supermundane traduntur, non secundum eam, quae apud nos est, demonstrationem; sed invisibiliter et simpliciter aspirata. Multa quidem hic dicenda fuerant de hoc contemplationis genere, quo theophaniae, id est divinae apparitiones divinitus aspiratae mentibus illuminandis superveniunt, et eas de occultis et invisibilibus Dei miro, et abscondito, et secreto, et 954Dsingulari modo erudiendo sapientes efficiunt: praecipue quoniam et hic quoque quidam in cogitationibus suis evanuisse inveniuntur, Deum rationali animo omnino incomprehensibilem et inaccessibilem, praedicantes, praeterquam quod theophaniis quibusdam, id est divinis apparitionibus, vel similitudinibus divinis in contemplationem propositis, de ipso eruditur. Ipsa autem quasi quaedam simulacra absconditae Divinitatis inter rationales animos ac Deum media ponunt, altiora quidem mente, inferiora autem Divinitate. Et hoc quidem solum de Deo videri, et in hoc solo Deum videri, utpote qui in ipso a nulla mente vel animo videri possit. Haec vero simulacra sunt eorum, et phantasmata vanitatis: in quibus dum solum Divinitatis lucem visibilem et perceptibilem 955Aconantur asserere, veram Deitatis cognitionem et visionem mentibus sanctis probantur auferre. Quid est enim in illis solum Deum videri, et extra illa non videri, nisi nunquam vere videri, et verum nunquam videri? Si enim imago sola semper videtur, et veritas nunquam videtur, quoniam imago veritas non est, etiam cum de veritate est. Tollant ergo phantasias suas, quibus lumen mentium nostrarum obumbrare nituntur; neque nobis Deum nostrum simulacris autumationum suarum intersepiant; quia nos sicut satiare non potest aliquid praeter ipsum, ita nec sistere usque ad ipsum. Ipsas igitur theophanias alio modo, et veritati consentaneo existimemus. Sicut enim duo sunt, lumen et quod suscipit lumen corpus: et ex his duobus unum efficitur 955Blucens, et ipsum lucens imago quodammodo est, et similitudo luminis, in eo quod lucet sicut ipsum lumen; ita et Deus noster lumen est, et verum lumen est, et ipsum lumen rationales animi mundi et puri concipiunt: et ex eo lucentes fiunt, et non sunt ipsi imago luminis in eo quod sunt; sed in eo quod lucent ex lumine, sicut ipsum lumen lucet; et sunt ipsa lucentia theophaniae luminis, in quibus lumen videtur, quoniam a nullo lumen videretur, si nullus a lumine illuminaretur. Nam et qui in se lumen videt, lucentem se videt; qui profecto non videret, si non luceret, et se lucentem non videret. Sic ergo non constituimus alium inter Deum nostrum et nos, sed immediate viam facimus, et nobis ad ipsum, et ipsi usque ad nos, ut simus in ipso, et 955Cipse in nobis: ut non sit aliud extra ipsum, in quo beatificemur, sicut aliud esse non potuit praeter ipsum, a quo crearemur. Propter hoc ergo supradictam sententiam theologiae ad commodiorem intelligentiam interpretemur. Quia enim dixerat invisibilia quaedam per eas quae determinatae sunt visibiles imagines, demonstrari, nunc generalem de ipsis invisibilibus sententiam subjungit, dicens: « Et quaecunque alia, etc. » Ac si diceret: Non solum illa invisibilia, quorum haec signa proposita sunt, in manifestationem venerunt; sed etiam quaecunque alia invisibilia, quae nobis quidem, scilicet hominibus symbolice, id est figurative et per sensibiles demonstrationes sunt tradita, id est proposita et manifesta; 956Acoelestibus autem essentiis, id est angelicis spiritibus supermundane et spiritualiter per nudam et simplicem veritatem impressam revelata.

Sequitur: « Propter hanc ergo nostram corrationalem theosin, » id est divinitatem, quae nobis est corrationalis, id est congrua vel apta. Congruum enim est ut per ea, quae nota sunt nobis, divinorum participes efficiamur, « Propter hanc ergo, etc., » quasi diceret: Quia humanus animus non potest de invisibilibus erudiri, nisi per visibilia et cognita, ac cognata sibi, igitur « misericors principium perfectionis, » id est Deus, a quo omnis perfectio initium habet, sicut in ipso consummationem capit, et finem sola gratia et misericordia, ut nos ad suam cognitionem revocaret, et similitudinem reformaret; 956B« manifestans nobis coelestes hierarchias, » id est angelicas potestates; « et perficiens etiam nostram hierarchiam comministram earum, » scilicet coelestium hierarchiarum, ut sit illis et in dignitate conformis, et in ministerio divino consimilis, servata in nobis similitudine deiformis earum sanctificationis, ut simus similes sanctificationi earum quae Deo conformes sunt, « ad virtutem nostram, » id est secundum possibilitatem nostram, hoc est quantum similes esse possumus, qui homines, et mortales, et peccato adhuc obnoxii sumus; « descripsit supercoelestes intellectus, » invisibiles spiritus, qui nobis incogniti erant, sensibilibus imaginibus, ut per nota incognita disceremus. Et hanc descriptionem fecit 956C« in sacris eloquiorum compositionibus, » id est in sacri eloquii descriptionibus: quae compositiones, et figuras, et similitudines proponunt nobis ad invisibilium demonstrationem. Et hoc ideo fecit, « ut nos reduceret per sensibilia ad intellectualia, » hoc est per visibilia ad invisibilia. Et ut nos etiam reduceret et « ex sacre figuratis symbolis, » id est de figuris sacris et sacrarum rerum figuris; « in simplas summitates, » id est in simplices et spiritales excellentias cognoscendas « coelestium hierarchiarum, » id est angelicarum potestatum. Propterea enim illas visibilibus signis nobis descripsit, ut eas nobis intelligibiles faceret, et ad earum nos imitationem conformaret.

EXPOSITION.

  • 935C

The first book of Dionysius the Areopagite the theologian, which is entitled On the Celestial Hierarchy, that is, on the celestial principate, is woven together of fifteen chapters: in which he carefully enumerates the gifts of the celestial spirits, and their offices, powers, and operations, through their several orders and grades and distributions and differences. And the title of the first chapter is: That every divine illumination, coming forth in various unforeseen ways according to goodness, remains simple, and not this alone, but also unifies the things illuminated. For grace itself is a divine illumination, and the gifts of grace themselves are lights illuminating those who partake of them; and all grace 935Ddescends from one fount, and every illumination from one light; and there are many rays, and one light: and the one light scatters itself, that it may illuminate many; and the many illuminated shine, and nothing is seen but one light, and they become one light in one light. By such a likeness theology shows how the one good offers itself to be partaken by many, that they may be one in it — they who draw one likeness from it. Then the theologian goes on, and shows that the invisible operations of grace, and the distributions of the invisible gifts, cannot be demonstrated or understood except by visible signs and likenesses; and that every visible appearance and sensible nature holds some likeness for the demonstration of invisible things. For as every good is from the 936Ahighest good, so in every good, according to the emulation of participation, the highest good can be contemplated. And therefore it is fitting for theology to conform, out of every appearance and form and sensible quality, to the signification of invisible things. And this is the sense of the first chapter. « Every best gift, and every perfect gift, is from above, descending from the Father of lights. » By apostolic authority, and that of divine theology, he first proves that every good is from the highest good; then from his own opinion he adds that every good looks toward and is poured back to the highest good; because, as it is divided among many by participation, so the many are united in one likeness and imitation. The best gifts are the gifts of nature; the perfect gifts are the gifts of grace; the Father of lights is the author and bestower of the gifts.

936B« Every best gift, therefore, and every perfect gift, is from above, descending from the Father of lights, » since all goods — whether those which nature, first well established, received, or those which afterward, glorified through grace, it merited to obtain — are given by one author of nature and bestower of grace. For which to descend, as it were, was to come from the fount of highest fullness to the participation of lower things. For every creature is by nature inferior to the excellence of the Creator; and therefore every good which by the Creator's gift is poured into the creature is rightly said, as it were, to descend to lower things. For it descends, because it pours itself into a nature subject and inferior in dignity. It descends also, because from a perfect and consummate fullness it divides itself into that participation 936Cwhich is in part. Yet in such a way that neither in descending is it enslaved, nor in being divided does it decrease; but, remaining in itself what it is, and in that from which it came, it offers itself, so far as it may, to those to whom it comes; and what being they receive, and how much being in that which they are, they have merited. Thus from one good all goods are; and in one good all goods are; and the good itself, from which all goods are, is good, and is light; and of the things which are from it, it is the author of goods and Father of lights; and the goods themselves are lights, and illuminating those things which are able to shine, and to become shining lights from the illuminating light. For this good leaves nothing established by it estranged from it; and yet it illuminates only those things which it created toward itself and formed according to itself. For those 936Dalone receive light which can shine from the light — which the coming light finds not unlike itself; and, poured in, it raises them to a greater likeness of itself and a more perfect outward image. These alone, therefore, receive the best gifts and the perfect gifts; because every creature (except that one which has the image of its founder and is capable of likeness), if in its own kind it is a good — which it received from the Creator to be — was neither best when it was given, nor perfect and consummate. But the rational creature, which alone was made to the image of its founder, has received both the given things and the gifts. The best, indeed, while it was being established toward the lowest; and the perfect, while it was being lifted toward the highest. For nothing better was given to any other nature than what it first received, nor anything more perfect than what it afterward 937Amerited to be, since it was both first established good before all the rest, and afterward perfected to the image and likeness of him by whom it was made. Therefore the best gifts and the perfect gifts, descending from the Father of lights, reach only the loftiness of the rational creature, which alone was made sublime. First, while it was being granted them, the best; and afterward, while it was being glorified, it is made perfect, in a certain manner conformed and coequal to the highest. For the best gifts themselves and the perfect gifts are lights, which descend from the Father of lights; and he from whom they descend, the Father of lights, is himself light, and those into whom they descend themselves become lights; because neither could the Father of light beget another than he himself is, nor can the receiver of light become other than light. If therefore he who begot light is light 937B, and he who received light is light, now in a certain manner both he who begot and he who received are found to be the same. Yet in such a way that the one is believed to be this by nature, but the other is acknowledged to be this by grace. For this reason, therefore, the one light poured itself out into many lights by participation, that it might reform the many illuminated toward the one light, so that, while many received it by partaking of it, all might appear one in its form. Therefore the theologian, when he had shown from divine authority that every good is from the highest good, at once adds from his own opinion: That every good is toward the highest good, and that it is both poured forth from it by the division of participation, and united to it by the likeness of conformation.

937C« Every best gift, and every perfect gift, is from above, descending from the Father of lights. » In this, therefore, he proves that every good is from the highest good. After this he adds that every good has its conversion, and its leading-back, and its end toward the highest good. « But also, the Father being moved, every procession of the manifestation of lights, coming forth into us most excellently and largely, again, as a unifying power, restoring us, fills us, and converts us to the unity of the gathering Father, and to the deifying simplicity. » The movement of the Father is the affection of fatherly kindness; for by kindness alone and by mercy alone the Father is moved to pour out his lights upon us. He is moved not by any disturbance of himself, but by compassion for us. He is moved, not shaking himself, but gathering us; not emptying himself, but filling us. 937DHe is moved, therefore, that he may come to us, and he is not moved so as to depart from himself. He is moved, that he may begin to be to us what he was not, and he is not moved so as to cease being to himself what he was. Thus, therefore, the Father of lights is moved upon us, and, the Father being moved, his lights descend into us, and by the things proceeding into us they are manifested through us. First to us, after this to others from us; and all this procession of the manifestation of lights — that is, through which the lights are manifested (for they would not be manifested unless they proceeded) — goes forth from the Father when he is moved. That is, all this procession of the manifestation of lights, coming forth into us, works this: namely, that it fills us — by nothing other, indeed, than itself, out of that with which it fills us — again restoring us by repairing, as it established us by punishments in creating. It restores us, namely, inasmuch as it is a unifying 938Apower, which gathers what is scattered, composes what is diverse, and out of many makes one; and thus, restoring and reforming, it converts us, who before had been turned away by unlikeness, made diverse by multitude, made perverse by depravity. It converts us, I say, to the unity of the gathering Father, and to the deifying simplicity. For the light of the Father, invisible in itself, proceeding into us and going forth to manifestation, finds us empty and void of the true good; and, pouring itself into us, fills us according to the power and capacity of each one of us; and when it has filled us, it converts us, that we may not be at variance with the Father, but in the same likeness and image may look toward him, by which we are not in discord with him. It fills, indeed, by illuminating; and it converts by making us lights. For we are filled in that we receive light; but we are converted 938Bin that, from the light received, we too are lights. For in this we are one with the light, and in the light we are one, that we are light; and there is unity in one likeness, in one light, in one brightness, and one illuminating and shining light. Since, therefore, every good is from the highest good, and every good is toward the highest good; for from it we receive that we are one with it; nor would there be in us anything by which we might look toward it, unless first what is its own became ours through it. « For from him are all things, and unto him, as the divine word says. » That is, as the authority of the divine word testifies, all things proceeding from him, converted unto him; from him as beginning unto him as end. But we can also, moreover, not unfittingly take the movement of the Father as the beginning of our 938Ccontemplation. For the mind, accustomed to its own darkness, when it strives to contemplate the inner brightness, as though with trembling and groping eyes not enduring the force of the unwonted radiance, is beaten back by the very first rays of the sight; and the light appears to it as though quivering; and the light itself seems to be moved, when rather its own darkness alone is moved and flees the presence of the flashing light. And this seems to be the movement of the light, when it is the light of the fleeing darkness; and after this movement the lights are poured out, and proceed to manifestation — lights which, while the darkness stood, could not be seen — and they fill us with light, that we may shine, and be lights, just as the light itself is which illuminates us, so that from it are all things 938Dand unto it; things which receive the beginning of their subsistence from it, and the end of their consummation in it, as the divine word through Paul the apostle testifies: « For from him, and through him, and in him are all things: to him be glory forever. Amen (Rom. XI). »

« Therefore, invoking Jesus, the paternal light, which is, [and] true, which illuminates every man coming into this world (Joan. I); through whom we have had access to the principal light, the Father; we shall look, as far as is possible, upon the illuminations handed down by the Father in the most sacred oracles, and we shall consider, as far as we are able, the hierarchies of the celestial spirits made manifest by them to us symbolically and anagogically. » In the preceding chapter he has briefly comprised the sum of the following work, namely 939Athat every good is from the highest good, and every good is toward the highest good. Now, before he enters upon the text of his subject-matter, he makes an invocation to Jesus, who is the paternal light, by whose mediation all spiritual illuminations and gifts of graces are bestowed on those to be illuminated, so that, with him illuminating and helping, according to the traditions of the divine oracles — which themselves too were handed down by the Father for the illuminating of the hearts of men — he may be able both truly to recognize and worthily to narrate the invisible illuminations and sacred dispositions of the celestial spirits. « Therefore, invoking Jesus; » as if he said: Every illumination indeed is from the Father, but without Jesus the mediator no illumination can be had. « Therefore » we, who ask to be illuminated, « invoking Jesus, » namely that we may merit to be illuminated 939B. Then there follows, concerning Jesus Christ himself, that it is « the paternal light; » instead of what he ought to have said, "who is the paternal light," the reference has been made to the following expression, "which is the paternal light." Or, « invoking Jesus, the paternal light, » which, namely, is light; that is, it has true and eternal and unchangeable being, and is light from that which it is. For it is as with the illuminated lights, which are lights not from that which they are, but from that which they have received. For which phrase "true light" — the word "light" too is understood — because from that which it is, it shines, and it shines not only for itself, but also illuminates others. Which « illuminates every man coming into this world. » Not because all are illuminated; but because of all men 939Cthere is none who has of himself why he should merit to be illuminated rather than another. For this illumination is of grace, not of nature; a gift, not a debt; the benefit of the giver, not the reward of the receiver. For either this light illuminates every man coming into this world inasmuch as all were made by nature capable of reason, and received the light of understanding. Or this light illuminates every man coming into the world; not because all, as has been said, are illuminated; but because all who are either illuminated or not illuminated have no means of being illuminated from elsewhere. For to illuminate belongs to none but the light; as to be illuminated belongs to none but the one receiving the light. Wherefore, as it belongs to all to receive light, so it belongs to the light alone to illuminate all.

939DThere follows: « Through whom we have had access to the principal light, the Father. » Through the light Jesus we have had access to the light the Father. For Jesus is light, and the Father of Jesus is light; and the Son, light, was begotten of the Father, light; and the Father and the Son are one light. And the Father is called the principal light, not because he is a greater light or a better light, since he is the same light; but because he is light not from light, therefore the principal light. The Son is light from light, the Father is light not from light; and yet the Father and Son are one light, as the Father and Son are one God. And therefore the Father is the principal light, because from the Father, light, the Son, light. It can, moreover, be understood also in another way, that the Father is called the principal light. For I see that the Son himself too is light in a certain respect, in which he cannot be equal 940Ato the Father. For the Father of Jesus is God, and God only; but the Son is God, and not only God, but also man and God; and Jesus is light in that he is God; and the same light which the Father, God, is. But in that he is man, he is light, since the very humanity of Jesus too was light in that it demonstrated the truth, and revealed the principal light, the Father. But the light of the humanity of Jesus was less than the light of the deity; and in the light of humanity indeed Jesus was inferior to the Father, but in the light of divinity the same as the Father. And we come through him — through the light of his humanity, in which was the Son alone — to the light of the divinity, in which was the Father and the Son. Therefore we have had access through the Son to the Father; and not to the Father alone, but both to the Son and to the Father. I see also another access 940Bthrough Jesus to the principal light, the Father. For Jesus is the wisdom of the Father, and this wisdom revealed the Father, and the wisdom of the Father went forth, the Father remaining in the hidden place: and the Father remained invisible, and his wisdom was made visible, that it might lead through to the invisible Father; and when it was made visible, it did not cease to be invisible, because it came thither where it was not: thence, where it was, it did not withdraw. And it went forth first through the creature of the world, and manifested itself in its works: and, invisible, it began to be seen visibly in that which was visible, and a certain light was shown, that it might lead to a greater light: and the first light was of wisdom, and the second light was wisdom. And Jesus was made for us the way to the Father; from the inferior light to the principal light. Then wisdom came a second time 940C, and went forth, as has been said, through the flesh, and became light in an earthen vessel, that it might illuminate us, and accustom us to the greater light, and lead us through to the principal light. But thus also we have had access through Jesus to the principal light, the Father. « Therefore, invoking Jesus, the paternal light, which is, which is true, which illuminates every man coming into this world: through whom we have had access to the principal light, the Father. » Up to this point the sentence hangs, until it is completed by what follows; and the sense is this. We, invoking Jesus, shall look, as far as is possible for us, upon the illuminations of the most sacred oracles — that is, upon the most sacred oracles, which illuminate us by the teaching of truth and the understanding of secrets — handed down 940Dby the Father. For the illuminations of the divine oracles were handed down by the Father, that we might be illuminated by them, until we are made capable of the contemplation of the principal light; and, with them illuminating us, we now recognize the celestial secrets which we are not yet able to comprehend by sense. We can also take the "illuminations of the most sacred oracles" to mean the descriptions of the sacred oracle, and the configurations drawn from visible forms, in which it demonstrates to us, from the proposed likeness, the state of invisible things and the reason and manner of the celestial secrets. For by these very visible signs the human mind is more conveniently instructed and illuminated to the knowledge of invisible things. Therefore almost everywhere in the sacred oracle the appearances of visible things are employed for signification, 941Awhen the human mind is instructed concerning those things which are hidden from human understanding, so that through the things it knows it may be able to grasp and understand the things it does not know. These illuminations, set before us outwardly for instruction, we ought — invoking Jesus, who inwardly illuminates hearts — to examine, and according to their demonstration to learn the celestial secrets.

This is what follows: « And we shall consider, as far as we are able, the hierarchies of the celestial spirits made manifest by them to us symbolically and anagogically. » The order, then, is this: that first we examine the illuminations of the Holy Scriptures with the invocation of Jesus, through whom the inward illumination is given and without whom the outward is empty; and then, with Jesus illuminating, from these illuminations and demonstrations of Holy Scripture 941Bwe consider the sacred principates and powers of the celestial spirits, that is, of the celestial spirits (which, unless they were made manifest to us through the traditions of Holy Scripture, would be altogether invisible and unknown to us). For this is what he says: « We shall consider, as far as we are able, » or as far as we can. For our ability is small and scanty for the magnitude of such great things. « We shall consider the hierarchies, » that is, the sacred principates of the celestial spirits, that is, of the angelic spirits. The hierarchies, I say, made manifest to us, that is, demonstrated, or revealed by them, namely by the illuminations, that is, by the demonstrations of the sacred oracle, symbolically and anagogically. A symbol is the bringing-together of visible forms for the demonstration of invisible things. But anagogy 941Cis the ascent, or elevation, of the mind for contemplating the things above. Here he notes a twofold mode of divine revelation, which was poured into the minds of the theologians and prophets through visions and demonstrations, which the Greeks call theophanies, that is, divine apparitions. Since sometimes invisible things were demonstrated through signs like to sensible things, sometimes through anagogy alone, that is, the ascent of the mind, purely contemplated in the things above. From these two kinds of visions, two kinds of descriptions also were formed in the sacred oracle. One, by which the truth of hidden things is shadowed forth by forms and figures and likenesses. The other, by which it is expressed nakedly and purely, as it is, without covering. When, therefore, 941Dthat which is hidden is manifested by forms and signs and likenesses, or that which is manifest is described, it is a symbolic demonstration. But when it is shown by pure by pure and naked revelation, or taught by plain and open narration, it is anagogic.

There follows: « And, looking with immaterial and untrembling eyes of the mind upon the principal and super-principal brightness of the divine Father, which manifests to us in figured symbols the most blessed hierarchies of the angels, again from it we are restored into the single ray of it. » Here he plainly teaches by what grades the procession of the divine illumination takes place down to us; and again by what advances our mind is led back to the contemplation of the highest brightness. For the divine light first descends into the angelic nature 942A, and from it, by revelations and divine demonstrations and the mystical narration of the sacred oracle, transfuses itself even to our understanding and participation. But the human mind, again ascending by the same grades to the things above, by the sacred inspection of the divine oracle weighs the celestial secrets and that illumination of the divine brightness which is in the angels: from which, gradually growing up into the recognition of invisible things, it at last becomes strong enough to contemplate the very splendor of the highest light; and there comes about what was said at the beginning, that the one light both divides itself for the illuminating of many, so that it may reform all the illuminated to the sight and likeness of one brightness. Therefore, the brightness of the celestial spirits being known from the sacred traditions of the divine oracle, he shows how the contemplation 942Bof the highest light follows upon this knowledge, saying: « And, looking with immaterial and untrembling eyes of the mind upon the principal and super-principal brightness of the divine Father, which manifests to us in figured symbols the most blessed hierarchies of the angels, again from it we are restored into the single ray of it. » The order of the words is: We, looking upon the principal and super-principal brightness of the divine Father with immaterial and untrembling eyes of the mind — which brightness manifests to us the most blessed hierarchies of the angels in figured symbols — again from it we are restored into its single ray. For, looking upon the brightness of the Father, we are restored, that is, reformed again — that is, being turned back reductively to that whence we came — into his single ray, 942Cthat in one light we may be one, we who shine from one light, and that there may be no discrepancy of the shining ones, just as there is no diversity of the lights. But the brightness of the Father is called principal and super-principal, because it is superior to all shining things not only in dignity or in being their cause, but also loftier in nature. And this brightness, because it is not corporeal but spiritual, and shines spiritually: therefore it can be seen only by immaterial, that is, incorporeal, eyes. Which eyes must also be untrembling, that is, sound and clear-sighted and unbeaten-back, lest, gazing upon so great a light with bleary keenness, they bring darkness upon themselves out of the very brightness. And rightly, after the brightness of the angels has been contemplated through the sacred oracles, 942Dwe are illuminated to the brightness of the divine Father; because the brightness of the angels itself too is made manifest to us, from the revelation of the sacred oracle, by the brightness of the Father descending through them into us. This is what he says: « Which, in figured symbols, » that is, in signs and conformations figured according to visible appearances, manifests to us the most blessed hierarchies of the angels, that is, the principates, dignities, and powers. The orders of the angels, and their powers, and their divine operations are altogether invisible: and unless they are demonstrated by visible signs and by likenesses drawn from visible things, they can in no way be understood by those who have known only visible things. Therefore the brightness of the Father, wishing to restore us to his principal light, first arouses us by the illuminations of the sacred oracle to contemplate the brightness of the angels 943A, and, illuminated from that brightness, at last reforms us to the recognition of his own brightness and light, that we may be one in it, we who have received one thing from it. But this brightness of the Father, by the emission and illumination of one simple ray, diffuses itself through all things, and penetrates all things, since the Father begot one wisdom, through which he made all his works. For the Word of the Father is light from light; one Word, and one ray, and the Word itself is wisdom, and this wisdom is a proceeding light, by which it is known: one from one, and therefore one ray from one brightness, by which they are illuminated who are reformed toward it, that they may shine from it, and be light with it, just as he is light. And although there are many illuminated lights, shining variously and dissimilarly, yet there is one 943Blight illuminating in all the illuminated.

This is what follows: « For neither anywhere, nor ever, is the ray itself forsaken by its own singular unity. » For the wisdom of God, although it pours itself variously and dissimilarly into the minds to be spiritually illuminated according to the capacity and possibility of those receiving it, yet in itself remains one and simple. Neither greater in itself in those who abound from it, nor less in those who, according to a lower grace of participation, receive to be united in it; but whole in the whole, and whole in each, transcending the highest and condescending to the lowest, offering itself to be partaken manifoldly, and remaining one in itself. Therefore it divides itself among many partakers, but by the participation of itself it restores the many partakers to unity. For we 943Ccan be gathered in it; but it cannot be divided in us. For the ray itself, that is, the illuminating wisdom itself, going forth from the principal light, the Father, and proceeding even to all things to be illuminated, is never forsaken by its own proper unity, since it is always with it; nor anywhere forsaken, since it is everywhere in it. For even when, through diverse times, it offers itself dissimilarly to the minds to be illuminated, it is the same and undissimilar. And when it shows itself present at once in diverse places and to diverse partners of participation, it is not manifold.

There follows: « But for the anagogic and unifying tempering-together of the things that have been provided, it is multiplied and comes forth most excellently and beautifully: and it remains within 943Ditself securely, uniformly fixed in the unchangeable likeness of its nature: and, to those looking upon it, as far as is right, it extends itself proportionally to them, and unifies them according to the simple unity of itself. » As if he said: The ray of divine brightness, which illuminates those who shine spiritually, although it remains one in itself, is nevertheless variously multiplied by the participation and distribution of gifts, since it is distributed and multiplied in many and diverse ways. But this multiplication and variation is the beauty of all things; since, unless the several things were beautiful dissimilarly, all things together would not be supremely beautiful. For no one thing out of all the diverse things could contain what was the whole of beauty: and therefore the highest beauty was distributed by varied participation among the several things, that 944Ait might be able to be perfect in all things together. But this distribution itself is multiplied most excellently and beautifully: most excellently in all things, and beautifully in the several, or, most excellently according to the disposition of the partakers. For it is multiplied most excellently, that the good which is perceived by many may be greater; and it is multiplied beautifully, that the comeliness of the whole may be greater — in that it is poured into the several partakers in varied and diverse ways, so that from the numerous multitude in the partakers there may come about the consummation of good, and from the dissimilar distribution the beauty of the partakers. Or the multiplication of the simple ray, by which we are illuminated, can suitably be understood according to the many and diverse figures and likenesses of the divine oracles: by which, taken according to the measure of us, the divine 944Bwisdom — which in its purity and simplicity is altogether incomprehensible — is declared to human minds variously and manifoldly, although it is itself always one and the same. It is multiplied, therefore, because it is declared in many ways: most excellently indeed as regards itself, and beautifully as regards us. It is multiplied most excellently, because from the very multiplication of declarations it is more perfectly recognized; it is declared beautifully, because it is manifested by the beautiful and seemly appearance and dissimilarity of the forms that declare it. And this multiplication takes place for the tempering-together of those things that have been provided — that is, of the elect and of those provided for life — that they may be tempered together and united by the concord of participation, like many members in one body, so that the very diversity of gifts may confirm among them the fellowship 944Cof unity and peace: so that each single member may not presume to divide itself from the framework of the whole body, since the fullness of good, which it has less in itself, it possesses in the fellowship of the others. For because each one has what another does not have, therefore each one has in the other what it does not have in itself, or has more in the other what it has less in itself. And therefore the several members tend toward one another and keep concord and peace among themselves: and this concord and peace is the tempering-together by which they agree with one another, that they may stand as one and be reformed to one. For this reason, therefore, he calls the tempering-together of those provided-for anagogic and unifying. Unifying indeed, that they may stand as one; anagogic, that they may be reformed 944Dto one. Unifying, because it gathers the dispersed into one; anagogic, because it leads back the cast-down to higher things. Unifying, through the love of neighbor; anagogic, through the love of God. Therefore it is beautiful in congregation, best in elevation. Therefore the ray of divine illustration itself, multiplied whether through the distribution of spiritual gifts, by which it is partaken inwardly, or through the variety of mystical demonstrations, by which it is declared outwardly in the sacred oracle, comes forth — that is, proceeds into the hearts to be illuminated — whether from within filling them by inspiration, or from without pouring itself into them by the instruction of the sacred word: and yet it remains within itself securely, so that, while it offers itself to be partaken variously and manifoldly by the minds to be illuminated, it nevertheless does not flow out beyond the simplicity of its 945Aunity. For its unity itself therefore always remains within itself, because a coessential unchangeableness guards and keeps it, so that, although a plurality of partakers approaches to the communication of it, yet the diversity of participation does not prevail to the division of it. It remains, therefore, within itself securely, that it may always be the same, and may not go out from that which it is into that which it is not: but remaining uniformly fixed in its unchangeable likeness, so that, namely, it may not differ from itself, as though made unlike itself. Nor does it alone remain one, but also to those looking upon it and turned toward it — as far as is right, that is, permitted and possible for them — it extends itself to them, that is, it reaches out so that it may come even to those who are far off, and yet does not withdraw from itself. It extends itself, namely, proportionally, 945Bthat is, so that some receive more, others miuus, according to the dispensation of the distribution of gifts, or the possibility of the capacity of the partakers. For those who are nearest receive more abundantly from it: and so then each one, the more they approach, the more they receive; and the more they withdraw, the less they receive. Yet all receive; each one according to his part. This is what he says: « It extends itself proportionally, because nevertheless it extends itself to all, and pours itself into all, illuminates all, and makes them to be lights from its own light, and through this makes them to be one, just as it itself is one. And this is what he says: « It unifies them according to the simple unity of itself. » For the one illumination of all is one likeness and one form, in which all are one from it — they who 945Care illuminated by it — and one with it, since the illuminated are lights, just as it itself is light. Yet those who are one from it are one by unification, not by unity, because what they are, one out of many, they are one in one. For they themselves are many, and therefore they are not one in that which they are; but, because they are many in one, from one the many are one, and they are one by unification, not by unity. But it itself is one not by unification but by unity, because it is one from that which it is, which is one. And therefore he said "simple unity," because it is one from one, and the same one from which it is, it itself is. Therefore unity in one is simple; but unification is manifold in one, because those are one from one, and one in one: but here 945Done out of many, because they are many in one, and one in many. Then he adds the reason why the divine ray, that is, the divine wisdom, which is one from the Father and simple with the Father, is variously multiplied through the likenesses and forms of demonstrations in the sacred oracle: namely, because the invisible wisdom of God could not otherwise become known to us, unless it conformed itself unto likeness to those forms of visible things which we know, and through them expressed to us, by signifying, its invisible things which we do not know. Therefore the divine ray, which in itself is one and simple, coming to us, is multiplied by the variety of significations and demonstrations, because the human mind is not able to grasp it in its purity and simplicity.
