946A« For neither is it possible for the divine ray to shine upon us otherwise, unless, by the variety of sacred things, or the mind, [it be] anagogically veiled about, and prepared, connaturally and properly, by the fatherly providence, for those things which are according to us. » The sacred veils, in which the divine ray shines for us, are the mystical descriptions in the sacred oracle, which bring forward visible forms and likenesses of invisible things for their declaration. By which veils, namely, the divine ray itself is anagogically veiled about. For anagogy, as has been said, is called the ascent of the mind, or elevation, into the contemplation of the things above. It is therefore anagogically veiled about, because it is veiled for this end, that it may grow more fully bright; it is covered for this, that it may appear the more. Its overshadowing, therefore, is our illumination; and its veiling-about 946Bis our elevation. Just as weak eyes freely behold the sun covered by a cloud, which cannot gaze upon its flashing light: so too it is impossible for the divine ray to shine upon the bleary eyes of the mind, unless it be veiled about by the variety of sacred veils and prepared, connaturally and properly, by fatherly providence, for those things which are according to us. For unless fatherly providence had provided for us in this with ineffable goodness, the light of it could not shine at all to our eyes: and therefore it provided for us fatherly and devoutly, that it might prepare that light for us and fit it to those things which are according to us — to things and likenesses and forms: and so, connaturally and properly, that is, according to our nature and the property of those things which belong to our nature, it might show it to us prepared 946Cand fitted. It conforms itself to our things, that through our things it may become known to us, so that those things which are connatural and proper to us, set forth in demonstration, may more easily be understood by us.

There follows: « For which reason also the most perfect disposition of sacred things, judging our most holy hierarchy worthy of the supermundane imitation of the celestial hierarchies, handed down the said immaterial hierarchies too, varying them by material figures and formal compositions. » As if he said: Because invisible things are suitably demonstrated through visible things, therefore the divine Wisdom, which disposes all things to the likeness of the angelic hierarchy, which had been invisibly 946Dordered in the heavens, formed the human hierarchy visibly on earth, so that in men too, as in the angels, there might be sacred powers and principates, by which human conduct, proceeding in time, might be governed, so that from the visible disposition of men the invisible disposition of the angels might become known. For this is what he says: For which reason the most perfect disposition of sacred things — that is, the highest hierarchy, the ineffable Trinity itself, from which, and according to which, all sacred things, that is, all sacred ordinations, are disposed — judging our most holy hierarchy, that is, the human, worthy of the supermundane, that is, spiritual or intellectual, imitation of the celestial hierarchies, so that it might imitate them spiritually and be disposed according to them. And therefore "varying," that is, variously and manifoldly 947Adeclaring those same already-mentioned immaterial, that is, spiritual and angelic hierarchies by material, that is, corporeal and visible, or figures taken according to visible things, and by formal compositions, that is, fittingly and competently expressed according to the plan of the formations, "he hands down," that is, institutes, namely our most holy hierarchy itself, so that in this too the reason of visible demonstrations to the invisible truth might be preserved, that we may ascend from these most sacred formations, which are set forth outwardly for demonstration, to the unfigured heights and likenesses, that is, the simple and spiritual ones. Let us ascend, I say, proportionally to our very selves, that is, according to the proportion and measure of spiritual gifts, illuminated 947Bthrough the things that are outward, into the recognition of invisible things, and to the sublime and simple truth that ever remains the same. For the heights and likenesses themselves are the invisible powers. Heights indeed by dignity, likenesses by unchangeableness, unfigured by simplicity. To the knowledge of which we ascend proportionally to our very selves, according to the difference of progressions and the increments of illuminations, by the grades of spiritual advancements in us, by the difference of gifts among us. For according to that proportion by which we now perceive the gifts of graces differently, we deservedly afterward pass over into the number of the angels — either here through the contemplation of the mind, or there through retribution. For thus we ascend proportionally to our very selves, when, according to 947Cthe fact that in the present we are disposed differently through the gifts of graces and the grades of dignities, we are lifted up to the participation of invisible truth by a secret and invisible promotion. But the truth itself, in us indeed, is figured figuratively and materially through the offices of spiritual dignities and the grades and distributions of the orders, and is formed according to habits and actions and visible signs, which are set forth in our hierarchy, as it were, for declaration — all which things, in the celestial and angelic hierarchy, according to the simple truth, in a manner sublime and superexcelling our nature, subsist purely and uniformly without signs and figures: according to which excellence theology calls the angelic orders themselves "heights" 947Dand "likenesses," either because through no mutability do they differ from themselves, or because those things which are in them according to the simple truth seem to be, as it were, certain likenesses and exemplars of the things which subsist through figures and images. For unless there were some likeness between these and those, through these there would be no declaration of those. But now, since the divine wisdom formed these visible things, for the emulation of invisible things, in the first creation, in the second disposition it also established from these same things, for the rational soul ascending to the recognition of invisible things, signs and examples of demonstrations.

For this is what follows: « Since it is not possible for our soul to ascend to that non-material imitation and 948Acontemplation of the celestial hierarchies, unless by that, » which is according to it, it make use of material hand-leading. By "non-material" he means the spiritual imitation, or contemplation, and the incorporeal; since everything that is corporeal is from matter. But the spiritual nature is rightly called immaterial, since it neither is from matter, so as to be from another, nor can be matter, so that something else be from it. But by "material hand-leading" he understands corporeal signs, by whose hand-leading, as it were, the human mind makes use, so that from visible things it may be directed to the imitation and contemplation of invisible things. To imitation indeed through the exercise of virtue; but to contemplation through the knowledge of truth. But note a new composition and a new likeness in the fact that he says "hand-leading." For the mind 948Bof man, wrapped about by the darkness of its own ignorance, cannot go out to the light of truth unless it be directed and, like a blind man using a hand to lead him, walk on where he does not see. But these hand-leadings and directions, which the mind uses in tending toward invisible things, are taken from visible signs and from demonstrations formed according to visible things. And all this was disposed and ordered by the most perfect disposition of sacred things, which in Greek is called hierothesia, that is, the placing of sacred things — namely the highest Trinity, from which and according to which all sacred things are disposed and ordered in heaven and on earth — and by another name is called teletarche, that is, the beginning of purgation, since from it is every cleansing and beginning of purgation — not only that the things which are evil may be made good; but also of illustration 948Cand deification, that the things which were good may be made better. Therefore this highest priesthood, or highest fatherhood, cleansing and sanctifying and illustrating all things, instituted and ordained this: that in the first place, according to it, the angelic nature might be invisibly formed, and in the second place the human nature, aroused through visible things, might be reformed to the same image; because the human soul cannot be led back to the knowledge or imitation of invisible things unless instructed through visible demonstrations, since the visible things themselves too were so made by God that, according to that likeness and emulation which they received toward those invisible things, they can suitably declare the same, so that our soul, using the leading of these, may be directed to those 948Daccording to these, estimating and weighing those things by the likeness of the demonstration.

As it follows: « judging the visible forms to be imaginations, or images, of invisible beauty, » namely our own mind; « and the sensible sweetnesses figures of the invisible distribution, » — understand, our own mind judging; « and the material lights an image of the immaterial brightness, » so that again it is understood, our own mind judging; « the sacred disciplines run through according to the understanding of contemplative fullness, » here more is to be understood, our mind judging them to be images; « and the ordered dispositions, gathered unto divine things and set in order, of those things which are here, the orders of dispositions, » again understand, our mind judging 949Athem to be images; « the very reception of the Eucharist of the participation of Jesus, that most divine reception, » again understand it, our mind judging it to be an image. The sum, then, of the whole chapter is this: Since our mind cannot ascend to the imitation and contemplation of invisible things unless it be directed through visible things — in such a way, namely, that from the visible things themselves it may know how to judge and estimate the invisible, according as they bear a likeness to those and effect a signification. But which likenesses of visible things unto invisible things our own mind ought to judge and estimate, he shows by subjoining certain distinct examples, as if he were saying: For this reason the truth of invisible things has been demonstrated through visible things: because our mind cannot ascend to the truth of those invisible things themselves unless it be instructed through the 949Bconsideration of visible things — in such a way, namely, that it may judge the visible forms to be imaginations of invisible beauty. For since in the forms of visible things their beauty consists, he fittingly says that invisible beauty is demonstrated from visible forms, since visible beauty is an image of invisible beauty. Yet because in visible things form is one thing and essence another, therefore whatever things are visible are mutably beautiful, since whatever things are diverse in number and by nature mutable do not inseparably subsist together. But invisible things, in which form is not one thing and essence another — since everything that is, is one and simple, and the same being — are beautiful from the very fact that they are; and their beauty is not compacted out of 949Cmany things running together into one, as the visible nature is seen to be, whose form is unfolded according to the spaces of places and is arranged through figures fitted together out of many. Therefore the beauty of the visible nature is one thing, and that of the invisible nature another, since the latter is simple and uniform, but the former manifold and led together by a varied proportion. There is nevertheless some likeness of visible beauty to invisible beauty, according to the emulation which the invisible Artificer established between the two, in which, as it were, certain reflections of diverse proportions fashion one image. According to this, then, the human mind, fittingly roused, ascends from visible beauty to invisible beauty; as though led 949Dfrom like to like, easily understanding within itself, invisibly, what kinship there is to invisible things in the things which it comprehends outwardly and visibly. For according to the invisible light implanted in it, our mind, looking to invisible things, easily judges the visible forms to be images of invisible beauty, corresponding by a certain friendly likeness to that which it itself has invisibly within, finding them according to its approval and affection. For what is in the mind is invisible, just as the mind itself is invisible; and yet it, which is invisible, conceives from those things which are visible joy, and love, and affection; and it loves out of these certain things as though like, and friendly, and akin, and yields itself to them willingly, and exults in them. But others it spurns, and hates, and shuns, and puts itself far 950Afrom them, in love and delight; and it judges them foreign to itself, and discordant, and having no likeness with itself. And in this manner our mind is taught, from its own nature, that visible things have kinship and likeness to invisible things; and that the visible things themselves are images and likenesses of those things which cannot be seen visibly, since from these are understood those things which are not seen; and because, according to something, the whole of that which the mutable nature has here received visibly and sensibly subsists there invisibly in the immutable nature, so that it may lead to invisible things. For here there is a shape and form which delights the sight; there is also the pleasantness of melody, which soothes the hearing; there is the sweetness of odor, which restores the smell; there is the sweetness of savor, which pours into 950Bthe taste; and the softness of bodies, which cherishes and gently receives the touch. But there the shape is virtue, and the form justice, the sweetness love, and the odor desire; the song indeed joy and exultation; and the touch the finding of the loved, and desired, and sought good. For all these things are there, and are true there, and have with these things, which are not true, some likeness according to which they are understood by us. For from these our mind ascends to the knowledge and imitation of those things, judging the visible forms — which either nature shows implanted according to the first condition, or the sacred word sets forth dispensatively as a signification, to make a declaration — to be images of invisible beauty; and the sensible sweetnesses, that is, the sensible delights, to be figures and likenesses 950Cof the invisible distribution, that is, of the sweetness which is distributed invisibly, that is, bestowed in diverse ways: namely, that one may receive more, another less, according to measure, and the gifts of the bounteous Giver. And likewise, that the material, that is, corporeal lights are an image of the immaterial brightness, that is, of spiritual light; and again, that the sacred disciplines, that is, the things investigated and searched out by the intellect, are images of contemplative fullness, that is, of full and perfect contemplation, which is both perceived and ministered according to the understanding, that is, intellectually only and invisibly. For all that knowledge which we now learn through the sacred word by the study of reading or meditation is, as it were, only an image of that full 950Dand perfect knowledge which we shall afterward draw from the contemplation that is to come. Whence the Apostle also says: « We see now through a glass, in a riddle; but then face to face (I Cor. XIII). » What wonder is it, then, if those sensible things which appear outwardly are said to be images of invisible things, when our very knowledge, which in comparison with these is believed to be spiritual and invisible, is reckoned to hold the place of an image and likeness in relation to those things?

There follows: « and the ordered dispositions, gathered unto divine things, of those things which are here, the orders of dispositions. » Again understand, our mind judging the orders of dispositions: « which dispositions are here, » that is, exteriorly, to be images of a state gathered unto divine things. For there is a certain state of the good mind gathered 951Aunto divine things, and, as it were, collected into one out of the various rents of desires, and set in order, so that it may go forward rightly. Gathered, namely, through love, and set in order through discretion. Gathered unto one, and ordered in one. Of which state, invisibly ordered and subsisting, the orders of dispositions are images, which are dispensed outwardly in the grades, and offices, and ministries in the holy Church. For just as in one Church diverse orders and dispositions effect one peace and concord in the whole, by ministering and cooperating, so in one soul many virtues, by cooperating and ministering to one another, compose one form of perfection. But also, in each one of us, the disposition of the outer man, and the order of living, and the manner of acting, demonstrate the form 951Band state of the inner man.

There follows: « and the very reception of the most divine Eucharist of the participation of Jesus. » Again understand, as above, our mind judging the reception itself of the most divine Eucharist to be an image of the participation of Jesus. For the very reception of the most divine Eucharist, that is, of the most holy partaking of the body and blood of Jesus Christ, which we now handle sacramentally and visibly upon the altar, is an image and form of that participation of Jesus by which either now we are joined to him in spirit through love, or afterward, appearing in the same form of glory, we shall be united to him in full likeness. Now here it is to be noted that certain men have thought to allege from this passage a bulwark for their error, saying that in the sacrament of the altar there is not the truth 951Cof the body and blood of Christ, but only an image and figure of it: for this reason, because the Scripture says that what is taken in the Eucharist of the altar is an image of that which will be received in the participation of Jesus. Who assuredly would not fall into this snare of error, if they either received the sacraments of God with a right and humble faith, or handled the sacred Scriptures with a fitting understanding. But now, because in the sacraments of God they prefer their own sense to faith, and in the sacred Scriptures scorn to hold the sound form of interpretation, it comes about that the very word of truth makes them grow yet more blind, while, not rightly understood, it ministers error in place of truth. Which, however, is not the fault of Scripture, but the blindness of those who read and do not understand; 951Dnor a confusion of the sacraments of God, but the depravity of the presumptuous. Here, however, they have erred perilously, preferring one ambiguous thing to so many manifest sentences and undoubted assertions, and choosing in it the lie rather than the truth — not because this was more said there, but because this was more believed by them. For what? Is the sacrament of the altar therefore not truth, because it is a figure? Then neither is the death of Christ truth, because it is a figure; and the resurrection of Christ is not truth, because it is a figure. For that both the death of Christ and the resurrection are a figure, and are an image, and a likeness, and a sacrament, and an example, the Apostle plainly declares, saying: « Christ died for our sins, and rose again for our justification 952A: that, dead to sins, we might live to justice (I Cor. XV). » And the apostle Peter said: « Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps (I Petr. II). » Therefore the death of Christ was an example, that we might die to sin, and his resurrection was an example, that we might live to justice. Was it therefore not truth? Then Christ did not truly die, and did not truly rise again, if his death, or resurrection, was not true. God forbid! For of him it is written: « Surely he himself hath borne our infirmities, and himself carried our sorrows » (Isa. LIII). Therefore the death of Christ was true, and yet was an example; and the resurrection of Christ was true, and yet was an example. Why then can the sacrament of the altar not be both a likeness and a truth? In one thing indeed 952Ba likeness, and in another a truth. For, since the sacrament is one, three distinct things are there set forth, namely: the visible appearance, and the truth of the body, and the virtue of spiritual grace. For the visible appearance, which is visibly discerned, is one thing. The truth of the body and blood, which under the visible appearance is invisibly believed, is another. And the spiritual grace, which is invisibly and spiritually received together with the body and blood, is yet another. For what we see is the appearance of bread and wine; but what we believe under that appearance is the true body and true blood of Christ Jesus, which hung upon the cross, and which flowed from his side. Nor is only the body and blood signified through the bread and wine; but under the appearance of bread and wine the true body and true blood is consecrated. And indeed the visible appearance 952Cis a sacrament of the true body and true blood; but the body and blood is a sacrament of spiritual grace. And just as there the appearance is discerned, whose reality or substance is not believed to be there, so there the reality is believed to be truly and substantially present, whose appearance is not discerned. For the appearance of bread and wine is seen, and the substance of bread and wine is not believed. But the substance of the body and blood of Christ is believed, and yet its appearance is not discerned.

What, then, is seen according to the appearance is a sacrament, and an image of that which is believed according to the truth of the body; and what is believed according to the truth of the body is a sacrament of that which is received according to spiritual grace. The sacrament, then, 952Dof the altar and the divine Eucharist is, in the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, both an image according to the appearance of bread and wine, in which it is discerned, and a reality according to the truth of its own substance, in which it is there believed and received. And again, that we now visibly, according to the appearance of the sacrament, and corporeally, according to the truth of flesh and blood, take Christ upon the altar, is a sacrament and image of the fact that we ought to take that same one invisibly and spiritually, according to the infusion of grace and the participation of his Spirit, in the heart. Therefore the most divine Eucharist, which upon the altar is handled visibly and corporeally both according to the appearance of bread and wine and according to the truth of the body and blood of Christ, is a sacrament, and a sign, and an image 953Aof the invisible and spiritual participation of Jesus, which is accomplished within, in the heart, through faith and love. For the Wisdom of God, which manifests itself through the visible, willed to show that it is itself the food and refreshment of minds; and therefore it set forth the assumed flesh as food, that through the food of the flesh it might invite to the taste of the Godhead. But, lest again human weakness should shrink from the touch of flesh in the receiving, it veiled it with the appearance of the accustomed and principal food, and thus set it forth to be taken, so that the sense might be cherished in the one, and faith built up in the other. For the sense is cherished in the one, while it perceives only the usual and accustomed; but faith is built up in the other, while in that which it sees it recognizes what manner of thing that is which it does not see. The appearance of bread and wine is therefore set forth, that it may be taught 953Bthat there is full and perfect refreshment in the taking of the body and blood of Christ from the Godhead of Christ. Now full refreshment is food and drink; but of food and drink, bread and wine is the principal substance. And the appearance is set forth from the principal substance of refreshment, that in it may be taken, and through it may be signified, the truth of the body and blood, as he himself testifies, saying: « My flesh is meat indeed, and my blood is drink indeed (Joan. VI). » Yet that this taking of the body and blood, alone and without a spiritual effect, does not confer salvation, the same Savior himself manifests, saying: « The flesh profiteth nothing; it is the spirit that quickeneth (ibid.). » Therefore the virtue and fullness of the spiritual refreshment which is in the body and blood of Christ is signified indeed through the appearance of bread and wine; 953Cbut it is accomplished in the receiving of grace, and in the infusion of the inward and eternal refreshment. And thus indeed, since three things are there in one, in the first is found a sign of the second; in the second the cause of the third; but in the third the virtue of the second, and the truth of the first. And these three are in one, and are one sacrament. It is clear, therefore, that the reception of the most divine Eucharist is a sacrament, and an image of the participation of Jesus; because this, that we visibly receive the sacrament of it, is a sign that we ought to be united to him spiritually and invisibly. But the Eucharist itself, that is, the good grace, that very sacred host, is called most divine, 953Dsince it makes divine, and partakers of the Godhead, those who partake of it. And because it is a sign, and a truth in which the true flesh of Christ is taken under the appearance of bread, and in his flesh, worthily taken, the reception too, and participation, and fellowship of his very Godhead is granted. Therefore it is most worthy, and most holy, and sanctifying all things that sanctify, and holy.

There follows: « And whatever other things have been handed down to the heavenly essences in a supramundane manner, but to us symbolically. » After he had set forth certain things, by way of example, to show the likeness of visible things to invisible, now he concludes generally about the whole, saying: « And whatever other things have been handed down to the heavenly essences in a supramundane manner, but to us symbolically, » as if he were saying: These things above mentioned, the visible things, our mind ought to judge 954Ato have a likeness to invisible things according to the examples set forth; and not these alone, but whatever other things have been handed down to us symbolically, or to the heavenly essences supramundanely. For not only these visible things which have been set down — that is, the forms, the sweetnesses, the lights, the disciplines, the orders, the sacred Eucharist — have the manifestation and demonstration of invisible things, even if a multitude of them; but also all other visible things whatsoever, which have been handed down to us — who are to be instructed visibly — symbolically, that is, figuratively, have been set forth for the signification and declaration of invisible things. And not only these visible things which have been handed down to us symbolically have a demonstration of invisible things; but those too which have been handed down to the heavenly essences, that is, to the angelic spirits, supramundanely, that is, invisibly and spiritually, and not 954Baccording to the appearances of this world, are signs of invisible things, and images of those things which, in the excellent and incomprehensible nature of the Godhead, subsist above all understanding and sense. For this is what he says: that not only those things which have been handed down to us symbolically are signs of invisible things; but those too which have been handed down to the heavenly essences supramundanely. For the angelic spirits themselves also have their signs, and demonstrations, through which they are instructed concerning the invisible things of God, and things exceedingly hidden, and secrets concealed within, immaterially, and invisibly, and simply. Which signs indeed, as far as concerns us and those things which are visible among us, are reckoned altogether invisible; but as far as concerns that light, much invisible, and inaccessible, and incomprehensible, 954Cof the Deity, they are as it were outside, and proceed from within into demonstration. On which account those very signs, which come upon minds, or upon souls divinely illuminated, are called theophanies, that is, divine apparitions; because in them, coming to manifestation, that which is altogether hidden of God is demonstrated. These, then, are the things which are handed down to the heavenly ones supramundanely, not according to that demonstration which is among us, but breathed in invisibly and simply. Many things indeed were here to be said about this kind of contemplation, by which theophanies, that is, divine apparitions divinely breathed in, come upon minds to be illuminated, and, by instructing them concerning the hidden and invisible things of God in a wondrous, and concealed, and secret, and 954Dsingular manner, make them wise: especially since here too certain men are found to have become vain in their thoughts, proclaiming God to be altogether incomprehensible and inaccessible to the rational mind, except that it is instructed concerning him by certain theophanies, that is, divine apparitions, or divine likenesses set forth for contemplation. But these they place, as it were, certain images of the hidden Godhead, as means between rational souls and God, higher indeed than the mind, but lower than the Godhead. And this alone, they say, is seen of God, and in this alone is God seen — inasmuch as he in himself can be seen by no mind or soul. But these are likenesses of them, and phantasms of vanity: in which, while they try to assert that only the light of the Godhead is visible and perceptible, 955Athey are proved to take away from holy minds the true knowledge and vision of the Deity. For what is it, that God is seen in those things alone, and outside them is not seen, save that he is never truly seen, and the truth is never seen? For if the image alone is always seen, and the truth is never seen, since the image is not the truth, even when it is of the truth. Let them therefore take away their phantasies, by which they strive to overshadow the light of our minds; nor let them fence off from us our God by the likenesses of their own conjectures; because, just as nothing besides himself can satisfy us, so neither can anything come to a stand short of himself. Let us therefore reckon these theophanies in another manner, and one consonant with truth. For just as there are two things, the light and the body that receives the light — and out of these two is made one thing that 955Bshines, and that shining thing is in a manner an image and likeness of the light, in that it shines as the light itself does — so also our God is light, and is true light, and rational souls, clean and pure, conceive that very light: and from it they become shining, and they themselves are not an image of the light in that they are; but in that they shine from the light, as the light itself shines; and those shining things are theophanies of the light, in which the light is seen, since by none would the light be seen, if none were illuminated by the light. For he too who sees the light in himself sees himself shining; who assuredly would not see, if he did not shine, and would not see himself shining. Thus, then, we set no other between our God and us, but make a way immediately, both for us to him, and for him even to us, that we may be in him, and 955Che in us: so that there be nothing outside himself in which we may be beatified, just as there could be nothing besides himself by which we might be created. On account of this, therefore, let us interpret the aforesaid sentence of theology to a more convenient understanding. For because he had said that certain invisible things are demonstrated through those visible images which are determinate, now he subjoins a general sentence concerning the invisible things themselves, saying: « And whatever other things, etc. » As if he were saying: Not only those invisible things, of which these signs have been set forth, came into manifestation; but also whatever other invisible things which have been handed down to us — namely to men — symbolically, that is, figuratively and through sensible demonstrations, that is, set forth and made manifest; 956Abut to the heavenly essences, that is, to the angelic spirits, supramundanely and spiritually, revealed through a bare and simple truth impressed.

There follows: « On account of this, then, our co-rational theosis, » that is, divinity, which is to us co-rational, that is, congruous or apt. For it is congruous that through those things which are known to us we should be made partakers of divine things: « On account of this, then, etc., » as if he were saying: Because the human mind cannot be instructed concerning invisible things save through visible things, and things known and akin to it, therefore « the merciful Principle of perfection, » that is, God, from whom all perfection has its beginning, as in him it takes its consummation and end — by grace and mercy alone, that he might call us back to his own knowledge, and reform his likeness; 956B« manifesting to us the heavenly hierarchies, » that is, the angelic powers; « and perfecting also our hierarchy as fellow-minister of them, » namely of the heavenly hierarchies, that it might be both conformable to them in dignity, and like them in divine ministry, the deiform likeness of their sanctification being preserved in us, that we may be like the sanctification of them who are conformed to God, « according to our virtue, » that is, according to our possibility, that is, as far as we are able to be like — we who are men, and mortal, and still liable to sin; « he described the supercelestial intellects, » the invisible spirits, who were unknown to us, by sensible images, that through the known we might learn the unknown. And this description he made 956C« in the sacred compositions of the words, » that is, in the descriptions of the sacred word: which compositions set forth to us both figures and likenesses for the demonstration of invisible things. And this he did for this reason, « that he might lead us back through sensible things to intellectual things, » that is, through visible things to invisible things. And that he might also lead us back and « from sacredly figured symbols, » that is, from sacred figures and the figures of sacred things; « into the simple heights, » that is, into the simple and spiritual excellences to be known « of the heavenly hierarchies, » that is, of the angelic powers. For this reason he described them to us by visible signs, that he might make them intelligible to us, and conform us to their imitation.

LIBER TERTIUS.

  • 955

THIRD BOOK.

  • 955

TITULUS CAPITULI II: Quod pulchre divina et coelestia etiam per dissimilia symbola manifestantur.

TITLE OF CHAPTER II: That divine and heavenly things are beautifully manifested even through dissimilar symbols.

LITTERA.

  • 955C

Oportet ergo, ut existimo, primum exponere quam quidem esse speculationem omnis hierarchiae existimamus, et quid ipsius unaquaeque divinis profuit laudatoribus. Deinde coelestes hierarchias laudare secundum ipsarum in eloquiis manifestationem consequentibusque his dicere, qualibus divinis formationibus coelestes figurant ordines eloquiorum sacrae 956Cdescriptiones, et ad qualem oportet ascendere per formas veritatem. Ut non et nos eodem modo multis immunde existimemus coelestes, et deiformes animos, multipedes esse quosdam, et multorum vultuum, et ad boum et pecudalitatem [pecuinitatem], aut ad leonum bestialem imaginationem formatos, aut ad aquilarum curvo rostro speciem, aut ad volatilium tripertitam alarum commotionem effiguratos: et rotas quasdam 957Aigneas super coelum imaginemur, et thronos materiales Divinitati ad recubitum necessarios; et equos quosdam multicolores, et armiferos archistrategos; et quaecunque alia ex eloquiis nobis sacrae, et formabiliter in varietate manifestativorum symbolorum tradita sunt (Ezech. I; Apoc. IV; Isa. VI; Dan. VII; Zach. I; Apoc. VI; Ezech. XXIII; Job. XVI; Sap. V; Josue V; II Machab. III). Etenim valde artificialiter theologia poeticis sacris formationibus in non figuratis intellectibus usa est: nostrum, ut dictum est, animum revelans, et ipsi propria, et connaturali reductione providens, et ad ipsam reformans anagogicas sanctas Scripturas, si cui autem videtur sacras quidem recipi debere compositiones tanquam simplicium in seipsis ignotorumque nobis, et incontemplabilium 957Bsubsistentium: inconvenientes vero existimat sanctorum intellectuum in eloquiis sacris descriptiones, et omne sic dicere durum, hoc angelicorum nominum theatrum; et debuisse, ait, theologos ad corpoream facturam universaliter in corporalium venientes propriis ea, et quantum possibile cognatis et formare, et manifestare figurationibus ex apud nos pretiosissimis, et immaterialibus quoquo modo, et supereminentibus essentiis, et non coelestibus, et deiformibus simplicitatibus terrenas novissimas circumpositas multiformitates. Hoc quidem et nostrum sublimius futurum esset, et supermundanas manifestationes non deduceret in inconvenientes dissimilitudines. Hoc etiam in divinas simul injuste non injuriam faceret virtutes, et aeque nostrum non seduceret 957Canimum in immundas se inserentem compositiones. Et fortassis etiam existimabuntur supercoelestia leoninis quibusdam, et equinis multitudinibus repleri; et mugitiva laudum oratione, et volatili angelorum praecipitatu, et animalibus aliis, et materiis ignobilioribus tanquam ad inconsequens, et ignobile, et passibile reclusa, dum describuntur per omnia deiformes clarae manifestativorum eloquiorum similitudines. Sed veritatis, ut existimo, inquisitio ostendit eloquiorum sacratissimam sapientiam (Ezech. XXVIII; Job. XXXVIII) in animorum coelestium formationibus utrumque valde providisse: ita ut neque in divinas (sic forsitan diceret quis) injuriam faceret virtutes; neque vos in viles passibiliter infigeret imaginum humilitates. Quia quidem enim pulchre procuratae 957Dsunt informium formae, et figurae carentium figuris, non unam causam diceret quis esse nostram analogiam non valentem immediate in invisibiles extendi contemplationes, et desiderantem proprias, et connaturales reductiones: quae passibiles nobis formationes praetendunt informium supernaturaliumque speculationum. Sed quia et hoc mysticis eloquiis est decentissimum, per incomprehensibilia divina aenigmat occultare, et inviam multis ponere sacram, abditamque supermundanorum intellectuum veritatem. Est enim non omnis sacer, neque omnium, ut eloquia aiunt, scientia (Matth. VII; I Cor. II). Si autem deformes imaginum descriptionis causas existimaverit quis inhonestum, dicens, referri sic turpes 958Aformationes deiformibus, et sanctissimis dispositionibus, sufficit ad eum dicere: Quomodo duplex est sanctae manifestationis modus? Unus quidem quasi consequens propter similes provenientium sacrarum figurarum imagines; alter vero propter dissimiles formarum facturas in omnino inconsequens, et indecorum conformatus. Itaque colendam super essentiam divinitatis beatitudinem manifestativorum eloquiorum mysticae traditiones, aliquando quidem ut rationem, et intellectum, et essentiam laudant; divinam rationalitatem, et sapientiam ejus declarantes, et vere existentem substantiam, et eorum, quae sunt substantiae, causam veram; et quasi lumen eam formant, et vitam vocant tantis mirabilibus formationibus castioribus manentibus, et materiales formationes 958Bexcellere quoquomodo probatis deficientibus; et sic divina ad veritatem similitudine. Est enim super omnem essentiam et vitam, nullo quidem ipsam lumine characterizante, omnique ratione, et intellectu similitudine ipsius incomparabiliter derelictis. Aliquando vero dissimilibus manifestationibus ab ipsis eloquiis (Rom. XI; I Tim. VI; Psalm. CXL) supermundane laudatur, eam invisibilem, et infinitam, et incomprehensam vocantibus: et quae, ex quibus non quid est, sed quid non est, significatur. Hoc enim, ut existimo, potentius est in ipsa. Quoniam quidem, ut occulta, et sacerdotalis traditio subintroduxit, hoc quidem non esse secundum quid eorum, quae sunt, eam vere dicimus. Ignoramus autem superessentialem ipsius, et invisibilem, et ineffabilem infinalitatem. 958CSi igitur negationes in divinis verae sunt affirmationes vero incompactae, obscuritati arcanorum magis apta per dissimiles formationes manifestatio. Et nunc itaque non turpes replent coelestes ornatus eloquiorum sacrae descriptiones dissimilibus eos formarum facturis manifestantes, et per has ostendentes materialibus simul omnibus supermundalium excellentias. Quin vero et nostrum animum reducant magis dissimiles similitudines: non existimo quemquam bene sapientum contradicere. Per quidem enim pretiosiores sacras formationes consequens est seduci, auriformes quasdam existimantes esse coelestes essentias, et quosdam viros fulgoreos decora indutos vestimenta, candidum, et igneum innocue respergentes, et quibuscunque aliis similibus imaginalis formis theologia 958Dcoelestes figuravit intellectus. Quod quidem ne paterentur, qui nihil visibilibus bonis altius intelligunt, sanctorum theologorum restitutiva sapientia ad indecoras dissimilitudines mirabiliter descendit: non concedens materiale nostrum in turpibus imaginibus remanens quiescere; purgans vero sursumque ferens, et animae suggerens deformitate compositionum, tanquam neque justo neque vero probante, esse nequaquam valde materialibus, quia sic turpibus, similia secundum veritatem supercoelestia, et divina spectacula. Sed itaque et hoc intelligere oportet: Nihil eorum, quae sunt, esse universaliter boni participatione privatum: siquidem, ut eloquiorum Veritas ait: « Omnia bona valde (Gen. I). » Est ergo ex omnibus intelligere bonas 959Aspeculationes, et invisibilibus, et intellectualibus, ex materialibusque formare dictas dissimiles similitudines: altero modo intellectualibus habentibus, quae sensibilibus aliter distributa sunt. Etenim furor in irrationalibus quidem ex passibili motu est: et omnis irrationabilitatis repletus est furibundus eorum motus; sed intellectualibus altero modo oportet irascibile intelligere, declarans, ut existimo, eorum virilem rationabilitatem, et immanem [immanentem] quietem in divinis, et immutabilibus fundamentis. Eodem modo concupiscentiam quidem esse dicimus in irrationabilibus inconsultam quamdam, et materialem ex naturali motu, aut consuetudine in mutabilibus incontinenter ingenitam impassibilitatem, et irrationabilem corporalis voluptatis continuitatem; simul omne animal 959Bcompellentis secundum sensum inconcupiscibile. Cum vero dissimiles similitudines intellectualibus circumponentes concupiscentiam eis circumformamus amorem divinum, ipsum intelligere oportet super rationem, et intellectum immaterialitatis, et inflexibile, et non indigens desiderium superessentialiter castae, et impassibilis contemplationis et illam puram, et sublimissimam claritatem, et invisibilem, et formificam pulchritudinem aeternae, verae et invisibilis societatis. Et veluti potentiam excipit quidem in sufficentia, et in conversibilitate; et a nulla affligitur virtute, per inconfusum, et immutabilem divinae pulchritudinis amorem, et universalem revocationem in id quod vere est appetendum. Sed et ipsam irrationabilitatem et insensualitatem 959Cin quidem irrationabilibus animalibus, aut in animatis materiis, defectum rationis, et sensus proprie vocamus; in autem immaterialibus et intellectualibus essentiis sanctae, et decenter supereminentias earum, ut super mundalium confitemur, nostram transitoriam, et corporalem rationem, et materialem, et alienatum incorporalibus animi sensum excellentes. Est itaque non dissonas formare coelestibus formas, et ex vilibus materiae partibus. Quoniam et ipsa ex vere bono subsistentiam possidens per omnem sui materialem dispositionem imagines quasdam intellectualis pulchritudinis habet; et possibile est per eas reduci ad immateriales primas formas dissimiliter, ut dictum est, similitudinibus acceptis, et eisdem non similiter: compacte autem, et pulchre intellectualibusque 959Det sensibilibus proprietatibus definitis. Haec mysticos theologos inveniemus non solum coelestium dispositionum declarationibus mirabiliter conformantes, sed ipsis aliquando divinis manifestationibus. Et aliquando quidem ipsam ex luminibus pretiosis laudant, ut solem justitiae, ut stellam matutinam in animum sancte orientem, et ut lumen incircumvolute, et invisibiliter resplendens (Malach. I; Apoc. II). Aliquando vero ex mediis, ut ignem innocue resplendentem, ut aquam vitalis plenitudinis datricem, et, ut symbolice dicendum, in ventrem subeuntem, fluminaque redundantem immensurabiliter refluentia. Aliquando autem ex novissimis, ut unguentum suave, ut lapidem angularem (Exod. III; Joan. I). » Sed et bestialem ipsi formam circumponunt; et leonis ei, et pantherae 960Aspecialitatem coaptant, et pardalineam vestiunt, et ur sam saevientem (Cant. II; Isa, XXVIII; Osee V). Ad dam vero, et quod omnium vilius esse, et magis significare visum est; quia et vermis specie ipsam seipsam circumformantem divina sapientes [divinam sapientiam] tradiderunt (Psal. XXI). Sic et omnes theosophi, et occulta inspiratione prophetae a sanctis incontaminatis distinguunt Sancta sanctorum, et dissimilem sanctam figurationem honorant, ut neque divina immundis recte accepta sint, neque mirabilium imaginum studiosi contemplationis tanquam veris remanent figuris. Divina itaque honorificant veris negationibus, et ad novissima compactarum imaginationum diversis similitudinibus. Nihil ergo inconsequens est, si et coelestes essentias ex inconvenientibus dissimilibus similitudinibus 960Bformant secundum dictas causas. Non enim fortassis utique, non nos in quaestionem quidem ex indigentia in anagogen per diligentem divinorum scrutationem veniremus, nisi deformitas nos extorqueret manifestatoriae angelorum deformationis: non sinens nostrum animum remanere in dissimilibus formarum facturis, sed reluctantem negare materiales passibilitates, et assuescentem pure extendere per visibilia in supermundanas altitudines. Tanta quidem a nobis dicta sunt propter materiales et inconvenientes divinorum eloquiorum angelicas imaginum descriptiones. Deinde autem segregare oportet quid ipsam quidem esse hierarchiam existimamus, quidque ab ipsa hierarchia prosunt hierarchiam sortientes. Dux vero sit Christus (siquidem mihi fas dicere) meus, totius 960Chierarchicae manifestationis inspiratio. Tu vero, o puer, secundum sanctam nostrae sacerdotalis traditionis legislationem, ipse sancte, et decenter ausculta, mirabiliter dictorum divinus divina in doctrina factus, secreto animi quae sancta sunt circumtegens, ex immunda multitudine tanquam uniformia custodi. Non enim fas, ut eloquia aiunt in porcos projicere invisibilium margaritarum inconfusum, et luciformem, beneficumque ornatum (Matth. VII).

THE TEXT.

  • 955C

It behooves us, then, as I judge, first to set forth what indeed we reckon the speculation of every hierarchy to be, and what each of them has profited the divine praisers of it. Then to praise the heavenly hierarchies according to their manifestation in the words, and, in what follows these, to say by what divine formations the sacred 956Cdescriptions of the words figure the heavenly orders, and to what truth one ought to ascend through the forms. That we too may not, in the same manner as the many, uncleanly reckon the heavenly and deiform minds to be certain many-footed things, and of many faces, and formed to oxen and to a cattle-like beastliness [pecuinitatem], or to the bestial imagination of lions, or figured to the appearance of eagles with curved beak, or to the tripartite motion of the wings of flying things: and imagine certain fiery 957Awheels above the heaven, and material thrones necessary for the Divinity to recline upon; and certain many-colored horses, and arms-bearing chief-commanders; and whatever other things have been handed down to us from the sacred words, and formatively, in the variety of manifesting symbols (Ezech. I; Apoc. IV; Isa. VI; Dan. VII; Zach. I; Apoc. VI; Ezech. XXIII; Job. XVI; Sap. V; Josue V; II Machab. III). For indeed most artfully has theology used poetic sacred formations in un-figured intellects: revealing, as has been said, our mind, and providing for it by a proper and connatural reduction, and reforming unto itself the anagogical holy Scriptures. But if to anyone it seems that the sacred compositions ought indeed to be received as of things simple in themselves and unknown to us, and of things incontemplable 957Bin their subsisting: but he reckons unfitting the descriptions of the holy intellects in the sacred words, and all such speaking hard — this theater of angelic names; and that the theologians ought, he says, coming universally to a corporeal fashioning among corporeal things, to form and manifest these by their proper figurations, and, as far as possible, akin, from the most precious things among us, and in any way immaterial, and supereminent essences — and not to set the earthly, most base, manifold forms round about the heavenly and deiform simplicities. This indeed would be both more sublime for us, and would not lead down the supramundane manifestations into unfitting dissimilitudes. This too would at once not unjustly do injury to the divine virtues, and likewise would not seduce our 957Cmind, thrusting itself into unclean compositions. And perhaps also the supercelestial things will be reckoned to be filled with certain leonine and equine multitudes; and with a bellowing utterance of praises, and with the flying headlong rush of angels, and with other animals, and with more ignoble matters, as though shut up unto the inconsequent, and ignoble, and passible, while there are described throughout as deiform the clear likenesses of the manifesting words. But the inquiry of truth, as I judge, shows that the most sacred wisdom of the words (Ezech. XXVIII; Job. XXXVIII) has in the formations of the heavenly minds provided exceedingly for both: so that neither would it (so perhaps someone might say) do injury to the divine virtues; nor would it fix you, in a passible manner, into the vile lownesses of images. For because indeed there have been beautifully procured 957Dforms of the formless, and figures of things lacking figures, one might say that it is not one single cause — that our analogy, not being able to be extended immediately into invisible contemplations, and desiring its proper and connatural reductions: which hold out to us the passible formations of formless and supernatural speculations. But because this too is most seemly for mystical words, to conceal by incomprehensible divine aenigmat, and to set trackless to the many the sacred and hidden truth of the supramundane intellects. For not every one is holy, nor is knowledge, as the words say, of all (Matth. VII; I Cor. II). But if anyone should reckon the deformed causes of the description of images dishonorable, saying that base 958Aformations are thus referred to deiform and most holy dispositions, it suffices to say to him: How is the mode of holy manifestation twofold? One indeed as it were consequent, on account of the like images of the sacred figures that come forth; but the other, on account of the dissimilar makings of forms, conformed to what is altogether inconsequent and unseemly. And so the mystical traditions of the manifesting words sometimes praise the blessedness of the Godhead, which is to be venerated above essence, as reason, and intellect, and essence; declaring the divine rationality and its wisdom, and the truly existing substance, and the true cause of those things which are substance; and they form it as though light, and call it life, so many wondrous, more chaste formations abiding, and the material formations 958Bbeing proved in some way to fall short of excelling; and thus by a likeness of the divine unto truth. For it is above all essence and life, no light indeed characterizing it, all reason and intellect being incomparably left behind by any likeness of it. But sometimes it is praised supramundanely by dissimilar manifestations from the very words (Rom. XI; I Tim. VI; Psalm. CXL), which call it invisible, and infinite, and incomprehensible: and by which is signified not what it is, but what it is not. For this, as I judge, is more powerful in its case. Since indeed, as the hidden and priestly tradition has introduced, we truly say that it is not according to anything of those things which are. But we do not know its superessential, and invisible, and ineffable infinitude. 958CIf, therefore, negations in divine matters are true, but affirmations incompact, the manifestation through dissimilar formations is more apt to the obscurity of the arcane things. And so now the sacred descriptions of the words do not fill up the heavenly ornaments with base things, manifesting them by dissimilar makings of forms, and through these showing, together with all material things, the excellences of the supramundane things. Nay rather, that dissimilar likenesses lead our mind back more — I do not think any of the well-wise contradict. For through the more precious sacred formations it is consequent to be seduced, reckoning the heavenly essences to be certain gold-formed things, and certain resplendent men clothed in comely garments, sprinkling harmlessly a white and fiery brightness, and by whatever other like imaginal forms theology has 958Dfigured the heavenly intellects. And lest they who understand nothing higher than visible goods should suffer this, the restorative wisdom of the holy theologians has wondrously descended to unseemly dissimilitudes: not granting our material part, remaining in base images, to rest; but purging, and bearing upward, and suggesting to the soul by the deformity of the compositions — as neither the just nor the true approving — that the supercelestial and divine spectacles are by no means, according to truth, like to things very material, because thus base. But so this too it behooves to understand: That nothing of those things which are, is universally deprived of the participation of the good: since indeed, as the Truth of the words says: « All things very good (Gen. I). » It is possible, then, from all things to understand good 959Aspeculations, and, of both invisible and intellectual things, to form from material things the said dissimilar likenesses: the intellectual things having in another way those things which are otherwise distributed to sensible things. For fury indeed in irrational things is from a passible motion: and the furious motion of them is filled with all irrationality; but in intellectual things one must understand the irascible in another way, declaring, as I judge, their manly reasonableness, and their immense [immanentem] rest in divine and immutable foundations. In the same way we say that concupiscence indeed is in irrational things a certain inconsiderate and material thing, from a natural motion, or from custom incontinently engendered in mutable things — an impassibility, and an irrational continuity of bodily pleasure; at once compelling every animal 959Baccording to sense to what is unfit to be desired. But when, setting dissimilar likenesses about intellectual things, we form concupiscence about them, we must understand it to be divine love — above reason, and above the intellect of immateriality, and the inflexible and needless desire of a superessentially chaste and impassible contemplation, and that pure and most sublime brightness, and the invisible and form-making beauty of eternal, true, and invisible fellowship. And as it were it receives power in sufficiency and in convertibility; and it is afflicted by no virtue, through the unconfused and immutable love of the divine beauty, and the universal recalling into that which is truly to be sought. But that very irrationality and insensibility 959C, in irrational animals indeed, or in animate matters, we properly call a defect of reason and sense; but in immaterial and intellectual essences we confess it, holily and fittingly, to be their supereminences, as of supramundane things, excelling our transitory and corporeal reason, and the material sense of the mind, alienated from incorporeal things. And so it is possible to form for the heavenly things forms not dissonant, even from vile parts of matter. Since it too, possessing subsistence from the truly good, has through all its material disposition certain images of intellectual beauty; and it is possible through them to be led back to the immaterial first forms — the likenesses being received dissimilarly, as has been said, and not in like manner with them: but compactly and beautifully, the intellectual 959Dand sensible properties being defined. These mystical theologians we shall find wondrously conforming not only to the declarations of the heavenly dispositions, but sometimes to the divine manifestations themselves. And sometimes indeed they praise it from precious lights, as the Sun of justice, as the morning star holily rising in the mind, and as a light shining unenveloped and invisibly (Malach. I; Apoc. II). But sometimes from middle things, as fire shining harmlessly, as water the giver of vital fullness, and, as it must be said symbolically, entering into the belly, and pouring back rivers that flow again immeasurably. But sometimes from the lowest things, as a sweet ointment, as a corner-stone (Exod. III; Joan. I). » But they set about it also a bestial form; and fit to it the special property of a lion and of a panther 960A, and clothe it with a leopard's skin, and a raging ur sam (Cant. II; Isa, XXVIII; Osee V). Ad dam indeed, and to that which seemed to be the vilest of all, and to signify more; since the divinely wise [divine wisdom] handed it down as forming itself even into the appearance of a worm (Psal. XXI). So too all the theosophers, and the prophets by hidden inspiration, distinguish the Holy of Holies from the undefiled saints, and honor the dissimilar holy figuration, so that neither may divine things be rightly received by the unclean, nor may the students of wondrous images remain in the figures of contemplation as though in true things. And so they honor divine things by true negations, and by diverse likenesses of images compacted unto the lowest things. Nothing, therefore, is inconsequent, if they form the heavenly essences too from unfitting, dissimilar likenesses 960Baccording to the said causes. For perhaps we would not indeed come to the question, out of need, unto the anagogy, through the diligent scrutiny of divine things, unless the deformity of the manifesting deformation of the angels forced us out: not suffering our mind to remain in the dissimilar makings of forms, but making it reluctant to deny the material passibilities, and accustoming it to extend itself purely through visible things into the supramundane heights. So much, then, has been said by us on account of the material and unfitting angelic descriptions of the images of the divine words. But then it behooves to set apart what indeed we reckon the hierarchy itself to be, and what those who obtain a hierarchy profit from the hierarchy itself. But let Christ be my leader (if indeed it is lawful for me to say), the 960Cinspiration of the whole hierarchical manifestation. But thou, O boy, according to the holy legislation of our priestly tradition, do thou holily and fittingly hearken, made divine in the divine doctrine of the things wondrously said, covering round in the secret of the mind the things that are holy, and, from the unclean multitude, guard them as uniform. For it is not lawful, as the words say, to cast to swine the unconfused, and light-formed, and beneficent ornament of the invisible pearls (Matth. VII).

EXPOSITIO.

Primum dixi, et dico nunc, ne vos expectatione detineam, quod in hierarchiam Dionysii petitionem vestram suscepi, non ut profunda rerum scrutari persequar, sed ut detegam solum, et in lucem exponam 960Dtecta verborum. Hoc enim introducendis primum magis conveniens est: praecipue quia illa, quae disserenda censuimus, magna nimis, et supra nostram possibilitatem agnoscimus. Titulus secundi capituli hic est. « Quod pulchre divina, et coelestia etiam per dissimilia symbola manifestantur. » Supra jam diximus quid sit symbolum, collatio videlicet, id est coaptatio visibilium formarum ad demonstrationem rei invisibilis propositarum. Verbi gratia, cum spirituum coelestium naturas exprimere visibiliter volumus humanos quidem vultus, sed alas avis in unam compositionis speciem coaptamus, ut pro vultu hominis, qui solus ex visibilibus ratione utitur, ipsi quoque invisibiles spiritus rationales et sapientes esse intelligantur per alas autem agilitas 961Anaturae illorum, et velox ad omnia motus exprimatur. Quia ergo in primo capitulo generaliter de omni hierarchia disseruit, quasi summam sequentis operis breviter ad doctrinam faciendam praelibans; primum, quia omne bonum a summo bono participatione multiplicatur, et omne bonum ad summum bonum similitudine et conversione unitur; deinde, quia convenienter Scriptura ad declarationem invisibilium visibilia signa assumpsit: nunc sequenti capitulo ostendit, sicut titulus ipse praeloquitur, quod videlicet pulchre, id est apte et convenienter manifestantur, hoc est repraesentantur et significantur, ut manifesta fiant, divina scilicet ea quae in summa sunt hierarchia, et coelestia quae in angelica sunt hierarchia. Utraque haec convenienter manifestantur, 961Bnon solum per similia symbola, id est non solum per pulchras et decentes, atque eorum majestati et puritati congruas, sive consimiles figuras et formas; sed etiam per dissimilia symbola, id est per tales formas et descriptiones, quae ab eorum excellentia alienae et puritate indignae videantur. Quod quidem aliquibus minus conveniens videatur esse. Sed bene considerantibus ratione magna, et dispensatione necessaria ordinatum invenitur. Ratione quidem, ut dum haec aliena in demonstrationem assumpta cernimus, illa quoque, quae propria esse videbantur secundum aliquid, aliena esse, et dissimilia a summa veritate agnoscamus. Dispensatione vero, ut dum illa, quae mens pia in divinis collocari secundum proprietatem non sustinet, significatione 961Cillorum cernit attribui: alia quoque quae digna videbantur, ac per hoc vera et propria credi poterant, figurativa esse, et per similitudinem veritati adducta nullatenus possit dubitari Ergo symbola similia in demonstrationem ad hoc proposita sunt, ut invisibilium veritatem specie consimili ostenderent; dissimilia autem, ut significando a figura ad veritatem exeundum, et non remanendum in iis, quae vera esse non poterant, demonstrarent. Ergo quantum similia symbola praecellunt specie, tamen dissimilia symbola transcendunt significatione; quoniam, etsi illa habent speciem pulchriorem, tamen ista significationem tenent manifestiorem. Illa veritatem ostendunt; ista a falsitate exire compellunt. Illa sic veritatem significant, ut facile 961Dpossit rudis animus in eis detineri; ista sic erudiunt, ut non sinat in sui veneratione animos considerantium falli. Illa, cum sint signa veritatis tamen, aliquando fortassis se pro veritate propter excellentem speciem recipi facerent, nisi ista signa essent, in quibus veritas non creditur, etiamsi per ipsa veritas significetur. Aliud enim est veritas, atque aliud signum veritatis; quia signum veritas non est, etiam eum veritatis signum est, et verum est. Illa igitur signa evidentiorem demonstrationem habent, quae et per similitudinem, qua appropinquant veritati, ipsam veritatem manifestant; et per dissimilitudinem, qua elongant a veritate, se non esse veritatem, sed signa tamen, et imaginem veritatis demonstrant. 962AHoc est ergo, quod in isto capitulo demonstrare intendit, sicut per titulum ipsius exprimitur: quod divina, et coelestia pulchre, et decenter non solum per similes, sed etiam per dissimiles formas, et figurationes demonstratur. Et quod nulla, sicut quidam existimaverunt, ipsis divinis et coelestibus injuria fiat, si aliquando in Scripturis sacris per humiles formationes, et quasi ab eorum excellentia remotas, et indignas figurentur, quemadmodum in Scriptura Deus plaustro, et angeli bobus comparantur: et caetera in hunc modum.

« Oportet ergo, ut existimo, primum exponere quam quidem esse speculationem omnis hierarchiae existimamus, etc. » Pudice temperat assertionem suam, ut prudentem decet; nec in rebus excellentibus, 962Bet a sensu humano remotis ultra hominis possibilitatem praesumere videtu, dicens: « Ut existimo. » Noverat enim hoc ipse, quod dicebat, quoniam ab eo doctus erat qui viderat, et sciebat. Sed servavit modestiam dictionis, ut haec humilitate, non elatione quaerenda et invenienda ostenderet. Oportet ergo, ut existimo, primum exponere quam quidem esse speculationem « omnis hierarchiae existimamus. » Quinque hic primum generaliter consideranda modo introductionis legentibus proponit: quae per sequentia capitula singillatim exponet. Primum, generalem omnis hierarchiae definitionem. Secundum, uniuscujusque hierarchiae utilitatem. Tertium, coelestium hierarchiarum secundum visibiles formationes, quae in eloquio sacro reperiuntur, 962Claudationem. Quartum, ipsarum formationum et descriptionum, quibus coelestes virtutes significantur, qualitatem. Quintum, qualem ex ipsis, quae visibiliter ad invisibilium declarationem et laudationem proponuntur, mens humana in ipsis invisibilibus concipere debeat, veritatem. Hoc est, considerare primum, quid sit hierarchia. Secundo, quid prosit, id est quae in unaquaque utilitas consistat. Tertio, quomodo excellentia invisibilium hierarchiarum per visibilia signa ostenditur. Quarto qualitatem signorum, et demonstrationum mysticarum cognoscere. Quinto, signatum a signo, veritatem a figura separare. Oportet primum exponere quam speculationem, id est quam definitionem existimamus esse omnis hierarchiae, hoc est quomodo generaliter 962Dvel universaliter definienda est hierarchia. Definitionem autem idcirco speculationem vocat; quoniam definitio rei quasi speculum est, in qua ipsius rei natura cernitur, sicut in speculo natura corporis appositi imago videtur. Generalis definitio est, quae definitio universaliter convenit, et in toto invenitur. Qui enim dicit principatus angelicos hierarchiam esse, verum dicit; sed universaliter non definit, quoniam in hominibus quoque hierarchia invenitur. Item, qui dicit hierarchiam esse ordinem, verum dicit; quoniam ubi potestas est, ordo est. Sed non totum dicit; quoniam non omnis ordo hierarchia est, quia non omnis ordo potestas est. Itaque generalis. definitio est, quae omni convenit et continet totum. 963AHanc itaque generalem definitionem hierarchiae speculationem omnis hierarchiae auctor nominavit: quae et omni convenit, et continet totum. Hanc autem quia in subsequentibus ipse positurus est et expositurus, nos in praesenti praeoccupare non oportet. Deinde subjungit aliud ex iis; quae exquirere vel exponere oportet, videlicet quod profuit unaquaeque hierarchia divinis laudatoribus ipsius, hoc est, quid vel quantum profuit unaquaeque hierarchia, id est sacra potestas, divinis laudatoribus suis, id est illis qui in ea constituti et ordinati Deum laudant, sive laudes divinas celebrant, et frequentant. Omnes enim hierarchiae ad laudem divinam ordinatae sunt et institutae, sivae superiores, sive inferiores, ut ab omnibus laudetur Deus: a quo et per quem sunt omnes et 963Bin omnibus omnia (I Cor. XV). Et qui excellentiores sunt, amplius laudant; et qui amplius laudant, sublimius remunerantur. Itaque omnis hierarchia tamen suis divinis laudatoribus prodest, quantum accepit secundum gratiae distributionem et dona largitionis, ut sit vel in cognitione sublimior, vel in amore ferventior. Secundum gratiam enim sunt dona, et secundum dona sunt merita, et secundum diversitatem meritorum, praemiorum diversitas constat. Omnis ergo hierarchia Dei laudatoribus suis tamen in praemio profuit quantum contulit in dono; quia omnis dignitas et potestas secundum ministerii et officii gratiam, qua Dei laudem, et honorem, et gloriam praedicare et amplificare potuit, in fructu retributionis excrescit. Sed et ipsae coelestes virtutes, 963Cquibus hoc ipsum praemium est Deum laudare, tantum singulae secundum ordines suos et dignitates in principatibus, et hierarchiis suis utilitatis accipiunt, quanto plus vel minus in laudem Creatoris per donum gratiae cooperantis assurgunt. Deinde, ait, « oportet, » id est post expositam divinam definitionem omnis hierarchiae et utilitatem, oportet laudare coelestes hierarchias, hoc est, angelicos principatus, id est laudes eorum describere et demonstrare secundum ipsarum, videlicet hierarchiarum, in eloquiis manifestationem, id est secundum hoc quod laudes earum in eloquiis, hoc est divinis Scripturis manifestantur. Proponuntur enim in sacro eloquio figurae et demonstrationes, quibus virtutes et laudes 963Dangelicarum potestatum declarantur: quas auctor inspiciendas, et considerandas dicit, ad angelicae hierarchiae manifestationem.

Sequitur; « Consequentibusque iis, » hoc est consequenter post ista supradicta, vel in consequentibus iis, qui sequuntur: Oportet « dicere qualibus divinis formationibus figurant sacrae descriptiones eloquiorum scilicet divinorum, coelestes ordines. » Ac si diceret: Primum oportet considerare quomodo divina eloquia coelestes virtutes per descriptionum formationes laudabiles praedicant. Deinde quales etiam sint ipsae descriptiones et formationes, quas divina quadam oratione in earum scilicet coelestium virtutum declarationem figurant. Novissime autem oportet considerare ad qualem oportet ascendere per 964Aformas veritatem. Non enim sufficit hoc solum, quod visibile est attendere, nisi etiam sciamus qualem oporteat ex eo quod visibiliter demonstratur, invisibiliter veritatem cogitare. Si enim putamus hoc solum esse quod visibiliter in demonstrationem cernitur, nunquam veritatis participes efficimur. Discernamus ergo signum a veritate, et sciamus aliud esse, quod foris sensui erudiendo apponitur; aliud autem, quod intus animo beatificando reservatur. Idcirco autem dicere oportet ad qualem veritatem ascendere debeamus, ab his figurationum visibilium formis, ne nos etiam, sicut multi, existimemus haec omnia, quae pro signis coelestium in Scripturis figurate proponuntur, ita esse illic quemadmodum hic mystice figurantur in similitudinibus et formis 964Bet figuris ad corporalia tamen, et sensibilia pertinentibus: quae in divina, et spiritualia omnino non cadunt.

Hoc est enim, quod sequitur: « Ut non et nos eodem modo multis immunde existimemus coelestes, et deiformes animos, multipedes esse quosdam, et multorum vultuum: et ad boum pecudalitatem, aut ad leonum bestialem imaginationem formatos: et ad aquilarum curvo rostro speciem, aut ad volatilium tripertitam alarum commotionem effiguratos. Et rotas quasdam igneas super coelum imaginemur; et thronos materiales Divinitati ad recubitum necessarios, et equos quosdam multicolores, et armiferos archistrategos; et quaecunque alia ex eloquiis nobis sacre et formabiliter in varietate manifestativorum 964Csymbolorum tradita sunt. » Ut ergo non existimemus etiam nos eodem modo multis, id est quemadmodum multi existimant, coelestes et deiformes animos, id est spiritus invisibiles, incorporeos, et Dei non corporum similitudinem ac formam habentes, multipedes esse; quemadmodum videlicet figurative in eloquio sacro sub figuris et formis animalium describuntur, ut in Ezechiele, in Isaia, et Zacharia, et Michea, et aliis prophetis, angelici spiritus per animalia figurantur quadrupedia, et volatilia, et caetera ad hunc modum. Et ne existimemus etiam quosdam illorum spirituum multorum vultuum esse, id est multos vultus sive facies habere, ut in Ezechiele scriptum est de animalibus sanctis: « Quatuor 964Dfacies uni erant (Ezech. I): » quod licet ad sanctos evangelistas, vel apostolos, vel quoslibet justos congrue referatur, tamen etiam de sanctis angelis, incarnationem Verbi, et passionem, et resurrectionem, et ascensionem annuntiantibus, et in his omnibus Verbum incarnatum ministerii famulatu prosequentibus, non inconvenienter accipitur.

Sequitur: « Et ad boum pecudalitatem, » subaudiendum est, et ne existimemus quosdam formatos ad boum pecudalitatem, hoc est ad similitudinem, formamque boum, quae pecudalis est, non angelica, sicut in Ezechiele forma bovis, vel vituli in animalium figuratione exprimitur. Aut etiam, ne existimemus eosdem spiritus formatos ad leonum bestialem. imaginationem hoc est ad imaginationem sive 965Aimaginem leonum, quae bestialis est, et spirituali ac rationali natura indigna, sicut in Ezechiele facies hominis, et facies leonis in figuratione animalium memoratur. Et ad aquilarum curvo rostro speciem, iterum subauditur, formatos non existimemus. Quod autem ait « curvo rostro, » expresse dignam movet irrisionem, sicut in caeteris, adversum eos qui haec putant spirituali naturae secundum proprietatem assignata. Notum est autem quod in discretione Ezechielis etiam facies aquilae memoratur.

Sequitur: « Aut volatilium tripertitam alarum commotionem effiguratos, » subauditur ne existimemus. Sicut enim in Isaia scriptum est de solio sedentis et templo: « Seraphim stabat super illud: 965Bsex alae uni, et sex alae alteri. Duabus velabant caput, duabus velabant pedes; et duabus volabant alter ad alterum (Isa. VI). » Et alibi: « Quoniam duabus tegebant corpora sua (Ezech. I). » Ubi quidem in sex alarum per binas et binas distinctiones terna vel tripertita commotio invenitur. Sex enim binae et binae junctae simul tria paria alarum conficiunt.

Sequitur: « Et rota quasdam igneas super coelum imaginemur. » Subauditur negativa particula a superiori, videlicet ne imaginemur rotas quasdam igneas super coelum, et ne imaginemur etiam thronos materiales quasi necessarios Divinitati ad recubitum, cum divina natura, quae sola omnia portat, fulcimento non egeat. De rotis autem igneis et thronis 965Cin libro Danielis testimonium habemus (Dan. VII), et in Isaia (Isa. VI), et Michea de solio excelso et sublimi sedentis.

Sequitur: « Et equos quosdam multicolores » (sicut in Zacharia leguntur equi albi, et nigri, et nigri, et varii (Zach. VI); et in Apocalypsi similiter (Apoc. VI) subauditur ne imaginemur. « Et armiferos archistrategos, » similiter ne imaginemur, id est principes, et duces militiae arma ferentes, sive armis indutos sicut in Zacharia legimus, et in Michea. Item Dominum sedentem super solium excelsum, et exercitum coeli a dextris ejus, et sinistris; et in libro Regum currus, et equos, et equites in montibus igneos demonstratos Eliseo, et puero ejus in auxilium venientes (IV Reg. VI), Archistrategi dicti sunt 965Dquasi duces, vel ductores principum exercitus. Compositum nomen ab eo quod est ἀρχός archos, id est princeps, et στρατηγος strategos, quod est dux et imperator exercitus, Archistrategi itaque duces intelliguntur principum exercitus: qui ipsis etiam princibus principantur, sive ducatum praebent superiores. Haec igitur omnia ab iis, quae secundum nos sunt per similitudinem sumpta, atque illis spiritibus coelestibus ad ea, quae ipsis invisibilia sunt, significanda attributa, sic a nobis accipienda sunt, ut haec ita in ipsis esse non existimemus, sed per haec alia, quae in ipsis, nobis sunt invisibilia, visibiliter proposita perpendere studeamus. Non enim species corruptibilis ad illorum munditiam attingit et propterea quodammodo 966Aimmunda existimatio est, quae sine discretione, tam humilia et indigna illi excellenti naturae per proprietatem attribuit. Sive igitur haec, sive quaecunque alia ex eloquiis, id est Scripturis, nobis sacre et formabiliter, hoc est sacra sive sacrae rei formatione vel figuratione, tradita sunt, in varietate manifestativorum symbolorum, id est figurarum et descriptionum sacrarum, quibus manifestantur secreta et abscondita: omnia sic accipiamus, ut secundum similitudinem et significationem eorum illa, de quibus facta sunt, omnia vera esse credamus: et tamen nihil horum in illis per proprietatem esse cogitemus.

Sequitur: « Etenim valde artificialiter theologia poeticis sacris formationibus in non figuratis intellectibus 966Busa est: nostrum, ut dictum est, animum revelans, et ipsi propria, et connaturali reductione providens: et ad ipsum reformans anagogicas sanctas Scripturas. » Ad hoc respondet, quod supradixerat, considerandum esse qualibus formationibus sacra Scriptura coelestes ordines figuraret. Ac si diceret: Propterea ipsae formationes coelestium ordinum in sacro eloquio diligenter inspiciendae sunt; quoniam idcirco factae sunt, ut nostrum animum ad invisibilium cognitionem per haec visibilia et nota revelarent, id est illuminarent. Etenim valde artificialiter vel prudenter, sive considerare usa est theologia, id est divina Scriptura, poeticis sacris formationibus, id est descriptionibus formarum vel figurarum ad sacra vel sancta repraesentanda propositarum, 966Cformationibus poeticis, id est excogitatis, vel adinventis ratione et expositis per similitudinem mysticae traditionis in non figuratis intellectibus, id est spiritibus sine figura et corporali forma in sua simplicitate consistentibus significandis. « Nostrum, ut dictum est, » videlicet in superiori capitulo « animum revelans » ab alto ignorantiae velamine, ut nuda et aperta facie coelestia contempletur: « et ipsi scilicet animo propria et connaturali reductione providens, » ut videlicet reducatur ad invisibilia cognoscenda instructus per ea quae connaturalia et propria illi sunt; et ad ipsum videlicet animum reformans vel coaptans, sive contemperans sanctas Scripturas anagogicas, ut prius nostra nobis conformata ad nos descenderent, et postea ad superiora 966Dreducendo illuminatos sublevarent. Hoc ergo theologia valde artificialiter fecit, ut nobis loquens nostra susciperet, et per nostra admonitos et eruditos ad sua sublevaret. Sed si cui fortassis hoc probandum videatur, inquantum ipsa theologia ad significationem visibilium pulchras et decentes ab iis quae nostra sunt, formationes assumpsit; reprehensibile autem et incongruum illud, quod indecoras etiam et indignas tantae puritati et majestati similitudines apposuit: illi respondendum, propterea theologiam non solum similes, sed etiam dissimiles in demonstrationem divinorum formas assumpsisse, ut per illud quod dissimile et quasi alienum manifeste de ipsis per figuram dicitur etiam id, quod 967Aproprium videri poterat, figuratum et alienum ad proprietatem agnoscatur:
