For there are set forth in the sacred word figures and demonstrations by which the virtues and praises 963Dof the angelic powers are declared: which the author says are to be inspected and considered, unto the manifestation of the angelic hierarchy.

There follows: « And in what follows these, » that is, consequently after those things aforesaid, or in those things which follow: It behooves « to say by what divine formations the sacred descriptions of the words, namely the divine words, figure the heavenly orders. » As if he were saying: First it behooves to consider how the divine words proclaim the heavenly virtues as praiseworthy through the formations of the descriptions. Then, of what quality these very descriptions and formations are, which by a certain divine speech they figure for the declaration of those heavenly virtues. But last of all it behooves to consider to what truth one ought to ascend through 964Athe forms. For it is not enough to attend to this alone, that it is visible, unless we also know of what quality we ought, from that which is visibly demonstrated, invisibly to think the truth. For if we think that this alone is what is visibly discerned in the demonstration, we are never made partakers of the truth. Let us therefore discern the sign from the truth, and let us know that one thing is that which is set outwardly for the instructing of the sense; but another that which is reserved within for the beatifying of the mind. Therefore it behooves to say to what truth we ought to ascend from these forms of the visible figurations, lest we too, like many, should reckon all these things, which are set forth figuratively in the Scriptures as signs of the heavenly ones, to be there just as here they are mystically figured in likenesses and forms 964Band figures pertaining nevertheless to corporeal and sensible things: which by no means fall into the divine and spiritual things.

For this is what follows: « So that neither may we too, in the same fashion as the many, impurely suppose the heavenly and deiform minds to be certain many-footed and many-faced things, and formed after the herd-nature of oxen, or after the bestial imagination of lions, and shaped after the appearance of eagles with a curved beak, or after the threefold beating of the wings of flying things. And that we should imagine certain fiery wheels above the heaven; and material thrones necessary to the Divinity for its reclining, and certain horses of many colors, and arms-bearing supreme commanders; and whatever other things have been handed down to us out of the sacred words, sacredly and in a form-giving way, in the variety of manifesting 964Csymbols. » So that neither may we too, then, in the same fashion as the many — that is, in the way that the many suppose — suppose the heavenly and deiform minds, that is, the invisible, incorporeal spirits, which have not the likeness and form of God nor of bodies, to be many-footed; namely, in the way in which they are figuratively described in the sacred word under the figures and forms of animals, as in Ezekiel, in Isaiah, and Zechariah, and Micah, and other prophets, the angelic spirits are figured by four-footed animals, and flying things, and the rest in this manner. And lest we also suppose certain of those spirits to be many-faced, that is, to have many countenances or faces, as it is written in Ezekiel concerning the holy living creatures: « Four 964Dfaces had one of them (Ezech. I): » which, although it may be fittingly referred to the holy evangelists, or the apostles, or any of the just, is nevertheless also not inconveniently taken of the holy angels, who announce the incarnation of the Word, and the passion, and the resurrection, and the ascension, and in all these things attend upon the incarnate Word in the service of ministry.

There follows: « And after the herd-nature of oxen, » — it is to be understood, and lest we suppose certain of them formed after the herd-nature of oxen, that is, after the likeness and form of oxen, which is that of the herd, not angelic, as in Ezekiel the form of an ox, or of a calf, is expressed in the figuration of the living creatures. Or again, lest we suppose the same spirits formed after the bestial imagination of lions, that is, after the imagination or 965Aimage of lions, which is bestial, and unworthy of a spiritual and rational nature, as in Ezekiel the face of a man and the face of a lion is mentioned in the figuration of the living creatures. And after the appearance of eagles with a curved beak, again it is understood, let us not suppose them formed. But in that he says « with a curved beak, » he plainly stirs a fitting derision, as in the rest, against those who think these things assigned to a spiritual nature according to property. It is known, moreover, that in Ezekiel's distinction the face of an eagle also is mentioned.

There follows: « Or shaped after the threefold beating of the wings of flying things, » — it is understood, let us not suppose. For as it is written in Isaiah of the throne of the one sitting and of the temple: « The seraphim stood above it: 965Bsix wings to the one, and six wings to the other. With two they veiled the head, with two they veiled the feet; and with two they flew, the one to the other (Isa. VI). » And elsewhere: « For with two they covered their bodies (Ezech. I). » Where indeed, in the six wings, by twos and twos in their distinctions, a threefold or tripartite beating is found. For six, joined two and two together, make three pairs of wings.

There follows: « And let us imagine certain fiery wheels above the heaven. » The negative particle is supplied from above, namely, let us not imagine certain fiery wheels above the heaven, and let us not imagine also material thrones as though necessary to the Divinity for its reclining, since the divine nature, which alone bears all things, has no need of a support. But of the fiery wheels and thrones 965Cwe have testimony in the book of Daniel (Dan. VII), and in Isaiah (Isa. VI), and Micah, concerning the one sitting upon a lofty and high throne.

There follows: « And certain horses of many colors » (as in Zechariah there are read white horses, and black, and black, and dappled (Zach. VI); and in the Apocalypse likewise (Apoc. VI)) — it is understood, let us not imagine. « And arms-bearing supreme commanders, » likewise let us not imagine, that is, princes and leaders of the army bearing arms, or clad in arms, as we read in Zechariah, and in Micah. Likewise the Lord sitting upon a lofty throne, and the host of heaven at his right hand and his left; and in the book of Kings the chariots, and horses, and horsemen of fire shown upon the mountains to Elisha, and coming to the aid of his servant (IV Reg. VI). They are called supreme commanders 965Das it were leaders, or conductors of the princes of the army. It is a compound name, from that which is ἀρχός archos, that is, prince, and στρατηγος strategos, which is leader and commander of an army; and so supreme commanders are understood as the leaders of the princes of the army, who rule over the princes themselves, or, being superior, afford them their leadership. All these things, therefore, taken by likeness from those things which are according to us, and attributed to those heavenly spirits for the signifying of those things which are invisible to themselves, are so to be received by us that we do not suppose these things to be in them in this way, but that through these things we may study to weigh other things, which are in them and are invisible to us, visibly set forth. For no corruptible appearance attains to their purity; and therefore in a certain manner 966Ait is an impure supposition which, without discretion, attributes things so lowly and unworthy to that excellent nature according to property. Whether therefore these things, or whatever other things out of the words, that is, the Scriptures, have been handed down to us sacredly and in a form-giving way — that is, by a sacred fashioning or figuring, or the figuring of a sacred thing — in the variety of manifesting symbols, that is, of sacred figures and descriptions, by which secret and hidden things are made manifest: let us so receive them all that, according to their likeness and signification, we believe all those things of which they are made to be true; and yet let us think none of these things to be in them according to property.

There follows: « For very artfully theology has used poetic sacred formations in unfigured intellects 966B— revealing, as has been said, our mind, and providing for it its own and connatural leading-back, and reforming unto it the anagogical holy Scriptures. » To this he responds to what he had said above, that it is to be considered with what sort of formations sacred Scripture would figure the heavenly orders. As if he said: For this reason the very formations of the heavenly orders in the sacred word are diligently to be inspected; because they were made for this end, that they might reveal, that is, illuminate, our mind unto the knowledge of invisible things through these visible and known things. For very artfully, or prudently, or with consideration, theology, that is, the divine Scripture, has used poetic sacred formations, that is, descriptions of forms or figures set forth for the representing of sacred or holy things — 966Cpoetic formations, that is, ones devised, or invented by reason and set forth through the likeness of mystical tradition — for the signifying of unfigured intellects, that is, of spirits subsisting without figure and corporeal form in their own simplicity. « Revealing, as has been said, » namely in the foregoing chapter, « our mind » from the deep veil of ignorance, so that with bared and open face it may contemplate heavenly things: « and providing for it, namely for the mind, its own and connatural leading-back, » so that, instructed, it may be led back to the knowing of invisible things through those things which are connatural and its own; and reforming, namely, or adapting, or tempering unto the mind itself the anagogical holy Scriptures, so that first, being conformed to us, they might descend to us, and afterward, by leading back to higher things, 966Dmight lift up the illumined. This, then, theology did very artfully, that, speaking to us, it might take up our things, and, through our things, might lift up those admonished and instructed unto its own. But if perchance it seem to anyone that this is to be approved insofar as theology itself, for the signifying of visible things, took beautiful and seemly formations from those things which are ours; but that it is reprehensible and unfitting that it also appended likenesses unseemly and unworthy of so great a purity and majesty: to him it is to be answered that theology took up not only like, but also unlike, forms for the demonstration of divine things for this reason — that through that which is unlike and, as it were, alien, said manifestly of them by figure, even that which 967Acould seem proper might be recognized as figured and alien to property:

This is what follows: « But if to anyone it seems that the sacred compositions ought indeed to be received, as of things simple in themselves, and unknown to us, and uncontemplable in their subsistence. » This is, that it is worthy that the sacred compositions be received, that is, the sacred figurations or formations which are made concerning the divine and invisible things themselves, inasmuch as they are of those things which are simple and uncompounded, without corporeal figuration and form, and thereby, to us who know only how to contemplate and think corporeal things, subsist unknown and uncontemplable, and cannot be shown, nor perceived by the human heart, save through visible signs and visible demonstrations. If, then, it seems to anyone worthy 967Band necessary, on account of causes of this sort, that the sacred compositions be received — provided only that they be formed beautifully and seemly, and befitting so great a purity — but now judges them to be unseemly « and unfitting, » namely whatever, « of the holy intellects, » that is, the descriptions of spirits, that are made « in the sacred words »; and he judges it also to be unfitting, all this figment of angelic names, as it seems to him theatrical — namely, that angels, oxen, and lions, and eagles, and horses, and wheels, and chariots, and thrones, and the rest of this sort should be introduced and named: which according to his supposition seems theatrical, and worthy of theatrical recitation and derision. 967CBut to us, thinking piously and believing rightly, to speak thus is hard, or, every such speaking is hard, that is, all such hard and unfitting sayings and descriptions, which is as it were a certain theater of angelic names; or, if he supposes that to speak thus, that is, that it must so be spoken, that which is feigned in Scripture, is as it were hard, that is, an inconsonant and unfitting theater of angelic names to be: and if he also says that the theologians, coming or descending to a corporeal fashioning, that is, a material figuration, of things universally, that is, altogether incorporeal — namely the heavenly and invisible — ought to have formed them, namely the invisible things, and to have made them manifest, as far as was possible for them, by proper and cognate figurations, that is, by unfitting and like figurations 967Dtaken from among us, that is, from among these visible things, out of the most precious ones — or taken out of the most precious things among us, that is, out of those things which are most precious among us; and out of things in some way immaterial, that is, out of those things which in any, that is, in some, way seem to be immaterial and incorporeal, such namely as light, and fire, and splendor, and heat, and the rest of this sort: which, though they be material and corporeal, nevertheless approach closely to a spiritual nature by their subtlety and purity. If then he say that out of these most precious things, and in some way immaterial and supereminent essences, the theologians ought to have taken the figures of those things which are altogether incorporeal, so that through those things which are almost immaterial and incorporeal, truly incorporeal things might be signified. And if he say further that there ought not to be set round about 968Aearthly and lowest, that is, last or least, or abject multiformities, that is, figures composed of many and various forms, upon the deiform simplicities, that is, the spiritual natures: which, because they are deiform in glory, earthly and lowest things, and because they are simple in essence, multiformities ought by no means to have been attributed to them. And if he say further: This indeed — that is, if out of precious and supereminent essences the figures of the invisible things were taken, and earthly and lowest formednesses were not set round about, or fitted to, the deiform simplicities — this indeed both would be our own more sublimely, that is, would advance us more sublimely to the knowledge of spiritual things. Or, this indeed both would be ours, because it would be corporeal and material; and would be more sublime, 968Bthat is, nearer to divine and spiritual things, so that on either part it would become reasonable: so that through that which was ours, that is, familiar and known to us, it could instruct; and through that which was more sublime and more worthy, it would befit the excellence and dignity of spiritual things. And it would also not lead the supermundane, that is, the heavenly and spiritual manifestations into unfitting unlikenesses, as these descriptions do; because out of earthly and lowest essences they bring likenesses unfitting and unlike to spiritual things. This also — that is, if only out of beautiful and seemly forms the figures of spiritual things were formed — would do no injury to the divine powers by attributing to them unfitting forms: 968Cwhich to do is unjust. And equally, that is, likewise, it would not seduce our mind, as this base and unseemly formation seduces it, into thinking things alien and unworthy of those powers, while it inserts, or intrudes, itself into these impure compositions: which have been made unseemly concerning them. And perhaps yet another evil may come from these base compositions, namely, that the supercelestial things will be supposed to be filled, or to have been filled, with certain leonine and equine multitudes, that is, of horses and lions, and with a lowing utterance of praises, and with a flying headlong of angels; because the figures of lions, and horses, and oxen, and birds, whose office is to roar, and to neigh, and to fly, and which cannot praise God save by lowing, or roaring, are ascribed to the angels. And the heavenly things themselves will be supposed 968Dto be filled not only with these, but also with other animals and baser materials, such as worms, and coals, and other things of this sort, which are found said by figure of spiritual things — as though the heavenly things themselves were laid open, that is, disclosed and opened, unto that which is inconsequent, that is, unfitting and ignoble, and it be possible above that things of this sort be admitted into them, or even passible, that is, corruptible. And all these things indeed will be supposed, while they are described, likenesses of the manifesting words: which the words set forth for manifestation clearly, that is, manifestly, as deformed. If then to anyone this whole thing seem so (so that up to this point the sentence hangs, and at last it is thus inferred) — to him indeed it so seems, namely that only beautiful and excellent appearances are to be set to the signification of spiritual 969Aand divine things. But nevertheless, if anyone diligently inquire into the truth, he recognizes that the wisdom of the divine words has fittingly set forth both.

This is what follows: « But the inquiry of truth, as I suppose, shows that the most sacred wisdom of the words, in the formation of the minds, or spirits, of the heavenly ones, has provided for both exceedingly, so that neither (as perhaps someone would say) should it do injury to the divine powers, » that is, so that neither through those lowly figurations should it do injury to the divine powers, that is, to the spirits, who are divine and sacred and incorporeal: which nevertheless perhaps someone would call injury, and would think ought to be called so, when yet it is no injury, « neither should it fix us » through the same figurations « passibly 969Bin the vile lownesses of images, » that is, in the vileness of lowly, or in the lowness of vile, images. For the wisdom of the divine word provided and took care of both: that through these lowly figurations it should neither do injury to the divine things, nor inform our mind to vile thoughts or false suppositions. And first, indeed, why corporeal and visible figures and forms have been set to the manifesting of divine and invisible things, a necessary and fitting cause is demonstrated — which perhaps someone would say is not one, but twofold, that is, not only because those things could not otherwise be made manifest to our mind save through these, but also because in the figures and enigmas of mystical descriptions the divine secrets were to be covered and concealed from impure minds and from the malevolent. 969CThus, he says, someone will state the cause of the mystical descriptions: which, though he himself could have said it indubitably and truly, he modestly attributes to another, lest perchance he should seem to commend his own authority.

This, then, is what he says: « For because indeed the forms of the formless, and the figures of things lacking figures, have been beautifully provided: one would not say the cause thereof to be one, our analogy. For because indeed. » Contrary to the usage of Latinity, according to the idiom of the Greek tongue, he has heaped up conjunctions, or quia is to be read for quod, so that this is the sense: That indeed one, that is, someone, would say the cause not to be one — namely this our analogy, that is, that not only our 969Danalogy is the cause of this thing, namely that the forms of the formless and the figures of things lacking figures have been beautifully, that is, fittingly, provided by the sacred word — that is, that in the sacred word forms and figures have been attributed to those heavenly spirits, which in their own nature have neither corporeal forms nor figures. Of this thing, I say, one would say the cause to be not only the analogy, that is, our condition, otherwise unable to attain to the knowledge of invisible things, nor able immediately, that is, without some intermediary, to extend itself through the intellect into the invisible contemplations, that is, into the contemplations of invisible things. Our analogy, I say, which also desires its own and connatural leadings-back, this is, to be led back to the knowledge and contemplation of invisible things 970Athrough those things which are its own and connatural, that is, visible and corporeal — which corporeal things, namely, put forth, that is, set forth, the formations of the formless, that is, of spiritual speculations, and the supernatural, that is, of speculations exceeding our nature, and altogether incomprehensible to us, unless through these passible formations they were demonstrated and insinuated to us. He calls analogy the human condition; because analogy is a property, according to reason and the agreement of several like things in one, just as grammarians too are wont to assign analogies of words according to the likeness of several falling under one property. The analogy, then, of human nature, that is, the condition or property, or 970Bagreement, is this: to be able and to know those things which pertain to man, and which man received to be and to be able. But above our analogy, that is, above our agreement and equality, is it to scrutinize heavenly things, unless we be instructed through those things which are with us visible and known to us. This analogy, then, that is, the human condition, was the cause why the sacred word, for the instructing of human minds, set forth visible signs of invisible things. And not this cause only, but also « because this also is most seemly for the mystical words, » namely to hide, « and to set as trackless to the many the sacred and hidden, » that is, the concealed truth « of the supermundane intellects, » that is, of the invisible spirits, « through incomprehensible divine enigmas. » 970CFor enigmas, and parables, and figures are set to the mystical word of the Scriptures for this reason: that the truth of spiritual things be not laid open to carnal and impure spirits, and that at once it may exercise the studious and devout by its very profundity. Which cause, however, the author here judges to mention out of superabundance. Therefore, then, the divine sacraments are covered lest they lie open to all, because not all are worthy of the recognition of truth. « For not everyone is holy, neither is knowledge of all, as the words say. » For because not every man is holy, therefore the truth is not to be made manifest to all; since, if it were made manifest to all, many would gnaw at it by contradicting through malice, or would defile it by living impurely. Whence it is said: « Give not the holy thing 970Dto dogs (Matth. VII), » namely to those who gnaw the truth set forth with the tooth of malice; « neither cast pearls before swine (ibid.), » namely before those who, as far as in them lies, pollute what is offered by living wickedly. For these are the unholy, that is, unworthy of holy things, whose knowledge it is not, « as the words say, » of the sacred Scripture. For the Apostle says that « faith is not of all (II Thess. III), » since that knowledge of truth, by which God is piously believed by the holy and just, is either not received by any of the perverse, or not worthily held.

« But if anyone should suppose the causes of the deformed descriptions of images to be dishonorable, saying that such base formations are thus referred to the deiform and most holy dispositions, it suffices to say to him: How 971Ais the mode of holy manifestation twofold? » Now at length he responds to the question objected above, in which it was contained that vile and abject formations are unfittingly set to sacred and divine things in the sacred word, saying: « If anyone should suppose the causes of the description of images to be deformed, » that is, if anyone should suppose the causes of describing images to be deformed, that is, unfitting, saying it to be dishonorable that such base formations be referred, that is, fitted, to the deiform and most holy dispositions, that is, orders. If anyone, I say, should so suppose, and so say: « It suffices to say to him how the mode of holy manifestation is twofold: » that is, to a supposition and objection of this sort it is sufficiently answered in this, that the holy manifestation which is made 971Bthrough the Scriptures is shown to have a twofold mode. « One indeed as it were consequent, » that is, fitting and seemly, in which the signs follow the signified truth by a like property: on account of like images of sacred figures agreeing, that is, proceeding to make the manifestation, or coming forth, that is, apt and concordant with that which they signify. « But the other mode is conformed unto the altogether inconsequent, » that is, discrepant, and unfitting, and unseemly, for the reason that the very figures and the very signs manifesting the truth seem not to say it. This is what he says: « On account of unlike fashionings of forms. »

There follows: « And so the mystical traditions of the manifesting words praise the venerable 971Cbeatitude of the superessential divinity — sometimes indeed as reason, and intellect, and essence, declaring the divine rationality and its wisdom, and the truly existing subsistence, and the true cause of those things which are subsistences. » As if he said: Since the mode of manifestation in the sacred word is twofold — one, namely, formed through like signs, the other through unlike signs — and so the sacred words themselves also sometimes represent the majesty of the divine nature through like, sometimes through unlike formations. Through like ones, sometimes indeed taken from corporeal things, sometimes from incorporeal. From incorporeal things, as when they name it reason and intellect; from corporeal, as when they name it light and 971Dsplendor, and the rest that are done in this manner. But sometimes through unlike formations, likewise taken from incorporeal, or from corporeal things, they manifest the divine nature. From incorporeal indeed, as when they attribute to it anger, zeal, repentance; but from corporeal, when they set to it, in signification, the forms or figures of beasts, or of any other corporeal things whatsoever. This, then, is what he says: « And so the mystical traditions of the manifesting words praise the venerable beatitude of the superessential divinity; sometimes indeed as reason, and intellect, and essence, declaring its divine subsistence truly existing, and the true cause of the subsistence of all those things which are; » since it both truly subsists in itself, 972Aand makes all subsistences to subsist, in that they call it essence — although it itself nevertheless, above all reason, and intellect, and essence, subsists in its majesty, neither intelligible nor comprehensible, above all subsistences.

There follows: « And they form it as light, and call it life. » Namely, the venerable beatitude the mystical traditions form, although it itself is light above all light and subsists as life above all life. By so many, then, and so great modes do the sacred words form the divine majesty in figuration. « These so great and wondrous formations remaining chaster than the rest, which seem incongruous, and unworthy, and these so great and wondrous formations being approved in some way to excel the other material formations. » As if he said: 972BAlthough unto that excellence every formation, or representation, is found inferior, yet in comparison with the other formations such beautiful and such seemly formations are proved to excel. When, namely, the nature of the divinity is named reason, and intellect, and essence, and light, and life — although even in these formations too the likeness fails in manifestation for the expressing of the ineffable truth. Whence he says: « These divine things also thus failing of likeness unto the truth. » Namely, even these more excellent likenesses thus failing, that is, even in so great excellence failing of the divine likeness — failing, namely, unto the truth, it is understood, to be expressed. For everything that here is in the sign is less than that which there is in the truth. « For it is, 972C« namely the divine nature, » above all essence and life, no light indeed characterizing, that is, figuring, or expressing, it: and it is excellent, all reason and intellect being incomparably left behind, or beneath the likeness of itself. Whence it appears that if its likeness is so far superior to reason and intellect, that neither reason nor intellect can advance to equal its likeness.

There follows: « But sometimes it is praised supermundanely by the words themselves through unlike manifestations, they calling it invisible, and infinite, and incomprehensible, and by those things from which is signified not what it is, but what it is not. » As if he said: Not only is it manifested by like and excellent manifestations, 972Dand by those approaching to its image: but sometimes also by unlike manifestations, and ones foreign to its nature, it is praised by the words « supermundanely, » that is, mystically and spiritually, and above the appearance of this world. For when it is praised through beautiful forms, it is praised according to the appearance of this world, that is, it is said according to something which is the very thing through which it is praised. But when it is praised through unlike formations, and ones alien from itself, it is praised supermundanely; since it is neither said to be the same, nor according to that, but above that, wholly other, through which it is praised. Therefore, then, it is praised supermundanely by the words themselves through unlike formations. The words, I say, or the formations themselves, calling it, namely the divine nature, invisible, and 973Ainfinite, and incomprehended: first, infinite in itself; then, invisible to us; after, incomprehended by us; and many other things also the words themselves calling the divine nature, which are such that from them is signified not what it is, but what it is not. For when God is said to be invisible, and infinite, and incomprehended: it is not said what he is, but what he is not — for he is not visible, because he cannot be seen, nor is he bounded, because he is not enclosed by place, nor terminated by time; nor is he comprehensible, because, even if it is believed what he is, how great he is is not grasped. Whoever, then, says him invisible, does not say to be that which is, but not to be that which is not. Likewise also whoever says him infinite, and incomprehended, does not say to be that which is, because he affirms nothing to be. But he says not to be that which is not, 973Bbecause he denies something to be; since both what he does not affirm is that which cannot be said, and what he denies is that which can be understood.

There follows: « For this, as I suppose, is more powerful in it. » This, namely, from which is signified not what it is, but what it is not, is more powerful, that is, more efficacious, and more proper, and more expressive in it; since he who says what it is not, says that which in some manner can be understood; but he who says what it is, says that which in no manner can be comprehended. But it is more powerful and more excellent, as regards the expression of truth, to say what God is not, than what he is. « Since indeed, as the hidden and priestly tradition has introduced, we truly say this to be it — not according to any of those things which are; but we are ignorant 973Cof its superessential, and invisible, and ineffable infinitude. » As if he said: As the authority of sacred Scripture testifies, introduced from the hidden unto manifestation, and handed down for correction and information. As, then, that tradition, that is, that authority which is handed down, hidden as regards the mysteries of hidden sacraments, and priestly as regards the dignity and holiness of the divine writings themselves, and its own sanctification, because it was both handed down by divine priests and prophets, and divinely sanctified for the sake of those to be sanctified through it. As, then, that hidden and priestly tradition introduced, we learned that this, that is, such a thing according to which 973Dwe truly say it, that is, the divine nature, to be, is not of all those things which are; because no species of created things so approaches to its likeness as to show expressly and according to property that which truly is in it. Or thus we learned that it is not truly what we say it to be according to something, that is, according to any of those things which are: for that which truly is according to any of those things which are, cannot be said to be the whole; and therefore when we say it to be something according to those things which are, we do not yet manifest by expression that which it truly is. But we are ignorant of its superessential, and invisible, and ineffable infinitude. For that which is infinite cannot be estimated by human knowledge: which, because it is ineffable, is not said; and because it is invisible, is not known; and 974Abecause it is superessential, is not comprehended. Of it, then, the human mind can grasp something, itself it cannot; and the human tongue can say something of it, itself it cannot; nor for that reason, however, is what is said of it to be supposed false; since it is only of it, and it itself is not this which is said; nor is what is thought of it vain, since it is only of it, and it itself is not this which is thought; since what is said is true, and what is thought is truth: which so leads unto it, although it subsists more sublimely and loftily in itself.

There follows: « If, then, the negations in divine things are true, but the affirmations incompact: the manifestation through unlike formations is more apt to the obscurity of hidden things. » As if he said: Since more expressly and more 974Bproperly we say God to be nothing that is, when we say both to be something, and not to be, truly, it is manifest that in divine things, that is, in those things which are said of God and attributed to God, the negations are true, that is, proper; but the affirmations incompact, that is, improper and not cohering, since they try to join and fit together unlike things, according to that mode of speaking by which human speech cannot otherwise be formed concerning God. But if the negations in divine things are true, that is, proper, and the affirmations incompact, that is, improper, it is manifest that the manifestation made through unlike formations is more apt to the obscurity of the hidden things to be revealed than that made through like ones; since the former strives to demonstrate, as it were by negation, by removing, what God is not, 974Cbut the latter tries to show, as it were by affirmation, by positing, what he is. « And now, therefore, the sacred descriptions of the words do not, as base, fill up the heavenly adornments, manifesting them by unlike fashionings of forms; and through these showing the excellences of the supermundane things above all material things together. And now therefore, » — since unlike figurations stand more properly in divine things, according to that mode by which, out of all things which are, nothing is properly named of God; according to this mode, therefore, they do not fill up, that is, assert to be filled up, the heavenly adornments, that is, the heavenly orders or dispositions, the base, that is, deformed, formations themselves which are set forth in the sacred word; manifesting 974Dthem, namely the adornments, by unlike fashionings, that is, by compositions of forms unlike and alien from their excellence; and through these fashionings showing the excellences of the supermundane, that is, of the heavenly and invisible things, above all material things together; this is, their excellences in relation to all material things; that is, showing that the supermundane and spiritual things themselves excel all material things. For in this, that they attribute unlike figures to them, they show that even those things too, which seem to be said of them according to likeness, do not rise up to their property.

There follows: « But that unlike likenesses lead our mind back more, I do not suppose that any of those who are well-wise contradicts. » As if he said: Not only for this reason are the unlike figurations approvable, 975Athat they show the excellences of the supermundane things; but also for this reason, that they lead our mind back from material and corporeal things more than like figurations do, nor suffer it to rest in itself. Hear a great mystery. That which God is, is above all; and when it is asked what he is, this cannot be said, because it cannot be thought. For that which can be thought ascends into the heart of man, and is grasped by the heart of man, either in those things which are seen according to appearance, or according to those things which are through imagination, or in those things which are perceived within by experience and truth; and the heart of man grasps only what it knows, or according to those things which it knows. But it knows those things which it conceives without by sense, and those things which it feels within by experience; and everything that it grasps, it either grasps in these, or conjectures according to 975Bthese. But that which is neither in these, nor according to these, the human heart cannot grasp. But that which God is, is neither any of these, because he is not a creature; nor is it according to these, because he is the Creator. That which God is, then, can neither be found in these, nor understood according to these what sort it is. For if it were understood according to these, it would be led down into the same likeness unto these, and there would be this in these which is in him. But whatever things are in creatures are more near and akin to one another, because they are made; than the work is to the artificer, and the thing fashioned to the fashioner. For all time compared to eternity, and all space composed to immensity, is found to have less, than any length of time set beside a moment, or an extension of quantity 975Chowever much increasing, referred to the proportion of an atom. So that which God is, compared to a creature, is found to excel more amply, than that which is highest among created things, compared to those things which are lowest, or made most extreme. God, then, cannot be thought according to these things, what he is; since he is other, and is otherwise, and far, and remotely, and unlikely; and what he is cannot be said. For if any of these things is said, he is other. If according to any of these things it is said, he is otherwise. What then is to be said, which God is? If he is called heaven, he is other. If he is called earth, he is other; and whatever is in heaven, and is on earth, is not this which God is. Therefore this which God is, is other. And what is this? Only this can be said, that he is other, 975Dand what he is cannot be said. We have, then, what we may say, God is not this; but we have not what we may say, this is God; because everything that we have, this is not God, and we have not in all these things, nor do we find, what God is. For all this is other than God; because God is not everything that is made by God, and the eye does not see, nor does the mind grasp, save this, or according to this, which is not God, but from God. For man has the sense of man, and feels according to the sense of man, either that which is without according to the flesh, or that which is within according to the mind, and man has no more. The eye of flesh those things which are unto the flesh, the eye of the mind those things which are unto the mind. What more? « No man knows the things which are of a man, save the spirit of a man, which is in the man. » 976A(I Cor. II). » So the things which are of God no one knows, save the Spirit of God; and he who has the Spirit of God knows through the Spirit of God the things which are of God. But the eye is threefold: the eye of flesh, the eye of reason, the eye of contemplation. The eye of flesh is open, the eye of reason bleary, the eye of contemplation closed and blind. By the eye of flesh is seen the world, and the things which are in the world. By the eye of reason the mind, and the things which are in the mind. By the eye of contemplation God, and the things which are in God. By the eye of flesh man sees those things which are outside himself; by the eye of reason those things which are in himself; by the eye of contemplation those things which are within himself and above himself. Therefore God, that which he is, is unthinkable, but to men, and to human reason: which perceives nothing save what it knows, or according to that which it knows, which is in itself or outside itself. But those who 976Bhave the Spirit of God in themselves, have God also: these see God, because they have an illumined eye by which God can be seen, and they feel him not in another, or according to another which he himself is not, but himself and in himself that which he is, which is present. Nor yet can it be said, because it is ineffable, because it is unthinkable; and it is felt, and not expressed. Therefore, everything that is said of God, that he is, is said according to that which can be said and thought, since it cannot be said otherwise; and everything that can be said and thought is less and is below than that which God is. This very thing which is said, is said as less, and this very thing is not said which God is, because he who says something says according to something, and thinks that which he says, and according to that which he says. You name 976CGod, and you form two syllables; and you think you have said the whole of that which he is. What have you thought? For that which you have thought, this you have said. I have thought, you say, that which is above all things: what is this? If you can think what it is, this you can say. But if you cannot think it, you cannot say it; because that which cannot be thought, cannot be said. You have said God: and what is God? What do you think, or of what sort do you think, when you say God? For that which sounds is this, either one beholding or running, or fear, or whatever else you shall have supposed of him as you are able. Therefore when you say God, you say one beholding and contemplating, and considering all things. And what is this? How does God behold, and how does he see? What is his seeing, save his being? And of what sort is this? But if you understand one running, because he penetrates 976Dall things, and apprehends, and contains everything that is, for him to run is this: to stand. And who may grasp this? But if you interpret it fear; and you assert that this itself is to be thought under this name when it is said God: who could explain how fear is God? But if for this reason you suppose fear to be said, because he is feared, how is that feared which is not seen? how can that be seen which cannot be thought? and how can that be feared which cannot be known? See therefore what you say, when you say God; or what you think, when you say God. The Creator, you say, of all things I think, when I say God, who made all things, and himself was not made. Therefore when you say God, you think that which made all things. You think that which he made, and you do not think that which he himself is who made. Not yet have you attained that which you had promised, that you should think, and understand 977Awhat God is. Less is this whole which you say; and this whole is not himself of whom you say it; and yet of him you say this, not that you may reach unto him, but that you may draw near to him. For it is a great thing for man now to go unto him, even if it be not granted to arrive. But it will be granted afterward, when that which is perfect shall have come; and man shall have begun to see as he is seen, not the image through a glass, but the truth face to face. But now meanwhile the whole is image, and the image itself is far from the truth; and yet it does what it can as an image; and it turns the mind, but does not lead it through. For this alone it can do in us, and we in it this alone, because neither can it show more, nor we grasp another, and yet there is a certain image more sublime, and more approaching to the truth, 977Bso that it can be more called truth by us, because there is nothing else above it, by which truth could be more expressly demonstrated. For it is said that God is fire; and the figure is manifest; since God, according to property, is not fire; since fire is a body, God is not a body. It is said also that God is light; and here likewise appears an image of the truth, other than the truth, since God is not light according to property, which is named according to figure. For all these things are visible, and are far from God by the property of nature, even if they are fitted to him according to likeness alone, which itself too is scanty in relation to the excellence of his majesty. But there is another incorporeal nature more near to God, between which and God there is no other intermediary nature; and this approaches more to likeness, 977Calthough it too is far from the truth. According to this, then, the highest nature to us, a sublime likeness to God is formed for us, when God is called spirit, and wisdom, and reason, and love; because the soul is spirit, and the angel is spirit, and in the spirit itself is reason, wisdom, and love. And we know what spirit is, as far as we know the soul, and know the angel; and through the soul we know the angel, as far as we know our own selves; although even this is little, and can scarcely be called knowledge. When therefore we hear that God is spirit, we think the soul, and the angel, and we suppose a likeness, since God is some such thing as the soul is, and the angel, because the soul and the angel 977Dare spirit. And we know not how far this is from the truth of the incomprehensible excellence. For whoever should call a body spirit, would say a falsehood, since a body is not spirit nor spirit a body. Whoever, then, should say this, would rightly be reprehended; and would be judged contrary to the truth; and yet whoever says God to be spirit is supposed to have said a truth. No one accuses him of falsity, although yet a body and a spirit are more near in nature and condition, than a spirit and God. For here each is a creature, and each is comprehensible, and each mutable, and finite. But there the one indeed is eternal, the other temporal; the one immense, the other comprehensible; the one always remaining the same, the other mutable; the one falling under knowledge, the other 978Aunthinkable. And yet, because another cannot be said, this is said; lest nothing be said, where another is to be said, and what is cannot be said; or if it can be said, it cannot be understood. This, then, is said, and the truth tolerates this of itself, and commends this to us for truth — to us who cannot yet grasp the truth itself, until the figure pass away, and the truth be manifested, above all this, and outside all this, nakedly and openly as it itself is. Now therefore up to this point the figures remain, and of these some are far, and appear to be likeness only; but some indeed are proper, and are received as it were for truth, though they be only signs of the truth and not the truth, in which indeed, if nothing higher shall have been unto it, the truth concedes these to us, and does not reckon the impossibility. But if 978Bthey shall have been near and closely alike, yet shall not have been nearest, and something more sublime appear for the manifesting of the truth; the truth does not suffer itself to be led down to them according to property, since in the other it demonstrates itself more perfectly, in which it proves itself here to be only through likeness. But in that supreme thing, than which nothing is higher, no other appears unto it by which the figure may be proved; and therefore it behooves to receive it so as it is, since no other is given, until that which is perfect shall come. Every figure, then, the more evidently demonstrates the truth, the more openly it proves itself, through an unlike likeness, to be a figure, and not the truth; and in this the unlike likenesses lead our mind back more unto the truth, in that they do not permit it to remain in likeness alone. 978C

Wherefore, he says, « I do not think that any of the well-wise would contradict » this — that dissimilar likenesses lead our mind back to the truth. For indeed « it follows, that men are led astray by the more precious sacred formations, » that is, it can follow, or come about, or easily happen, that through those formations of sacred things which are represented as more precious in the sacred discourse, the thoughts of men are led astray, « thinking certain celestial essences to be gold-formed, » just as in certain places of the Scriptures they are represented by likeness; and thinking also that there are in heaven certain flashing men clothed in comely garments, just as 978Dangels are read to have appeared in splendid garments and with flashing countenances, « sprinkling forth, harmlessly, what is white and fiery, » that is, emitting, or pouring out, brightness and light; the white indeed as to the garments, and the fiery as to the flaming and burning countenances; harmlessly, that is, without injury — this itself holding firm in the very divine miracle, because in the divine and celestial natures, which are here shown by appearance, they are otherwise there according to truth: in which the appearance of visible nature is discerned, but the effect is not found.

There follows: « And by whatever other similar imagined forms, » that is, expressed according to imaginable things, « Theology has figured the celestial intellects, » that is, has represented the spiritual natures — so that from the things above 979A(understand) here it follows that men are led astray, thinking the celestial essences to exist in their own nature such as these. « Now that they might not suffer this — those who understand nothing higher than visible goods, » that is, that those might not think this who do not suppose there to be other goods higher, or better, than these visible goods; therefore « the restorative wisdom of the holy theologians wondrously descended to unseemly likenesses, » that is, therefore the holy theologians, who by their wisdom — which restores and reforms us unto the knowledge of truth — handed down to us the divine discourses, by a wondrous consideration descended to the taking up of unseemly likenesses, that they might fit them to the divine and celestial natures; and through these they might show that the other things too, which seem to be said of them magnificently and becomingly, are to be referred to likeness, and not to 979Bproperty. This, then, the wisdom of the holy theologians did, « not granting that our material part, remaining in base images, should rest; but purging, bearing upward the powers of the soul, and suggesting by the deformity of the compositions that these are approved by neither the just nor the true; and that the super-celestial and divine spectacles are not, according to truth, so very like to things material and thus base. » As if he were saying: The wisdom of the theologians, descending to unseemly likenesses, in this very thing wondrously provided for our restoration, not granting that our material part — that is, our carnal sense, which cleaves to material things — should rest; the material part, I say, which remains in base images, that is, which so far as in it lies wills to remain, so that it may think only these things, 979Cand accept only these as though true, if it were permitted to rest in them, and were not compelled by the very baseness of the images to go out to seek other things beautiful and true; or, not granting that our material part should rest, remaining in base images — that is, not granting that it either rest or remain, but by the very baseness of the images expelling it, and advancing it to higher things; but purging, bearing upward, namely, the power of the soul, that is, the intellectual force of the soul, which bears it upward and strains toward higher things; purging it from the admixture of images, that it may grow accustomed to contemplate spiritual and invisible things purely and simply; and suggesting, that is, admonishing and persuading the soul from the very deformity of the compositions, 979Dthat the super-celestial and divine spectacles are not, according to truth, very like to material things — especially to things so base — as neither the just nor the true approves, namely that those are like to these; or, suggesting by the deformity of the compositions that it is approved by neither the just nor the true — understand, in that manner, in the property of spiritual and invisible natures, as it is shown in the appearance and image of visible things; and suggesting also, that the super-celestial and divine spectacles are not very — that is, not much — like, according to their own truth, to material things thus base.

There follows: « But so too this must be understood: that none of the things which are is universally deprived of the participation of the good. For indeed, as the truth of the discourses 980Asays, all things are very good. » Above he demonstrated that dissimilar representations are for this reason fittingly brought forward for the manifestation of divine things: that from those which evidently appear dissimilar, those too which seemed similar may be recognized to be outside the property of the thing. But now he demonstrates that for this reason also dissimilarities are not unfittingly taken up; because those too which seem to be dissimilar from the truth of divine and spiritual things have something in common with them, in which they can be called similar, since there is nothing in the universe which does not draw participation from the highest good; and through this — in that it participates with it — it fittingly represents its image and likeness. And so it behooves us not only to consider the former cause, but 980Balso to understand this: that none of the things which universally are is deprived of the participation of the good. For « as the truth of the discourses says, » that is, the true discourses say, « all things are very good. » For thus it is written in Genesis: « God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good (Gen. I). » If therefore all things were good, in all things there was the good, and all things participated in the good, and from the good all things had something similar to the good; from which the good itself may be understood and known in them. Whence there follows: « It is possible, then, » that is, it happens, « from all » namely things « to understand good speculations; and to form, » or fit, « to invisible and intellectual things the likenesses called dissimilar; » namely those which above we called dissimilar: « to form, » I say, « from these very 980Cmaterial things, » that is, corporeal and visible ones. Yet in such a way that those things which, according to the likeness of visible things, are attributed to invisible things, be recognized to subsist otherwise in the visible things themselves, and otherwise in the invisible. For this indeed he says: « the intellectual things having them in another manner, » namely those things which are distributed otherwise to sensible things.

There follows: « For indeed anger is present in irrational beings from a passible motion; and their raging motion is full of all irrationality. » Now, certain examples having been set forth, he proves that those things which are referred from the nature of visible things to invisible things subsist otherwise here and otherwise there; as anger, and concupiscence, and the rest, which are referred from visible things to invisible things 980Dby likeness; as if he were saying: Those things which are fitted from visible things to invisible things must be believed to be otherwise in the visible things themselves, and otherwise in the invisible; as can be plainly understood in the things which follow. For « anger » « in irrational beings, » that is, in those proceeding and acting irrationally — whether they have no reason, or, having reason, do not proceed according to reason. In these, indeed, anger is present from a passible motion, that is, one impetuous and fervent, and born according to a dominating passion; and their raging motion is full of all irrationality. For that motion is named anger which, seething wholly outside reason, is borne by the impulse of passion alone. « But in intellectual beings the irascible must be understood in another manner; » 981Ain this manner, namely, that the irascible itself be understood in them as declaring their manly rationality, and their vast quiet in the divine and immutable foundations. For when anger is named in the spiritual and celestial nature, it is not an impulse or a motion that is named, but quiet and immutability that is understood. By this reasoning — these things being considered among the dissimilar and contrary: that just as in these beings anger strives by impulse and vehemence to drive off a supervening annoyance, so there an immovable quiet, persisting, is disturbed by no supervening shock — for this reason he calls that quiet itself "vast," that is, strong, and robust, and imperturbable; repelling every motion without motion, and suppressing every violence without shock and disturbance of itself; which quiet, however, 981Bis not from themselves, but from the divine and immutable foundations to which they cleave, that is, from divine love and contemplation, by which they are made firm unto eternity, that they can in no way henceforth be moved. But this quiet, since it is not of necessity — as though they were held unwilling — but of will — as though, loving indefatigably, they are not forsaken — therefore he joined manly rationality to the quiet, showing that through illuminating reason they manfully reject the evils which they discern, and through affecting love they are at rest in the goods which they perceive, so that the quiet may be fortified by reason, lest it take on an affection for evils; and reason may be guarded by the quiet, lest, setting itself in opposition in hatred of evil, it overstep the bounds of tranquillity. This manly reason, then, and vast quiet, free and 981Cabsolute, and receiving no perturbation, is what anger — when fitted to divine things — signifies; because, as we have said, just as here anger repels an assailing annoyance through madness, so there a rational and voluntary quiet receives no shock, through its immutability.

There follows: « In the same manner we say that concupiscence in irrational beings is a certain ill-considered and material passibility, engendered incontinently from a natural motion or from custom in mutable things, and an irrational continuity of bodily pleasure; at once compelling every animal toward the concupiscible according to sense. » After he demonstrated what anger signifies when attributed to sensible and material 981Dthings, and likewise what it signifies when fitted to immaterial and invisible natures, now he consequently shows the difference of concupiscence — whether when it is said of corporeal things, or when it is named in spiritual and divine things. Defining the concupiscence of corporeal beings, indeed, to be a certain passibility, or passion, that is, a dominating affection — ill-considered indeed, because it is not borne by reason, but is drawn by rash appetite into those things by whose delight it is affected; and material, that is, rising from the flesh and from the carnal sense, and showing forth things carnal and sensible — a passibility, I say, engendered either from a natural motion, namely when its appetite is according to nature; or from custom incontinently held in those mutable things, when its desire is borne outside nature, 982Aor against it: and an irrational continuity of bodily pleasure; understand, we say that concupiscence itself is an irrational continuity, that is, a prolongation, or straining, or effusion of bodily pleasure — that is, of pleasure rising from the body, and tending toward corporeal things, and even compelling every animal, namely by the violence of its appetite, toward that which is concupiscible according to sense. And such indeed we understand the concupiscence of corporeal things to be. « But when, placing dissimilar likenesses about the intellectual and spiritual things, » or clothing them: « being formed about them, » that is, we adapt « to them concupiscence; » then we must understand that concupiscence itself not such as before, but rather divine love, 982Band a desire of immateriality, or incorporeality, and of divinity, existing above reason and intellect; since it can be loved more than investigated or understood; and inflexible, since it is always toward the one; and not needy, since what is loved is present. A desire, I say, of contemplation superessentially chaste and impassible — that is, of that thing which they contemplate superessentially, passing over in mind, namely, every essence and nature — the love of which thing is both chaste, since it brings no corruption upon the lover, and impassible, since, sweetly refreshing the one who desires, it does not afflict him. « And it must also be understood that concupiscence itself is a desire, tending toward that pure and most sublime brightness; and toward the invisible 982Cand form-making beauty of the eternal, true, and invisible fellowship » — which beauty, namely, is called form-making, because it conforms to itself those turned toward it, that they may become beautiful, loving the true beauty, not as in the flesh and according to the flesh, where a lover of beauty can be base, and a possessor of beauty be found not good; but there he who loves, possesses; and he who loves to have, begins to be it. Such a love, then, and such a desire, we must understand in the concupiscence of spiritual and divine things.

There follows: « And it receives, as it were, a power in its sufficiency and in its convertibility; and is afflicted by none; by virtue, through the unconfused and immutable love of divine 982Dbeauty, and the universal recalling unto that which is truly to be desired. » As if he were saying: Concupiscence itself, or the chaste desire of eternal and invisible goods, because it is inflexible, as was said, and not needy, therefore has received, or receives, in its sufficiency and its convertibility toward God and toward divine things, as it were a certain power, or excellence and firmness, so that it cannot at all be afflicted by any contrary power, or violence, or strength. For no one can be hurt or afflicted, except in that which he loves; and therefore he who loves that alone which cannot be taken away can in no way be hurt, because he neither desires anything else outside it, having his sufficiency in it, nor is he anxious about its loss, holding it immutably. Because, then, 983Ait is sufficient, it suffers no need; and because it is inflexible, it can undergo no violence. And this indeed is conferred on it through the unconfused and immutable love of divine beauty, and the universal recalling unto that which is truly to be desired. For because in them the love of God is unconfused, or, to say it otherwise, unmingled and pure, therefore their desire is not split toward diverse things. And because it is immutable, it is not bent away from the same object. And because they are universally recalled and gathered together unto that which is truly to be desired, it is disturbed by no exterior violence. For if with their whole desire they were not recalled to loving the truth, nor gathered together, without doubt they could be hurt and afflicted, wherever they cleaved in mind to mutable and transitory things. But now, because they are wholly there where all things 983Bimmutably stand fast, it comes about that they too, through the cohesion of love, cannot feel the mutability of affliction.

There follows: « But irrationality itself too, and insensibility, in irrational animals or in animated matters, we properly call a defect of reason and sense; but in immaterial and intellectual essences we confess, holily and becomingly, their supereminences as of super-mundane beings, surpassing our transitory and corporeal and material reason, and the mind's sense that is estranged from incorporeal things. » Other examples being set forth, he shows that the same things which are said of visible and invisible things are not said similarly, nor in the same manner. As if he were saying: Not only anger and concupiscence must be understood otherwise 983Chere and otherwise there. For irrationality, which signifies the loftiness of reason; and insensibility, which demonstrates the excess of sensibility, when they are named here, that is, in irrational things and things not having sense, show a defect of reason and sensibility; but when they are said there, that is, in divine and intellectual natures, something above reason and sense is signified — not by defect, but by advance. For an excess of reason and sensibility happens either upward or downward: namely when something, either falling short of reason and sense, sinks down, so that it has not this; or, advancing beyond, transcends it, so that it has more. Whence also in Holy Scripture we find that holy men, breathed upon by the Spirit of God, at times suffered ecstasy, that is, an excess of mind 983D; since, led above human reason and sense, they went beyond reason and sense in this: that, reaching to that which was higher than reason, they began to be vivified in it and illumined by it. For them, then, the excess was in that they received more, just as for these others the excess came about in that they lost that very thing. Therefore, then, irrationality and insensibility in irrational animals and in inanimate matters we properly call a defect of reason and sense; but in immaterial and intellectual essences, as often as we name irrationality and insensibility, we confess not a defect of them, but rather their supereminences, inasmuch as they are super-mundane. We confess, I say, holily and becomingly, 984Athat is, attributing nothing to them irreverently or unbecomingly; but, as befits the supereminences or excellences of super-mundane beings, that is, of spiritual essences, which surpass our transitory and corporeal reason — that is, a reason which can neither ascend above transitory things, nor comprehend anything at all outside corporeal things; and surpassing the material sense of our mind, estranged among corporeal things — that is, a sense flourishing only toward material things, and, through material and corporeal things, estranged from immaterial and incorporeal things, unable to perceive the same. Because, then, they are established above such reason, above such sense, through the excellence of contemplation, they are rightly reported to be estranged from such reason and sense — so that this very insensibility and irrationality of theirs 984Bbe understood not as stupor or ignorance, but to be something other — both a manly knowledge and a perception of the good; and not to be such as it is with us, or according to us.

There follows: « It is possible, therefore, to form for celestial things forms not discordant, even from the base parts of matter; since matter itself too, possessing its subsistence from the truly good, has, throughout its every material disposition, certain images of intellectual beauty; and it is possible through them to be led back to the immaterial first forms — the likenesses being taken, as was said, dissimilarly, and not similarly for the same things; yet compactly and beautifully, the intellectual and sensible properties being defined. » He subjoins another cause to the former, for which likenesses are fittingly drawn from visible things to invisible ones 984C, even according to those things which seem contrary; namely not only because the things which are said are understood to subsist otherwise here and otherwise there, but for this reason too: because whatever things are here have, according to something, a likeness to those which subsist there, since both these and those are, whatever they are, from the one good; and according to the image which these possess toward that good, they also put forth the figure and likeness of those there. This is what he says: « It is possible, » that is, it happens, « to form for celestial things, » namely for the essences, forms not discordant, even « from the base parts of matter, » that is, of corporeal substance, since matter itself too, namely, possessing its subsistence from the truly good, has certain 984Dimages of intellectual beauty throughout its every material disposition: and through them, namely the images, it is possible for the mind to be led back to those first immaterial forms, that is, to the forms of immaterial and spiritual essences, which are prior to these — because these exist according to those, and these tend toward those, and these exist on account of those. It is possible, I say, to be led back from these — yet to those — the likenesses themselves being taken dissimilarly, so that, namely, the things which are here, and are said of those, be understood to be and subsist otherwise there. And the same properties being not similarly defined. But yet compactly, that is, fittingly, and aptly, and beautifully, that is, becomingly — understand, the same properties being defined, on both sides namely, both intellectual and insensible. He speaks of likeness 985Awhen, through extrinsic forms or figures or qualities, descriptions of invisible things are taken from visible ones; but of property, when the likeness is drawn from the inner nature. Whether, then, likenesses from visible things be set forth to be transferred extrinsically to the nature of invisible things, or properties be taken up intrinsically from those same visible and material things for the demonstration of invisible ones, the comparison and adaptation on both sides must be so tempered, that the likenesses themselves, which seem to be set forth similarly on both sides, be nevertheless taken dissimilarly, and be understood to be otherwise here, otherwise there; and the properties themselves, which seem to be attributed the same to both, be defined otherwise in these, and otherwise in those, and be understood to be different — so that to each may be attributed what is 985Bfitting and apt to it according to its nature.

There follows: « We shall find the mystical theologians wondrously conforming these things not only to the declarations of the celestial dispositions, but sometimes also to the very divine manifestations. » He recalled the same thing above: namely that the mystical theologians — that is, theologians who narrate mystical and secret things — conform and fit these things, that is, these likenesses and properties taken from visible things, not only to the declarations of the celestial dispositions, that is, of the celestial orders, namely of the angelic spirits — that is, they set forth these likenesses and properties of visible things not only to declare or demonstrate the celestial dispositions and angelic orderings; 985Cbut they sometimes bring them also to the very divine manifestations, that is, to manifesting and indicating the divinity itself. « And sometimes indeed they praise it » namely the divinity, « from precious lights, » by comparing it to precious lights, and by demonstrating its praise through that thing which, among the other visible things, is precious and comely, as, for example, when they call it the sun — not this visible one, which illumines even the bodily eyes for perpetrating iniquity; but the sun of justice, which enlightens the spiritual eyes for knowing truth and virtue. And as when they call it the « morning star, » whose rising puts darkness to flight — not rising to illumine this world visibly, 985Dbut rising into the rational mind, which alone can receive this light, holily, that is, for making sanctification. And as also when they call it « light shining without being wrapped about, and invisibly; » not as this visible light, which can be both darkened by shadows, and wrapped about, and enclosed in place, and constrained by a bound. If, then, mystical theology praises the excellence of the divine majesty through the appearances and forms of the highest and most precious things. « But sometimes from the middle things, » understand, which in the order of creation are neither highest nor lowest, that theology praises the divine majesty, namely by calling it fire; not such as this corporeal fire is, which, though it profit by illumining, harms by burning and consuming; but « fire harmlessly shining; » 986Anamely illumining, and not burning up; kindling, and not consuming. And as when it calls it « water, giver of vital fullness; » which gives, namely, the fullness of life, and fills with life those who draw and carry it; and water also, « that it be so said symbolically, » that is, figuratively, « entering into the belly; and overflowing with rivers immeasurably flowing back. » For all these things are said of it not in property, but in figure alone. In all these things mystical theology praises the majesty and goodness of the divinity. « But sometimes also from the lowest things » — as from the inferior and earthly ones — it praises it, and manifests its praise figuratively, as when it names it « sweet ointment, » and likewise when it calls it « corner 986Bstone. » And to such a degree does it fit the appearances of lowly things to it by likeness, that sometimes it seems even to descend, in describing it, to unfitting and contrary forms. Which nevertheless, according to the cause mentioned above, is carried through by a fitting and necessary dispensation. « But they even set a bestial form about it. » As if he were saying: Not only in the declaration of the divinity do the theologians take up likenesses from inferior things, but (what seems marvelous!) they even descend to contrary and dissimilar formations — ones which, if they were understood according to property, would be wholly unworthy of its majesty. « For they even set a bestial form about it; and to it the particularity of a lion and of a panther, » that is, the appearance, or form, or figure, « they fit; 986Cand they clothe it, » namely the divinity: « with a leopard-like form, » understand form, that is, the form of a leopard. « And they clothe it, » understand again the divinity; a raging she-bear, that is, with the appearance of a raging she-bear; or they call it « a raging she-bear, » so that in both the incongruity may appear, since they attribute even deformity to the beautiful, and cruelty to the mild.

There follows: « But I will add also that which has seemed to be, of all things, among the base, and to signify more. » As if he were saying: Although in the preceding things which have been mentioned, and in the rest of this kind, a great unworthiness may seem to appear, nevertheless in this which I subjoin a much greater affront appears. « But I will add, » I will indeed presume, and I shall seem to speak boldly, 986DI who add this too to the divine significations, « what has seemed to be the basest of all; » and through this, according to the aforesaid reasoning by which dissimilar symbols make the declaration greater, it is proved to signify more than the rest. Which nevertheless perhaps a man would not dare to fit to the divine majesty, if the wisdom of God itself did not take these things to itself by spontaneous condescension. « For those wise in divine things have handed it down as forming itself even under the appearance of a worm. » As it is written: « I am a worm, and no man; the reproach of men, and the outcast of the people (Psal. XXI). » For unless it had first said this of itself, who would dare to say this of it? For since nothing seems to be baser and lowlier than a worm, who would presume to bring the highest majesty down to this abasement, 987Aunless it had first, by its own dispensation, formed itself about with such an appearance, signifying itself thereby. Therefore it deigned first to say this of itself, because it knew that human conscience would not, of itself, dare this against its own Creator. « Thus all the theosophists, and the prophets by hidden inspiration, distinguish the Holy of Holies from the undefiled holy things. » Theosophists, that is, those wise in divine things and who have been made prophets by hidden inspiration. All these, when they wish to designate invisible things through visible appearances and the properties of visible things, distinguish, as we demonstrated above, « the Holy of Holies from the undefiled holy things. » The undefiled holy things are the symbols of divine things taken from beautiful and becoming forms; the Holy of Holies are the divine things themselves, which 987Bare figured through these. The theosophists, then, by the fact that they attribute dissimilar figures to divine things, also separate the similar formations — even those which seemed worthy — from the excellence and majesty of those divine things. For because they fit even those figures which are not doubted to be foreign to the signification of them, they show that the others too, which could seem true, are not, according to property, similar. Thus, then, in one and the same thing, both in the similar figures they separate the figure from the truth, and in the dissimilar ones, by the fellowship of truth, they honor the figure of truth — since those figures, when they are shown to be foreign, are distinguished, and these, when they are fitted to likeness, are honored. For thus it was fitting that all that was made, compared to the excellence of the Creator, should be shown both in sublime things not 987Cto be equal, and in the lowest things not to be dissimilar. For because it was made, it cannot be comparable unto equality; and because it was made by him, it cannot be wholly dissimilar to him by whom it was made.

There follows: « So that neither may divine things be rightly received by the unclean, nor may the zealous of the contemplation of marvelous images remain in the figures as though they were true. » This, then, is effected through dissimilar figurations: that in the consideration of them the unclean of heart, and those unworthy of the knowledge of truth, may be the more blinded; and those who are zealous, in the contemplation of marvelous images — that is, of sacred representations marvelously made — may be the more exercised.
