For thus on both sides 987Da just design is accomplished: that while the truth, in its manifestation, covers itself as with a base garment, it both provokes the unworthy to contempt of it, and invites the worthy to desire and to seek that appearance of its own which lies hidden, so that they be not content with what they look upon outwardly, but, repelled by the very deformity of the exterior demonstration, do not remain in the figures as though they were true — since a sign cannot be the truth, even when it is a sign of the truth.

There follows: « They therefore honor divine things by true negations, and by the diverse likenesses of imaginations compacted unto the lowest things. » As if he were saying: Since negations made concerning divine things signify their truth more expressly, and dissimilar formations of images demonstrate their purity more evidently, 988Atherefore the holy theologians do no affront to the divine things themselves, both by making true negations concerning them, and by attributing dissimilar formations to them, but rather they honor the divine things themselves by true negations, by which they show their excellence to be so great that what they are can in no way be expressed, even if in some way what they are not can be said; and they honor them also by likenesses diverse from their sublimity through a humble formation; and by the likenesses of imaginations compacted unto the lowest things — that is, composed and joined together out of the lowest things, that is, out of the basest and vile appearances of corruptible things.

There follows: « Nothing therefore is inconsequent, if they also form the celestial essences from unfitting, dissimilar 988Blikenesses, according to the causes stated. » As if he says: Since divine things are honored by true negations and by diverse formations, nothing is inconsequent — that is, unfitting — if the theologians form, that is, represent, the celestial essences from dissimilar and unfitting likenesses; that is, through representations of figures dissimilar from their nature, and in a certain way unfitting. It is not inconsequent, I say, according to the causes stated above.

There follows: « For perhaps indeed we would not, from need, come into inquiry, and into anagogy through a diligent scrutiny of divine things, unless the deformity of the manifesting formation of angels wrested us thereto. » As if he were saying: From our need 988Cinto this inquiry — that is, to seeking these things as regards the composition of visible images — or into anagogy as regards the investigation of invisible truth; from our need, I say — we who, knowing the truth, do not need these inquiries — into this inquiry, I say, we would not come, unless (on account of others who might be scandalized thereby, if they were not instructed) the deformity wrested us to it. First, note the doubling of the negation, by which the expression is made: or in this it is manifest that deformed formations are useful in divine things, because we too would not scrutinize the truth of divine things so diligently, unless the deformity of the manifestations wrested us, that is, compelled us. This is what he says: « Perhaps we would not indeed 988Dcome into an inquiry leading into anagogy, » that is, the contemplation of things above; from need, namely, of the understanding of truth: we would not come, I say, through a diligent scrutiny of divine things, « unless it wrested us, » that is, compelled us « to come into inquiry from need, and through inquiry into anagogy, » — the very deformity of the manifesting deformation of the angels, that is, unless the deformity of the formation through which the angels are manifested in Holy Scripture should compel us; I say: « Not allowing our mind to remain in the dissimilar makings of forms, » that is, in the deformed compositions of representations, which are dissimilar from the truth of spiritual things. Unless, then, the very deformity of the representations should compel our mind from the visible figures to 989Aseek the truth, our mind itself would remain in those things which are set forth outwardly, as things only to be believed and venerated, and would not recognize its own need, so as to think that other things, beyond these, were to be desired and sought by it. But now the very deformity, intervening, compels the mind to go forth from the figure to the truth — the mind, I say, unable to remain in those things which are in themselves unworthy, and incongruous with the truth of divine things. « But the mind struggling to deny » of the divine things themselves those « material possibilities » which are set forth outwardly in signs; and through the fact that it thus holily abhors them, « growing accustomed purely to extend itself through visible things, » roused « into the super-mundane heights »: that is, the angelic excellences, which are supereminent over and excel all worldly things. For unless, roused from these 989Bby the advancement of contemplation, it should wholly leave these very things behind, it would not be able purely to behold those things which it strives to contemplate.

There follows: « So many things indeed have been said by us, » etc. He himself connects the preceding matters to the following narration. « So many things indeed, » as many as we have said thus far, « have been said by us on account of the angelic descriptions of images, » that is, on account of the descriptions of angels, which are made through images and visible forms, and forms taken from visible things — which descriptions are « of the divine discourses, » that is, made through the divine discourses, and set forth in the divine discourses, which descriptions are also material, that is, formed according to the nature and likeness of material and corporeal things; and they are also unfitting 989Con account of the incongruous and base figurations of those things to which excellences have been attributed. For on account of such a thing the inquiry which has been ventilated thus far was set forth. « But next it behooves us to set apart what we consider the hierarchy itself to be, and what benefit those who obtain the hierarchy receive from the hierarchy itself. It behooves us, he says, next, » that is, after the aforesaid, to set apart, that is, to distinguish what we consider the hierarchy itself, taken generally, to be, its definition being set forth. « Next » also « it behooves us to set apart what benefit they receive, » that is, what of usefulness those who obtain the hierarchy receive from the hierarchy itself, namely, which each one obtains. And in saying this, he says, I pray that « my Christ » may be the « leader » of my discourse 989D; yet only if it is lawful for me, that is, permitted, to say « my. » For this is a great thing, and seems as it were close to presumption, that a sinner should receive the reward of the just, and one cast down should be confident of the familiarity of the Most High. Therefore I say 990Alet « Christ » (and if I dare more, I say « my ») be the leader of my discourse. Without whom neither can discourse be right, because he is the Word; nor understanding be true, because he is Wisdom. For all who savor the true, savor through him; and he himself is the inspiration « of every hierarchical manifestation, » since he himself, being Wisdom breathed into the minds of the holy theologians, manifests the whole account of the hierarchical disposition — whether that which is in heaven, or that which is on earth — to those to whom he wills, in the ways he wills. « But you, O boy, » etc. He speaks to Timothy, the disciple of Paul, to whom he is said to have written these things — whom he also calls a boy for this reason: either because he preceded him in age, or because he held toward him the place and dignity of a teacher and master. « But you, O boy, hearken. » As if he says: 990BBecause the things which are to be said are great, therefore hearken holily and becomingly, as befits the very holy things which are to be said. « Hearken, » I say; according to the holy legislation of our priestly tradition, which bids us not to contend, nor to resist in doctrine, but reverently and humbly to hearken. Or hearken to these things which have been said « according to the holy legislation of our priestly tradition, » that is, which have been said according to the holy law, that is, the Holy Scripture, which has been brought to us by God through the priestly tradition, that is, through the tradition of the holy and the sanctified. Thus, then, « hearken to the wondrously said things, » that is, those things which have been wondrously said: « you, » I say, who have been made divine in the divine doctrine, which makes those who hear and do it divine; 990Cor, having been made divine in the divine doctrine of the wondrously said things, hearken to the things I propose to be said. And not only hearken, so as to receive the things said reverently, but also « in the secret of your mind covering about the things which are holy, keeping them from the unclean multitude, » that is, from those who are both unclean in conduct and divided in desires: « as uniform things, » that is, undivided and untouched, « guard them, » lest you imprudently expose them to be torn and defiled. « For it is not lawful, as the discourses say, to cast to swine the unconfused, and light-formed, and beneficent adornment of the invisible pearls. » For those are that unclean multitude who are signified by swine in Holy Scripture, who defile the Word of God by living wickedly, and defile the invisible pearls, that 990Dis, the spiritual understandings — which adorn the understandings with morals, shine through pure truth, are unconfused through the affluence of grace, and are beneficent toward those who touch them with reverence and honor.

LIBER QUARTUS.

  • 989

BOOK FOUR.

  • 989

TITULUS CAPITULI III. Quid est hierarchia et quae per hierarchiam utilitas.

TITLE OF CHAPTER III. What the hierarchy is, and what the benefit is through the hierarchy.

LITTERA.

  • 989D

Est quidem hierarchia, secundum me, ordo divinus, et scientia, et actio deiforme quantum possibile similans, 990Det ad inditas ei divinitus illuminationes proportionaliter in Dei similitudinem ascendens. Divina pulchritudo ut simpla, et optima ut consummativa. Pura 991Aquidem est universaliter omnium dissimilitudine, distributiva vero secundum dignitatem uniuscujusque proprii luminis: et perfectiva in sacrificio divinissimo secundum ad ipsam perfectorum compacte immutabilem formationem. Interpretatio igitur hierarchiae est ad Deum, quantum possibile est similitudo, et unitas, ipsum habens omnis sanctae actionis, et scientiae ducem; et ad suum divinissimum decorem immutabiliter quidem definiens: quantum vero possibile reformat, et suos laudatores agalmata divina perficit specula clarissima, et munda receptiva principalis luminis, et divini radii, et inditae quidem claritatis sacrae repleta: eamque iterum copiose in ea, quae sequuntur declarantia divinas leges. Non enim fas est sanctorum perfectoribus ac sancte perfectis; operari quod omnino 991Bpraeter hostiarum + mysteria, aut sacras ordinationes; sed neque subsistere aliter si divinam ipsius claritatem appetunt; et ad ipsam sacre et decenter respiciunt, et reformantur, secundum uniuscujusque sanctorum intellectuum anagogiam. Nonne ergo hierarchiam qui dicit, sacram quamdam universaliter declarat dispositionem, imaginem divinae speciositatis in ordinibus, et scientiis hierarchicis propriae illuminationis sacrificantem mysteria, et ad proprium principium, ut licet, assimilatam? Est enim unicuique hierarchiam sortientium perfectio; hoc est secundum propriam analogiam in Dei imitationem ascendere, et omnium divinius, ut eloquia aiunt, Dei cooperatorem fieri (I Cor. III; III Joan. I; Matth. V), et ostendere divinam in seipso actionem, secundum 991Cquod possibile est, relucentem. Utpote quoniam ordo hierarchiae est quosdam quidem purgari, quosdam vero purgare; et quosdam quidem illuminari quosdam vero illuminare; et quosdam quidem perfici, quosdam vero perficere; unicuique deiforme adunationi qualicunque modo. Divina beatitudo, quantum in hominibus dicendum, pura quidem est sine omni dissimilitudine, plena vero luminis aeterni, perfecta et non indigens, simul omnis perfectionis; purgans, et illuminans, et perficiens; magna autem purgatio, sancta et illuminatio, et perfectio, super purgationem, super lumen, ante perfecta; per seipsam perfecta perfectionis principium; et omnis quidem hierarchiae causa, omnisque sacri secundum supereminentem celsitudinem. 991DOportet itaque, ut existimo, purgandos quidem puro perfici omnino, et omni liberari dissimilitudinis confusione. Illuminandos vero repleri divino lumine ad contemplativam habitudinem et virtutem in castissimis mentis oculis reducendos. Ex imperfecto restaurando participes fieri exploratorum sacrorum perfectivae scientiae. Purgatores vero magnitudine purgationis aliis tradere ex propria castitate. Illuminatores autem luculentiores animos, et ad participationem luminis, et distributionem proprie habentes, et ditissime sanctae repleti charitatis, omnino suum superexcellens lumen in eos qui digni sunt lumine, supervehere. Perfectores vero tanquam praeceptores perfectivae traditionis perficiendos sacratissima doctrina per inspectorum sacrorum scientiam. Nonne ergo 992Aunusquisque hierarchia dispositionis ordo secundum propriam analogiam reducitur ad divinam cooperationem, illa perficiens gratia, et Deo data virtute, quae divinitati naturaliter, et supernaturaliter insunt, et ab ea superessentialiter acta, et ad possibilem Deum diligentium animorum imitationem hierarchiae manifestata.

THE TEXT.

  • 989D

The hierarchy is, according to me, a divine order, and a knowledge, and an activity assimilating itself, as far as possible, to the deiform, 990Dand, proportionally to the illuminations divinely implanted in it, ascending into the likeness of God. The divine beauty, as simple, and best, as consummative. It is pure 991Aindeed, universally, from all dissimilarity; distributive according to the worth of each one's proper light; and perfective, in the most divine sacrifice, according to the compactly immutable formation of those perfected unto it. The interpretation, therefore, of the hierarchy is, unto God, as far as is possible, a likeness and unity, having Him as the leader of every holy action and knowledge; and unto its own most divine comeliness immutably defining them; but, as far as possible, it reforms, and perfects its own praisers as divine statues, mirrors most clear, and pure, receptive of the principal light and of the divine ray, and filled indeed with the implanted sacred brightness: and pouring it out again copiously into the things which follow, declaring the divine laws. For it is not lawful for the perfecters of the holy, and for the holily perfected, to do anything at all 991Bapart from the + mysteries of the sacrificial victims, or the sacred ordinations; but neither to subsist otherwise, if they seek His divine brightness; and they look unto it holily and becomingly, and are reformed, according to the anagogy of each of the holy intellects. Does not, therefore, he who says "hierarchy" declare universally a certain sacred disposition, an image of the divine beauty, in the hierarchical orders and knowledges celebrating the mysteries of its own illumination, and assimilated to its own principle, as is permitted? For to each of those who obtain the hierarchy this is the perfection: to ascend, according to one's own analogy, into the imitation of God, and — most divine of all, as the discourses say — to become a fellow-worker of God (I Cor. III; III Joan. I; Matth. V), and to show forth the divine action shining again in oneself, according 991Cas is possible. Inasmuch as the order of the hierarchy is that some be purged, but some purge; and some be illumined, but some illumine; and some be perfected, but some perfect; for each in a deiform union, in whatever manner. The divine blessedness — as far as it is to be spoken of among men — is indeed pure, without any dissimilarity; full of eternal light; perfect and not needy, at once of all perfection; purging, and illumining, and perfecting; but a great purgation, and holy illumination, and perfection, above purgation, above light, perfect beforehand; through itself perfect, the principle of perfection; and the cause indeed of every hierarchy, and of everything sacred, according to its supereminent loftiness. 991DIt behooves, therefore, as I consider, that those to be purged be wholly perfected by the pure, and be freed from all confusion of dissimilarity. But that those to be illumined be filled with divine light, and be led back unto a contemplative habit and power in the most chaste eyes of the mind. That from the imperfect, being restored, they become partakers of the perfective knowledge of the sacred things searched out. But that the purgers, by the greatness of purgation, impart to others out of their own chastity. But that the illuminators — having more luminous minds, and being properly suited both for the participation of light and for its distribution, and most richly filled with holy charity — convey their own super-excellent light entirely upon those who are worthy of light. But that the perfecters, as teachers of the perfective tradition, perfect those to be perfected by a most sacred doctrine, through the knowledge of the sacred things beheld. Is not, therefore, 992Aeach order of the hierarchy's disposition led back, according to its own analogy, to divine cooperation — accomplishing those things by grace and by the power given by God, which are present in the divinity naturally and supernaturally, and, by it superessentially enacted, are manifested unto the imitation of the hierarchy, as far as is possible, by minds loving God.

EXPOSITIO.

Hactenus quae universaliter dicenda erant introducendis in hierarchiarum cognitionem pro ratione demonstrationum visibilium in significationem visibilium propositarum theologus disseruit. Deinde nunc principalem narrationem ingrediens primum definit quid sit hierarchia; non universaliter tamen, sed secundum eam tantum, quae in angelis et 992Bhominibus constat hierarchiam, significatione restricta. « Est quidem, » inquit, « hierarchia, secundum me, ordo divinus, et scientia, et actio, deiforme, quantum possibile similans; et ad inditas ei divinitus illuminationes proportionaliter in Dei similitudinem ascendens. » Quod ait, « secundum me, » ita accipiendum, ac si dixisset, secundum existimationem meam. Pudice enim temperat assertionem suam, ne de sua existimatione plus justo praesumere videatur. Deinde tria in definitione hierarchiae principalia proponit, quae perficiunt ipsam hierarchiae definitionem. Sunt autem haec: ordo, scientia et actio. Horum trium si defuerit omnium aliquod, non constat hierarchia. Primum est ordo divinus; quia non est potestas, si ordinata non est 992Ca Deo; propter hoc ait, ordo divinus. « Omnis » enim « potestas a Deo est; et quae a Deo sunt, omnia bona et ordinata sunt; propterea qui potestati resistit a Deo ordinatae, Deo resistit (Rom. XIII). » Propter hoc ergo hierarchia est ordo divinus, id est potestas a Deo ordinata, et secundum Deum disposita. A Deo quippe est per ordinationem; et secundum Deum est per imitationem; et propterea ordo divinus, quia a Deo est, ut sit; et secundum Deum est, ut qualis et quantus sit. Deinde quia omnis potestas, quae a Deo ordinata est, ad aliquid perficiendum, atque complendum ordinata est; sequitur in definitione post ordinem « scientia et actio. » Scientia quidem, qua quid faciendum sit intelligant; 992Dactio vero, qua quod intellexerint agendum, perficiant. In ordine officium; in scientia discretio; in actione ministerium. Sine ordine praesumptio est actio, sine actione negligentia est ordo, sine scientia vero et actio reprehensibilis et ordo inutilis. Propter haec ergo hierarchia est ordo divinus, et scientia, et actio. Hierarchia dico tam in ordine quam scientia et actione, similans deiforme, hoc est conformitatem Dei imitans quantum possibile scilicet illi est; et ascendens in Dei similitudinem proportionaliter ad illuminationes, id est secundum illuminationes divinitus ei inditas: unaquaeque scilicet secundum modum et mensuram gratiae divinitus ei infusae in ordine suo perficiens, et ascendens ad imitationem Dei, ut recte discernendo et bene operando 993Aipsum imitetur. In utroque enim divinam similitudinem aemulatur omnis hierarchia, sive in eo videlicet quod ab ipso disponitur sive in eo quod secundum ipsum operatur. Haec autem definitio, sicut diximus, angelicam tantum et humanam hierarchiam complectitur, quae ad similitudinem summae et aeternae factae sunt hierarchiae: et ipsam imitantur secundum ipsam dispositae.

Sequitur: « Divina pulchritudo ut simpla, et optima ut consummativa; pura quidem est universaliter omni dissimilitudine; distributiva vero secundum dignitatem uniuscujusque proprii luminis; et perfectiva in sacrificio divinissimo secundum ad ipsam perfectorum compacte immutabilem formationem. » Sensus hic est. Quod divina pulchritudo, 993Bquam summam nominamus hierarchiam, secundum quam caeterae factae sunt hierarchiae, pura est universaliter, id est omnino, utpote quae semper simpla quidem est unitate, optima bonitate, consummativa perfectione. Ubi enim unitas est, diversitas non est; et ubi diversitas non est, dissimilitudo nulla esse potest. Item ubi perfectio est, ibi gradus non est; ubi gradus non est, differentia non est; ubi differentia non est, dissimilitudo nulla est. Ergo divina pulchritudo, quae forma et exemplar est bene, et pulchre dispositorum omnium; quia una est, pluralitatem non recipit; et quia optima est, et consummata, nec solum consummata, sed etiam consummandorum omnium consummativa, et consummationis causa, diversitatem non admittit, ac per 993Choc omnino dissimilitudinem nescit; quae et una est simplicitate et eadem perfectione. Et cum in semetipsa talis sit, ut nec dividatur pluralitate, nec inferior sit diversitate; in ipsis tamen qui participes fiunt gratiae, distributiva est proprii luminis, proprium lumen diversis modis tribuens; secundum dignitatem, videlicet uniuscujusque participantium; altioribus quidem majora, inferioribus autem minora largiendo dona gratiarum, ut in ipsis pulchre multiplicetur, quae in se vere una consistit. Perfectiva est et ipsa divina pulchritudo, quoniam perficit, et consummatos facit participes luminum suorum; perfectiva dico in sacrificio divinissimo, quo perficit perficiendos secundum immutabilem formationem compacte perfectorum ad ipsam. Divinissimum 993Dsacrificium vocat ipsam illuminationem divinam, et gratiam, et propitiationem; quo purgantur, et emundantur purgandi omnes, et salvandi, non solum a corruptione mali, ut boni fiant; sed a defectu quoque boni purgantur, ut meliores assistant. Ipsa ergo oblatio summa, et teletargis, id est principalis purgationis hostia; ipsa videlicet gratia divina quae nobis offertur et pro nobis offertur. Offertur nobis ad purgationem, offertur pro nobis ad propitiationem. Offertur nobis, ut eam habeamus; offertur pro nobis, ut per eam placeamus. Offertur nobis per infusionem, offertur pro nobis per emundationem. Offertur nobis dum incipimus esse quod non fuimus; offertur a nobis, dum exhibemus et praesentamus 994Aquod sumus. Ipsa ergo teletargis, id est principalis purgationis hostia, et sacrificium divinissimum, sine quo omnes hostiae et sacrificia omnia nec affectum habere possunt, nec prodesse; ipsum est, quo divina pulchritudo perficit, et perfectos facit eos, qui perfecti sunt, ad ipsam, id est ad similitudinem ipsius reformati, id est concorditer, ut ab ea videlicet non discrepent secundum immutabilem formationem ipsorum scilicet perfectorum, ad ipsam, id est secundum similitudinem ejus, quam semel acceptam immutabiliter servant, ut non defluant ab ipsa. Divina enim pulchritudo quae in se una est, et perfecta perficiendos ad se per principalis purgationis hostiam id est infusionem gratiae suae, quam a sua plenitudine propter purgandos, et 994Bperficiendos in participatione diffudit, purgat et perficit, secundum uniuscujusque modum, et mensuram, et capacitatem, quam dono ejusdem gratiae perceperunt secundum immutabilem formationem illorum ad ipsam; quae videlicet formatio vel ideo immutabilis, sicut diximus, vocatur, quod ipsos, quod formantur et reformantur ad immutabilitatem convertat; vel quia immutabilis consistit in eo, a quo est, etiam si mutetur iis quibus est et in quibus est.

Sequitur: « Interpretatio [ intentio ] igitur hierarchiae est ad Deum, quantum possibile, similitudo et unitas. » Quod in Graeco dicitur σκοπός scopos, et quod translator interpretationem vocat, magis proprie intentio vel directio nominatur. Est enim intentio 994Csive directio, quae scopos dicitur, certa destinatio in aliquem finem. Omnis enim actio in aliquem finem tendit et per aliquam directionem tendit. Scopas autem, id est directio vel destinatio, est qua tendit. Omnis ergo hierarchia scopon habet, id est directionem secundum quam incedat in ministerio suo explendo; imitationem scilicet, et similitudinem divinam, ut quemadmodum ab ipso ordinata est in officio et dignitate, ita secundum ipsum incedat in ministerio et operatione, ut praeter modum, et mensuram ab ipso assignatam et ordini suo debitam, nihil agere praesumat. Est ergo interpretatio, id est definitio, sive potius directio et contemplatio hierarchiae, qua intendere debet et dirigit omnis hierarchia: similitudo, et unitas, hoc est 994Dimitatio et identitas ad Deum, ut in nullo deviet vel declinet ab ipsius similitudine, in qua posita est; sed eum quantum possibile est aemuletur per omnia. Similitudo ad Deum est ipsum imitari; unitas vero solum sequi. Et hic est scopus, id est directio, vel destinatio omnis hierarchiae, ut secundum ipsum ad ipsum incedat, ipsum habens omnis sanctae et scientiae, et actionis ducem, ipsum sequens judicio, et actione illuminata ab ipso ad cognitionem veritatis, et adjuta ad exsecutionem boni operis. « Ipsum habens ducem » intus praesidentem in demonstratione veritatis, et foris praecedentem in exemplo bonae actionis. « Et ad suum divinissimum decorem immutabiliter quidem definiens; 995Aquantum vero possibile, reformat, et suos laudatores agalmata divina perficit. » Ipsa quidem scilicet hierarchia immutabiliter definiens, hoc est invariabiliter sive inflexibiliter conversa, vel intendens per suum scopum ad divinissimum decorem ipsius Dei, imitando, et sequendo ipsum, ut pulchritudini ipsius et decori divinissimo conformetur, secundum quem omnis hierarchia pulchre et decenter in suo ordine et gradu disposita est: quantum possibile est reformat suos laudatores, hoc est eos qui in ipsa Deum laudant, et ad laudem Dei dispositi sunt et ordinati: reformat, dico, in eo ipso quod imitatores Dei facit, et ad similitudinem ipsius in suo ministerio convertit, et convertendo, ac reformando agalmata divina perficit, ut sint ipsi divina 995Bagalmata, id est sancta simulacra et receptacula divinitatis, et specula clarissima; ut sint ipsi agalmata quidem divina, divinum lumen perficiendo, specula autem clarissima lucenda ex suscepto lumine. Perficit etiam ipsos laudatores suos, « munda receptiva, » sive receptacula « principalis luminis, et divini radii » hoc est luminis immediate illuminantis, et ad ipsa prima illuminanda descendentis, ut post susceptum quidem lumen repleta sint claritatis sacrae, inditae sibi, hoc est, infusae: et ut sint etiam declarantia eam, videlicet claritatem, « iterum, » hoc est secundo loco, « in ea, quae sequuntur, declarantia » copiose secundum « divinas leges. » Sensus hic est: Quoniam hierarchia secundum illam dispositionem, qua divinam pulchritudinem 995Cimitatur, laudatores suos universaliter quidem, id est sive superiores, sive inferiores, tales facit ut digni sint, et lumen divinum percipere et lucere ex lumine: specialiter autem quosdam ita mundos perficit ut sint capaces principalis luminis, et immediate illuminentur a Deo, ac deinde ad eos, qui sequuntur post se et dignitate constituti sunt sub se, lumen suum transfundant: copiose quidem ex abundantia perceptionis primae secundam participationem ministrantes, servata duntaxat lege divina, in qua unicuique perscriptum est quid, vel quantum, aut cui ex dono gratiae sibi concesso debeat impertiri. Nam quod non sine divina lege, id est ea dispensatione divina, qua dona gratiae in participes largitionis secundum 995Dcertam mensuram, et proportionem tribuuntur: et assignantur officia, ut sciat unusquisque quantum sibi liceat secundum ministerium assignatum vel fieri liceat, manifestat cum subdit:

« Non enim fas est sanctorum perfectoribus, ac sancte perfectis operari quid omnino praeter propria mysteria hostiarum, ac sacras ordinationes. » Ac si dicat: Propterea ii qui in ordine hierarchiarum superiores sunt secundum divinas leges, lumina sua ad inferiores transfundunt; quia fas non est, hoc est, licitum omnino aliquid operari, aut sanctorum perfectoribus, id est iis qui alios in sanctitate perficiunt, aut sancte perfectis, id est iis qui ab aliis in sanctitate perficiuntur, praeter propria hostiarum mysteria, id est propria gratiarum dona, et proprias 996Asacras ordinationes, id est sacros ordines unicuique proprios assignatos. Nam sine gratia operari, vanum est; praeter ordinem operari aut contra, perversum. Habent namque singuli propria dona, secundum quae valeant operari; et ordines proprios secundum quos debeant operationem suam moderari. Propterea necesse est ut studeat unusquisque gratiam, quam accepit, agnoscere, ne incipiat praesumere in eo quod non potest; et officium proprium, ordinemque attendere, ne audeat transgredi in eo quod non debet. Hunc namque ordinem divinae dispositionis diligenter servandum esse Petrus apostolus admonet, dicens: « Unusquisque sicut accepit gratiam, in alterutrum administrantes » (I Petr. IV). Et Paulus apostolus eos qui hanc divinam ordinationem, 996Bet dispensationem tenere noluerunt, reprehendit, dicens: « Nunquid omnes apostoli? Nunquid omnes prophetae? Nunquid omnes doctores? Nunquid omnes virtutes? Nunquid omnes gratiam curationum habent? Nunquid omnes linguis loquuntur? Nunquid omnes interpretantur? Aemulamini charismata meliora. » (I Cor. XII.) Propterea igitur fas non est iis, qui divinae gratiae participes facti sunt, sive immediate a Deo, sive per hominem eam acceperint, aliquid operari praeter propria dona, et officia, ut divina pulchritudo in omnibus conservetur, et ordo dispensationis summae perseveret. Sanctorum perfectores vocat eos, qui tantam a Deo gratiam perceperunt, ut alios etiam illuminando, et erudiendo ad sanctitatem perficiant. Sancte perfecti sunt, qui 996Cab ipsis superioribus illuminati, et eruditi in sanctitate perficiuntur. Mysteria hostiarum, sive dona gratiarum intelligi vult: quae propterea mysteria dicuntur, quia occulte inspirantur; hostiae autem, quia ad emundationem et expiationem percipientium tribuuntur. Sive ministeria hostiarum exhibitiones sanctorum operum dicit, et administrationes divinorum sacramentorum: quae et hostiae sunt, quia offeruntur per exhibitionem actionis, et mysteria per sacramenta significationis; quia per id, quod foris visibiliter in sacramento agitur, invisibilis virtus veritatis significatur. Ita ergo praeter propria hostiarum mysteria, id est dona, vel ministeria propria, fas non est operari aliquid, vel sanctorum perfectoribus, id est iis qui gratiam acceptam aliis perficiendis 996Dadministrant, vel ipsis perfectis, id est qui per acceptam gratiam, in sanctitatis perfectionem perficiuntur. Neque fas est etiam sive his, sive illis aliquid operari, praeter sacras ordinationes suas, hoc est, praeter id quod ad sacras ordinationes suas spectat, ut videlicet id solum unusquisque operari praesumat, quod ad ordinem, et officium sibi assignatum spectare probatur.

Sequitur: « Sed neque subsistere aliter, si divinam ipsius claritatem appetunt, et ad ipsam sacre, et decenter respiciunt, et reformantur, secundum uniuscujusque sanctorum intellectuum analogiam. » Quasi dicat: Non solum debitum illis est ut sacra mysteria et ordinationes sacras custodiant, sed necessarium 997Aquoque, quoniam aliter subsistere non possunt, in eo videlicet statu, quo divinam pulchritudinem imitantur, nisi ordines suos servando secundum leges divinas incedant. Si ergo appetunt divinam ipsius Creatoris sui claritatem, et ad ipsam percipiendam respiciunt imitando, et desiderando sacre per affectum, decenter per habitum, et reformamur ad ipsius similitudinem imitando ipsam, et sequendo: unusquisque videlicet sanctorum intellectuum, id est angelorum, « secundum uniuscujusque analogiam, » id est secundum modum et mensuram possibilitatis suae, quam habet secundum ordinem, et gradum, et proprietatem suam unusquisque; aliter nullatenus subsistere possunt in eo bono, quod appetunt, nisi secundum leges divinas incedant, 997Bordinationes suas servando, et ministeria propria exsequendo.

Sequitur: « Nonne ergo hierarchiam qui dicit, sacram quamdam universaliter declarat dispositionem, imaginem divinae speciositatis in ordinibus, et scientiis hierarchicis propriae illuminationis sacrificantem mysteria, et ad proprium principium, ut licet, assimilatam? » Quando, inquit, necesse est ut omnis hierarchia divinam appetat similitudinem, neque aliter subsistere potest, nisi in ejus imitatione perseveret. Ergo qui dicit hierarchiam, declarat sacram dispositionem quamdam, quae imago est divinae speciositatis, id est pulchritudinis. Dispositionem, dico sacrificantem mysteria, id est exercentem sive exhibentem mystica opera, vel divina ministeria 997Cpropriae illuminationis, hoc est secundum propriam illuminationem in ordinibus et scientiis hierarchicis, quantum videlicet unicuique datum est operi secundum ordinem, et gradum suum, et donum gratiae illuminantis; et operando assimilatam, ut licet, id est quantum possibile est creaturae secundum modum et dignitatem suam ad proprium principium suum a quo et facta est ut aliquid sit, et secundum quod disposita est ut talis sit. « Nonne ergo qui hierarchiam dicit declarat dispositionem quamdam sacram universaliter, » id est in omni ordine et gradu suo sic se habentem; quoniam, videlicet disposita est et ordinata ad imaginem divinae pulchritudinis in ordinibus, et scientiis hierarchicis, et sacrificat 997Dmysteria propriae illuminationis, ut in omni dispositione sua, et ordine dignitatis, et scientia discretionis, et imitatione operis, principium suum aemuletur. Mysteria propriae illuminationis sacrificat, qui ex occulto aspirationis dono bonum opus repraesentat; mysteria etiam propriae illuminationis sacrificat, qui perceptam gratiam ad alios transfundens talentum commissum multiplicat; mysteria etiam propriae illuminationis sacrificat, qui ea solum quae suo ordini et officio conveniunt administrat. « Est enim unicuique hierarchiam sortientium perfectio, hoc est, secundum propriam analogiam in Dei imitationem ascendere, et omnium divinius [divinissime], ut eloquia aiunt, Dei cooperato em fieri, et ostendere divinam in seipso actionem, secundum quod possibile est 998Arelucentem. » Propterea ait: Qui dicit: hierarchiam generalem quamdam dispositionem significat, pulchritudinem divinam in sua ordinatione imitantem, quia haec est perfectio unicuique ordini scilicet sive personae omnium hierarchiam sortientium ascendere, videlicet secundum propriam analogiam, id est modum et mensuram in Dei imitationem, et fieri cooperatorem Dei, ut eloquia aiunt, divinius omnium, id est quo nihil divinius aiunt eloquia, vel omnium divinius fieri cooperatorem Dei, id est, quo nihil magis divinos facit quam scilicet Dei cooperatorem fieri, et ostendere in seipso divinam actionem relucentem: ut scilicet ad alios relucendo transfundat per exemplum operis, quod primum percipere meruit per donum occultae aspirationis. Sic ergo 998Bperfectio constat hierarchiae, ut qui purgantur purgent, et qui illuminantur illuminent, et qui perficiuntur perficiant. « Utpote quoniam ita scilicet est ordo hierarchiae: Quosdam quidem purgari, quosdam vero purgare; et quosdam quidem illuminari, quosdam vero illuminare; et quosdam quidem perfici, quosdam vero perficere: unicuique deiforme adunationi qualicunque modo. » Primum purgantur, postea illuminantur, deinde perficiuntur. Nisi enim praecederet purgatio, non sequeretur illuminatio; et nisi esset illuminatio, non veniret consummatio. Sicut enim illuminari non potest qui non est purgatus, sic consummari non potest qui non est illuminatus; quia cognitio veritatis nonnisi mundos illuminat, et perfectio virtutis nonnisi illuminatis 998Cveritate appropinquat. Sed sunt superiores et sublimes, et ipsi appropinquantes divinitati immediate ab ipsa accipientes et purgationem ut sint mundi, et illuminationem ut sint clari, et perfectionem ut sint sancti. Et ab illis rursum secundum ordinem divinae dispositionis, iis qui sequuntur, et in ordine subjecti sunt, et purgantur, et illuminantur, et perficiuntur. Et sic secundum hunc modum unicuique adunationi, id est ordini et distributioni qualicunque modo deiforme, id est deiformitas sive similitudo, ipsum videlicet purgari, illuminari et perfici, ut in hoc suo modo, et mensura singuli deiformitatem, et Dei similitudinem habeant: qui sunt purgatione mundi, veritate illuminati, bonitate perfecti.

998DSequitur: « Divina beatitudo (quantum in hominibus dicendum) pura quidem est simul omni dissimilitudine; plena vero luminis aeterni: perfecta et non indigens simul omnis perfectionis; purgans, et illuminans, et perficiens. » Nunc demonstrare vult, quod bonum, quod in creatura sive purgata, sive illuminata, sive perfecta constat per gratiam, in ipso Creatore, a quo est, subsistit per naturam: cujus divina beatitudo, et munda est sine purgatione, et lucens sine illuminatione, et perfecta sine susceptione. Non enim ut munda sit, purgatur; neque ut luceat, illuminatur; neque accipit, ut perficiatur. Sed habens in se totum alieno non indiget; et suum ministrans, ea, quae per se indigentia sunt, replet. Pura quidem, inquit, est ab omni pariter dissimilitudine, 999Ahoc est ergo, propter quod munda jure nominatur, et dissimilitudinem non habet ullam. Ubi enim puritas est, dissimilitudo non est; quia id ipsum est totum, et concordans unum. Corruptio enim dissimilitudinem inducit, et alterum facit quod a suo esse recedit, et deficit ut si alterum quam fuit. Quod ergo semper idem est, dissimilitudinem non capit; et quod immutabile perseverat, corruptionem non admittit. Propterea divina beatitudo munda est, et incorrupta, et ab omni dissimilitudine aliena, consistens in eo, quod est, et incorruptum servans quod habet. Est quoque plena luminis aeterni, non tamen quasi illuminata, quoniam ipsa lumen est; nec lucere incipiens, quoniam aeterna est; nec crescens in lumine, quoniam plena 999Best. Perfecta quoque est, et non indigens simul omnis perfectionis, hoc est nullo indigens, quod ad perfectionem pertineat; quia totum habet et possidet, et est totum ipsa, quod possidet: et idcirco nec major esse potest, quia totum habet; nec minor, quoniam immutabiliter et aeternaliter habet. Et cum in se talis sit, ut nec purgari egeat, pura; nec illuminari, lumine plena; nec perfici, consummata: purgat tamen, et illuminat et perficit omnes, qui purgari, et illuminari, et perfici merentur, sive primo loco immediate gratiam accipientes, sive mediate per eos, qui primum accipere meruerunt, participantes. Hoc vero totum, videlicet quod divina beatitudo plena, et lumine plena, et perfecta vocatur: dicendum est quantum in hominibus, id est 999Csecundum eum modum, quo id, quod ineffabile est, ab hominibus dici potest. Nam quantum ad ipsam ineffabilem summae veritatis puritatem, magis dicenda est ipsa divina natura purgatio sancta, et illuminatio, et perfectio, ut parum id esse intelligatur, quod pura dicitur, sed magis ipsa purgatio; quod illuminata, sed magis ipsa illuminatio; quod perfecta, sed magis ipsa perfectio: quod et ipsum tamen minus adhuc invenitur, nisi cogitetur purgatio super omnem purgationem, illuminatio super omnem illuminationem, perfectio super omnem perfectionem. Propterea ait: « Purgatio, illuminatio, perfectio, super purgationem, super lumen ante perfecta, » sive plusquam perfecta, id est supra perfectionem; quia omne hoc, quod dicitur, secundum 999Daliquid dicitur, a quo longe est qui summe est, et propterea supra omne hoc est, quod est. Idcirco purgatio est, quoniam in se coinquinatum non recipit, coinquinationem vel corruptionem recipientibus et patientibus corruptionem tollit: et tamen supra purgationem, quoniam corruptionem non contingit. Et est illuminatio, quoniam in se lucet, et a se tenebrosa clarescere facit, et supra illuminationem, quoniam omnia irradians, et penetrans a se non exit; et est perfectio, quoniam nihil minus habet in se, et minus habentibus quod deest largitur, et praestat ex se; et tamen ante perfecta, sive plusquam perfecta, quoniam in singularitate boni constat tota, et in participatione indivisa, ut nec minus ejus 1000Abonum sit, quia unum est, nec multiplex, quia participatum. Propter hoc, « per seipsam perfecta est, » quia quod habet, aliunde non accepit; et « per seipsam perfectionis principium, » quia perficiendis quod habet largiendo ipsa non amittit. Et est « causa omnis hierarchiae, et omnis sacri secundum supereminentem celsitudinem. » Principium est, quoniam ab ipsa; et causa, quoniam per ipsam, et propter ipsam; et forma, quoniam secundum ipsam omnis hierarchia in ordine dignitatis, et omne sacrum in ministerio actionis dispensatur. Ab ipsa, praedestinatione; per ipsam, creatione; propter ipsam, glorificatione; ad ipsam, conversione, ut ipsam imitetur et in ipsa beatificetur.

Sequitur: « Oportet itaque, ut existimo, etc. » 1000BPostquam demonstravit divinam beatitudinem formam esse, et causam omnis sacrae potestatis et dispositionis; ipsamque et mundam esse, et lucentem, et perfectam: mundam quidem ac puram in eo quod omni dissimilitudine, et confusione careat; lucentem autem in eo quod aeterni luminis plenitudinem in se contineat; perfectam vero in eo quod omnia habens nullo indigeat. Modo infert, probans eos quoque, qui ad ipsius similitudinem et imitationem in sacris dispositionibus ordinati sunt, similiter mundos esse debere ab omni contagione, et confusione, et lucentes veritate, et perfectos bonitate, ut et ipsi quoque alios emundare possint, et illuminare, et perficere doctrina, et exemplo, ut in utroque ad imaginem et similitudinem Creatoris sui assurgant, 1000Csive in eo videlicet quod ipsi mundi, et clari, et perfecti sunt, sive in eo quod alios mundant, et illuminant, et perficiunt. « Oportet, » inquit, « ut existimo purgandos quidem, » sive eos videlicet, qui primo loco, sive eos, qui mediantibus aliis purgationem accipiunt; « puros perfici omnino, et liberari ab omni dissimilitudinis confusione, » quam vel ignorantia veri, vel concupiscentia mali induxit. « Illuminandos vero oportet repleri divino lumine, » utpote reducendos in castissimis mentis oculis « ad contemplativam habitudinem, et virtutem, id est ut mentis oculis castis, et mundis ex praecedenti purgatione peccati, et erroris existentibus « contemplativam habeant habitudinem, et virtutem. » Habitudinem videlicet per mentis puritatem; virtutem autem per 1000Dcontemplationis stabilitatem, ut possint contemplari divina, quae et veraciter apprehendunt, et retinent perseveranter. « Ex imperfecto » autem « restaurandos oportet participes fieri exploratorum sacrorum perfectivae scientiae, » ut videlicet vera bona, et sacra illa, quae per scientiam perfectam explorant, dilectione sequendo, et sanctitate participando apprehendant; ut sicut per scientiam perfectam perfecti sunt in cognitione, ita per bonitatem perfectam perfecti sint in participatione. « Purgatores vero magnitudine purgationis aliis tradere ex propria castitate, » id est ipsos purgatores, quorum scilicet ministerium est, ut per eos alii purgentur ab errore et culpa: oportet tales esse, ut magnitudine 1001Apurgationis suae, id est munditiae suae, quam in se habent, aliis tradant purgationem propria castitate, non alieno, sed proprio exemplo purgandorum vitam castificantes. « Illuminatores autem oportet suum superexcellens lumen in eos, qui digni sunt lumine, supervehere, » utpote habentes luculentiores animos ad participationem luminis, qua lumen ipsi percipiunt, et ad distributionem luminis, qua perceptum lumen ad alios illuminandos transfundunt: « habentes » dico « proprie, » id est singulariter et excellenter, quia qui alios illuminare debent, plus aliis lucere debent: « et ditissime, » id est abundanter repleti esse debent sanctae claritatis, ut ex abundantia perceptionis singulis tribuere possint quod opus est. Nam qui omnes docere debet, omnium 1001Bscientiam habere debet; quia non potest unicuique quod expedit, ministrare, qui causas omnium non novit, et utilitates. Supervehere autem debent lumen suum, ut quod verbo docent, per excellentiam vitae commendent, quasi in sublimi lucentes, et lumina fundentes ad eos, qui conversatione inferius manent. Perfectores vero oportet perficiendos sacratissima doctrina per inspectorum sacrorum scientiam, tanquam praeceptores perfectivae scientiae. Sacra veraciter inspicit, qui habitum per experientiam cognoscit; sacra veraciter inspicit, qui interna bona gustando percepit. Sacratissimam ergo doctrinam habet, qui docet quod sapit; qui instruit quod sentit; qui docet non solum cognoscere verum, sed apprehendere bonum 1001Cet amare justum. Quae traditio idcirco perfectiva vocatur, quia hoc solum hominem ad perfectum ducit, quando bona, quae per intelligentiam cognoscere non potuit, per studium boni operis apprehendit. Tali ergo doctrina ipsi perfectores perficiendos perficere debent, ut sint sancti et perfecti bonitate, imitantes illum, ad cujus formam et similitudinem reformantur, et superiores tribuendo, et inferiores percipiendo gratiae divinae participationem.

Unde sequitur: « Nonne ergo unusquisque hierarchiae dispositionis ordo secundum propriam analogiam, id est, » modum, et mensuram, et ordinem, « reducitur ad divinam cooperationem: illa agens et perficiens per gratiam et virtutem a Deo datam, 1001Dquae divinitati naturaliter, et supernaturaliter insunt, et ab ipsa » scilicet divinitate « superessentialiter acta, postea manifestata sunt hierarchiae ad possibilem imitationem animorum, id est, » spirituum « Deum diligentium? » Nisi enim illa bona, quae in Deo sunt per naturam, ad istos descenderent per gratiam, non essent illi similes; et nisi ipsi agendo obtinerent, quae ipse non agendo sed habendo possidet, non essent illius imitatores. Postremo, nisi ab ejus secreto invisibili, bona illa ad manifestationem deducta essent, nequaquam possibilitati creaturae imitabilia fuissent; nec dignitas secundum ipsum esset, nisi gratia ab ipso exisset. Ecce quid charitas facit. Solis animis diligentibus Deum, abscondita 1002Adivina manifesta facta dicuntur, et ad imitandum possibilia. Interna namque, et aeterna bona rationales animi per solam charitatem percipiunt: illa per dilectionem et gustando ut intelligant, et sequendo ut apprehendant. Nisi enim diligerent non intelligerent, quia non intelliguntur nisi cum diliguntur; et rursum nisi amarent non quaererent, et nisi quaererent non invenirent, quia non inveniuntur, si non quaeruntur. Hinc enim scriptum est: « Jam non dicam vos servos, quia servus nescit quid faciat Dominus ejus. Vos autem dixi amicos, quia omnia quaecunque audivi a Patre meo, nota feci vobis (Joan. XV). » Et iterum: « Pater, gratias ago tibi, quia abscondisti haec a sapientibus et prudentibus, et revelasti ea parvulis (Luc. X). » Ecce 1002Bergo quomodo sola charitas revelat ea quae abscondita sunt Dei, similiter quoque et ipsa ad possibilitatem deducit, quae sunt ineffabilia, et superessentialia, et supernaturalia omni creaturae, secundum incomprehensibilem sublimitatem Dei. « Si quis, inquit, diligit me, sermonem meum servabit; et Pater meus diliget eum, et ad eum veniemus, et mansionem apud eum faciemus (Joan. XIV). » Sic ergo omnis ordo dispositionis hierarchiae gratia, et virtute accepta a Deo per solam charitatem perficitur, agendo, et imitando Deum, ut illi actione et imitatione inesse incipiant, quae divinitati naturaliter insunt, quoniam ex ipsa sunt; et supernaturaliter, quoniam idem cum ipsa sunt: naturaliter, quoniam coaeterna; supernaturaliter, quoniam 1002Ccoessentialia: quod enim semper inest, naturale est; quod autem idem est, supernaturale est, quoniam natura ipsa est, et ipsum natura est.

Sequitur: « Et ab ea superessentialiter acta; et ad possibilem Deum diligentium animorum imitationem hierarchiae manifestata. » Quae sunt ea, quae divinitati supernaturaliter insunt, et ab ea superessentialiter acta sunt, postremo ad possibilem imitationem animorum Deum diligentium hierarchiae manifestata. Bona quaedam intelligi vult invisibilia, et ineffabilia, quae apud Deum fuerunt, et in Deo fuerunt, et non venerant adhuc in cognitionem per participationem, ut cognoscerentur et haberentur nisi ab eo solo cujus erant, in quo erant: et postea ab ipso facta sunt, quando factum est, ut fierent in 1002Dnobis; et superessentialiter facta sunt, quoniam primum ab ipso facta sunt, nobis, ut postmodum per ipsum fierent in nobis. Facta nobis praedestinatione, ut fierent in nobis perceptione; facta nobis cum tribuuntur, ut fierent in nobis cum percipiuntur. Facta supra nos, cum incipiunt venire ad nos; facta in nobis, cum incipiunt haberi a nobis. Facta in nos, cum descendunt ab ipso; facta in nobis, cum tribuuntur per ipsum. Haec ergo sunt, quae divinitati ante nos supernaturaliter insunt, et ab ea ad nos superessentialiter facta sunt: postremo in nobis per eam manifestata. « Manifestatae, inquit, sunt hierarchiae, » id est sacrae dispositioni, quae secundum Deum ordinata est, et incedit: et hoc factum 1003Aest « ad possibilem imitationem animorum Deum diligentium, » id est, ut animi Deum diligentes eum imitari possint; quia, nisi manifestata fuissent, imitabilia non essent. Nisi enim cognoscerentur non quaererentur, et nisi quaererentur non cognoscerentur. Hoc autem diligenter attendendum est, quod non singulis quibusque, sed hierarchiae, id est universitati, bona illa manifestata dicuntur. ita tamen ut a singulis 1004Ain universitate imitationis studio exerceantur, quia gratia ad universos effunditur et in singulis operatur. Extra unitatem nullus illam accipere potest, et in unitate alteri data nulli sufficere potest. Propterea hierarchiae manifestantur ad possibilem imitationem Deum diligentium animorum deducendam.

EXPOSITION.

Up to this point the theologian has discoursed on the things that had to be said in a general way for those being introduced into the knowledge of the hierarchies, in proportion to the visible demonstrations set forth for the signifying of visible things. Then now, entering upon the principal exposition, he first defines what a hierarchy is; not universally, however, but with a restricted meaning, only according to that hierarchy which consists in angels and 992Bmen. « A hierarchy, » he says, « is, in my view, a divine order, and knowledge, and activity, likening the deiform as far as is possible; and ascending, in proportion to the illuminations divinely implanted in it, into the likeness of God. » What he says, « in my view, » is to be taken as though he had said, according to my own estimation. For he modestly tempers his assertion, lest he seem to presume upon his own estimation more than is right. Then he sets forth three principal things in the definition of a hierarchy, which complete the very definition of a hierarchy. And these are: order, knowledge, and activity. If any one of all these three be lacking, there is no hierarchy. The first is a divine order; because there is no power, if it is not ordained 992Cby God; for this reason he says, a divine order. For « all » « power is from God; and the things that are from God are all good and ordained; therefore he who resists the power ordained by God, resists God (Rom. XIII). » For this reason, then, a hierarchy is a divine order, that is, a power ordained by God and disposed according to God. For it is from God by ordination; and according to God by imitation; and therefore a divine order, because it is from God, that it may be; and it is according to God, as to what kind and how great it is. Then, because every power that is ordained by God is ordained for the accomplishing and completing of something, there follows in the definition, after order, « knowledge and activity. » Knowledge, indeed, by which they may understand what is to be done; 992Dbut activity, by which they may accomplish what they have understood must be done. In order, duty; in knowledge, discernment; in activity, ministry. Without order, activity is presumption; without activity, order is negligence; but without knowledge, both activity is blameworthy and order is useless. For these reasons, then, a hierarchy is a divine order, and knowledge, and activity. A hierarchy, I say, both in order and in knowledge and in activity, likening the deiform, that is, imitating conformity to God as far as is possible for it; and ascending into the likeness of God in proportion to the illuminations, that is, according to the illuminations divinely implanted in it: each one, namely, according to the manner and measure of the grace divinely infused into it, accomplishing its task in its own order, and ascending to the imitation of God, so that by discerning rightly and working well 993Ait may imitate him. For in both respects every hierarchy emulates the divine likeness: namely, both in that it is disposed by him, and in that it works according to him. But this definition, as we have said, embraces only the angelic and human hierarchy, which were made after the likeness of the supreme and eternal hierarchy; and, being disposed according to it, they imitate it.

There follows: « The divine beauty, as simple, and as best because consummative; it is pure, indeed, universally from all unlikeness; but distributive, according to the dignity of each, of its proper light; and perfective in the most divine sacrifice, according to the unchangeable formation of those made perfect, closely joined unto it. » The sense is this. That the divine beauty, 993Bwhich we name the supreme hierarchy, according to which the other hierarchies were made, is universally pure, that is, wholly so, inasmuch as it is always simple in unity, best in goodness, consummative in perfection. For where there is unity, there is no diversity; and where there is no diversity, there can be no unlikeness. Likewise, where there is perfection, there is no degree; where there is no degree, there is no difference; where there is no difference, there is no unlikeness. Therefore the divine beauty, which is the form and exemplar of all things well and beautifully disposed — because it is one, it does not admit plurality; and because it is best, and consummate, and not only consummate but also consummative of all things to be consummated, and the cause of consummation, it does not admit diversity, and thereby 993Cknows no unlikeness at all; it that is both one in simplicity and the same in perfection. And although in itself it is such that it is neither divided by plurality nor made lesser by diversity, yet in those who become partakers of grace it is distributive of its proper light, bestowing its proper light in diverse ways, according to the dignity, namely, of each of the participants — granting to the higher greater, but to the lower lesser, gifts of graces, so that it may be beautifully multiplied in them, it which in itself truly abides one. The divine beauty itself is also perfective, since it perfects and makes the partakers of its lights consummate; perfective, I say, in the most divine sacrifice, by which it perfects those to be perfected according to the unchangeable formation of those closely joined and made perfect unto it. By the most divine 993Dsacrifice he means the divine illumination itself, and grace, and propitiation; by which all who are to be purged and to be saved are purged and cleansed, not only from the corruption of evil, that they may become good, but they are purged also from the defect of good, that they may stand present as better. It is therefore the supreme offering, and the teletargis, that is, the victim of the principal purgation; namely, the divine grace itself which is offered to us and offered for us. It is offered to us for purgation; it is offered for us for propitiation. It is offered to us, that we may have it; it is offered for us, that through it we may be pleasing. It is offered to us by infusion; it is offered for us by cleansing. It is offered to us while we begin to be what we were not; it is offered by us, while we exhibit and present 994Awhat we are. It is therefore the teletargis itself, that is, the victim of the principal purgation, and the most divine sacrifice, without which all victims and all sacrifices can have neither effect nor profit; it is that by which the divine beauty perfects, and makes perfect those who are perfect unto it — that is, reformed unto its likeness, that is, harmoniously, so that, namely, they may not diverge from it — according to the unchangeable formation of those very ones made perfect, unto it, that is, according to its likeness, which, once received, they keep unchangeably, so that they do not flow away from it. For the divine beauty, which in itself is one and perfect, purges and perfects those to be perfected unto itself through the victim of the principal purgation — that is, the infusion of its grace, which from its own fullness it poured out into participation for the sake of those to be purged and 994Bperfected — according to the manner and measure and capacity of each, which they received by the gift of that same grace, according to the unchangeable formation of them unto it; which formation, namely, is called unchangeable, as we have said, either because it turns those who are formed and reformed toward unchangeability; or because it abides unchangeable in him from whom it is, even if it be changed for those for whom it is and in whom it is.

There follows: « The interpretation [ intentio ], therefore, of a hierarchy is likeness and unity with God, as far as is possible. » What in Greek is called σκοπός scopos, and what the translator calls interpretation, is more properly named intentio or directio. For the intention 994Cor direction which is called scopos is a fixed aiming toward some end. For every action tends toward some end, and tends by some direction. But scopas, that is, the direction or aim, is that by which it tends. Every hierarchy, therefore, has a scopon, that is, a direction according to which it may proceed in fulfilling its ministry; namely, the imitation and divine likeness, so that, just as it has been ordained by him in office and dignity, so according to him it may proceed in ministry and operation, so that it presume to do nothing beyond the manner and measure assigned by him and owed to its own order. The interpretation, then — that is, the definition, or rather the direction and contemplation of a hierarchy, toward which every hierarchy ought to aim and does direct itself — is likeness and unity, that is, 994Dimitation of and identity with God, so that in nothing it may deviate or decline from his likeness, in which it has been placed, but may emulate him in all things as far as is possible. Likeness to God is to imitate him; but unity is to follow him alone. And this is the scopos, that is, the direction or aim of every hierarchy: that according to him it may proceed toward him, having him as the leader of all holy knowledge and activity, following him in judgment and in action — illumined by him unto the knowledge of truth, and aided unto the carrying out of good work. « Having him as leader, » presiding within in the demonstration of truth, and going before without in the example of good action. « And unto its own most divine comeliness defining unchangeably indeed; 995Abut, as far as is possible, it reforms, and perfects its own praisers as divine images. » The hierarchy itself, namely, defining unchangeably — that is, invariably or inflexibly turned, or aiming through its scopos toward the most divine comeliness of God himself, by imitating and following him, so that it may be conformed to his beauty and most divine comeliness, according to which every hierarchy is beautifully and becomingly disposed in its own order and rank: as far as is possible it reforms its own praisers, that is, those who in it praise God, and are disposed and ordained unto the praise of God: it reforms them, I say, in this very thing, that it makes them imitators of God, and turns them unto his likeness in their ministry; and by turning and reforming them it perfects them as divine agalmata, so that they themselves may be divine 995Bagalmata, that is, holy images and receptacles of divinity, and most bright mirrors; so that they themselves may be divine agalmata, indeed, by perfecting the divine light, but most bright mirrors, to shine from the light received. He also perfects those praisers of his as « pure receptacles, » or vessels « of the principal light, and of the divine ray » — that is, of the light immediately illuminating, and descending to illuminate those first things — so that, after the light is received, they may be filled with the sacred brightness implanted in them, that is, infused; and so that they may also be things declaring it, namely the brightness — « again, » that is, in the second place, « in those things which follow, declaring it » abundantly, according to « the divine laws. » The sense is this: Since a hierarchy, according to that disposition by which it imitates the divine beauty, 995Cmakes its praisers universally — that is, whether the higher or the lower — such that they are worthy both to receive the divine light and to shine from the light: but in particular it makes certain ones so pure that they are capable of the principal light, and are immediately illumined by God, and then transfuse their light to those who follow after them and are set beneath them in dignity: administering, indeed, abundantly, out of the abundance of the first reception, the second participation — provided only that the divine law is observed, in which it is prescribed for each one what, or how much, or to whom he ought to impart out of the gift of grace granted to him. For that it is not without the divine law — that is, that divine dispensation by which the gifts of grace are bestowed upon the partakers of the largess according to 995Da fixed measure and proportion, and duties are assigned, so that each one may know how much is permitted to him according to the ministry assigned, or is permitted to be done — he makes clear when he adds:

« For it is not lawful for the perfecters of holy things, and for the holily perfected, to work anything at all beyond their proper mysteries of victims, and their sacred ordinations. » As if he should say: For this reason those who in the order of the hierarchies are superior transfuse their lights to the inferiors, according to the divine laws; because it is not lawful, that is, not at all permitted, to work anything either for the perfecters of holy things, that is, for those who perfect others in holiness, or for the holily perfected, that is, for those who are perfected by others in holiness, beyond the proper mysteries of victims, that is, the proper gifts of graces, and the proper 996Asacred ordinations, that is, the sacred orders proper and assigned to each one. For to work without grace is vain; to work beyond order, or against it, is perverse. For individuals have their proper gifts, according to which they are able to work; and their proper orders, according to which they ought to moderate their working. Therefore it is necessary that each one strive to recognize the grace which he has received, lest he begin to presume in that which he cannot do; and to attend to his proper office and order, lest he dare to transgress in that which he ought not. For that this order of the divine disposition must be diligently observed, the Apostle Peter admonishes, saying: « Each one, as he has received grace, ministering it one to another » (I Petr. IV). And the Apostle Paul reproves those who were unwilling to hold this divine ordination 996Band dispensation, saying: « Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all doctors? Are all workers of powers? Have all the grace of healings? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret? Be zealous for the better charisms. » (I Cor. XII.) Therefore, then, it is not lawful for those who have been made partakers of divine grace, whether they have received it immediately from God, or through man, to work anything beyond their proper gifts and offices, so that the divine beauty may be conserved in all, and the order of the supreme dispensation may persevere. He calls perfecters of holy things those who have received so great a grace from God that, by illuminating and instructing, they perfect others also unto holiness. The holily perfected are those who, 996Cillumined and instructed by those very superiors, are perfected in holiness. By mysteries of victims he wishes gifts of graces to be understood: which are for this reason called mysteries, because they are secretly inspired; but victims, because they are bestowed for the cleansing and expiation of those who receive them. Or by ministries of victims he means the exhibitions of holy works, and the administrations of the divine sacraments: which are both victims, because they are offered through the exhibition of action, and mysteries through the sacraments of signification; because through that which is done visibly without in the sacrament, the invisible power of truth is signified. So, then, beyond the proper mysteries of victims, that is, the proper gifts or ministries, it is not lawful to work anything, either for the perfecters of holy things, that is, for those who administer the grace they have received to others to be perfected, 996Dor for the perfected themselves, that is, for those who, through the grace received, are perfected unto the perfection of holiness. Nor is it lawful either for these or for those to work anything beyond their sacred ordinations, that is, beyond that which pertains to their sacred ordinations, so that, namely, each one may presume to work that alone which is proved to pertain to the order and office assigned to him.

There follows: « But neither can they subsist otherwise, if they desire his divine brightness, and look toward it sacredly and becomingly, and are reformed, according to the analogy of each of the holy intellects. » As if he should say: Not only is it a debt for them to keep the sacred mysteries and the sacred ordinations, but it is also necessary, 997Asince they cannot subsist otherwise, namely in that state in which they imitate the divine beauty, unless, by keeping their orders, they proceed according to the divine laws. If, therefore, they desire the divine brightness of their Creator himself, and look toward the receiving of it by imitating and desiring — sacredly by affection, becomingly by habit — and we are reformed unto his likeness by imitating and following it: each of the holy intellects, namely, that is, of the angels, « according to the analogy of each, » that is, according to the manner and measure of his possibility, which each has according to his order, and rank, and property; otherwise they can in no way subsist in that good which they desire, unless they proceed according to the divine laws, 997Bkeeping their ordinations, and executing their proper ministries.

There follows: « Does not, therefore, he who says a hierarchy universally declare a certain sacred disposition, an image of the divine beauty, in the hierarchical orders and knowledges sacrificing the mysteries of its proper illumination, and, as far as is allowed, assimilated unto its proper principle? » Since, he says, it is necessary that every hierarchy desire the divine likeness, nor can it subsist otherwise, unless it persevere in his imitation. Therefore he who says a hierarchy declares a certain sacred disposition, which is an image of the divine beauty, that is, comeliness. A disposition, I say, sacrificing the mysteries, that is, exercising or exhibiting the mystical works, or the divine ministries 997Cof its proper illumination, that is, according to its proper illumination, in the hierarchical orders and knowledges — as far, namely, as is given to each for the work, according to his order, and rank, and the gift of illuminating grace; and, by working, assimilated, as far as is allowed, that is, as far as is possible for the creature according to its manner and dignity, unto its proper principle, from which also it was made that it might be something, and according to which it was disposed that it might be such. « Does not, therefore, he who says a hierarchy declare a certain sacred disposition universally, » that is, so holding itself in every order and rank of it; because, namely, it is disposed and ordained after the image of the divine beauty in the hierarchical orders and knowledges, and sacrifices 997Dthe mysteries of its proper illumination, so that in all its disposition, and order of dignity, and knowledge of discernment, and imitation of work, it may emulate its principle. He sacrifices the mysteries of his proper illumination who, out of the hidden gift of inspiration, represents good work; he also sacrifices the mysteries of his proper illumination who, transfusing the grace he has received to others, multiplies the talent committed to him; he also sacrifices the mysteries of his proper illumination who administers those things alone which befit his order and office. « For the perfection of each of those who are allotted a hierarchy is this: namely, according to his proper analogy, to ascend into the imitation of God, and to become, most divinely of all [divinissime], as the words say, a fellow-worker of God, and to show forth the divine action in himself, shining, as far as is possible, 998Arelucent. » For this reason he says: He who says a hierarchy signifies a certain general disposition, imitating the divine beauty in its ordination, because this is the perfection of each order, namely, or person, of all who are allotted a hierarchy: to ascend, namely, according to his proper analogy, that is, manner and measure, into the imitation of God, and to become a fellow-worker of God, as the words say, most divinely of all, that is, than which the words say nothing more divine, or, most divinely of all, to become a fellow-worker of God, that is, than which nothing makes men more divine than, namely, to become a fellow-worker of God, and to show forth in himself the divine action relucent: so that, namely, by being relucent to others, he may transfuse through the example of work that which he first merited to receive through the gift of hidden inspiration. Thus, then, 998Bthe perfection of a hierarchy stands, that those who are purged may purge, and those who are illumined may illumine, and those who are perfected may perfect. « Inasmuch as the order of a hierarchy is thus, namely: that some indeed are purged, but some purge; and some indeed are illumined, but some illumine; and some indeed are perfected, but some perfect: for each one a deiform union in whatever mode. » First they are purged, afterward they are illumined, then they are perfected. For unless purgation preceded, illumination would not follow; and unless there were illumination, consummation would not come. For just as he cannot be illumined who is not purged, so he cannot be consummated who is not illumined; because the knowledge of truth illumines none but the pure, and the perfection of virtue 998Capproaches none but those illumined by truth. But there are the superior and sublime, who themselves also, approaching the divinity, receive immediately from it both purgation, that they may be pure, and illumination, that they may be clear, and perfection, that they may be holy. And from those in turn, according to the order of the divine disposition, those who follow, and are subject in order, are both purged, and illumined, and perfected. And thus, according to this mode, for each union — that is, order and distribution — in whatever mode the deiform, that is, deiformity or likeness, is: namely, this very being purged, illumined, and perfected, so that in this their mode and measure the individuals may have deiformity and the likeness of God: they who are pure by purgation, illumined by truth, perfected by goodness.

998DThere follows: « The divine beatitude (as far as it must be said among men) is indeed pure at once from all unlikeness; but full of eternal light: perfect, and at once not lacking any perfection; purging, and illuminating, and perfecting. » Now he wishes to demonstrate that the good which, in the creature — whether purged, or illumined, or perfected — stands by grace, in the Creator himself, from whom it is, subsists by nature: whose divine beatitude is both pure without purgation, and shining without illumination, and perfect without reception. For it is not purged in order that it may be pure; nor is it illumined in order that it may shine; nor does it receive in order that it may be perfected. But having the whole in itself, it does not lack what is another's; and, administering its own, it fills those things which of themselves are in need. It is indeed pure, he says, from all unlikeness equally; 999Athis, then, is the reason for which it is rightly named pure, and has no unlikeness whatsoever. For where there is purity, there is no unlikeness; because it is the very same throughout, and a concordant one. For corruption introduces unlikeness, and makes other that which withdraws from its own being, and fails as though it were other than it was. That, therefore, which is always the same admits no unlikeness; and that which perseveres unchangeable admits no corruption. Therefore the divine beatitude is pure, and incorrupt, and foreign to all unlikeness, abiding in that which it is, and keeping incorrupt what it has. It is also full of eternal light, yet not as if illumined, since it is itself light; nor beginning to shine, since it is eternal; nor growing in light, since it is 999Bfull. It is also perfect, and at once not lacking any perfection, that is, lacking nothing that pertains to perfection; because it has and possesses the whole, and it is itself the whole which it possesses: and therefore it can be neither greater, because it has the whole; nor lesser, since it has it unchangeably and eternally. And although in itself it is such that it needs neither to be purged, being pure; nor to be illumined, being full of light; nor to be perfected, being consummate: yet it purges, and illumines, and perfects all who merit to be purged, and illumined, and perfected — whether receiving grace immediately in the first place, or partaking mediately through those who first merited to receive it. But this whole, namely that the divine beatitude is called full, and full of light, and perfect: is to be said as far as among men, that is, 999Caccording to that mode by which that which is ineffable can be said by men. For as regards that ineffable purity of the supreme truth, the divine nature itself is rather to be called holy purgation, and illumination, and perfection, so that it may be understood to be little that it is called pure, but rather purgation itself; that it is called illumined, but rather illumination itself; that it is called perfect, but rather perfection itself: which itself, however, is still found to be too little, unless there be thought purgation above all purgation, illumination above all illumination, perfection above all perfection. For this reason he says: « Purgation, illumination, perfection, above purgation, above light, before perfect, » or more than perfect, that is, above perfection; because all this that is said is said according to 999Dsomething, from which he who supremely is is far removed, and therefore he is above all this, which is. Therefore it is purgation, since it receives nothing defiled into itself, and takes away defilement or corruption from those receiving and suffering corruption: and yet above purgation, since it touches no corruption. And it is illumination, since it shines in itself, and makes dark things grow bright from itself, and above illumination, since, irradiating and penetrating all things, it does not go out from itself; and it is perfection, since it has nothing less in itself, and to those having less it grants what is lacking, and supplies it out of itself; and yet before perfect, or more than perfect, since it stands wholly in the singularity of good, and undivided in participation, so that its good is neither less 1000Abecause it is one, nor manifold because it is participated. For this reason, « it is perfect through itself, » because what it has it did not receive from elsewhere; and « through itself the principle of perfection, » because, by granting to those to be perfected that which it has, it itself does not lose it. And it is « the cause of every hierarchy, and of every holy thing, according to its supereminent loftiness. » It is a principle, since it is from it; and a cause, since it is through it, and on account of it; and a form, since according to it every hierarchy in the order of dignity, and every holy thing in the ministry of action, is dispensed. From it, by predestination; through it, by creation; on account of it, by glorification; unto it, by conversion, that it may imitate it and be beatified in it.

There follows: « It behooves, therefore, as I suppose, etc. » 1000BAfter he has demonstrated that the divine beatitude is the form and cause of every sacred power and disposition; and that it is both pure, and shining, and perfect: pure indeed and clean in that it lacks all unlikeness and confusion; shining in that it contains in itself the fullness of eternal light; but perfect in that, having all things, it lacks nothing. Now he infers, proving that those too who are ordained unto its likeness and imitation in the sacred dispositions ought likewise to be pure from all contagion and confusion, and shining with truth, and perfect in goodness, so that they too may be able to cleanse, and illumine, and perfect others by doctrine and by example, so that in both respects they may rise up unto the image and likeness of their Creator, 1000Cnamely, both in that they themselves are pure, and clear, and perfect, and in that they cleanse, and illumine, and perfect others. « It behooves, » he says, « as I suppose, that those to be purged indeed » — namely, whether those who in the first place, or those who, with others mediating, receive purgation — « be made altogether pure, and be freed from all confusion of unlikeness, » which either ignorance of the true, or concupiscence of evil, has introduced. « But those to be illumined it behooves to be filled with the divine light, » inasmuch as they are to be led back, in the most chaste eyes of the mind, « unto a contemplative habitude and power — that is, so that, the eyes of the mind being chaste and pure from the preceding purgation of sin and of error, they « may have a contemplative habitude and power. » A habitude, namely, through purity of mind;
