but a power through 1000Dthe stability of contemplation, so that they may be able to contemplate divine things, which they both truly apprehend, and retain perseveringly. « But those to be restored from the imperfect it behooves to become partakers of the perfective knowledge of the explored holy things, » so that, namely, they may apprehend the true goods, and those holy things which they explore through perfect knowledge, by following them with love and partaking of them with holiness; so that, just as through perfect knowledge they are perfected in cognition, so through perfect goodness they may be perfected in participation. « But the purgers, by the greatness of purgation, to hand on to others out of their proper chastity, » that is, the purgers themselves, whose ministry it is, namely, that through them others be purged from error and fault: it behooves them to be such that, by the greatness 1001Aof their own purgation, that is, of their own cleanness which they have in themselves, they may hand on purgation to others by their proper chastity, chastening the life of those to be purged by their own, not another's, example. « But the illuminators it behooves to convey their supereminent light upon those who are worthy of light, » inasmuch as they have more luminous souls for the participation of light, by which they themselves receive light, and for the distribution of light, by which they transfuse the light received to others to be illumined: « having » I say « properly, » that is, singularly and excellently, because those who ought to illumine others ought to shine more than others: « and most richly, » that is, they ought to be abundantly filled with the sacred brightness, so that out of the abundance of reception they may be able to bestow upon individuals what is needful. For he who ought to teach all ought to have the knowledge of all; 1001Bbecause he cannot administer to each one what is expedient, who does not know the causes of all things, and their utilities. And they ought to convey their light aloft, so that what they teach by word they may commend by the excellence of life, as though shining on high, and pouring lights upon those who remain lower in their manner of life. But the perfecters it behooves to perfect those to be perfected by most sacred doctrine, through the knowledge of the holy things beheld, as teachers of the perfective knowledge. He truly beholds holy things who knows the habit through experience; he truly beholds holy things who has perceived the interior goods by tasting. He therefore has most sacred doctrine who teaches what he savors; who instructs in what he feels; who teaches not only to know the true, but to apprehend the good 1001Cand to love the just. Which handing-on is for this reason called perfective, because this alone leads a man to the perfect, when he apprehends, through the pursuit of good work, the goods which he could not know through the understanding. By such doctrine, therefore, the perfecters themselves ought to perfect those to be perfected, so that they may be holy and perfect in goodness, imitating him unto whose form and likeness they are reformed — the superiors by bestowing, and the inferiors by receiving, the participation of divine grace.

Whence there follows: « Is not, therefore, every order of the hierarchic disposition, according to its proper analogy, that is, » manner, and measure, and order, « led back unto the divine cooperation: doing and perfecting those things through the grace and power given by God, 1001Dwhich are in the divinity naturally and supernaturally, and, having been » — namely by the divinity — « superessentially wrought by it, were afterward manifested to the hierarchy for the possible imitation of the souls, that is, » of the spirits « that love God? » For unless those goods which are in God by nature descended to these by grace, they would not be like him; and unless they themselves, by acting, obtained those things which he possesses not by acting but by having, they would not be his imitators. Finally, unless those goods had been led forth from his invisible secret unto manifestation, they would in no way have been imitable by the possibility of the creature; nor would there be dignity according to him, unless grace had gone forth from him. Behold what charity does. To those souls alone that love God are the hidden 1002Adivine things said to be made manifest, and possible to imitate. For rational souls perceive the interior and eternal goods through charity alone: those goods, through love, both by tasting that they may understand, and by following that they may apprehend. For unless they loved they would not understand, because they are not understood except when they are loved; and again, unless they loved they would not seek, and unless they sought they would not find, because they are not found if they are not sought. For hence it is written: « Now I will not call you servants, because the servant knows not what his Lord does. But I have called you friends, because all things whatsoever I have heard from my Father, I have made known to you (Joan. XV). » And again: « Father, I give thee thanks, because thou hast hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones (Luc. X). » Behold, 1002Btherefore, how charity alone reveals the things of God that are hidden, and likewise it too leads unto possibility the things that are ineffable, and superessential, and supernatural to every creature, according to the incomprehensible sublimity of God. « If anyone, he says, loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him, and will make our abode with him (Joan. XIV). » Thus, therefore, every order of the disposition of the hierarchy, the grace and power having been received from God, is perfected through charity alone, by acting and imitating God, so that by action and imitation there may begin to be present in them those things which are in the divinity naturally, since they are from it; and supernaturally, since they are the same with it: naturally, since coeternal; supernaturally, since 1002Ccoessential: for that which is always present is natural; but that which is the same is supernatural, since it is nature itself, and it itself is nature.

There follows: « And superessentially wrought by it; and manifested to the hierarchy for the possible imitation of the souls that love God. » What are those things which are supernaturally in the divinity, and were superessentially wrought by it, and finally were manifested to the hierarchy for the possible imitation of the souls that love God. He wishes certain goods to be understood, invisible and ineffable, which were with God, and were in God, and had not yet come into knowledge through participation, so as to be known and possessed except by him alone whose they were, in whom they were: and afterward they were made by him, when it was brought about that they should come to be in 1002Dus; and they were superessentially made, since first they were made by him, for us, so that afterward through him they might come to be in us. Made for us by predestination, that they might come to be in us by reception; made for us when they are bestowed, that they might come to be in us when they are received. Made above us, when they begin to come to us; made in us, when they begin to be had by us. Made unto us, when they descend from him; made in us, when they are bestowed through him. These, therefore, are the things which are supernaturally in the divinity before us, and were superessentially made from it unto us: finally manifested in us through it. « They were manifested, he says, to the hierarchy, » that is, to the sacred disposition which is ordained according to God, and proceeds: and this was done 1003A« for the possible imitation of the souls that love God, » that is, so that the souls that love God might be able to imitate him; because, unless they had been manifested, they would not be imitable. For unless they were known they would not be sought, and unless they were sought they would not be known. But this is to be diligently attended to, that those goods are said to be manifested not to any single individuals, but to the hierarchy, that is, to the whole; yet in such a way that they are exercised by the individuals 1004Awithin the whole by the zeal of imitation, because grace is poured out upon all and works in individuals. Outside unity none can receive it, and, given to another within unity, it can suffice for no one. For this reason they are manifested to the hierarchy, to bring forth the possible imitation of the souls that love God.

LIBER QUINTUS.

  • 1003

BOOK FIVE.

  • 1003

TITULUS CAPITULI IV. Quid significat angelorum cognominatio.

TITLE OF CHAPTER IV. What the appellation of the angels signifies.

LITTERA.

  • 1003B

Igitur hierarchia quid est, ut existimo, bene a nobis definita angelica hierarchia, deinde laudanda, mirabilesque ejus in eloquiis formarum facturae supermundanis oculis intuendae, ut ascendamus in deiformissimam eorum simplicitatem per mysticas formationes. Et simul omnis hierarchiae scientiae principium laudabimus in divina religiositate, et perfectissimis gratiarum actionibus: primum simul omnium illud dicere verum, ut bonitate universali, superessentialis divinitas eorum quae, sunt essentias ad esse substituens adduxit. Est enim hoc omnium causae, et super omnia bonitatis, proprium, ad communionem suam ea, quae sunt, vocare, ut unicuique eorum, quae sunt, ex propria definitur analogia. Omnia igitur 1003Cquae sunt participant providentiam ex superessentiali, et causalissima divinitate manantem. Non enim fortassis essent nisi eorum, quae sunt, essentiae principii assumptione. Existentia igitur omnia ejus esse participant. Esse enim omnium est superesse divinitatis: viventia autem eamdem super omnem vitam vivificam virtutem. Rationabilia, et intellectualia eamdem super omnem, et rationem, et intellectum per se perfectam, et ante perfectam sapientiam. Clarumque quod circa eam illae essentiarum sunt, quaecunque innumerabiliter ab ea acceperunt. Sanctae ergo coelestium essentiarum dispositiones super ea, quae tantum sunt et irrationabiliter viventia (secundum quae nos rationalia) in hierarchiae traditionis participatione facta sunt. Invisibiliter enim in divinam similitudinem supermundane 1003Daspicientes, et formare appetentes intellectualem suam speciem copiosiores pulchre habent ad eam communiones. Attendentes enim sunt omnem vitum. Ipsae ergo sunt primo, et multipliciter, et semper ad summum, quantum fas est, in conformatione divini, et inflexibilis amoris intentae, et principales illuminationes immaterialiter, et pure recipientes, et ad ipsas ordinatae, et intellectualem habentes omnem vitam. Ipsae ergo sunt primo, et multipliciter in participatione Dei factae: et primo, et multipliciter manifestatrices divinae occultationis. Propterea et ultra 1004Bomnia cognominatione angelica et selectim dignae factae sunt: eo quod primo in seipsas edunt divinam illuminationem, et per se in nos deferunt, quae supra nos sunt, manifestationes. Sic quidem, ut theologia ait, per angelos nobis donatae sunt. Et gloriosos quoque ante legem, et post legem nostros patres angeli ad divinum reducebant: quod agendum introducentes, et ad rectam veritatis viam ex errore, et vita immunda reducentes, aut ordines sacros mysteriorum supermundalium, aut occultas visiones, aut divinas quasdam ante praedicationes [praedictiones] prophetice revelantes (Gen. XIX, XXII, XXXI; Judith. VI; Dan. VII; Matth. II; Act. X; Apoc. IV). Si autem quis dixerit et inde immediate fuisse quibusdam sanctorum theophanias, discat et hoc sapienter ex sacratissimis 1004Celoquiis, quomodo hoc quidem quid est, Dei occultum nemo videt, neque videbit (Num. XII; I Tim. VI). Theophaniae autem sanctis factae sunt, [sed] secundum decentes Deum, perque quasdam sacras videntibus proportionalium visionum manifestationes. Ipsa igitur sapientissima theologia visionem illam, quae in ipsa est descripta, revelavit divinam, quasi in forma informium similitudinem ex videntium in divinum reductione pulchre vocari theophaniam, quasi per ipsam videntibus divina facta illuminatione, et quidem divinis ipsis sancte perficientibus. Has autem divinas visiones gloriosi patres nostri perfecerunt per medias coelestes virtutes. An non et sacram legislationem eloquiorum traditio velut per se quidem dicit ex Deo Moysi donatam, ut etiam nos 1004Dvere doceat, divinos eam esse, et sacros characteres? (Deut. IX.) Docet autem et sapienter theologia per angelos eam in nos pervenire, tanquam divino legali ordine illud legaliter ponente, hoc est, per prima secunda in divinum reduci. Etenim non solum in superpositis, et subjectis animis sed et aeque potentibus ipsa lex definitur ex superessentiali omnium ordinationis principio. Hoc est per unam quamque hierarchiam primas, et medias, ultimas esse, et ordinationes, et virtutes, et minimorum esse diviniores doctores, et manuductores in divinam adductionem, et illuminationem, 1005Aet communicationem. Video autem quod et divinum humanitatis Christi mysterium angeli primum docuere deinde per ipsos in nos scientiae gratia descendit (Matth. I; Luc. I, II). Sic ergo divinissimus Gabriel Zachariam quidem summum sacerdotem mysteria edocuit (Luc. I), hoc est, prophetam fore ex ipso contra spem, gratia divina nasciturum puerum divinitus, et salutariter mundo manifestandae virilis Jesu divinae operationis. Mariam quoque quomodo in ipsa foret divinum ineffabilis divinae formationis mysterium (ibid.). Ast alius angelorum Joseph erudiebat, quomodo vere implerentur divinitus promissa progenitori David (Matth. I; Luc. II). Alius vero pastores tanquam multorum reditu, et silentio purgatos evangelizavit, et cum eo multitudo exercitus coelestis 1005Billam valde laudabilem tradebant iis, qui in terra sunt, doxologiam. Respiciamque et ad excellentissimas eloquiorum luminis apparitiones. Video enim quoniam et ipse Jesus supercoelestium essentiarum superessentialis essentia, ad id, quod secundum nos est, immutabiliter veniens, non resilit a se ordinata, et assumpta humana ordinatione, sed obediens subditur Patris, et Dei per angelos dispositionibus. Et per medios ipsos annuntiatur Joseph a Patre disposita Filii ad Aegyptum recessio, et iterum ad Judaeam ex Aegypto traductio (Matth. II). Et per angelos ipsum videmus sub paternis legislationibus ordinatum (Luc. XXII). Insto enim dicere (ut scienti nostris sacerdotalibus traditionibus expressa) et de angelo ipsum Vesum confortante; aut quia et ipse Jesus per nostram 1005Csalutarem, beneficam, et manifestatoriam veniens ordinationem Angelus magni consilii appellatur. Etenim, ut ipse angelus dixit, quaecunque audivit a Patre, annuntiavit nobis (Joan. XV; Isai. IX).

THE TEXT.

  • 1003B

What a hierarchy is, therefore, having been, as I suppose, well defined by us — the angelic hierarchy — is then to be praised, and its wondrous makings of forms in the words are to be beheld with supermundane eyes, that we may ascend into their most deiform simplicity through the mystical formations. And at the same time we shall praise the principle of all hierarchic knowledge in divine religiosity, and in the most perfect givings of thanks: first of all, at once, to say this true thing — that by universal goodness the superessential divinity, setting up the essences of the things that are unto being, led them forth. For this is proper to the cause of all things, and to the goodness that is above all: to call unto its own communion the things that are, as for each one of the things that are it is defined out of its proper analogy. All things, therefore, 1003Cthat are participate the providence flowing from the superessential and most causal divinity. For perhaps they would not be, save by the assumption of the principle of the essences of the things that are. All existing things, therefore, participate its being. For the being of all things is the superbeing of the divinity: but living things participate the same vivific power above all life. Rational and intellectual things participate the same wisdom, above all reason and intellect, perfect through itself, and before perfect. And it is clear that about it are those of the essences which have innumerably received from it. The holy dispositions, therefore, of the heavenly essences, above the things which merely are and live irrationally (according to which we are rational), have been made in the participation of the hierarchic tradition. For, invisibly looking supermundanely 1003Dinto the divine likeness, and desiring to form their intellectual appearance, they beautifully have the more copious communions toward it. For they are attentive to all life. They, therefore, are first, and manifoldly, and ever to the utmost, as far as is lawful, intent upon the conformation of the divine and inflexible love, and receiving the principal illuminations immaterially and purely, and ordained unto them, and having all intellectual life. They, therefore, are first, and manifoldly made in the participation of God: and first, and manifoldly the makers-manifest of the divine hiddenness. For this reason also, beyond 1004Ball things, they have been made worthy of the angelic appellation, and by selection: in that they first bring forth into themselves the divine illumination, and through themselves convey to us the manifestations which are above us. Thus indeed, as theology says, they were given to us through angels. And our glorious fathers also, both before the law and after the law, the angels led back unto the divine: introducing what was to be done, and leading them back unto the right way of truth from error and from an unclean life; or revealing prophetically the sacred orders of the supermundane mysteries, or the hidden visions, or certain divine prior proclamations [praedictiones] (Gen. XIX, XXII, XXXI; Judith. VI; Dan. VII; Matth. II; Act. X; Apoc. IV). But if anyone should say that from thence also there were, immediately, theophanies to certain of the holy ones, let him learn this too wisely from the most sacred 1004Cwords: how this indeed is a certain thing — no one sees the hidden of God, nor will see (Num. XII; I Tim. VI). But theophanies were made to the holy ones, [sed] according to what befits God, and through certain sacred manifestations of proportional visions to those who see. Therefore the most wise theology itself revealed that vision which is described in it to be divine, so that, as it were, a likeness in the form of the formless, from the leading-back of the seers into the divine, is beautifully called a theophany, as though through it divine things were made to the seers by illumination, the divine ones themselves indeed holily perfecting them. But these divine visions our glorious fathers accomplished through the mediating heavenly powers. Does not also the tradition of the words say that the sacred legislation was given, as it were of itself indeed, from God to Moses, so that it may truly teach us also 1004Dthat it and the sacred characters are divine? (Deut. IX.) But theology also wisely teaches that it came unto us through angels, as though the divine legal order legally set that down — that is, that the second things are led back into the divine through the first. For not only in the superposed and subject souls, but also in the equally powerful, is the law itself defined out of the superessential principle of the ordination of all things. This is: through each single hierarchy there are the first, and the middle, and the last, and ordinations, and powers, and the teachers of the least are the more divine, and the guides-by-hand unto the divine leading, and illumination, 1005Aand communication. But I see that the angels first taught the divine mystery of the humanity of Christ, and then through them the grace of knowledge descended unto us (Matth. I; Luc. I, II). Thus, therefore, the most divine Gabriel taught the mysteries to Zacharias, the high priest (Luc. I), that is, that from him a prophet should come to be, against hope — a boy to be born divinely by divine grace — and, for the salutary manifestation to the world of the manly divine operation of Jesus. And Mary too, how in her there should be the divine mystery of the ineffable divine formation (ibid.). But another of the angels was instructing Joseph, how the things divinely promised to the forefather David were truly to be fulfilled (Matth. I; Luc. II). But another evangelized the shepherds, as those purged, as it were, by the return of the many and by silence, and with him a multitude of the heavenly host 1005Bwas delivering to those who are on earth that greatly laudable doxology. And let us look also to the most excellent apparitions of the light of the words. For I see that Jesus himself, the superessential essence of the supercelestial essences, coming unchangeably unto that which is according to us, does not recoil from the human ordination ordained and assumed by himself, but, obedient, is made subject to the dispositions of the Father, and of God, through angels. And through those very mediators there is announced to Joseph the withdrawal of the Son to Egypt, disposed by the Father, and again the leading-across into Judaea out of Egypt (Matth. II). And through angels we see him ordained under the paternal legislations (Luc. XXII). For I press on to say (as to one who knows the things expressed in our priestly traditions) also concerning the angel strengthening Vesum himself; or because Jesus himself too, coming through our 1005Csalutary, beneficent, and manifesting ordination, is called the Angel of great counsel. For indeed, as the angel himself said, whatsoever things he heard from the Father, he announced to us (Joan. XV; Isai. IX).

EXPOSITIO.

Postquam demonstravit, data et exposita generali definitione, quomodo intelligenda sit hierarchia secundum angelicam et humanam ordinationem (divina enim, quae infinita est, definiri non potest), nunc de angelica hierarchia specialiter tractare incipit, primum ostendens quomodo nomina angelorum, quae ab hominibus, et secundum homines data sunt, in illa spirituali, coelestique natura intelligenda sunt. Continuat praecedentia ad narrationem subsequentem dicens: « Igitur hierarchia quid est, ut 1005Dexistimo, bene a nobis definita angelica hierarchia, deinde laudanda: mirabilesque ejus in eloquiis formarum facturae supermundanis oculis intuendae. » Ac si diceret: Postquam secundum nostram existimationem bene ostendimus quid sit hierarchia ex definitione ejus proposita; nunc consequens est, ut laudemus angelicam hierarchiam, id est ut ostendamus quantum laudata sit in Scripturis sacris, sive quantum ex iis, quae de ipsa dicta sunt, laudabilis appareat, demonstremus. Et ad hoc demonstrandum conveniens est ut intueamur supermundanis oculis, id est spiritualibus, et spiritualiter videntibus oculis mirabiles facturas, id est compositiones vel adaptiones formarum, quae in eloquiis sacris illi 1006Aattribuuntur, ad invisibilem ejus naturam demonstrandam. Ideo enim spiritualibus oculis ea, quae visibiliter proponuntur, intuenda sunt, ne hoc solum esse putetur quod videtur, ne mens in illo remaneat quod foris conspicit. Sed per illud quod exterius in demonstrationem proponitur, ad illud verius et sublimius contemplandum invitatur.

Ideo sequitur: « Ut ascendamus in deiformissimam eorum » scilicet angelorum, « simplicitatem per mysticas formationes. » Ideo, inquit, « super mundanis oculis intuendae sunt mirabiles formarum facturae, ut per ipsas mysticas formationes » extrinsecus consideratas excitati, intrinsecus « ascendamus ad deiformissimam » ipsorum angelorum « simplicitatem. » Quasi enim multiplicitas quaedam angelis 1006Best ipsa, per quam exterius demonstratur mysticarum formationum veritas. Simpliciter autem illorum spiritualis et invariabilis naturae suae unitas est. In multiplicitate ergo sua deiformitatem non habent, sed in simplicitate: quia in ea parte, qua per visibiles formas demonstrantur, corporeae naturae similitudinem assumunt. In ea autem parte, qua spirituales ipsi et incorporea natura intelliguntur, ad imaginem, et similitudinem Dei respiciunt. Quae similitudo non solum deiformis, sed etiam deiformissima appellatur; quia cum eadem ipsa in hominibus quoque inveniatur, in angelis tamen excellentior creditur.

Sequitur: « Et simul omnis hierarchiae scientiae principium laudabimus in divina religiositate, et 1006Cperfectissimis gratiarum actionibus. » In eo, inquit, quod angelicam hierarchiam laudabimus, simul etiam laudabimus divinam, et summam hierarchiam, quae principium est omnis scientiae hierarchiae, id est quam habet omnis hierarchia, et per quam disposita est omnis hierarchia, quia omnis hierarchia et per eam disponitur et ab ea illuminatur. « Laudabimus, inquam, principium omnis hierarchiae, » scientiae, non tamen definitione et demonstratione sicut angelicam, nec definitione et comprehensione sicut humanam, quarum altera invisibilis per visibilia demonstratur; altera visibilis in seipsa cognoscitur. Sed laudabimus divina religiositate, et perfectissimis gratiarum actionibus. 1006DNeque enim demonstratione laudatur, quod incogitabile est, neque comprehensione laudatur, quod est incomprehensibile. Sola ergo religione et gratiarum actione Deus laudari potest, qui investigari et comprehendi non potest. Si ergo dicendo non potes, lauda vivendo. Quod lingua non explicat vita bona commendat; bona voluntate contingitur, qui per scientiam non investigatur. Si ergo non comprehendis ipsum, vivendo secundum ipsum, tende ad ipsum; hoc est laudare divina religione. Rursum si dicere non potes ipsum, dicere potes quae data sunt ab ipso; dona ejus optima commendare, ipsum ineffabiliter bonum praedicare; hoc est laudare perfectissima gratiarum actione, sic ergo laudabimus principium nostrum divina religiositate, 1007Aet perfectissimis gratiarum actionibus. In ipsa autem laudatione principii nostri primo omnium hoc commemorandum est, qualiter divina bonitas, quae ad omnia diffunditur, primum creanda ad esse adduxit; postea gubernanda sub se constituit et nutrienda ad se reformavit. Hoc est, quod dicit: « Primum simul omnium, » id est primum ante omnia, oportet « illud dicere verum, » id est illam veritatem dicere, « ut, » hoc est qualiter, scilicet superessentialis divinitas « universali bonitate sua adduxit ad esse essentias eorum, quae sunt; substituens, » post creationem, videlicet disponens et ordinans, vel statuens sub se, et ordinans secundum se. « Est enim, » etc. Ac si diceret: Propter hoc divina bonitas ea, quae creavit, 1007Bad se revocat et reformat, quia proprium illi est ex insita benignitate illa, quae esse acceperunt ab ea, ut beate esse possint, ad suam communionem vocare; quantum scilicet unumquodque secundum ordinem conditionis suae, et modum capax esse potest participationis illius. « Est enim, inquit, hoc proprium causae omnium, et bonitatis super omnia, » id est bonitatis, quae causa est omnium, quia per eam facta sunt omnia, et super omnia est, quia trahit ad se facta a se; hoc scilicet proprium illi est, vocare ea, quae sunt, ad communionem suam, ut hoc est, sicut unicuique eorum quae sunt, definitur vel dispensatur ex propria analogia, id est mensura, et modo, et ordine. Nam in hoc ipso pulchritudo 1007Cuniversitatis perficitur, quod non uno et eodem modo omnia, sed singula quaeque secundum ordinem et gradum suum varie, ac multifariam ad communionem divinae bonitatis revocantur, ut in eo quod non deseruntur, compleatur opus bonitatis; in eo vero, quod varie disponuntur ad decorem et pulchritudinem omnium opus sapientiae perficiatur. « Omnia igitur, quae sunt, participant providentiam ex superessentiali, et causalissima divinitate manantem. » Quandoquidem, inquit, hoc proprium est divinae bonitatis, ut omnia revocet ad sui participationem, ut conversa ad eam subsistant, quae ab ea processerunt, ut esse acciperent. Ergo « omnia quae sunt, participant providentiam, » id est provisum bonum, et provisam gratiam manantem ex 1007Dipsa divinitate, quasi de fonte, et primo principio omnis bonitatis, quae superessentialis est, quia in suae naturae excellentia omnibus essentiis, et subsistentibus naturis supereminet; et causalissima est, id est causarum omnium causa, et prima causa, quoniam ab ejus bonitate procedit bonum omne quod rebus a se conditis omnibus, ut subsistant, participandum praebet. « Non enim fortassis essent nisi eorum, quae sunt, essentiae, et principii assumptione. » Ex hoc, inquit, probari potest, omnia quae sunt, divinam providentiam participare, quia aliter subsistere non possent, nisi ipsius divinae bonitatis, a qua omnia esse acceperunt, et in qua omnia subsistunt, participatione subsisterent. Omnia enim, quae sunt, nisi a divina bonitate principium accepissent, 1008Anon incoepissent; et nisi in illa essentiam haberent, in eo quod sunt, non permanerent. Propterea ipsa principium omnium est, quam assumendo, et participando incipiunt; et essentia omnium est, quam assumendo, et participando subsistunt.

Unde sequitur: « Existentia igitur omnia ejus esse participant. » Ac si diceret: Quia sine ea nihil subsistere potest, manifestum est, quod esse ejus participant omnia, quae subsistunt. Ipsa ergo una et eadem existens in se divina natura quantum ad effectum, et virtutem, et operationem, omnibus subsistentibus, et a se creatis essentiis, et naturis, et principium est, a quo esse accipiunt, et essentia omnium est, in qua subsistunt; et vita est non 1008Bomnium quidem (quia non omnia vivunt) sed viventium omnium vita est, ex qua, et per quam vivificantur, et vivunt; et sapientia est non omnium existentium, aut viventium, quia non omnia existentia, aut viventia sapiunt, sed sapientium omnium sapientia est; et intellectus, et ratio, a qua et per quam illuminantur, et sapiunt, et intelligunt, et discernunt.

Hoc est quod dicit: « Esse enim omnium est superesse divinitatis, » quia per esse divinitatis, quod super omne esse est, esse habet et subsistit quidquid est. « Viventia autem, » quae jam non solum esse sed et vivere ab ea accipiunt, participando eamdem vitam, quae est super omnem vitam, et 1008Ceamdem vivificam virtutem participando, vivificantur, et vivunt. « Rationalia autem, et intellectualia, » participando « eamdem » ipsam sapientiam existentem « super omnem et rationem, et intellectum, per se perfectam, et ante perfectam, » id est supra omnia perfectam sapientiam participando, ratiocinantur, et intelligunt, et sapiunt. Ratiocinantur quidem investigando, intelligunt cognoscendo, sapiunt participando, ut una et eadem divina bonitas et subsistentibus essentia sit, et viventibus vita, et sapientibus sapientia. Ex quo claret, quod illa creata creatrici naturae similitudine, et veritate magis propinqua sunt, quae ab illa magis in dono perceperunt.

1008DHoc est quod sequitur: « Clarumque quod circa eam illae essentiarum sunt, quae innumerabiliter ab ea acceperunt. » Circa eam videlicet divinam naturam, id est propinquae et vicinae illi sunt, et immediate conjunctae, illae essentiarum, hoc est illae essentiae, sive naturae, quaecunque post ipsum esse datum innumerabiliter, vel multipliciter ab ea dona virtutum acceperunt. In quibus primo loco censentur coelestes illae et spirituales naturae angelorum, quae non solum per subtilitatem sapientiae rationabilia sunt, quia intellectu discernunt; sed per subtilitatem quoque spiritualis naturae intellectualia, quia solo intellectu in sua natura percipiuntur, et sensum corporis non contingunt; ac per hoc super omnia, quae sunt, factae sunt, quia vivunt; et super 1009Aomnia, quae irrationabiliter vivunt, quia discernunt.

Hoc est, quod ait: « Sanctae ergo coelestium essentiarum dispositiones, » id est sancti coelestium spirituum ordines, « factae sunt participatione traditionis hierarchiae, » id est participatione gratiae, quae traditur hierarchiae secundum Deum ordinatae, « super ea, quae tantum sunt, » quia vivunt: « et super ea, » quae « irrationabiliter viventia sunt, » quia discernunt; secundum quae irrationabiliter viventia nos homines rationalia animalia vocamur et sumus. Nec mirum, inquit, est, si spiritus angelici non solum super existentia et non viventia et super viventia et non discernentia, sed etiam super rationalia et corporalia dignitate facti sunt, quia rationalia 1009Bcorporalia, id est homines, licet ad divinam similitudinem reformentur, non nisi corporalibus tamen mediantibus eruditi et excitati ad illam respiciunt. Angelica autem sublimitas super corporalia omnia constituta invisibiliter, et immediate nulla alia creatura inter ipsam, et Deum constituta, ad divinam similitudinem conformatur copiosius, et multiplicius ab illa gratiam hauriendo, et vicinius illam, ut proximam contemplando. « Invisibiliter, » ait, hoc est sine materialibus et corporalibus instrumentis et signis visibilibus in divinam imitationem seipsas conformantes; ipsae scilicet coelestium essentiarum dispositiones. « Et ad divinam similitudinem, » per imitationem et conformationem « supermundane, » id est spiritualiter « aspicientes copiosiores pulchre 1009Chabent ad eam communiones, » id est multipliciores ab ea videlicet divina similitudine sumunt donorum spiritualium perceptiones, in quibus communionem cum ipsa habent, quia bonum ejus in ipsis spiritualibus donis percipiendo et communicando, in ipsa et cum ipsa possident. Pulchre quidem, et pure, et sine corporali contagione, et materiali attactu; simpliciter in illud assumpto. « Attendentes » quidem « sunt omnem vitam, » id est summam vitam, in qua est omnis vita; et quae tota est vita, nec aliunde vivens, sed vita; ac per hoc percipientes ex summa vita omnem vitam, ut in ea ipso quod immediate plenitudinem vitae accipiunt in ipsis, vita nunquam deficiat.

1009DSequitur: « Ipsae ergo sunt primo, et multipliciter; et semper ad summum, quantum fas est, in conformatione divini, et inflexibilis amoris intentae; et principales illuminationes immaterialiter, et pure recipientes, et ad ipsas ordinatae, et intellectualem, habentes omnem vitam. » Ipsae, inquit, sunt intentae, ad summum videlicet bonum, primo quia immediate, et multipliciter quia perfecte, et semper quia sine intermissione intentae, « videlicet quantum fas est, » id est licitum, vel possibile creaturae positae, « in conformatione divini et inflexibilis amoris, » id est creaturae inflexibiliter vel immutabiliter Deum amanti; et per inflexibilem et divinum amorem ad Deum se convertenti, et reformanti. « Sunt etiam ipsae, » scilicet coelestes virtutes « recipientes principales 1010Ailluminationes, » hoc est primo, et principaliter datas, immaterialiter sine corpore, et pure sine contagione. Immaterialiter sine visibili significatione, et pure sine erroris contagione. « Sunt etiam ordinatae ad ipsas, » videlicet illuminationes percipiendas, ut secundum differentiam ordinis differentia sit perceptionis; vel ordinatae ad illas per justitiam sunt subjicientes se, et coaptantes divinae voluntati per omnia, ut in eo ipso gratiae illuminationem sine impedimento percipiant, quo ab ejus veritate per desiderium iniquitatis non discordant. « Sunt » etiam « habentes intellectualem omnem vitam, » quia ipsum quod sunt, vita sunt, et eorum spirituales substantiae hoc ipsum vivere habent quod esse. Quia ergo in eis aliud non est, quod vivificat; 1010Bet aliud quod vivificatur, sed unum ipsum totum; omnem vitam habere dicuntur, vel omnis vita esse, quia totum quod sunt, vita sunt, sicut et ipsa summa vita, in qua sunt, et in qua vivunt, omnis vita est; quia ex se vivit, et vita est, et totum quod est ipsum, vita est.

Sequitur: « Ipsae ergo sunt primo, et multipliciter in participatione Dei factae, et primo, et multipliciter manifestatrices divinae occultationis. » Ipsae, inquit, coelestes dispositiones « factae sunt in participatione Dei, » id est ut Deum et gratiam divinam participent; primo, quia nulla creatura ante ipsas: « et multipliciter, » quia nulla creatura supra ipsas. « Primo, » quia ante omnia: « et multipliciter, » quia plus omnia. Et sunt « manifestatrices divinae occultationis, » 1010Cid est divinae gratiae invisibiliter et occulte sibi aspiratae, dum id quod ipsae intus ex occulta inspiratione percipiunt ad alios postmodum manifestando transfundunt. Vel « divinae occultationis, » id est divinitatis occultae et invisibilis manifestatrices sunt; quia in eis, et per eas invisibilia Dei ad manifestationem exeunt, cum claritas divina et in eis primum lucet, et per eas postea illuminat subjectos ordines provisorum. Propterea, ait, « dignae factae sunt selectim, » id est specialiter vel singulariter, « ultra omnia cognominatione angelica, eo quod primo in seipsas edunt divinam illuminationem, et per se in nos deferunt, quae supra nos sunt, manifestationes. » Propterea quia divinum lumen in 1010Dipsas primo loco se effundit, et per ipsas ad nos illuminandos postea descendit, dignae factae sunt ultra omnia, cognominatione angelica. Angelus quippe nuntius interpretatur. Qui ergo acceptam gratiam aliis ministrando deferunt, quid aliud quam auctoris et largitoris gratiae ejusdem nuntii sunt? Sed sunt nuntii, alii priores, alii posteriores. Angeli enim, qui primo loco gratiam divinam percipientes illam postmodum ad hominum cognitionem deferunt, quasi ejusdem gratiae primi nuntii sunt. Ipsi vero homines cum gratiam perceptam aliis praedicando, et annuntiando deferunt, nuntii quidem nominantur, sed primi nuntii non sunt, quia ab aliis primo illuminatis, et prius nuntiantibus, quod nuntiant, perceperunt. Propterea coelestes illi, et invisibiles 1011Aspiritus et singulari dignitate, et propria cognominatione angeli nominantur; quia eis primum per occultam aspirationem manifestatur, quod de invisibili divinitatis luce in semetipsis aspiciant, et per eos primo loco ad nos transfunditur, quod per se ipsi ad nostram cognitionem manifestandum portant. Primo namque loco quasi ex occulto conceptionis divinae parturiendo, in seipsos divinam illuminationem edunt, non extrinsecus hauriendo, sed ab intus concipiendo lucem claritatis aeternae, ut abintus prodeat ad se, quod videant in se, et ad nos transfundant per se. Sic enim primo in semetipsis illuminationes divinas percipiendo per se, postea deferunt ad nos manifestationes ipsarum illuminationum, quae sunt supra nos. Nam « sic quidem donatae 1011Bsunt nobis per angelos manifestationes, » scilicet divinae, « sicut theologia, » id est, sacra Scriptura « testatur. Et gloriosos quoque ante legem, et post legem nostros patres angeli ad divinum reducebant, quod agendum introducentes, et ad rectam veritatis viam ex errore, et vita immunda reducentes, aut ordines sacros mysteriorum supermundalium, aut occultas visiones, aut divinas quasdam ante praedicationes prophetice revelantes. » Ita, ait, sicut theologia, id est sacra Scriptura, testatur, manifestatur, manifestationes divinae nobis per angelos donatae sunt; quia et ante legem, scilicet datam, et post legem datam, id est sub lege et gratia, gloriosos patres nostros, id est electos et justos, quorum vitam imitando filii sumus, angeli ad divinum, id est 1011Cad divinam cognitionem reducebant: quod agendum scilicet erat introducentes, id est juste et pie ducentes vivere, et ad rectam veritatis viam ex errore, et vita immunda reducentes, hoc est, docentes recte credere, ut et fides illorum esset recta, et vita munda. Aut etiam revelantes ordines sacros mysteriorum supermundalium, id est secretorum coelestium de vita scilicet beata, et coelestis patriae gaudiis, et invisibili beatorum spirituum ordinatione, qualiter omnes in uno bono felices sunt, non tamen coaequales; et quod superiores sine superbia praelati sunt, inferiores sine miseria subjecti; aut ordines sacros mysteriorum supermundalium, id est secretorum divinorum revelantes, qualiter scilicet visibiliter 1011Det temporaliter ab hominibus impleri oportet, quod Deus invisibili, et secreta dispensatione agendum disposuit; aut etiam revelantes occultas aliquas visiones de praeteritis, sive praesentibus, sive futuris aliquid significantes; aut revelantes divinas quasdam ante praedicationes prophetice factas, id est praedicationes divinas, in quibus aliquid antequam fieret prophetice praedicabatur, revelantes, ut iis videlicet, quae dixerunt cognitionem futurorum, vel iis qui audierunt intelligentiam dictorum ministrantes, et in his omnibus sanctos viros sive ad rectam fidem, sive ad bonam operationem instruendo, ad divinam cognitionem et participationem reducentes.

Sequitur: « Si autem quis dixerit, et inde immediate 1012Afuisse quibusdam theophanias, discat et hoc sapienter ex sacratissimis eloquiis: quomodo hoc quidem quid est: Dei occultum nemo vidit, neque videbit. » Si quis, inquit, contra hoc, quod dixi, revelationes divinas per angelos ad hominum cognitionem venire dixerit, etiam angelis non mediantibus nonnunquam quosdam sanctorum Patrum ab ipsa divinitate revelationes accepisse, discat ex sacratissimis eloquiis hoc, quod, ipsum Dei occultum nemo vidit, aut videbit. Si ergo quis, hoc est aliquis dixerit inde, id est, a secreto divino fuisse scilicet factas quibusdam sanctorum theophanias, id est divinas apparitiones immediate, hoc est, primo loco in ipsos descendentes nulla alia creatura mediante; si quis, inquam, hoc dixerit, discat ille 1012Betiam hoc sapienter intelligere ex sacratissimis eloquiis, quomodo « nemo » unquam « vidit, neque videbit occultum Dei, » hoc est divinam naturam, quae occulta est et ab omni sensu remota. Vidit, dico, quid scilicet est hoc ipsum occultum; hoc est: Et si vidit in figura, non vidit in essentia; non vidit in specie, etsi vidit in significatione. Cumque hoc ex sacratissimis eloquiis cognoverit, intelligat quod humana mens ad inaccessibilis lucis contemplationem per semetipsam immediate accedere non potest, nisi theophaniis, id est apparitionibus divinis excitata sublevetur. « Theophaniae autem sanctis factae sunt [sed] secundum decentes Deum: perque quasdam sacras videntibus proportionalium visionum manifestationes. » Theophaniae inquit, id 1012Cest divinae revelationes vel divinitatis revelationes sanctis factae sunt, non hoc quidem modo, ut mens humana in carne mortali posita, et intra sensum humanum constituta ad incomprehensibilem naturam contingendam immediate accederet; sed factae sunt secundum quasdam sacras manifestationes, sive visibilium formarum extrinsecus sensui adhibitas, sive imaginationum secundum visibilia intrinsecus animo ingestas, sive alio qualicunque modo altiori et excellentiori spiritaliter humanae rationi impressas, tali convenientia coaptatas, ut et ipsum Deum, de quo factae erant, decerent, et ipsis, quibus fiebant videntibus secundum proportionem uniuscujusque, et capacitatem congruerent.

1012DHoc est, quod dicit: Sanctis factae sunt theophaniae secundum quasdam sacras manifestationes decentes Deum, et per manifestationes visionum proportionalium videntibus. Quae scilicet ita proportionaliter contemperatae erant possibilitati videntium, ut imperfectiores quidem inferiori et imperfectiori genere visionis coelestium veritatem perciperent; excellentiores autem sublimiori modo secreta divina cognoscerent. Et tamen sive in istis, sive in illis quidquid de Deo ad humanam cognitionem venire potuit, minus ipso, et quodammodo infra ipsum fuit. Hinc enim scriptum est: « Ea, quae sub ipso erant, replebant templum (Isai. VI): » quia omne quod mens humana in hac vita de cognitione 1013Aillius capere potest, ineffabili majestati ejus aequari non potest. Tamen divina Scriptura manifestationes illas, quibus Deus mentibus humanis se revelat, theopbanias, id est divinas apparitiones vocare consuevit; quoniam, etsi natura Deus non est, quod cernitur, secundum demonstrationem est, quia tamen per ipsum, et in ipso Deus manifestatur.

Hoc est, quod sequitur: « Ipsa igitur sapientissima theologia visionem illam, quae in ipsa est descripta, revelavit divinam, quasi in forma informium similitudinem ex videntium in divinum reductione pulchre vocari theophaniam. » « Ipsa, inquit, sapientissima theologia, » id est, divina Scriptura, quae secreta divina sapienter ad humanam cognitionem educit, « revelavit pulchre, » id est, convenienter vocari 1013Btheophaniam visionem illam, quae in ipsa descripta est, utpote « divinam similitudinem informium, » id est spiritualium, et corporalem formam non habentium naturarum, in forma visibili vel secundum visibilia sumpta expressam. Revelavit, dico, pulchre vocari theophaniam ex reductione videntium in divina, id est, quia per eam videntes in divina cognoscenda reducuntur, quasi per ipsam videntibus divina facta illuminatione et quidem divinis ipsis sancte perficientibus, id est, non solum ideo quia divina videntibus manifestavit, sed quia ipsos etiam videntes divinos effecit.

Sequitur: « Has autem divinas visiones gloriosi patres nostri perfecerunt, per medias coelestes virtutes, » 1013Cid est mediantibus coelestibus virtutibus, per quas ad hominum cognitionem deductae sunt: adepti sunt, et consecuti, et perfecte comprehenderunt visiones istas gloriosi patres nostri.

Sequitur: « An non et sacram legislationem eloquiorum traditio velut per se quidem dicit ex Deo Moysi donatam, ut etiam nos vere doceat divinos eam esse, et sacros characteres? » Nonne, inquit, « traditio eloquiorum, » id est, auctoritas Scripturarum, « dicit sacram legislationem, » id est, lationem sacrae legis, « donatam esse Moysi ex Deo per se, » nullum videlicet mediatorem commemorans in latione legis inter Deum et Moysen. Sed ipsum per se Deum Moysi locutum fuisse contestans: ut etiam doceat nos eam, videlicet legem, sacros esse, et divinos 1013Dcharacteres, hoc est sacrorum et divinorum signa, ut per ea, quae visibiliter in legislatione gesta sunt, alia quaedam invisibilia significata et demonstrata ostendat, sicut scriptum est: « Facies ergo tabernaculum juxta exemplar, quod tibi monstratum est in monte (Exod. XXVI). » Secundum hunc ergo modum et ipsa visibilis manifestatio ac materialis allocutio, qua invisibilis Dei hominibus se demonstrare voluit, Deus esse vel Dei esse dicitur, quia in ea invisibilis Deus ad manifestationem prodiit, et quae occulta erant sua ad cognitionem eduxit. In qua tamen visibili manifestatione ministerio angelorum mediante cuncta operatus est, ut id quidem quod visibile factum est, et Dei dici possit per primam 1014Aauctoritatem, et angelorum per subjectam operationem.

Hinc est enim quod sequitur: « Docet autem et hoc sapienter theologia, per angelos eam in nos pervenire. » Non solum, inquit, testatur theologia legislationem donatam Moysi ex Deo immediate, sed docet etiam eam, scilicet legem, pervenire in nos, hoc est ad nostram cognitionem expositam per angelos, ut aperte demonstretur quod illa legislatio et Dei erat, ex cujus auctoritate processit; et angelorum erat, quorum etiam ministerium exhibuit. « Tanquam, inquit, divino legali ordine illud legaliter ponente, hoc est, per prima secunda in divinum reduci. » Ita, inquit, Scriptura legislationem Deo per angelos in hominibus ordinatam ostendit, tanquam 1014Bipso legali ordine divinitus facto illud legaliter ponente, id est instituente, vel sanciente, hoc est, secunda reduci in divinum per prima. Cum enim divina lex primum a Deo in angelos, ac deinde per angelos in homines processisse perhibetur, manifeste ostenditur quod per prima et superiora, secunda et inferiora ad divinam cognitionem reducuntur: et hoc non solum inter Deum et angelos, vel inter angelos et homines, sed in ipsis quoque angelis intelligi oportet, quoniam superiores inferiores ad divinam reducunt cognitionem. Quoniam et in ipsis angelis ordines sunt, alii superiores, alii inferiores: et qui superiores sunt, copiosius lumen divinitatis hauriunt, et ad eos qui sequuntur post se, illuminandos transfundunt. Et in ipsis quoque ordinibus, 1014Cin quibus secundum parem dispositionem multi aequales sunt, haec legis definitio servatur, ut sint in divinae gratiae perceptionem alii primi, alii secundi, alii ultimi; et ii etiam, qui ordine pares sunt, non sint in gratiae perceptione aequales. Hoc est, quod dicit: « Etenim non solum et in super positis, et in subjectis animis, id est spiritibus; sed et in aeque potentibus ipsa lex definitur ex superessentiali principio ordinationis omnium, hoc est, » id scilicet, « per unamquamque hierarchiam, » id est sacram ordinationem, « esse et primas, et medias, et ultimas, et ordinationes, et virtutes: » et in ipsis ordinationibus, et virtutibus diviniores semper esse doctores, « et manuductores » divinorum, 1014Dut eos doceant, et adducant « in divinam adductionem, et illuminationem, et communicationem. In adductionem » per conversionem, « in illuminationem » per cognitionem; « in communicationem » per perceptionem.

Sequitur: « Video autem quod et divinum Christi humanitatis mysterium angeli primum docuere. Deinde per ipsos in nos scientiae gratia descendit. » Ex hoc, inquit, patet quod quae a Deo mandantur hominibus per angelos nuntiantur, quoniam et ipsum divinum mysterium humanitatis Christi angeli docuerunt, tam eos qui praedixerunt et crediderunt, quam eos qui viderunt et susceperunt. Et deinde, hoc est, consequenter per ipsos angelos in nos hujus scientiae gratia descendit. Sic ergo, sicut videlicet 1015AChristi nativitas per angelos nuntiata est: nativitas quoque praecursoris ejus per Gabrielem angelum legitur nuntiata. « Sic, inquit, divinissimus Gabriel Zachariam quidem summum sacerdotem docuit mysteria, hoc est, puerum nasciturum ex ipso contra spem, » quia ex sterili matre et sene patre: gratia divina « Prophetam fore manifestandae virilis divinae operationis Jesu mundo divinitus et salutariter. » Ac si diceret: Divinissimus Gabriel docuit Zachariam summum sacerdotem, quod puer nasciturus ex ipso propheta foret operationis Jesu virilis; quia in natura humanitatis, qua sexum carnis assumpsit, exhibita est; et divinae, quia per potentiam divinitatis, in qua etiam carnem suam condidit, est perfecta. Operationis, dico, manifestandae mundo per eum 1015Bdivinitus, et salutariter, hoc est ad salutem mundi divinitus proventuram. Docuit enim idem divinissimus Gabriel « Mariam quomodo, » scilicet « in ipsa foret complendum divinum mysterium ineffabilis divinae formationis. » Quod scilicet divina operatio ineffabiliter super usum, et legem naturae de carne ipsius virginis sine virilis seminis admistione carnem sumeret, et eam indumentum Verbi aeterni mirabiliter formaret. « Ast alius angelorum Joseph erudiebat, quomodo vere implerentur divinitus promissa progenitori David. » Id est, quomodo implerentur ea, quae promissa erant divinitus, hoc est, a Deo progenitori ejus David.

« Alius vero pastores tanquam multorum reditu, et silentio purgatos evangelizavit: et cum eo multitudo 1015Cexercitus coelestis illam valde laudabilem tradebant iis, qui in terra sunt, doxologiam. Alius, inquit, rursum angelus evangelizavit pastores, tanquam purgatos, et puros effectos multorum reditu, » id est separatione vel segregatione multitudinis, et tumultus, et strepitus; et purgatos etiam silentio, id est quiete mentis et pace interna, ut in hoc ipso digni Evangelio, et Evangelico fierent alloquio, quod seorsum a multitudine ad semetipsos redeuntes in silentio, et quiete mentis constituti spiritalis annuntiationis capaces exstiterant. Unde paulatim crescente gratia post unius evangelizationem coelestis exercitus multitudo auditur, qui illam valde laudabilem doxologiam, id est hymnum gloriae, tradebant iis qui in terra sunt hominibus scilicet bonae voluntatis.

1015DSequitur: « Respiciamque et ad excellentissimas eloquiorum luminis apparitiones. » Ac si diceret: Non solum in iis, quae de Verbi incarnatione hominibus per angelos nuntiata sunt, apparet, quod divinorum cognitio ipsis angelis mediantibus et ministrantibus ad homines descendit; sed in ipsa quoque persona Verbi incarnati idem videri potest: quae licet divinitatis majestate angelis imperaret, ea tamen, quae circa ejus humanitatem temporaliter facienda fuerant, per angelos voluit dispensari: in hoc ipso conditionem humanitatis dignanter suscipiens, quod omni necessitate carens sola dispensatione ad exemplum humanitatis, et documentum veritatis 1016Adispositionibus angelicis se inclinavit. « Respiciam, inquit, etiam ad excellentissimas apparitiones eloquiorum luminis, » id est apparitiones ipsius Jesu Christi, quando videlicet ipse Jesus, qui lumen est verum, in carne assumpta visibilis apparuit. Quae apparitiones luminis excellentissimae existunt, prae caeteris omnibus apparitionibus eloquiorom, id est prae caeteris omnibus apparitionibus quae in eloquiis sacris referuntur; quia nunquam prius ita excellenter Deus mundo se manifestavit, sicut quando in carne assumpta ipse visibilis apparuit. Ad has igitur, inquit, apparitiones luminis excelsissimas prae omnibus apparitionibus eloquiorum respiciam, ut in eis etiam hoc probem, quod divina arcana in homines per angelos dispensantur. Si enim circa illum 1016Bhominem, qui super homines est angelica dispensatio non est repudiata, quanto magis in eis, qui peccato obnoxii sunt, et in tenebris ignorantiae constituti probatur esse necessaria. In illo ergo homine, qui caput est hominum, agnoscere possumus quid de aliis hominibus, membris ejus sentire debeamus.

« Video enim, inquit, quoniam et ipse Jesus supercoelestium essentiarum in superessentialis essentia ad id, quod secundum nos est, immutabiliter veniens, non resilit a se ordinata et assumpta humana ordinatione. » Ipse, inquit, Jesus, qui secundum divinitatem suam, qua universa subsistunt supercoelestium quoque essentiarum, id est angelicorum spirituum, qui non solum terrena puritate, sed et 1016Ccoelestia quoque subtilitate transcendunt, essentia est; nec solum essentia, quia in eo subsistunt; sed superessentialis essentia, quia ad ejus aequalitatem non pertingunt. Ipse Jesus cujus ineffabilis majestas et divinitatis potentia ipsos quoque angelos et portat per gratiam, et transcendit per naturam, veniens ad id quod secundum nos est, hoc est, ad susceptionem carnis, quae nostrae naturae erat, et nobis similis erat; et immutabiliter veniens, hoc est, sine diminutione, vel mutatione suae divinitatis, non resilit ab humana ordinatione, hoc est, ab ordinatione sive lege humanitati debita. Ordinatione, dico, primum ab eo ordinata, quando prius hominem instruxit: postea ab eo assumpta quando humanitatis formam et naturam suscepit. Si autem humanam 1016Dnaturam assumpsisset, et humanam conditionem respueret, ab humana ordinatione resiliret. Quasi enim resilire illi esset, id, quod per naturam assumpserat, per conditionem nolle tolerare. Nunc autem veniens ad humanam naturam per assumptionem carnis, ab humana ordinatione non resilit per custodiam humilitatis. « Sed obediens subditur dispositionibus Dei Patris per angelos, » circa ejus humanitatem administratis: « et per medios ipsos » angelos, id est mediantibus ipsis angelis « annuntiatur Joseph, » utpote paedagogo infantiae ejus, « recessio » ipsius « filii » Dei « ad Aegyptum » a Patre Deo disposita, « et iterum ad Judaeam ex Aegypto traductio, » sive reductio. « Sed et ipsum, inquit, 1017Avidemus per angelos sub paternis legislationibus ordinatum. » Ipsum videmus ordinatum per angelos, hoc est, dispositum, « sub paternis legislationibus, » id est sub mandatis legalibus, quae mandata ii, quos secundum carnem patres habuit et antecessores, acceperant observanda. Sub his itaque mandatis legalibus ordinatus est per angelos, quando secundum legis paternae praecepta et circumcisus est die octava, et quadragesima die in templo cum muneribus, et hostiis praesentatus, legem per angelos datam observans Dominus angelorum.

Sequitur: « Insto enim dicere, ut scienti nostris sacerdotalibus traditionibus expressa, et de angelo ipsum Jesum confortante. » Parum est, inquit, quod dico, quod Jesus in humanitate ab angelis sub paternis 1017Blegibus ordinatus est: qui in eadem humanitate ab angelo passioni propinquans etiam est confortatus. Insto dicere, quod fortasse si prius dictum non esset, credibile omnino non esset. Insto dicere et de angelo ipsum Jesum confortante. Insto dicere, quod et ipse ego sine admiratione proferre non possum, quod credo certe, et studeo: quod si inscienti dicturus essem, dicere omnino non praesumerem. Insto dicere, quod tam magnum est, ut a parvis scientia comprehendi non possit; tam mirabile, ut a parvis fide non possit credi, de angelo ipsum confortante. Insto dicere, quod si a me dictum putaretur, non crederetur. Tibi autem scienti quae expressa sunt, id est manifeste prolata a nostris traditionibus sacerdotalibus, id est a Scripturis, 1017Cquae nobis traditae sunt a sacerdotalibus, et sacra ministrantibus ac sanctificatis viris, tibi audacter insto dicere veritatem, nihil haesitans de tua fide, quae firma est, et scandalum non recipit, habens discretionem quid factum, quid dictum sit. Tibi ergo, o Timothee fili, ut scienti nostris sacerdotalibus traditionibus expressa, tibi fiducialiter « insto dicere et de angelo Jesum confortante, » ut in hoc sine dubitatione patescat, quantum humanitas 1018Asecundum divinam ordinationem angelicae dispensationi subjecta sit quae in homine de tempore passionis ab angelo confortari voluit; non tamen quaerens auxilium, sed formans exemplum; non habens necessitatem, et tamen monstrans conditionem. Propterea ergo « insto » tibi « dicere, et de angelo ipsum Jesum confortante. » Aut etiam hoc « insto » tibi « dicere, quod ipse Jesus per nostram salutarem beneficam, et manifestatoriam veniens ordinationem, angelus magni consilii appellatur. » Hoc est quod ipse Jesus appellatur « magni consilii angelus, veniens, » hoc est, in eo quod venit ad nos, per nostram ordinationem, id est secundum quod ordinaverat, vel ordinatum erat venire in nostra natura: quae ordinatio salutaris erat, et benefica, et manifestatoria. 1018BSalutaris in redemptione, benefica in gratiae largitione, manifestatoria in glorificatione. Salutaris, quia a morte redemit; benefica, quia redemptis ad justificationem dona gratiarum contulit; manifestatoria, quia primum justificandis Deum in humanitate visibiliter videndum proposuit, et postea justificatos per visionem humanitatis ad contemplationem divinitatis perducit. Secundum hanc ergo « manifestatoriam ordinationem veniens Jesus angelus magni consilii appellatur. » Quia, « ut ipse angelus dicit, quaecunque audivit a Patre, annuntiavit nobis. » Si ergo angelus nuntius dicitur, merito et ipse Salvator nuntius vocatur. Qui voluntatem Dei Patris nobis annuntiat, et interna bona per Spiritum suum nostris mentibus aspirando revelat. In 1018Cquo etiam dignitas angelica manifeste ostenditur, quod et ipse Salvator ad nos mandata Patris deferens angelus cognominatur. Nam, cum summa nostrae salutis per redemptionem non sine angelica cognominatione perficitur, patet quod et caetera quoque, quae ad eamdem salutem pertinent, angelica, administratione dispensantur. Et haec quidem de angelica cognominatione dicta sunt.

EXPOSITION.

After he has shown — the general definition having been given and set forth — how the hierarchy is to be understood according to the angelic and human ordering (for the divine hierarchy, which is infinite, cannot be defined), he now begins to treat especially of the angelic hierarchy, first showing how the names of the angels, which have been given by men and after the manner of men, are to be understood in that spiritual and heavenly nature. He links what precedes to the narrative that follows, saying: « Therefore, what the hierarchy is, as 1005DI think, the angelic hierarchy having been well defined by us, is next to be praised; and its wondrous fashionings of forms in the sacred words are to be beheld with supramundane eyes. » As if he should say: After we have, according to our estimation, well shown what the hierarchy is from the definition of it set forth, now it follows that we praise the angelic hierarchy — that is, that we show how greatly it has been praised in the Holy Scriptures, or that we demonstrate how praiseworthy it appears from the things that have been said about it. And to demonstrate this it is fitting that we behold with supramundane eyes, that is, with spiritual eyes and eyes that see spiritually, the wondrous fashionings, that is, the compositions or adaptations of forms, which in the sacred words are 1006Aattributed to it, in order to demonstrate its invisible nature. For the things that are set forth visibly are to be beheld with spiritual eyes for this reason: lest what is seen be thought to be the only thing that is, lest the mind remain in that which it looks upon outwardly. But through that which is set forth outwardly for demonstration, it is invited to contemplate that which is truer and more sublime.

Therefore there follows: « That we may ascend to the most deiform » — namely of the angels — « simplicity through the mystical formations. » Therefore, he says, « the wondrous fashionings of forms are to be beheld with supramundane eyes, so that through those very mystical formations » — considered outwardly — being roused, we may inwardly « ascend to the most deiform » « simplicity » of the angels themselves. For it is as though a certain multiplicity belongs to the angels 1006B, through which the truth of the mystical formations is demonstrated outwardly. But their simplicity is the unity of their spiritual and unvarying nature. Therefore in their multiplicity they do not have deiformity, but in their simplicity; because in that part in which they are shown through visible forms, they take on the likeness of corporeal nature. But in that part in which they themselves are understood as spiritual and as an incorporeal nature, they look toward the image and likeness of God. Which likeness is called not only deiform but even most deiform; because, although the very same is found in men too, yet in the angels it is believed to be more excellent.

There follows: « And at the same time we shall praise the principle of the knowledge of every hierarchy in divine religiousness, and 1006Cin most perfect acts of thanksgiving. » In this, he says, that we shall praise the angelic hierarchy, at the same time we shall also praise the divine and highest hierarchy, which is the principle of all the knowledge of the hierarchy — that is, the knowledge which every hierarchy has, and through which every hierarchy is ordered, because every hierarchy is both ordered through it and illumined by it. « We shall praise, I say, the principle of every hierarchy, » of knowledge — yet not by definition and demonstration as we praise the angelic hierarchy, nor by definition and comprehension as we praise the human, of which the one, invisible, is demonstrated through visible things, the other, visible, is known in itself. But we shall praise it with divine religiousness and most perfect acts of thanksgiving. 1006DFor that which is unthinkable is not praised by demonstration, nor is that which is incomprehensible praised by comprehension. Therefore God, who cannot be searched out and comprehended, can be praised by religion and thanksgiving alone. If, then, you cannot praise by speaking, praise by living. What the tongue does not unfold, a good life commends; he who is not searched out through knowledge is attained by good will. If, then, you do not comprehend him, by living according to him, reach toward him; this is to praise with divine religion. Again, if you cannot speak him, you can speak the things that have been given by him; to commend his best gifts, to proclaim him ineffably good — this is to praise with a most perfect act of thanksgiving. Thus, then, we shall praise our principle with divine religiousness 1007Aand most perfect acts of thanksgiving. But in the very praising of our principle, first of all this must be called to mind: how the divine goodness, which is poured out upon all things, first brought into being the things to be created; then established beneath itself the things to be governed, and reformed unto itself the things to be nourished. This is what he says: « First of all together, » that is, first before all things, one must « speak that true thing, » that is, speak that truth, « namely how, » that is in what manner, the superessential divinity « by its universal goodness brought into being the essences of the things that are; substituting, » after creation, namely disposing and ordering, or establishing beneath itself, and ordering according to itself. « For it is, » etc. As if he should say: For this reason the divine goodness recalls to itself and reforms the things which it created, 1007Bbecause it is proper to it, out of its innate kindness, to call to its own communion the things which have received being from it, so that they may be able to be blessed — namely, as far as each one, according to the order of its condition and its measure, can be capable of that participation. « For this, he says, is proper to the cause of all things, and to the goodness that is above all things, » that is, to the goodness which is the cause of all things, because through it all things were made, and is above all things, because it draws to itself the things made by it; this, namely, is proper to it: to call the things that are to its own communion — that is, as it is defined or dispensed to each one of the things that are according to its proper analogy, that is, its measure, and mode, and order. For in this very thing the beauty 1007Cof the universe is perfected: that not all things in one and the same way, but each single thing according to its own order and grade, are variously and manifoldly recalled to the communion of the divine goodness — so that, in that they are not forsaken, the work of goodness may be completed; but in that they are variously disposed unto the comeliness and beauty of all, the work of wisdom may be perfected. « All things, therefore, that are, participate in the providence flowing from the superessential and most causal divinity. » Since, he says, this is proper to the divine goodness — that it recall all things to participation in itself, so that, turned back to it, the things which proceeded from it in order to receive being may subsist — therefore « all things that are participate in providence, » that is, in the provided good and the provided grace flowing from 1007Dthe divinity itself, as from a fountain and the first principle of all goodness, which is superessential, because in the excellence of its nature it is supereminent over all essences and subsisting natures; and is most causal, that is, the cause of all causes and the first cause, since from its goodness proceeds every good which it offers to be participated by all the things founded by it, that they may subsist. « For perhaps they would not be, except by the assumption of the essences of the things that are, and of their principle. » From this, he says, it can be proved that all things that are participate in divine providence, because they could not otherwise subsist, unless they subsisted by participation in the divine goodness itself, from which all things received being, and in which all things subsist. For all things that are, unless they had received their principle from the divine goodness, 1008Awould not have begun; and unless they had their essence in it, they would not remain in that which they are. Therefore it is the principle of all things, by assuming and participating in which they begin; and it is the essence of all things, by assuming and participating in which they subsist.

Whence there follows: « All existing things, therefore, participate in its being. » As if he should say: Because without it nothing can subsist, it is manifest that all things which subsist participate in its being. Therefore the divine nature, being one and the same in itself, as regards effect and power and operation, is, to all subsisting essences and natures created by it, both the principle from which they receive being, and the essence of all in which they subsist; and it is the life, not 1008Bof all indeed (because not all things live), but is the life of all living things, from which and through which they are made alive and live; and it is the wisdom, not of all existing or living things — because not all existing or living things are wise — but is the wisdom of all wise things; and it is the intellect and reason, from which and through which they are illumined and are wise and understand and discern.

This is what he says: « For the being of all things is the super-being of the divinity, » because through the being of the divinity, which is above all being, whatever is has being and subsists. « But living things, » which now receive from it not only being but also life, by participating in that same life which is above all life, and 1008Cby participating in that same life-giving power, are made alive and live. « But rational and intellectual things, » by participating in « that same » wisdom itself, existing « above all reason and intellect, perfect through itself and pre-perfect, » that is, by participating in the wisdom perfect above all things, reason and understand and are wise. They reason indeed by searching out, they understand by knowing, they are wise by participating — so that one and the same divine goodness is both essence to subsisting things, and life to living things, and wisdom to wise things. From which it is clear that those created things are nearer to the creating nature in likeness and in truth which have received more from it as a gift.

1008DThis is what follows: « And it is clear that those of the essences are around it which have received innumerably from it. » Around it, namely the divine nature — that is, they are near and neighboring to it, and immediately joined to it, those of the essences, that is those essences or natures, whichever, after being itself was given, have received innumerably or manifoldly from it the gifts of powers. Among which in the first place are reckoned those heavenly and spiritual natures of the angels, which are rational not only through the subtlety of wisdom, because they discern by intellect; but are also intellectual through the subtlety of their spiritual nature, because they are perceived in their nature by intellect alone, and do not touch the sense of the body; and through this they have been made above all things that are, because they live; and above 1009Aall things that live irrationally, because they discern.

This is what he says: « The holy dispositions, therefore, of the heavenly essences, » that is, the holy orders of the heavenly spirits, « have been made by participation in the tradition of the hierarchy, » that is, by participation in the grace which is handed on to the hierarchy ordered according to God, « above those things which only are, » because they live; « and above those things » which « are living irrationally, » because they discern; in comparison with which irrationally living things we men are called, and are, rational animals. Nor is it any wonder, he says, if the angelic spirits have been made superior in dignity not only to existing and non-living things, and to living and non-discerning things, but even to rational and corporeal things; because rational 1009Bcorporeal things, that is, men, although they are reformed unto the divine likeness, nevertheless look toward it only when instructed and roused by the mediation of corporeal things. But the angelic sublimity, established above all corporeal things, invisibly and immediately, no other creature set between it and God, is conformed to the divine likeness more copiously, drawing grace from it more manifoldly, and contemplating it more nearly, as being close at hand. « Invisibly, » he says, that is, conforming themselves unto the divine imitation without material and corporeal instruments and visible signs — namely the dispositions themselves of the heavenly essences. « And unto the divine likeness, » through imitation and conformation, « supramundanely, » that is, spiritually, « looking, they have beautifully more copious 1009Ccommunions with it, » that is, they take more manifold perceptions of spiritual gifts from it, namely from the divine likeness, in which they have communion with it; because, by perceiving and sharing its good in those very spiritual gifts, they possess it in it and with it. Beautifully indeed, and purely, and without corporeal contagion and material contact; being simply taken up into it. « They are attending » indeed « unto all life, » that is, unto the highest life, in which is all life; which is wholly life, not living from elsewhere, but is itself life; and through this, perceiving all life from the highest life, so that, by the very fact that they receive the fullness of life immediately in themselves, in them life may never fail.

1009DThere follows: « They themselves, therefore, are — firstly, and manifoldly, and always, unto the highest, as far as is lawful — intent upon the conformation of divine and inflexible love; and receiving the principal illuminations immaterially and purely, and ordered unto them, and having all intellectual life. » They themselves, he says, are intent — namely upon the highest good — firstly because immediately, and manifoldly because perfectly, and always because intent without intermission, « namely as far as is lawful, » that is, permitted or possible to a creature so placed, « in the conformation of divine and inflexible love, » that is, of a creature loving God inflexibly or immutably, and turning itself and reforming itself toward God through inflexible and divine love. « They themselves also are, » namely the heavenly powers, « receiving the principal 1010Ailluminations, » that is, those given firstly and principally — immaterially, without body, and purely, without contagion. Immaterially, without visible signification, and purely, without the contagion of error. « They are also ordered unto them, » namely unto the illuminations to be received, so that according to the difference of order there may be a difference of perception; or, ordered unto them, they are by justice subjecting themselves and fitting themselves to the divine will in all things, so that in this very thing they may perceive the illumination of grace without impediment, in that they do not disagree from its truth through desire of iniquity. « They are » also « having all intellectual life, » because the very thing that they are, they are life, and their spiritual substances have this very same thing — to live — that they have to be. Because, therefore, in them there is not one thing which gives life 1010Band another which is given life, but the whole is one and the same; they are said to have all life, or to be all life, because the whole of what they are, they are life — just as the highest life itself also, in which they are and in which they live, is all life; because it lives of itself, and is life, and the whole of what it is, is life.

There follows: « They themselves, therefore, have been made — firstly, and manifoldly — in the participation of God, and are — firstly, and manifoldly — the manifesters of the divine hiddenness. » They themselves, he says, the heavenly dispositions, « have been made in the participation of God, » that is, so that they may participate in God and in the divine grace; firstly, because no creature is before them; « and manifoldly, » because no creature is above them. « Firstly, » because before all; « and manifoldly, » because more than all. And they are « manifesters of the divine hiddenness, » 1010Cthat is, of the divine grace invisibly and secretly breathed into them, while that which they inwardly perceive from a hidden inspiration they afterward transfuse to others by manifesting it. Or « of the divine hiddenness, » that is, they are manifesters of the hidden and invisible divinity; because in them and through them the invisible things of God come forth unto manifestation, when the divine brightness both first shines in them and afterward, through them, illumines the subject orders of those provided for. Therefore, he says, « they have been made worthy, by selection, » that is, specially or singularly, « beyond all things, of the angelic appellation, in that they first put forth into themselves the divine illumination, and through themselves bring down to us the manifestations which are above us. » Therefore, because the divine light pours itself into 1010Dthem in the first place, and afterward descends through them to illumine us, they have been made worthy, beyond all things, of the angelic appellation. For 'angel' is interpreted messenger. Those, therefore, who bring down the grace they have received by ministering it to others, what else are they than messengers of the author and bestower of that same grace? But there are messengers — some prior, some posterior. For the angels, who, perceiving the divine grace in the first place, afterward bring it down to the knowledge of men, are, as it were, the first messengers of that same grace. But men themselves, when they bring down the grace they have received to others by preaching and announcing it, are indeed called messengers, but are not the first messengers, because they have perceived what they announce from others first illumined and first announcing. Therefore those heavenly and invisible 1011Aspirits are named angels both by a singular dignity and by a proper appellation; because to them first, through hidden inspiration, is manifested that which they behold in themselves of the invisible light of the divinity, and through them in the first place is transfused to us that which they themselves carry to be manifested to our knowledge. For in the first place, as though giving birth out of the hidden womb of divine conception, they put forth into themselves the divine illumination — not by drawing it from without, but by conceiving from within the light of eternal brightness — so that there may come forth from within, to themselves, that which they see in themselves, and that they may transfuse to us through themselves. For thus, by first perceiving the divine illuminations in themselves through themselves, they afterward bring down to us the manifestations of those very illuminations, which are above us. For « thus indeed the manifestations, » namely the divine ones, « have been given 1011Bto us through the angels, as theology, » that is, Holy Scripture, « testifies. And the angels led back also our glorious fathers, both before the law and after the law, unto the divine, introducing that which was to be done, and leading them back from error and unclean life unto the right way of truth; either revealing the sacred orders of the supramundane mysteries, or the hidden visions, or certain divine fore-preachings prophetically. » Thus, he says, as theology, that is, Holy Scripture, testifies and manifests, the divine manifestations have been given to us through the angels; because both before the law, namely before it was given, and after the law was given, that is, under law and under grace, the angels led back our glorious fathers, that is, the elect and just, by imitating whose life we are sons, unto the divine, that is, 1011Cunto the divine knowledge: introducing, namely, that which was to be done, that is, leading them to live justly and piously, and leading them back from error and unclean life unto the right way of truth, that is, teaching them to believe rightly, so that both their faith might be right and their life clean.
