Or also revealing the sacred orders of the supramundane mysteries, that is, of the heavenly secrets — namely concerning the blessed life, and the joys of the heavenly fatherland, and the invisible ordination of the blessed spirits: how all are happy in the one good, yet not co-equal; and how the superior are set above without pride, the inferior subjected without misery; or revealing the sacred orders of the supramundane mysteries, that is, of the divine secrets: namely how it must be fulfilled visibly 1011Dand temporally by men, which God disposed to be done by an invisible and secret dispensation; or also revealing certain hidden visions, signifying something concerning things past, or present, or future; or revealing certain divine fore-preachings made prophetically, that is, divine preachings in which something, before it came to pass, was prophetically foretold — ministering, namely, to those who spoke them the knowledge of things to come, or to those who heard them the understanding of what was said, and in all these things, by instructing holy men either unto right faith or unto good working, leading them back unto divine knowledge and participation.

There follows: « But if anyone should say that there have also been theophanies to certain persons immediately 1012Afrom thence, let him learn this too wisely from the most sacred words: how this indeed is a certain thing: No one has seen, nor will see, the hidden thing of God. » If anyone, he says, against what I have said — that divine revelations come to the knowledge of men through the angels — should say that sometimes, without the angels mediating, certain of the holy Fathers received revelations from the divinity itself, let him learn from the most sacred words this: that the hidden thing of God itself no one has seen, nor will see. If, then, anyone — that is, some person — should say that from thence, that is, from the divine secret, theophanies were made to certain of the holy ones, that is, divine apparitions immediately, that is, descending into them in the first place with no other creature mediating; if anyone, I say, should say this, let him 1012Balso learn to understand this wisely from the most sacred words: how « no one » ever « has seen, nor will see, the hidden thing of God, » that is, the divine nature, which is hidden and removed from every sense. He has seen, I say — namely what this very hidden thing is; that is: even if he has seen it in a figure, he has not seen it in essence; he has not seen it in its proper form, even if he has seen it in signification. And when he has come to know this from the most sacred words, let him understand that the human mind cannot by itself approach immediately unto the contemplation of the inaccessible light, unless, roused by theophanies, that is, by divine apparitions, it be lifted up. « But theophanies have been made to the holy ones [but] according to what befits God: and through certain sacred manifestations of proportional visions to those who see. » Theophanies, he says, that 1012Cis, divine revelations, or revelations of the divinity, have been made to the holy ones — yet not in this manner, that the human mind, placed in mortal flesh and established within human sense, should approach immediately to touch the incomprehensible nature; but they were made according to certain sacred manifestations, whether of visible forms applied outwardly to the sense, or of imaginations brought inwardly into the mind according to visible things, or impressed spiritually upon human reason in some other, higher and more excellent way whatsoever — fitted with such suitability that they both befitted God himself, concerning whom they were made, and were congruous to those very seers to whom they were made, according to the proportion and capacity of each.

1012DThis is what he says: To the holy ones there have been made theophanies according to certain sacred manifestations befitting God, and through manifestations of proportional visions to those who see. Which, namely, were so proportionally tempered to the capacity of those seeing, that the more imperfect indeed perceived the truth of heavenly things by an inferior and more imperfect kind of vision; but the more excellent came to know the divine secrets in a more sublime manner. And yet, whether in these or in those, whatever could come from God unto human knowledge was less than himself, and in a certain manner beneath himself. For hence it is written: « The things that were under him filled the temple (Isai. VI): » because everything that the human mind in this life can grasp of the knowledge 1013Aof him cannot be made equal to his ineffable majesty. Nevertheless Holy Scripture has been accustomed to call those manifestations, by which God reveals himself to human minds, theopbanias, that is, divine apparitions; because, although that which is discerned is not God by nature according to demonstration, yet through it and in it God is manifested.

This is what follows: « That most wise theology, therefore, revealed that vision which is described in it to be a divine one, and to be beautifully called a theophany, as a likeness of formless things in a form, from the leading-back of those who see unto the divine. » « That most wise theology itself, he says, » that is, Holy Scripture, which wisely brings forth the divine secrets unto human knowledge, « revealed that that vision which is described in it is beautifully, » that is, fittingly, called 1013Ba theophany — inasmuch as it is « a divine likeness of formless things, » that is, of spiritual natures, and of natures not having corporeal form, expressed in a visible form, or taken according to visible things. It revealed, I say, that it is beautifully called a theophany from the leading-back of those who see unto divine things — that is, because through it those who see are led back to knowing divine things, as though, through it, divine things were made illumination to those who see, and indeed the divine things themselves holily perfecting them; that is, not only because it manifested divine things to those who see, but because it also made the seers themselves divine.

There follows: « But these divine visions our glorious fathers accomplished, through the mediating heavenly powers, » 1013Cthat is, by the heavenly powers mediating, through which they were brought down to the knowledge of men: our glorious fathers attained, and obtained, and perfectly comprehended those visions.

There follows: « Does not the tradition of the words also say that the sacred legislation was given to Moses by God, as it were through himself, so that it may also truly teach us that they are divine and sacred characters? » Does not, he says, « the tradition of the words, » that is, the authority of the Scriptures, « say that the sacred legislation, » that is, the giving of the sacred law, « was given to Moses by God through himself, » namely commemorating no mediator in the giving of the law between God and Moses. But testifying that God himself, through himself, spoke to Moses: so that it may also teach us that it, namely the law, are sacred and divine 1013Dcharacters, that is, signs of sacred and divine things, so that through the things which were done visibly in the legislation it may show certain other invisible things signified and demonstrated, as it is written: « Thou shalt therefore make the tabernacle according to the pattern which was shown thee in the mount (Exod. XXVI). » According to this manner, therefore, the visible manifestation itself and the material address, by which the invisible God willed to show himself to men, is said to be God, or to be of God, because in it the invisible God came forth unto manifestation, and brought forth to knowledge the things of his own which were hidden. In which visible manifestation, nevertheless, he worked all things by the mediating ministry of the angels, so that that which was made visible might be said to be both of God, by the first 1014Aauthority, and of the angels, by the subordinate operation.

For hence it is that there follows: « But theology also teaches this wisely: that it came unto us through the angels. » Not only, he says, does theology testify that the legislation was given to Moses by God immediately, but it also teaches that it, namely the law, came unto us — that is, was set forth to our knowledge through the angels — so that it may be openly demonstrated that that legislation was both of God, from whose authority it proceeded, and of the angels, whose ministry too it employed. « As though, he says, the divine legal order itself was setting that down legally, that is, that through the first things the second are led back unto the divine. » Thus, he says, Scripture shows the legislation to have been ordained by God through the angels among men, as though 1014Bthe legal order itself, divinely made, established that legally, that is, instituted or sanctioned it — namely, that the second things are led back unto the divine through the first. For when the divine law is declared to have proceeded first from God unto the angels, and then through the angels unto men, it is manifestly shown that through the first and superior things, the second and inferior things are led back unto the divine knowledge: and this must be understood not only between God and the angels, or between the angels and men, but also among the angels themselves, since the superior lead back the inferior unto the divine knowledge. Since among the angels themselves too there are orders, some superior, some inferior; and those who are superior draw more copiously the light of the divinity, and transfuse it to those who follow after them, to be illumined. And in those very orders too, 1014Cin which, according to an equal disposition, many are equal, this definition of the law is kept: that in the perception of divine grace some are first, some second, some last; and even those who are equal in order are not equal in the perception of grace. This is what he says: « For indeed not only among the placed-above and among the subject minds, that is, spirits, but even among the equally powerful, the very law is defined from the superessential principle of the ordering of all things, that is, » namely this, « that through each hierarchy, » that is, sacred ordination, « there are both first, and middle, and last ordinations and powers: » and that in those very ordinations and powers, the more divine are always the teachers « and hand-leaders » of divine things, 1014Dso that they may teach them and lead them « into the divine leading, and illumination, and communication. Into the leading » by conversion, « into illumination » by knowledge, « into communication » by perception.

There follows: « But I see that the angels first taught the divine mystery of Christ's humanity. Then through them the grace of that knowledge descended unto us. » From this, he says, it is clear that the things which are commanded by God to men are announced through the angels, since the angels taught even the divine mystery of Christ's humanity itself — both those who foretold and believed, and those who saw and received. And then, that is, consequently, through those very angels the grace of this knowledge descended unto us. Thus, therefore, just as 1015AChrist's nativity was announced through the angels, so too the nativity of his forerunner is read to have been announced through the angel Gabriel. « Thus, he says, the most divine Gabriel taught Zachariah, the high priest, the mysteries, that is, the boy to be born of him against hope, » because of a barren mother and an aged father: by divine grace « that he would be a Prophet, to manifest to the world the manly divine operation of Jesus, divinely and salvifically. » As if he should say: The most divine Gabriel taught Zachariah the high priest that the boy to be born of him would be a prophet of the operation of Jesus — a manly operation, because it was displayed in the nature of humanity, in which he took on the sex of flesh; and a divine operation, because it was accomplished through the power of the divinity, in which also he founded his own flesh. An operation, I say, to be manifested to the world through him 1015Bdivinely and salvifically, that is, one to come forth divinely unto the salvation of the world. For the same most divine Gabriel taught « Mary how, » namely, « in her the divine mystery of the ineffable divine formation was to be completed. » Namely, that the divine operation, ineffably, above the use and law of nature, would take flesh from the flesh of the Virgin herself without the admixture of male seed, and would wondrously form it as the garment of the eternal Word. « But another of the angels was instructing Joseph, how the things divinely promised to his forefather David were truly fulfilled. » That is, how those things were fulfilled which had been promised divinely, that is, by God, to his forefather David.

« But another evangelized the shepherds, as those purged by the withdrawal of the many and by silence: and with him the multitude 1015Cof the heavenly host were delivering to those who are on earth that most praiseworthy doxology. Another angel again, he says, evangelized the shepherds, as those purged and made pure by the withdrawal of the many, » that is, by the separation or segregation from the multitude and the tumult and the din; and purged also by silence, that is, by quiet of mind and inner peace, so that in this very thing they might become worthy of the Gospel and of the evangelic address, in that, returning apart from the multitude unto themselves, established in silence and quiet of mind, they had shown themselves capable of the spiritual announcement. Whence, the grace gradually growing, after the evangelization of the one, the multitude of the heavenly host is heard, who were delivering that most praiseworthy doxology, that is, hymn of glory, to those who are on earth, namely to men of good will.

1015DThere follows: « And let me look also to the most excellent apparitions of the light of the words. » As if he should say: Not only in the things which were announced to men through the angels concerning the incarnation of the Word does it appear that the knowledge of divine things descends to men by the mediation and ministry of the angels themselves; but the same can also be seen in the very person of the incarnate Word: who, although by the majesty of his divinity he commanded the angels, nevertheless willed that the things which had to be done temporally about his humanity should be dispensed through the angels: in this very thing deigning to take up the condition of humanity, in that, lacking all necessity, by dispensation alone, for an example of humanity and a lesson of truth, 1016Ahe inclined himself to the angelic dispositions. « I shall look, he says, also to the most excellent apparitions of the light of the words, » that is, to the apparitions of Jesus Christ himself, namely when Jesus himself, who is the true light, appeared visibly in the flesh he had assumed. Which apparitions of the light are the most excellent, beyond all the other apparitions eloquiorom, that is, beyond all the other apparitions which are reported in the sacred words; because never before did God manifest himself to the world so excellently as when he himself appeared visibly in the flesh he had assumed. To these apparitions of the light, therefore, he says, the most lofty above all the apparitions of the words, I shall look, so that in them too I may prove this: that the divine secrets are dispensed to men through the angels. For if, about that 1016Bman who is above men, the angelic dispensation was not repudiated, how much more is it proved to be necessary in those who are subject to sin and established in the darkness of ignorance. In that man, therefore, who is the head of men, we can recognize what we ought to think about other men, his members.

« For I see, he says, that Jesus himself too, coming immutably — in the superessential essence of the supercelestial essences — unto that which is according to us, does not recoil from the human ordination ordained and assumed by himself. » Jesus himself, he says, who according to his divinity, by which all things subsist, is also the essence of the supercelestial essences, that is, of the angelic spirits, who transcend not only earthly things by purity, but also 1016Cthe heavenly things by subtlety; and not only their essence, because in him they subsist, but the superessential essence, because they do not attain to his equality. Jesus himself, whose ineffable majesty and power of divinity both bears up the angels themselves through grace and transcends them through nature, coming unto that which is according to us, that is, unto the taking-on of flesh, which was of our nature and was like unto us; and coming immutably, that is, without diminution or change of his divinity, does not recoil from the human ordination, that is, from the ordination or law owed to humanity. An ordination, I say, first ordained by him, when he earlier instructed man; afterward assumed by him, when he took on the form and nature of humanity. But if he had assumed the human 1016Dnature and yet spurned the human condition, he would recoil from the human ordination. For it would be, as it were, a recoiling for him to be unwilling to endure by condition that which he had assumed by nature. But now, coming unto the human nature through the assumption of flesh, he does not recoil from the human ordination, by the keeping of humility. « But, obedient, he is made subject to the dispositions of God the Father through the angels, » administered about his humanity: « and through those very » angels as intermediaries, that is, by the mediation of the angels themselves, « there is announced to Joseph, » as to the guardian of his infancy, « the withdrawal » of the « Son » of God himself « into Egypt, » disposed by God the Father, « and again the leading-across, or leading-back, from Egypt into Judea. » « But we see him too, he says, 1017Aordained through the angels under the paternal legislations. » We see him ordained through the angels, that is, disposed, « under the paternal legislations, » that is, under the legal commandments, which commandments those whom he had as fathers and forefathers according to the flesh had received to be observed. Under these legal commandments, therefore, he was ordained through the angels, when, according to the precepts of the paternal law, he was both circumcised on the eighth day, and on the fortieth day presented in the temple with gifts and victims — the Lord of the angels observing the law given through the angels.

There follows: « For I am urgent to say, as to you who know the things expressed in our priestly traditions, also concerning the angel comforting Jesus himself. » It is a small thing, he says, that I say, that Jesus in his humanity was ordained by the angels under the paternal 1017Blaws: he who, in the same humanity, drawing near to the passion, was even comforted by an angel. I am urgent to say what perhaps, if it had not been said before, would not be credible at all. I am urgent to say, also concerning the angel comforting Jesus himself. I am urgent to say what I myself too cannot utter without wonder — what I certainly believe and pursue: which, if I were about to say it to one who did not know, I would not presume to say at all. I am urgent to say what is so great that it cannot be comprehended by the little in knowledge; so wondrous that it cannot be believed by the little in faith — concerning the angel comforting him. I am urgent to say what, if it were thought to have been said by me, would not be believed. But to you, who know the things which are expressed, that is, manifestly set forth by our priestly traditions, that is, by the Scriptures, 1017Cwhich were handed on to us by priestly men who minister sacred things and are sanctified, to you I boldly am urgent to say the truth, hesitating nothing about your faith, which is firm and admits no scandal, having discernment of what was done, what was said. To you, therefore, O Timothy, son, as to one who knows the things expressed in our priestly traditions, to you confidently « I am urgent to say, also concerning the angel comforting Jesus, » so that in this it may become plain without doubt how greatly the humanity 1018Awas subjected, according to the divine ordination, to the angelic dispensation — the humanity which, in the man, at the time of the passion, willed to be comforted by an angel; yet not seeking aid, but forming an example; not having necessity, and nevertheless showing the condition. Therefore, then, « I am urgent » to « say to you, also concerning the angel comforting Jesus himself. » Or also I « am urgent » to « say this to you: that Jesus himself, coming through our salvific, beneficent, and manifestative ordination, is called the angel of great counsel. » This is that Jesus himself is called « the angel of great counsel, coming, » that is, in that he came to us, through our ordination, that is, according to what he had ordained, or what had been ordained — to come in our nature: which ordination was salvific, and beneficent, and manifestative. 1018BSalvific in redemption, beneficent in the bestowal of grace, manifestative in glorification. Salvific, because he redeemed from death; beneficent, because to the redeemed he conferred the gifts of graces unto justification; manifestative, because he first set forth God, in his humanity, to be seen visibly by those to be justified, and afterward leads the justified, through the vision of his humanity, unto the contemplation of the divinity. According to this « manifestative ordination, therefore, Jesus, coming, is called the angel of great counsel. » Because, « as the angel himself says, whatsoever he heard from the Father, he announced to us. » If, then, an angel is called a messenger, deservedly the Savior himself too is called a messenger. Who announces to us the will of God the Father, and reveals the inward goods to our minds by breathing them in through his Spirit. In 1018Cwhich the angelic dignity is also manifestly shown: that the Savior himself too, bringing down to us the commands of the Father, is surnamed an angel. For since the sum of our salvation through redemption is accomplished not without the angelic appellation, it is clear that the rest too, which pertain to that same salvation, are dispensed by angelic administration. And these things indeed have been said concerning the angelic appellation.

TITULUS CAPITULI V Quare omnes coelestes essentiae communiter angeli dicuntur, et specialiter proprias, praeterquam primi et ecundi ordinum habent agnominationes.

TITLE OF CHAPTER V Why all the heavenly essences are commonly called angels, and specially have their own proper appellations, except those of the first and second orders.

LITTERA.

  • 1017D

Haec quidem est, quantum ad nos, causa angelicae in eloquiis cognominationis. Scrutari autem, ut existimo, oportet, ob quam causam theologi omnes quidem simul coelestes essentias angelos vocant: ad manifestationem autem venientes supermundalium ipsarum dispositionum ordinem angelicum specialiter nominant, completive terminantem divinas, et coelestes res: ante ipsum vero superpositae archangelicos ordinant ornatus, principesque, et potestates, et virtutes, et quascunque his superfirmatas essentias eloquiorum cognoscunt manifestatoriae traditiones. Dicimus autem, quod per omnem sanctam dispositionem excellentes quidem ordines habent inferiorum dispositionum, et illuminationes, et virtutes, non autem participantes 1018Dexcellentium se, sunt ultimi. Ergo sanctissimos excellentissimarum essentiarum ordines angelos vocant theologi; etenim sunt manifestatores et ipsi divinae illuminationis (Hebr. I). Ordinem vero extremum animorum coelestium non habent rationem archas, aut thronos, aut seraphim nominandi. Neque enim est in participatione excelsissimarum virtutum. Sed sicut ipse, nostros divinos summos sacerdotes reducit ad cognitos ei divinitatis fulgores, sic et ipsum ante se essentiarum [adhuc immundae] omnino sacrae virtutes reducunt, et ad divinum sunt consummanti angelicas hierarchias dispositioni. Nisi quidem quis et hoc dixerit, communes esse omnes angelicas nominationes secundum omnium coelestium virtutum in deiforme, et ex Deo datum lumen subjectionem, et supereminentem 1019Acommunicationem. Sed ut magis a nobis ratio dijudicata sit, considerabimus sacrae in eloquiis expressas sanctas, et decoras proprietates uniuscujusque coelestis dispositionis.

THE TEXT.

  • 1017D

This indeed is, as far as concerns us, the cause of the angelic surname in the oracles. But it is fitting, as I think, to search out for what cause the theologians call all the heavenly essences at once angels, yet, coming to the manifestation of the supramundane dispositions themselves, they specially name the angelic order, which completively terminates the divine and heavenly things; but before it they set in order, placed above, the archangelic adornments, and the princes, and the powers, and the virtues, and whatever essences the manifestative traditions of the oracles know to be established above these. But we say that, throughout every holy disposition, the excelling orders have the illuminations and virtues of the inferior dispositions, but they that do not participate 1018Din the things that excel them are last. Therefore the theologians call the most holy orders of the most excellent essences angels; for these too are manifesters of the divine illumination (Hebr. I). But the lowest order of the heavenly minds have no ground for being named principalities, or thrones, or seraphim. For it is not in the participation of the most lofty virtues. But just as he himself leads back our divine high priests to the brightnesses of the divinity known to him, so also the wholly sacred virtues of the essences [still unclean] altogether lead back that which is before it, and they are ordered unto the divine, unto the disposition that consummates the angelic hierarchies. Unless indeed someone should say this too: that all the angelic namings are common, according to the subjection of all the heavenly virtues unto the deiform and God-given light, and their supereminent 1019Acommunication. But that the matter may be the more discerned by us, we shall consider the holy and comely properties of each heavenly disposition, expressed in the sacred oracles.

EXPOSITIO.

« Haec quidem est, » etc. Hoc quinto capite disquiritur quare omnes coelestes essentiae angeli cognominantur. Haec autem quaestio ex eo orta videtur, quod in sacro eloquio coelestium spirituum quidam Deo sempe assistere, faciemque ejus semper videre perhibentur; quidam vero foras ad exteriora ministeria complenda mitti dicuntur. Hinc namque consequens esse videtur quod ii, qui semper vultui divino assistunt, ad exteriora nuntianda non exeant; ii autem, 1019Bqui foras mittuntur, divino conspectui immobiliter, sive immutabiliter non assistant. Scriptum quippe est in libro Danielis prophetae: « Millia millium ministrabant ei, et decies millies centena millia assistebant ei (Dan. VII). » In qua distinctione per assistentes quidem ii significati esse videntur, qui ad exteriora non exeunt; per ministrantes vero ii qui ad exteriora exeundo non semper assistunt. Propter quod quia inferiores simul, et postremi ordines ad exteriora exeunt, superiores tantum, et excellentiores divinae contemplationi sine intermissione assistunt; pauciores assistentes, plures vero ministrantes esse perhibentur. Nam cum novem sint ordines angelorum, duo tantum, id est angeli et archangeli pro eo quod specialiter ex officii sui distributione 1019Cmitti habent, ex re ipsa cognominationem susceperunt. Angeli videlicet nuntii, archangeli vero principales nuntii dicti; quoniam et illi minora, isti vero majora quasi ex ministerii dignitate annuntiant. Sed quia rursum in Scriptura sacra quosdam de superioribus ordinibus missos legimus, sicut in Isaia unus de seraphim volasse ad prophetam, atque labia ejus carbone, quem forcipe de altari tulerat, tetigisse memoratur (Isa. VI); et in Epistola ad Hebraeos Apostolus omnes administratorios spiritus, et in ministerium missos testatur, propter eos, qui haereditatem capiunt salutis (Hebr. I): magna nobis ambiguitatis difficultas oboritur, et quid potius hinc asserendum sit non facile invenitur. Auctor hanc quaestionem in hunc modum solvit. Nomen angelorum 1019Dinferioribus tantum ordinibus, et qui ex officio proprie exteriora nuntiare habent, convenire testatur. Sed quia divina secreta, quae ab ipsis inferioribus exterius ad hominum cognitionem deferuntur, eisdem a superioribus nuntiantur: nomen quoque angelorum superioribus esse communicabile: qui licet ad exteriora nuntianda non exeant, ea tamen, quae exterius nuntianda sunt, desuper ipsi accipiendo secundum legem divinae ordinationis ad inferiores, et post se subsequentes ordines nuntiando transportans, omnemque virtutem, et gratiam, et proprietatem inferiorum superiores participare: proptereaque etiam cognominationes inferiorum ad superiores transire; virtutem autem, et gratiam, et 1020Aproprietatem superiorum non omnem inferioribus esse communicabilem, et idcirco cognominationes quoque ipsorum simili ratione ad inferiores universaliter non posse deduci. Aliquando tamen inferiores quando superiorum proprietatem ex officii qualitate suscipiunt, nomen quoque ipsorum in ejusdem officii exsecutione assumunt. Hinc esse illud, quod superius commemoravimus, quod angelus, qui prophetae labia accendere, et purgare venerat, seraphim dicitur, quia in hujus operis qualitate accendentis sive inflammantis proprietatem exsequebatur. Illud vero quod Apostolus dicit, omnes esse administratorios spiritus, et in ministerium missos, hoc modo intelligendum putant, quod sicut superius diximus, illi quoque non inconvenienter missi dicuntur; 1020Bquia, licet ad exteriora non exeant, ea tamen quae exterius nuntianda sunt, inferioribus et subsequentibus ordinibus nuntiando apportant. Alii putant omnes coelestes ordines tam superiores, quam inferiores pro tempore, et loco, et causa ad exteriora dirigi; eos tamen, qui hoc ex officio proprium habent, specialiter angelos sive archangelos cognominari. Nam, quod omnes aliquando mittantur, apostolus, in eo quod superius commemoravimus, testimonio asserere videtur, dicens: « Nonne omnes sunt administratorii spiritus in ministerium missi, propter eos, qui haereditatem capiunt salutis? » Quod autem etiam superiores quidam aliquando non ex officio, sed ex causa accidentali ad exteriora dirigantur, Psalmista asserere videtur, cum dicit: « Qui 1020Cfacit angelos suos spiritus, et ministros suos ignem urentem (Psal. CIII). Sic ergo et alii sunt, qui ex officio assistunt; atque alii, qui ad exteriora complenda exeunt, et tamen assistentes aliquando in ministerium missi, dum proprietatem inferiorum suscipiunt, nomen quoque ipsorum in significatione assumunt. Qui tamen cum ad exteriora exeunt, ab interiori contemplatione non recedunt, quia illum aspiciunt, qui praesens ipsis est, quocunque vadunt. Et hoc modo quidem priusquam verba libri discuteremus, ad evidentiam dicendorum hujusmodi quaestionis mentionem breviter faciendam esse putavimus, nihil temere definientes, sed secretum venerantes, quod fortassis nescisse, venialis est infirmitas, 1020Dasserere autem praesumptuose, damnabilis temeritas. Hoc tamen sciendum est quod auctor illi potius parti assensum praebere videtur, quosdam solummodo, non omnes coelestes ordines ad exteriora mitti; et tamen propter ejusdem proprietatis participationem, qua superiores inferiorum gratiam et virtutem communicant, nomina quoque inferiorum a superioribus assumi. Sicut etiam aliquando inferiores, quando superiorum proprietatem ex officii qualitate suscipiunt nomen quoque illorum in significatione assumunt. Nunc ad litteram: « Haec quidem est, quantum ad nos, causa angelicae in eloquiis cognominationis. » « Haec, inquit, est, » quam superius diximus, « causa angelicae cognominationis; » quia videlicet secreta divina per eos nobis 1021Anuntiantur, et idcirco quia ad nos divina praecepta nuntiando deferunt, quantum ad nos, id est quantum ad id, sive propter id quod erga nos operantur, angelorum nomen assumunt. Sed quia hoc, id est interni praeceptoris nuntia foras ad hominum cognitionem efferte, utrum omnibus conveniat nondum manifesta ratione, vel auctoritate probatur, quaerendum nunc est, inquit, quare angelorum nomen in sacro eloquio omnibus communiter coelestibus virtutibus attribuit.

Hoc est, quod ait: « Scrutari, ut existimo, oportet, ob quam causam theologi omnes quidem simul coelestes essentias angelos vocant; ad manifestationem autem unientes supermundalium ipsarum dispositionum ordinem angelicum specialiter nominant, 1021Bcompletive terminantem divinas et coelestes res; » ac si diceret: Hoc nunc quaerendum restat quare theologi omnes illas coelestes naturas universaliter angelos nominant, cum tamen specialiter unum ordinem illorum videlicet spirituum, qui veniunt ad nos ad manifestandas ipsas supermundales dispositiones, id est spirituales, et divinas, et invisibiles ordinationes, ordinem angelicum nominant; « completive terminantem divinas, et coelestes res, » id est usque ad completionem, et terminum perducentem res divinitus in coelesti, secretaque ordinatione dispositas. Praeceptum namque divinum a summo deorsum currens, per superiores ordines ad inferiores defertur, donec tandem ad hominum cognitionem veniens opere compleatur: propter quod 1021Cet ille ordo coelestis, ad quem novissime per superpositas virtutes mandatum divinitatis descendit; ac deinde per ipsum foras nuntiatur, completive sive ad completionem illud terminare dicitur, quia per ejus illuc, ubi novissimae visibili operatione complendum est, annuntiationem defertur. Hoc ergo quaerendum est quare scilicet, cum novissimus iste ordo specialiter angelica cognominatione signetur, omnes coelestium essentiarum ordines angeli nominantur. « Ante ipsum vero superpositae archangelicos ordinant ornatus principesque et potestates, et virtutes, et quascunque his superfirmatas essentias eloquiorum cognoscunt manifestatoriae traditiones. » Ac si diceret: Ipsum quidem angelicum ordinem 1021Dultimum et novissimum, rebusque humanis proximum, divinasque visiones postremo annuntiatione efferentem, et determinantem theologi constituunt; ante ipsum autem ordinant superposite, id est in ordine superpositos describunt. « Archangelicos ornatus. » id est choros archangelorum ordinatos, et pulchre dispositos, qui in ordine ipsis angelis et superiores sunt dignitate, et priores annuntiatione. Deinde etiam constituunt ipsi theologi non solum scilicet super angelos, sed etiam super archangelos: principes, id est principatus, et potestates, et virtutes, et alias essentias, id est « spirituales naturas quascunque cognoscunt, » id est ad cognitionem proponunt manifestatoriae traditiones eloquiorum sacrorum. Essentias, dico, superfirmatas his videlicet 1022Aangelis, vel quascunque alias his supradictis omnibus superfirmatas, ut sint non solum dignitate sublimiores, sed etiam perfectionis firmitate fortiores, et magis ad aeternitatem et immutabilitatem stabiles.

Sequitur: « Dicimus autem quod per omnem sanctam dispositionem excellentes quidem ordines habent inferiorum dispositionum et illuminationes et virtutes; non autem participantes excellentium se sunt ultimi. » Ac si diceret: Cum in illa coelestium spirituum dispositione alii superiores sint, alii inferiores, superiores quidem omnem illuminationem, et virtutem inferiorum habent; sed inferiores superiorum ordinum illuminationes, et virtutes non omnes habent. Proptereaque inferiorum nomina 1022Baliquando ad superiores ordines transferuntur, utpote qui ipsis in eisdem nominum proprietatibus participant. Nomina vero superiorum non ita ab inferioribus assumi possunt, quoniam ad eos proprietates nominum universaliter non transeunt: hoc est quod ait: « Dicimus autem, quod per omnem sanctam dispositionem » coelestium videlicet spirituum, « excellentes quidem » sive superiores « ordines habent » omnes illuminationes, et virtutes « inferiorum dispositionum, » hoc est subjectorum ordinum. Sed ultimi, id est inferiores, et in ordine sequentes non sunt participantes, omnes subauditur illuminationes et virtutes excellentium se, id est eorum qui ipsis sunt excellentiores. Illuminationes intelligimus 1022Cin cognitione veritatis; virtutes autem in amore bonitatis et perfectione operis.

Sequitur: « Ergo sanctissimos excellentissimarum essentiarum ordines angelos vocant theologi. Etenim sunt manifestatores et ipsi divinae illuminationis. » Quia ait superiores ordines omnes proprietates habent inferiorum: ergo theologi sanctissimos ordines excellentissimarum essentiarum, id est excellentissimorum spirituum, vocant angelos; quoniam ipsi angelicam proprietatem participant, in eo quod, licet ad exteriora nuntianda non exeant, tamen eis, qui post se sequuntur ordinibus divinam illuminationem, quam de se accipiunt transfundendo, et quasi nuntiando manifestant. « Ordinem vero extremum animorum coelestium non habent 1022Drationem archas, aut thronos, aut seraphim nominandi. » -- « Non habent, inquit, rationem » ipsi theologi « nominandi extremum ordinem animorum coelestium, » id est ultimum ordinem spirituum coelestium, angelos videlicet: « archas, » id est principes, aut thronos, aut seraphim, quia ipse scilicet extremus ordo angelorum non est in participatione excelsissimarum virtutum. Propterea enim non possunt angeli principes, aut throni, aut seraphim nominari, sicut principes, et throni, et seraphim angeli nominantur; quia superiores angelicam proprietatem universaliter participant, angeli vero superiorum illuminationes, et virtutes non universaliter participant: et eas praecipue, pro quibus speciales cognominationes acceperunt, sed ex parte 1023Apossident; dignitatem tamen, ac proprietatem cognominationis ejus non habent. Neque enim omnis, qui aliquam virtutem aut proprietatem participando habet, secundum illam statim proprietatem cognominari debet, nisi illam vel inter caeteros singulariter, vel prae caeteris excellenter obtineat. Non enim omnis; qui aliquid sapit, statim sapiens nominatur; nec qui rectum quidpiam fecerit, continuo justus dicitur. Sed hic solus qui sapientiam et justitiam vel singulariter, vel excellenter obtinet, sapiens et justus propria et expressa cognominatione appellari debet. Sic itaque coelestes illi ordines spirituum sanctorum proprias cognominationes habent, in quibus designatur, non quod singulariter acceperint, sed quid possideant excellenter. Seraphim 1023Bnamque, quia ex amore Creatoris sui tanquam vicini et proximi, et in se ardentes sunt et ex se alios accendunt, ardentes sive incendentes interpretantur, non quod soli hoc inter caeteros habeant singulariter, sed cum caeteris, et prae caeteris excellenter. Omnes enim amore Dei ardent, et tamen ipsi specialiter ardentes vocari debuerunt, qui ipsius amoris ignem et primi concipiunt, et fortius ardentes ad caeteros quoque accendendos flammam dilectionis emittunt. Sic et cherubim (quod nomen plenitudo scientiae interpretatur) quia majorem caeteris cognitionem Dei habent, ex eo soli nomen accipiunt quod cum caeteris possidentes prae caeteris omnibus excellentius percipere meruerunt. Throni quoque dicti sunt, non quod in eis solis Deus sedeat, et judicia 1023Csua discernat; sed quia hoc excellentius caeteris in munere acceperunt, propter hoc ex ipso specialiter cognominationem trahunt. Et ad hunc modum quidem de caeteris etiam ordinibus intelligendum est, ut videlicet inde credantur singuli proprias cognominationes accipere, quod excellentius probantur ex dono gratiae possidere.

Sed oritur non contemnenda quaestio, et quae magnam animo confusionem inducat, si ratione adhibita discussa non fuerit. Si enim, ut dictum est, in illa coelesti dispositione singuli quique ordines ex ea proprietate singulares cognominationes trahunt, in qua caeteris excellentiores esse comprobantur, cum subjectorum ordinum omnes illuminationes et 1023Dvirtutes superiores universaliter et excellenter possideant, nihil suppositis consequentibusque ordinibus singulare relinquitur, ex quo propriam discretamque inter caeteros cognominationem sortiantur. Unde oportet diligentius considerare quemadmodum utrumque simul verum sit: quod videlicet subjectorum ordinum superiores universaliter et excellenter illuminationes et dona possident, et tamen singuli quique aliquid proprium ac speciale retinent unde propria discretaque appellatione signari valent. Seraphim namque ex nomine singularem dilectionem exprimunt. Cherubim autem excellentiorem cognitionem innuunt. Throni vero majorem vim discretionis ostendunt. Constat tamen, quod qui ardentius diligunt, profundius prospiciunt, et subtilius discernunt. 1024AQui enim magis e vicino respiciunt, procul dubio evidentius agnoscunt. Quomodo ergo ordo cherubim ex singularis gratiae privilegio cognominatus, dicitur, si hoc alter in munere excellentius retinet, unde ipse appellationem sortitur? Haec vero quaestio hac fortassis ratione non inconvenienter solvitur: ita tamen, si secretum veritatis nulla praejudicii temeritate violetur. Fieri namque potest ut, licet omnia virtutum dona superiores ordines excellentius possideant, ab iis tamen quae inter ipsa dona virtutum sublimiora sunt, solum cognominationem trahant; atque alia quae ordine dignitatis sequuntur, post se sequentibus ad denominationem relinquant, ut primus a prima, secundus a secunda, tertius a tertia vocabulum sortiatur. Scimus scilicet, 1024Bteste Scriptura, quod inter omnia virtutum dona charitas excellit propter quod consequens erat, ut ille ordo, qui omnium eminentissimus est, a charitate sola singularem sumeret in sui discretione appellationem, quamvis et alia quoque dona virtutum excellentius possideret, a quibus appellationem et vocabulum sumere potuisset. Quia autem cognitio veritatis, post amorem virtutis proxima dignitate cognoscitur: idcirco ab ipsa dignitate qui secundi sunt, post primos angelici spiritus merito cognominantur. Judicium autem discernendae veritatis quia sententiam adhuc quasi dubiam habere videtur, et suspensam quodammodo minus perfecta cognitione apparet: et idcirco quia ipsum post plenam contemplationem, in qua veritas non quaeritur, sed 1024Chabetur, ad eamden veritatis summae cognitionem respicit, tertio post duos priores ordini nomen dedit: hoc tamen secundum hominem propter quem nomina spiritibus ipsis data sunt, intelligi oportet. Nam illic judicium non est ambiguitatis definitio, sed veritatis discretio; neque ibi ubi manifesta sunt omnia, aliquid, quod latet, discutitur, sed quod certum est, pro merito existimatur. Quocirca in hoc quoque judicio scientiam veritatis anteponendam existimamus, quoniam sapientia simplicitatem et unitatem judicat; judicium autem per vim discretionis ad diversa se, contrariaque respicere probat. Unde excellentior cognominatio ab ipsa sapientia sumenda erat, per quam ordo excellentior designandus 1024Derat: qui licet et sapientiam, et judicium utpote sublimior et perfectior plenius possideret, a sola tamen sapientia vocabulum sumens, sequentis post se ordinis judicium cognominationis relinqueret. Secundum hanc itaque considerationem quisquis angelorum cognominationes interpretari voluerit, nihil fortassis inconvenientiae erit, si omnia virtutum dona superiores ordines perfectius possident, et tamen inferiores ordines ex quibusdam specialiter donis proprias cognominationes habent. De ipsis autem ordinibus angelorum in primis quidem, et ultimis eadem omnium sententia constat. Nam seraphim, loco supremo positos, et post illos cherubim, ac deinde thronos nulli, qui sanctarum Scripturarum testimonia novit, ignotum esse potest. 1025AInferioribus quoque ab imo sursum ascendentibus primum angelos atque archangelos collocari manifestum est. Sequentes quatuor ordines quidam hoc modo disponunt, ut a thronis deorsum primum dominationes, deinde principatus, deinde potestates, deinde virtutes constituant, ut in hunc modum novem ordines tribus ternariis distinguantur: quorum primus, et supremus seraphim, cherubim, thronos continet; secundus et medius dominationes, principatus, et potestates complectitur; tertius, et infimus virtutes, archangelos et angelos simul disponit. Sicque ab imo sursum primum angeli numerantur; deinde archangeli, deinde virtutes, deinde potestates, deinde principatus, deinde dominationes, deinde throni, deinde cherubim, deinde seraphim. Theologus 1025Bautem primum angelos ponit, deinde archangelos, deinde principatus, et hos primo ternario deputat. In secundo autem primum potestates, deinde virtutes, deinde dominationes constituit. In tertio vero primum thronos, postea cherubim, postea seraphim ab inferiori ad superiora progressione facta collocandos censet. Sed in hac terna triplici distinctione hoc maxime considerare oportet quod supremi quidem tres ordines, id est seraphim, et cherubim, et throni ex virtute singularis excellentiae, et vi denominationis suae ad interiora tantummodo respicere videntur. Amare enim et cognoscere, et judicare intus praesidentium, et conversionem ad interiora habentium proprium est. Ultimi vero tres, et extremi ordines ex proprietate cognominationis 1025Csuae ad exteriora solum secundum officium ministerii sui dispositi esse probantur; sive angeli et archangeli pro eo quod, agenda quaeque et manifestanda hominibus, exterius nuntiant; sive principatus pro eo quod, quae circa homines administranda sunt et disponenda, invisibili potestate dispensant. Medii autem ordines sicut dispositione, ita officio quoque inter invisibilia et visibilia ferri videntur; et quae a superioribus ad inferiores deferenda sunt secundum dignitatem, et officium suum administrare. In his autem dominationes primae sunt, quae singulari excellentia invisibilem annuntiationem in virtutibus solo imperio formant; virtutes autem secundae, quae praeceptum imperium exsequendo in 1025Dpotestatibus edunt. Potestates vero tertiae, quae conceptum mandatum in principatibus, archangelis et angelis sibi ad operationem subjectis perficiunt. Qui autem post angelos et archangelos constituit virtutes, illos nimirum spiritus intelligi volunt, per quos frequentius signa et miracula fiunt. In hoc quoque postremae dispositionis proprietas servetur, cujus ministerium ad exteriora sola dispensanda ordinatum esse putamus. Potestates vero dicunt illos spiritus vocari, qui adversas virtutes subjectas habent, et eas secundum datam potestatem libere comprimunt, ne tantum nocere valeant, quantum volunt. Principatus autem appellatos putant eos nimirum spiritus, qui ipsis etiam bonis angelorum spiritibus praelati sunt: quibus dum agenda quaeque imperant, 1026Asubjectis ad explenda divina ministeria principantur, et superiores existunt. Dominationes autem dictos, qui etiam principatus excellentiori potestate transcendunt, ut ipsos quoque subjectos habeant, qui aliis ad ministerium implendum imperare meruerunt. Haec breviter de ordinibus angelorum, et nominibus ad futuram narrationem necessaria praelibanda esse putavimus, ut semel dicta lector ad singula quaeque, prout ratio poposcerit, et causa, in sequentibus commemoranda, super his, et fortassis sine his obscura dicenda assumat. Nunc ad ipsius textus seriem explanandam revertamur. Superius dixit, quod non habent rationem theologi nominandi angelicum ordinem archas, aut thronos, aut seraphim; quia ipse videlicet angelicus ordo 1026Bnon est in participatione illarum excelsissimarum virtutum, ut ipsis participet in nomine, quibus non participat in nominis proprietate. Nunc idipsum sequentibus probat verbis, quod videlicet angelicus ordo excelsissimis virtutibus non participat. Non, inquit, participat cum ipsis; sed quod participat, participat ex ipsis. Aliud quippe est in plenitudine participare, atque aliud ex plenitudine participationem accipere. Sic itaque angelicus ordo excelsissimis virtutibus subjectus est, ut non participet cum ipsis, sed ex ipsis; quia, sicut ipse eos, qui in hominibus ad divinam cognitionem reducuntur, illuminando, et erudiendo reducit; sic et ab iis, qui ante ipsum sunt, virtutibus divinam ipse illuminationem percipit.

1026CHoc est, quod ait: « Sicut ipse, » videlicet angelicus ordo, « nostros divinos summos sacerdotes, » id est sanctos viros, qui sacra divina ab angelis immediate perceperunt, et nobis tradiderunt, « reducit ad cognitos ei divinitatis fulgores, » id est divinam cognitionem quam ipse percepit, et perceptam tribuit, « sic ipsum etiam reducunt virtutes essentiarum quae sunt ante se, » id est ante ipsum, vel super ipsum, « virtutes dico mundae, » id est valde sacrae, vel omnino sacrae, ut possint per excellentiam sanctitatis forma perfectionis esse subjectis. Et sunt etiam ipsae « virtutes sacrae ad divinum, » scilicet conferendum; id est divinitatis cognitionem dandam, « dispositioni consummanti, angelicas hierarchias, » 1026Did est dispositioni, quae perficit, vel perfectas continet sive terminat angelicas hierarchias; hoc est, videlicet ultima dispositio, in qua et ordo angelicus in eo quod perfecta est, consummatur, et in eo quod ultima est, omnium spirituum hierarchiae terminantur. Sane hic exsecrabilis interpretis error cavendus est, qui coelestes virtutes immundas dici existimavit. Nam Graecum πανιερὸν panieron, quod valde sacrum, vel omnino sacrum, vel universaliter sacrum interpretatur, hic ἀνιερὸν anieron, id est insacrum, vel non sacrum, vel sine sacro intelligendum putavit.

Sequitur: « Nisi quidem quis et hoc dixerit communes esse omnes angelicas nominationes secundum omnium coelestium virtutum in deiforme, et 1027Aex Deo datum lumen subjectionem, et supereminentem communicationem. » Non possunt, inquit, inferiores ordines superiorum nomina assumere, quia in eadem excellentia virtutum cum eis non participant, nisi quis dicere velit, propterea nominationes angelorum omnes communes esse debere, quod omnes pariter unum lumen a Deo datum subjecti percipiunt, et ex ipso lumine percepto omnes Deo conformes fiunt, et unius supereminentis communicationis in uno lumine participes existunt. Nisi, ait, quis etiam hoc dixerit, omnes angelicas cognominationes communes esse, secundum omnium coelestium virtutum subjectionem in lumen, sive ad lumen deiforme, et ex Deo datum percipiendum, et secundum communicationem supereminentem gratiae spiritualis vel specialis: ut quemadmodum una 1028Agratia ad omnium participationem se diffundit, sic una omnibus cognominatio rationabiliter tribui possit. « Sed ut magis a nobis ratio dijudicata sit, considerabimus sacrae in eloquiis expressas sanctas, et decoras proprietates uniuscujusque coelestis dispositionis. » Ut magis possimus, inquit, judicare hanc rationem, utrum videlicet cognominationes angelicae communes esse debeant an non, considerabimus sanctas et decoras proprietates uniuscujusque coelestis dispositionis sacrae expressas in eloquiis. Ex proprietatibus enim uniuscujusque diligenter consideratis fortassis poterit agnosci, utrum communicatio nominationis eadem esse possit: quibus et si gratia una infunditur, una tamen mensura, ac proportione non datur.

EXPOSITION.

« This indeed is, » etc. In this fifth chapter it is inquired why all the heavenly essences are surnamed angels. But this question seems to have arisen from this: that in the sacred word certain of the heavenly spirits are declared sempe to stand by God and always to see his face; but certain others are said to be sent forth outward, to fulfill exterior ministries. For hence it seems to follow that those who always stand by the divine countenance do not go forth to announce exterior things; but those 1019Bwho are sent forth do not stand by the divine sight immovably, or immutably. For it is written in the book of the prophet Daniel: « Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood by him (Dan. VII). » In which distinction, by those who stand by seem to be signified those who do not go forth to exterior things; but by those who minister, those who, by going forth to exterior things, do not always stand by. On which account, because the inferior and lowest orders together go forth to exterior things, while only the superior and more excellent stand by the divine contemplation without intermission, those who stand by are declared to be fewer, but those who minister more. For since there are nine orders of angels, only two, that is, angels and archangels — inasmuch as they specially, from the distribution of their office, 1019Care appointed to be sent — have received their surname from the very thing. Angels, namely, are called messengers, but archangels chief messengers; since the former announce lesser things, the latter greater, as it were from the dignity of their ministry. But because again, in Holy Scripture, we read that certain ones of the superior orders were sent — as in Isaiah one of the seraphim is recorded to have flown to the prophet and to have touched his lips with a coal which he had taken with tongs from the altar (Isa. VI); and in the Epistle to the Hebrews the Apostle testifies that all are ministering spirits, and sent into ministry, for the sake of those who receive the inheritance of salvation (Hebr. I): a great difficulty of ambiguity arises for us, and what is rather to be asserted here is not easily found. The author solves this question in this manner. He testifies that the name of angels belongs 1019Donly to the inferior orders, and to those which, from their office, are properly appointed to announce exterior things. But because the divine secrets, which by those inferior ones are brought down outwardly to the knowledge of men, are announced to those same ones by the superior: the name of angels too is communicable to the superior: who, although they do not go forth to announce exterior things, nevertheless — themselves receiving from above the things which are to be announced outwardly, according to the law of the divine ordination, and by announcing carrying them across to the inferior orders that follow after them — and the superior participate in every virtue, and grace, and property of the inferior: and therefore the surnames of the inferior also pass over to the superior; but the virtue, and grace, and 1020Aproperty of the superior are not all communicable to the inferior, and therefore their surnames too, by a like reasoning, cannot universally be brought down to the inferior. Yet sometimes the inferior, when they take up the property of the superior from the quality of an office, assume their name too in the execution of that same office. Hence is that which we commemorated above, that the angel who had come to kindle and purge the lips of the prophet is called a seraph, because in the quality of this work he was carrying out the property of the one who kindles or inflames. But that which the Apostle says, that all are ministering spirits and sent into ministry, they think is to be understood in this way: that, as we said above, those too are not unfittingly said to be sent; 1020Bbecause, although they do not go forth to exterior things, nevertheless they bring the things which are to be announced outwardly, by announcing them to the inferior and following orders. Others think that all the heavenly orders, both superior and inferior, are directed to exterior things according to time, and place, and cause; yet that those which have this as proper from their office are specially surnamed angels or archangels. For that all are sometimes sent, the Apostle seems to assert by testimony, in that which we commemorated above, saying: « Are they not all ministering spirits, sent into ministry, for the sake of those who receive the inheritance of salvation? » But that even certain superior ones are sometimes directed to exterior things not from office, but from an accidental cause, the Psalmist seems to assert, when he says: « Who 1020Cmakes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire (Psal. CIII)." Thus, then, there are some who stand by from office; and others who go forth to fulfill exterior things; and yet those who stand by, being sometimes sent into ministry, while they take up the property of the inferior, assume their name too in signification. Who, nevertheless, when they go forth to exterior things, do not withdraw from the interior contemplation, because they behold him who is present to them wherever they go. And in this way indeed, before we should examine the words of the book, we thought that mention of a question of this kind should be made briefly, for the clearness of the things to be said — defining nothing rashly, but venerating the secret, of which perhaps to have been ignorant is a venial infirmity, 1020Dbut to assert presumptuously is a damnable rashness. This, however, must be known: that the author seems rather to lend his assent to that part which holds that only certain, not all, of the heavenly orders are sent to exterior things; and yet that, on account of the participation of the same property, by which the superior share the grace and virtue of the inferior, the names of the inferior too are assumed by the superior. Just as also sometimes the inferior, when they take up the property of the superior from the quality of an office, assume their name too in signification. Now to the text: « This indeed is, as far as concerns us, the cause of the angelic surname in the words. » « This, he says, is » — which we have said above — « the cause of the angelic surname; » namely because the divine secrets are announced to us through them, 1021Aand therefore, because they bring down to us the divine precepts by announcing them, as far as concerns us — that is, as far as regards that, or on account of that, which they work toward us — they assume the name of angels. But because this — that is, carry ye the messages of the interior teacher outward to the knowledge of men — whether it befits all is not yet proved by manifest reason or authority, it must now be inquired, he says, why in the sacred word he attributes the name of angels commonly to all the heavenly virtues.

This is what he says: « It is fitting, as I think, to search out for what cause the theologians call all the heavenly essences at once angels; but, uniting unto the manifestation, they specially name the angelic order of the supramundane dispositions themselves, 1021Bwhich completively terminates the divine and heavenly things; » as if he should say: This now remains to be inquired: why the theologians universally name all those heavenly natures angels, when nevertheless they specially name one order of them — namely of the spirits who come to us to manifest the supramundane dispositions themselves, that is, the spiritual, and divine, and invisible ordinations — the angelic order; « completively terminating the divine and heavenly things, » that is, leading through, unto completion and end, the things divinely disposed in a heavenly and secret ordination. For the divine precept, running down from the highest, is brought through the superior orders to the inferior, until at last, coming to the knowledge of men, it is completed in work: on which account 1021Cthat heavenly order too, to which the command of the divinity descends last of all through the powers placed above, and then through it is announced outwardly, is said to terminate it completively, or unto completion, because through its announcement it is brought to that place where it is last to be completed by visible operation. This, therefore, must be inquired: why, namely, although this last order is specially marked with the angelic surname, all the orders of the heavenly essences are named angels. « But before it, those placed above set in order the archangelic adornments, and the princes, and the powers, and the virtues, and whatever essences established above these the manifestative traditions of the words know. » As if he should say: The theologians indeed establish the angelic order itself 1021Das the last and latest, and nearest to human things, and as carrying forth the divine visions by a final announcement, and determining them; but before it they set in order those placed above, that is, they describe those placed above in the order. « The archangelic adornments, » that is, the choirs of the archangels, ordered and beautifully disposed, who in order are both superior to the angels themselves in dignity, and prior in announcement. Then the theologians themselves also establish — not only above the angels, but even above the archangels — the princes, that is, the principalities, and the powers, and the virtues, and other essences, that is, « whatever spiritual natures the manifestative traditions of the sacred words know, » that is, set forth to knowledge. Essences, I say, established above these, namely 1022Athe angels, or whatever others established above all these aforesaid, so that they are not only more sublime in dignity, but also stronger in firmness of perfection, and more stable unto eternity and immutability.

There follows: « But we say that, throughout every holy disposition, the excelling orders have the illuminations and virtues of the inferior dispositions; but they that do not participate in the things that excel them are last. » As if he should say: Since in that disposition of the heavenly spirits some are superior, others inferior, the superior indeed have every illumination and virtue of the inferior; but the inferior do not have all the illuminations and virtues of the superior orders. And therefore the names of the inferior 1022Bare sometimes transferred to the superior orders, inasmuch as these participate with them in the same properties of names. But the names of the superior cannot be so assumed by the inferior, since the properties of the names do not universally pass over to them: this is what he says: « But we say that, throughout every holy disposition » — namely of the heavenly spirits — « the excelling, » or superior, « orders have » all the illuminations and virtues « of the inferior dispositions, » that is, of the subject orders. But the last, that is, the inferior, and those following in order, do not participate — "in all," it is understood, the illuminations and virtues of those that excel them, that is, of those who are more excellent than they. We understand the illuminations 1022Cas being in the knowledge of truth; but the virtues as being in the love of goodness and the perfection of work.

There follows: « Therefore the theologians call the most holy orders of the most excellent essences angels. For they too are manifesters of the divine illumination. » Since he says that the higher orders have all the properties of the lower ones: therefore the theologians call the most holy orders of the most excellent essences — that is, of the most excellent spirits — angels; because they too partake of the angelic property, in this respect, that although they do not go out to announce outward things, nevertheless to those orders which follow after them they manifest, by transfusing and as it were by announcing, the divine illumination which they receive concerning themselves. « But the lowest order of the heavenly minds does not have 1022Dthe ground for being named archas, or thrones, or seraphim. » — « They do not have, he says, the ground, » those same theologians, « for naming the lowest order of the heavenly minds, » that is, the last order of the heavenly spirits, namely the angels, « archas, » that is princes, or thrones, or seraphim, because that lowest order of the angels is not in participation of the most exalted powers. For this reason the angels cannot be named princes, or thrones, or seraphim, as princes and thrones and seraphim are named angels; because the higher ones partake of the angelic property universally, whereas the angels do not partake universally of the illuminations and powers of the higher ones; and those very ones especially, for which the higher ones received their special surnames, the angels possess only in part 1023A, and yet they do not have the dignity and the property of that surname. For not everyone who has some power or property by partaking of it ought at once to be surnamed according to that property, unless he holds it either singularly among the rest or excellently above the rest. For not everyone who knows something is at once called wise; nor is he who has done something right forthwith called just. But he alone who holds wisdom and justice either singularly or excellently ought to be called wise and just by a proper and express surname. So then those heavenly orders of the holy spirits have proper surnames, in which is signified not what they have received singularly, but what they possess excellently. For the seraphim 1023B— because out of love of their Creator, as neighbors and those nearest, they both are burning in themselves and set others alight from themselves — are interpreted burning or kindling, not because they alone among the rest have this singularly, but because with the rest, and above the rest, excellently. For all burn with the love of God, and yet they especially ought to be called burning, who both first conceive the fire of that love and, burning more strongly, send out the flame of love to set the rest also alight. So too the cherubim (which name is interpreted fullness of knowledge) — because they have a greater knowledge of God than the rest — take their name from that alone which, possessing it with the rest, they merited to perceive more excellently than all the rest. The thrones too are so called, not because in them alone does God sit and discern 1023Chis judgments, but because they received this in their office more excellently than the rest, and on that account they draw their surname specially from it. And in this manner indeed the other orders too must be understood, namely, that each is believed to receive its proper surnames from that which it is proved to possess more excellently by the gift of grace.

But there arises a question not to be despised, and one which would bring great confusion to the mind if it were not examined by applying reason. For if, as has been said, in that heavenly arrangement each and every order draws its own surnames from that property in which they are proved to be more excellent than the rest, since the higher ones possess universally and excellently all the illuminations and 1023Dpowers of the subject orders, nothing singular is left to the orders placed beneath and following, from which they might obtain a surname proper to them and distinct among the rest. Whence it behooves us to consider more diligently in what way both are at once true: namely, that the higher ones possess universally and excellently the illuminations and gifts of the subject orders, and yet that each and every one retains something proper and special from which it can be marked by a proper and distinct appellation. For the seraphim by their name express a singular love. The cherubim, however, intimate a more excellent knowledge. But the thrones show a greater force of discernment. Yet it is established that those who love more ardently look more deeply, and discern more subtly. 1024AFor those who look from nearer at hand undoubtedly recognize more evidently. How then is the order of the cherubim said to be surnamed from the privilege of a singular grace, if another retains this more excellently in its office, from which the cherubim obtains its appellation? But this question is perhaps not unfittingly solved by this reasoning: yet only so, if the secret of truth be violated by no rashness of prejudgment. For it can come to pass that, although the higher orders possess more excellently all the gifts of the powers, nevertheless they draw their surname only from those which among the gifts of the powers themselves are the more sublime; and they leave the others, which follow in the order of dignity, to those following after them for their denomination, so that the first may obtain its name from the first, the second from the second, the third from the third. For we know, 1024BScripture bearing witness, that among all the gifts of the powers charity excels; wherefore it was consequent that that order which is the most eminent of all should take its singular appellation, in its own distinction, from charity alone, although it might possess the other gifts of the powers too more excellently, from which it could have taken its appellation and name. But because the knowledge of truth is recognized as next in dignity after the love of virtue: therefore from that same dignity those who are second are, after the first, deservedly surnamed angelic spirits. But the judgment of discerning truth, because it seems to have a verdict still as it were doubtful, and appears in a certain manner suspended by a less perfect knowledge; and therefore because it, after full contemplation, in which truth is not sought but 1024Cpossessed, looks back to that same knowledge of the highest truth, gave its name to the third order after the two former: this, however, must be understood according to man, for whose sake the names were given to those spirits themselves. For there judgment is not the settling of ambiguity, but the discernment of truth; nor there, where all things are manifest, is something that lies hidden discussed, but what is certain is esteemed according to its merit. Wherefore in this judgment too we hold that the knowledge of truth is to be preferred, since wisdom judges simplicity and unity; but judgment proves itself, through the force of discernment, to look toward diverse and contrary things. Whence the more excellent surname was to be taken from wisdom itself, by which the more excellent order was to be designated 1024D: which order, although, as more sublime and more perfect, it possessed both wisdom and judgment more fully, yet, taking its name from wisdom alone, left judgment as the surname of the order following after it. According to this consideration, therefore, whoever should wish to interpret the surnames of the angels, there will perhaps be no unfittingness, if the higher orders possess more perfectly all the gifts of the powers, and yet the lower orders have their proper surnames from certain gifts specially. But concerning the orders of the angels themselves, in the first and the last at least, the same opinion of all is established. For that the seraphim are placed in the highest place, and after them the cherubim, and then the thrones, can be unknown to no one who knows the testimonies of the holy Scriptures. 1025AIt is manifest too that, for the lower ones ascending from the bottom upward, the angels and archangels are placed first. The four following orders certain men arrange in this manner, that from the thrones downward they set first the dominations, then the principalities, then the powers, then the virtues, so that in this manner the nine orders are distinguished by three triads: of which the first and highest contains the seraphim, cherubim, thrones; the second and middle comprises the dominations, principalities, and powers; the third and lowest arranges together the virtues, archangels, and angels. And so from the bottom upward the angels are numbered first; then the archangels, then the virtues, then the powers, then the principalities, then the dominations, then the thrones, then the cherubim, then the seraphim. But the Theologian 1025Bplaces first the angels, then the archangels, then the principalities, and these he assigns to the first triad. But in the second he sets first the powers, then the virtues, then the dominations. And in the third he judges that first the thrones, afterward the cherubim, afterward the seraphim are to be placed, the progression being made from the lower to the higher. But in this threefold triple distinction it especially behooves us to consider this: that the highest three orders, that is, the seraphim, and the cherubim, and the thrones, by the power of their singular excellence and the force of their denomination, seem to look only toward the interior. For to love and to know and to judge is proper to those presiding within, and having their conversion toward the interior. But the last three, and lowest orders, by the property of their surname 1025C, are proved to be arranged toward outward things only according to the office of their ministry; whether the angels and archangels, in that they announce outwardly whatever is to be done and manifested to men; or the principalities, in that they dispense by invisible power whatever things are to be administered and arranged concerning men. But the middle orders, as in arrangement, so also in office, seem to be borne between the invisible and the visible things; and to administer, according to their dignity and office, the things which are to be brought down from the higher ones to the lower. And among these the dominations are first, which by a singular excellence form by command alone the invisible announcement in the virtues; but the virtues are second, which, executing the enjoined command, publish it in 1025Dthe powers. But the powers are third, which perfect the mandate conceived in the principalities, archangels, and angels, subjected to them for the operation. But those who set the virtues after the angels and archangels understand thereby, of course, those spirits through whom signs and miracles are more frequently done. In this too let the property of the last arrangement be preserved, whose ministry we hold to have been ordained for dispensing outward things alone. But the powers, they say, are those spirits so called who have the adverse virtues subjected to them, and freely restrain them according to the power given, lest they be able to harm as much as they will. But the principalities, they hold, are those spirits so named who are set over even the good spirits of the angels themselves: to whom, while they command whatever is to be done, 1026Athey act as princes over their subjects for the fulfilling of the divine ministries, and stand as superiors. But the dominations are those so called who surpass even the principalities by a more excellent power, so that they have as subjects even those who merited to command others for the fulfilling of the ministry. These things briefly concerning the orders of the angels, and their names, we thought had to be tasted beforehand as necessary for the coming narration, so that the reader, once these things are said, may take up the several matters — as reason and cause shall demand, to be recalled in what follows — that concern these things, and perhaps, without these, the obscure things that are to be said. Now let us return to explaining the sequence of the text itself. Above he said that the theologians do not have the ground for naming the angelic order archas, or thrones, or seraphim; because that angelic order 1026Bis not in participation of those most exalted powers, so as to partake with them in name, when it does not partake in the property of the name. Now he proves this same thing by the following words, namely, that the angelic order does not partake of the most exalted powers. It does not, he says, partake with them; but what it partakes, it partakes from them. For it is one thing to partake in the fullness, and another to receive participation from the fullness. And so the angelic order is subjected to the most exalted powers in such a way that it does not partake with them, but from them; because, just as it, by illuminating and instructing, leads back those men who are led back to divine knowledge, so also it receives divine illumination from those powers which are before it.

1026CThis is what he says: « As it, » namely the angelic order, « leads back our divine highest priests, » that is, the holy men who received the sacred divine things immediately from the angels and handed them on to us, « to the splendors of the divinity known to it, » that is, the divine knowledge which it received, and, having received, bestowed, « so also it is led back by the virtues of the essences which are before it, » that is, before it, or above it, « the virtues, I say, pure, » that is, exceedingly sacred, or wholly sacred, so that by the excellence of holiness they can be a form of perfection to those subject to them. And these same « virtues are also sacred toward the divine, » namely, toward what is to be conferred; that is, toward the knowledge of divinity to be given, « to the arrangement consummating the angelic hierarchies, » 1026Dthat is, to the arrangement which perfects, or contains as perfected, or terminates the angelic hierarchies; this is, namely, the last arrangement, in which both the angelic order, in that it is perfected, is consummated, and, in that it is last, the hierarchies of all spirits are terminated. Indeed, here the execrable error of the interpreter must be guarded against, who supposed that the celestial virtues are called unclean. For the Greek πανιερὸν panieron, which is interpreted exceedingly sacred, or wholly sacred, or universally sacred, he thought was here to be understood as ἀνιερὸν anieron, that is, unsacred, or not sacred, or without the sacred.

There follows: « Unless indeed someone should also say this: that all the angelic namings are common, according to the subjection of all the celestial virtues to the deiform, and 1027AGod-given light, and their supereminent communication. » The lower orders cannot, he says, take up the names of the higher, because they do not partake in the same excellence of virtues with them, unless one should wish to say that, for this reason, all the namings of the angels ought to be common, because all alike, as subjects, perceive the one light given by God, and from that same perceived light all are made conformed to God, and exist as partakers of one supereminent communication in one light. Unless, he says, someone should also say this: that all the angelic surnames are common, according to the subjection of all the celestial virtues into the light, or toward the deiform and God-given light to be perceived, and according to the supereminent communication of spiritual or special grace: so that, just as one 1028Agrace diffuses itself for the participation of all, so one surname may reasonably be attributed to all. « But, that the reason may be more judged by us, we shall consider the holy and comely properties, expressed in the sacred oracles, of each celestial arrangement. » That we may be more able, he says, to judge this reason — namely, whether the angelic surnames ought to be common or not — we shall consider the holy and comely properties of each celestial arrangement, expressed in the sacred oracles. For from the properties of each, diligently considered, it will perhaps be able to be recognized whether the communication of the naming can be the same: to whom, even if one grace is infused, yet it is not given in one measure and proportion.

TITULUS CAPITULI VI. Quae sit prima coelestium essentiarum dispositio: quae media, et quae ultima.

TITLE OF CHAPTER VI. What is the first arrangement of the celestial essences: what the middle, and what the last.

LITTERA.

  • 1027B

Quanti quidem sunt et quales supercoelestium essentiarum ornatus, et quomodo secundum eos Hierarchiae perficiuntur, solam diligenter scire dico contemplativam eorum perfectionis principem; adhuc et eos ignorare proprias virtutes et illuminationes, et suam sacram, et superornatam ordinationem.
