Non ergo dici potest a nobis bonum illud, quod illos beatos animos per gaudium aeternae contemplationis juxta se immobiles tenet, ut ad caduca non effluant; et rursum per desiderium movens ad se trahit, ut ipsum incessabili dilectione appetant. Sed ne omnino taceatur, quod prorsus dici non potest, audi quid sit, quod illos et tenet juxta se, et trahit ad se. Bonum quoddam, et magnum supra 1063Cbona ista omnia, quae nosti, aliud prorsus non solum differentia, sed supereminentia, ut tamen secundum haec, quae nosti, bona tibi insinuetur, et notum fiat, sicut potest esse, dicamus: lumen est et dulcedo bonum illud. Quare lumen? quia oculos clarescere facit. Quare dulcedo? quia reficit. Duo sunt ista apud nos magna bona, et non inveniuntur alia majora his, neque ad gaudium vel ad felicitatem nostram magis operantia: lumen et dulcedo. Alterum est ad illuminationem, alterum ad refectionem. Si illuminaris et non satiaris, magnum bonum est sed non plenum. Si satiaris et non illuminaris; magnum item bonum est sed non perfectum. Refectio jucundum facit, quod intus est; illuminatio 1063Djucundum exhibet, quod foris est, utrumque ad gaudium plenum exigitur. Si enim in altero reficeris, et in altero afficeris, non est laetitia perfecta, cui tristitia mista est. Quaere ergo refectionem, ut jucundum tibi sit quod in te est, quaere et illuminationem, ut jucundum tibi sit, quod extra te est. Videtur quidem refectio magis necessaria esset, quemadmodum magis proprium est tibi bonum, quod in te est, quam quod extra te est bonum. Verumtamen illuminatio contemplationis quantum jucunditatis apponit? Dulce lumen, et delectabile oculis videre solem. Aspice mundum istum, qui multa spectacula jucunditatis praebet? Et omnia haec per sapientia Dei facta sunt. Totum quod vides, inde exivit, ubi ratio, et causa est omnium. Si ergo tam pulchrum 1064Aest videre dispositionem et formam operis; quam jucundum esse putas et delectabile sapientiam artificis contemplari? Noli autem cogitare, quia una sapientia nominatur quasi solitariam quamdam et fastidiosam contemplationem videntium illam, una est, sed non ita una. Quomodo enim putas esse unam sapientiam Dei? Forte, quemadmodum dicis essentiam unam, speciem unam et formam unam, locum unum et tempus unum: haec omnia numero unum sunt. Quid est numero? discretione. Quid est numero? parvitate. Quid est numero? imperfectione. Sic enim numeras hoc et illud. Cum enim numeras, dicis hoc et non illud. Quod ergo unitate numeratur, unitate separatur; et eadem unitate probatur ab omnibus esse diminutum, a quibus ostenditur 1064Bipsa unitate discretum. Nunquid sapientiam Dei ita unam esse putas? Ergo ipsam numeras, et dicis, recte hoc, et non illud. Si ergo ipsa est, et non illud; ergo non totum est ipsa; et aliquid est extra ipsam, quod non est in ipsa. Si totum in ipsa est, totum ipsa est; quomodo tu dicis hoc et non illud ipsa est? Noli ergo numerare. Scriptura tibi dicit: « Sapientia ejus non est numerus. Omnia, quae ex ipsa sunt, in numero facta sunt et pondere, et mensura. Ipsa autem sub numero non est; » in qua vera unitas est sine parvitate, et universitas sine multiplicitate; nec sub pondere est, inaestimabilis; nec sub mensura, incomprehensibilis. Quid ergo putas esse videre sapientiam Dei? Quando mundum istum vides, quanta in ipsos vides? Et totum 1064Choc inde venit; et ibi est totum, ubi est sapientia Dei. Et quid dico totum hoc? Parum enim est hoc, ut in sapientia Dei non aliud sit. Si intelligit opus suum Deus, et seipsum non intelligit, quae est sapientia ista? Plus enim est quod est Deus quam quod est factum a Deo. Si ergo novit quod fecit, et non novit quod est ipse qui fecit; quod majus est ignorat, et non est sapientia perfecta in eo. Si cor tuum capere potest, et comprehendere ea quae facis et quae explicas opere, universa ratione intus dictante disponis, et quae facturus es omnia prius in ratione concipis; et cum ad opus exeunt, a ratione non recedunt: quomodo in aeterna ratione Conditoris non esse potest omne 1064Dquod factum est? Rursum si parum est animo rationali videre et comprehendere quae foris sunt, nisi ea quae intus sunt, multo majora et mirabiliora contempletur, et majus agnoscit esse quod ipse est, quam omne quo extra ipsum est: non potest aeternus artifex in ea sapientia, qua videt omne quod ipse fecit, ignorare quod majus omnibus est; quod est ipse qui fecit. Attende ergo quae sit sapientia ista, in qua sunt omnia quae facta sunt, et praeter omnia, et super omnia, quod majus omnibus est ille, a quo omnia facta sunt. Qualis putas est species ista, in qua tanta pulchritudo est? Cum ergo audis sapientiam Dei nominari, hoc totum cogita, hoc totum in ipsa est; et ipsam videre, totum hoc videre est. In ipsa videntur omnia quae facta sunt; 1065Aet in ipsa videtur a quo omnia facta sunt. Propterea summi illi spiritus, qui per excellentiam supereminentis gratiae immediate appropinquant, ab ipsa illuminantur ad contemplandam ipsam, et in ejus contemplatione vident, et quod factum est per ipsam, et quod est in ipsa, et eum qui per ipsam fecit in quo est ipsa. Istae ergo sunt contemplationes, quas pure videt prima hierarchia, ad simplos fulgores immediate illuminata, quae contemplationes et multae sunt, in quantum illic omnia videntur; et beatae sunt, quia cum omnibus ille etiam qui fecit omnia videtur. Non enim praeter ipsum videtur quod in ipso videtur, quia et unum est quod videtur, quod ipse est; et in ipso uno omnia videntur, in quo omnia unum et unum omnia est. Vide quam 1065Bmultae sunt contemplationes, ubi nihil omnium absconditur, quam beatae contemplationes, ubi in summo bono cuncta videntur; ubi videre et habere; amare et gustare bonum idem est; ubi non videtur, nisi veritas; non amatur, nisi bonitas. Duo sunt enim, cognitio et amor. Alterum ad illuminationem pertinet; alterum ad refectionem. Cognitio illuminat, dilectio satiat. Cognitio veritatis, amor bonitatis: in his beatitudo constat cognoscere et amare bonum. « Gustate, inquit Scriptura, et videte, quoniam suavis est Dominus (Psal. XXXIII). » In « gustate » dilectio; in « videte » cognitio est. Duo ista distincte commendat, scilicet cognitionem et dilectionem. « Multas quidem, et beatas videns pure contemplationes simplosque, et immediate fulgores 1065Cilluminata. » Hoc de illuminatione et cognitione dictum est.

Sequitur: « Divino alimento repleta. Multa quidem primo data fusione, solaque domestica, et unifica divinae refectionis unitate. » Hoc dictum est de dilectione et refectione. Utramque multis modis commendat. Primo cognitionem in contemplationibus multis et beatis pure visis per illuminationem fulgorum simplicium. Qui sunt simplices fulgores? purae illuminationes. Per puras illuminationes venitur ad puras contemplationes. Pura illuminatio est quando veritas per semetipsam concipitur; pura contemplatio est quando veritas in semetipsa videtur. Quando per subjectam imaginem vel figuram 1065Dveritas addiscitur, non est pura illuminatio; quando in subjecta imagine vel figura veritas cognoscitur, non est pura contemplatio. Neque enim simplicitas esse potest, nisi ubi solum est; neque puritas, nisi ubi verum est. Simplicitas in solo; puritas in vero. Propterea qui immediate contemplantur, et per semetipsos ad veritatem accedunt, soli simplices illuminationes habent et puras contemplationes.

Sequitur: « Divino alimento repleta. » Quod est divinum alimentum? divina refectio. Et ipsa refectio quae est, nisi Dei dilectio? Propterea cum dixisset, « Supereminentem illam dispositionem angelicam repletam divino alimento, » adjunxit etiam, dicens: « repletam unitate divinae refectionis. » Quid autem est divina refectio, nisi divinum alimentum? 1066AUnitas ergo refectionis, et unitas alimenti una est refectio, et unum alimentum. Ergo in mensa Dei non nisi unum ferculum apponitur. Sed noli contemnere. Satietas multa est. « Satiabor, » inquit Psalmista, « cum apparuerit gloria tua (Psal. XVI). » Multa in hoc mundo sunt, et haec omnia cor hominis satiare non possunt. Unum autem bonum est apud Deum, et hoc solum cum percipitur, satietas invenitur. Ergo non in multitudine, sed in unitate satietas est. Quando satietas? quando satis est satietas. Pone modo, ut ex his multis, quae in mundo sunt, quaedam aliqua habeas, quae diligis et videbis, quod non sufficit. Veniant plura: adhuc non dices, sufficit. Apponantur universa; et invenies te egentem adhuc, et nondum satis habentem. In omnibus ergo his satietas 1066Besse non potest, ubi satis esse non potest. Veniet autem unum illud bonum; et satietas erit, quia satis erit. Non mireris. Omnia haec multa sunt, sed multum non sunt. Illud unum est, et multum est. Propterea peccatrix illa quia multa dimittenda habuit, non multa sed multum dilexit. Multa dimisit, et multum elegit. Sapiens erat; non attendit acervum, sed pretium pensavit. In multis parum; in uno multum. Propterea non atttendas ad numerum, sed fructum inquire. Unum est bonum, quod tibi praeparavit Deus. Noli timere cum audis unum; unum bonum est, sed in illo bono omne bonum est. Unam refectionem, unum cibum, unum ferculum, unum panem praeparavit, sed ne despicias. Audi quod scriptum est: « Habentem omnem saporem, et 1066Comne oblectamentum suavitatis (Sap. XV). » Hoc divinum alimentum, et multa fusio, vel abundans effusio, qua videlicet fusione beata illa societas primo loco sibi data repletur. Est etiam unitas divinae refectionis, qua scilicet unitate sola, hoc est singulari et domestica, et unifica specialiter digna effecta est. Ipsa vero una, et simplex divina refectio, idcirco singularis dicitur, quia cum aliena delectatione et dulcedine extranea non percipitur; domestica, quia amicis tantum et familiaribus praeparatur. Unifica, quia unum secum efficit omnes, quibus se sumendam et participandam concedit.

Sequitur: « Multaque communione Dei et cooperatione: » subauditur repleta est dispositio, vel hierarchia 1066Dprima coelestium essentiarum. Ipsa dico, digna effecta ad eam, scilicet communionem et cooperationem Dei, ut possibile sibi est; similitudine bonarum habitudinum, id est virtutum et actionum. Per bonas enim habitudines, digna effecta est communione; per bonas actiones, digna cooperatione. Et rectus est ordo. Primum per claritatem cognitionis illuminatur; postea per dulcedinem dilectionis reficitur, ut sic Deo et communicet in virtute, et cooperetur in actione, sicut scriptum est: « Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum servabit; et Pater meus diliget eum, et ad eum veniemus, et mansionem apud eum faciemus (Joan. XIV). »

Sequitur: « Multaque divinorum superposite cognoscens, et divinae scientiae et cognitionis in participatione, 1067Asecundum quod fas est, facta. » Hoc est, ipsa hierarchia cognoscens est multa divinorum, id est multa de divinis, sive de Deo superposite, id est excellenter super alias hierarchias « et facta est in participatione, » hoc est, particeps facta est divinae scientiae et cognitionis divinae, secundum quod fas est illi, id est concessum.

Sequitur: « Propterea et laudes ipsius theologia iis qui in terra sunt, tradidit in quibus mirabiliter manifestatur excelsissimae ipsius illuminationis eminentia. » Ac si diceret: Quia tanta est excellentia hierarchiae primarum essentiarum, propterea theologia, id est divina Scriptura tradidit iis, qui in terra sunt, hoc est, hominibus, laudes sive laudationes ipsius. In quibus scilicet laudationibus 1067Bmirabiliter manifestatur eminentiam excelsissimae illuminationis ipsius. Ac si diceret: Quia tanta est sublimitas ejus, propterea theologia hominibus laudationes ejus, quibus ipsa Deum laudat, manifestavit, ut per excellentiam laudationis manifestaretur eminentia illuminationis.

Sequitur: « Alii enim quidam ejus sensibiliter dicendo tanquam vox aquarum reboant. Benedicta gloria Domini ex loco suo. » Ac si diceret: Vere excellentes sunt laudationes hujus hierarchiae, quae a Scriptura divina manifestantur, quia alii ejus, id est quidam ex ea sensibiliter sonando reboant, vel resonant, sive clamant tanquam vox aquarum: Benedicta gloria Domini ex loco suo. Vel sic legi potest. Theologia tradidit laudes ipsius sensibiliter, id est 1067Cper similitudinem sensibilium, et corporalium de spiritalibus dicendo, quod « alii ejus. » Hoc est, de numero ipsius « reboant tanquam vox aquarum. Benedicta gloria Domini ex loco suo. » Hoc testimonium de Ezechiele sumptum est, ubi propheta vocem commotionis magnae post se factam commemorat. Quae vox, quamvis ibi prolata non dicitur, tamen iste a summis eam coelestium ordinum spiritibus sine ambiguitate factam esse testatur.

Sequitur: « Alii vero illam valde laudabilem et piissimam reclamant theologiam: Sanctus, sanctus sanctus: Dominus Deus Sabaoth. Plena omnis terra gloria ipsius (Isa. VI). » Hoc testimonium de Isaia sumptum est, ubi duo seraphim volantes alter ad 1067Dalterum, hanc theologiam, id est divinam allocutionem, sive laudationem ad invicem proclamasse commemorantur.

Sequitur: « Has autem excelsissimas coelestium animorum hymnologias, jam quidem in iis, quae sunt de divinis laudibus, quantum possibile, aperuimus. Et dictum est de his in illis quantum ad nos, sufficienter. » Has supradictas hymnologias, id est divinas laudationes coelestium animorum, hoc est, coelestium spirituum; dicit se aperuisse, vel exposuisse, quantum sibi possibile fuit, in aliis Scripturis, quae sunt ab ipso factae de divinis laudibus; et de his scilicet hymnologiis, in illis (subauditur) Scripturis sufficienter dictum esse testatur, quantum ad eum, hoc est ad ejus possibilitatem pertinuit. Haec 1068Aautem Scriptura, quam se de divinis laudibus fecisse asserit, inter haec ejus scripta, quae apud nos sunt, minime reperitur. Ex hac tamen sententia possumus cognoscere de divinis laudibus ipsum scripsisse, quoniam in libro de divinis nominibus ex amatoriis hymnis sancti Hierothei quaedam introduxit, in quibus de supradictis laudibus nonnihil tractatur.

Sequitur: « Ex quibus in recordationem sufficit dicere tantum secundum praesens tempus, quod theologicam scientiam ipsa prima dispositio, quantum fas, illuminata est a divina bonitate, per quam tanquam deiformem hierarchiam et aliis seipsam deinde tradidit. » Ac si diceret: Ex quibus, scilicet laudibus divinis in supra memorato libro sufficienter 1068Bexpositis, nunc secundum praesens tempus in recordationem, vel admonitionem tantum sufficit dicere hoc, scilicet quod ipsa prima dispositio, hoc est, prima hierarchia angelorum illuminata est theologicam, id est divinam scientiam ab ipsa divina bonitate. Nota constructionem in eo quod ait, illuminata scientiam. Sic enim dicitur: Erudior autem, doceor disciplinam. Dicit ergo, quod prima dispositio a sola divina bonitate illuminata est ad scientiam; per quam videlicet scientiam ipsa dispositio tradidit seipsam; deinde, hoc est, consequenter aliis hierarchiis post se sequentibus. « Tradidit, » dico, « seipsam tanquam deiformem hierarchiam, » hoc est, Dei conformitatem et similitudinem habentem, et Deum imitantem in eo quod ab ipso illuminata 1068Calios illuminat, et seipsis quasi formam, et exemplar proponit divinae conformitatis. Hoc ergo nunc sufficit dicere de supradictis laudibus, quod in eis prima dispositio angelorum Creatorem suum laudans, formam laudandi aliis post sequentibus hierarchiis semetipsam tradidit, « subintroducens, » hoc est, suggerens eis, vel insinuans « illud per brevitatem dicendo. » Subintroduxit enim, vel suggessit quasi occultum quiddam, et paucis manifestum. Suggessit autem per brevitatem dicendo aliud quod suggessit. Et recte nonnisi occulte suggerebatur, quod erat invisibile, et nonnisi breviter dicebatur, quod erat ineffabile. Quantumcunque enim exponeretur ad cognitionem, ocultum esset, quod erat impenetrabile; 1068Det quantumcunque extenderetur per sermonem, breve esset ad ipsum, quod erat interminabile. Suggessit tamen, et insinuavit, et exposuit, ut per eam ad aliorum cognitionem veniret, quod ipsa nullo mediante perceperat. Quid suggessit?

Audi: « Ipsam piissimam, et summe benedictam, et omnino benedictam divinitatem, fas est benedictam esse ex Deum recipientibus quantum possibile est eam cognosci, et laudari intellectibus. Ipsi enim sunt tanquam deiformes divini loci, divinae, ut eloquia aiunt, quietis. » Exponit supra memoratum testimonium de Ezechiele sumptum. « Benedicta gloria Domini ex loco suo. » Ipsa, inquit, prima hierarchia clamans, « benedicta gloria Domini ex loco 1069Asuo, » docet, quod fas est, hoc est justum, vel debitum, vel dignum, ipsam piissimam et summe benedictam, et omnino benedictam divinitatem, benedictam esse ex intellectibus Deum recipientibus et in tantum benedictam, quantum possibile est eam cognosci et laudari. Justum est, inquit, ut ipsa divinitas, quae in se semper piissima est, parata scilicet largiri, et non indigens accipere: et quae summe benedicta est, et omnino, vel fortissime benedicta, hoc est, cujus gloria in semetipsa tanta est, ut nec alieno beneficio augeri, nec aliena laude amplius commendari possit. Fas, inquit, est, ut quamvis in se ita perfecta sit, ut benedici, vel laudari non egeat: tamen ut intellectus, id est, corda rationalia, eam benedicant et laudent, quantum scilicet eam cognoscere, 1069Bet secundum cognitionem perceptam laudare possunt. Quamvis enim gloria ejus ex semetipsa perfecta sit, nos tamen a benedictione et laude ejus cessare non debemus: qui et si benedicendo et laudando illi non perficimus, perficimur tamen ex illa. Vel aliter intelligi potest, quod dicit, justum esse, ut divinitas, quae in se summe benedicta est, ex intellectibus Deum recipientibus benedicatur. Ac si diceret: Quamvis laus Dei in semetipsa summe perfecta sit, hoc tamen laudi ejus jure addicitur, quod per gratiam corda a se facta inhabitare dignatur. Sic ergo justum est divinitatem in semetipsa summe benedictam pro eo etiam benedici, et benedictam esse, quod se mentibus beatificandis recipiendam praebet, et eas tanquam locum proprium 1069Cinhabitare dignatur. Non enim ita in eis habitat quasi stabilimentum quaerens, et velut ruitura, si fulcimentum non habeat. Non enim locum quaerit Deus sibi, quasi esse non posset, nisi contineretur; sed quasi receptaculum quaerit cui se infundendum praestet: quod utique beatum esse non posset, nisi ab ipso repleretur. Adjicitur ergo super omnem laudem ejus, quod summe benedictus in se alios benedictos facit ex se. Benedicatur ab illis, benedicatur et pro illis. Ab illis benedicatur quantum illis cognoscendus et laudandus revelatur; pro illis benedicatur, quantum in illis manifestatur.

Sequitur: « Ipsi enim sunt tanquam deiformes divini loci, divinae, ut eloquia aiunt, quietis. » Reddit causam, quare ex eo, quod dictum est, « benedicta 1069Dgloria Domini ex loco suo: » signatum intelligat, gloriam benedictam esse debere ex intellectibus Deum recipientibus, quia, inquit, ipsi intellectus Deum recipientes, ipsi sunt loci divini. Theodocos enim Graece dicitur, hoc est, Dei receptor. Quo nomine omnis purus animus sive humanus, sive angelicus potest significari. In ipsis enim duobus Deus habitat, et quiescit. Ipsi ergo tanquam deiformes divini loci sunt. Quasi rationem reddit, quare divini loci dicuntur. Eadem enim causa est, quare loci sunt, et quare deiformes sunt. Ex eo quippe, quod lumen capiunt, locus luminis fiunt. Et rursum ex eo ipso, quod lumen capiunt, lucentes fiunt, et conformes lumini existunt. Sunt ergo divini loci, utpote 1070Adeiformes, et ex inhabitante Deo Dei similitudinem habentes. Rursum quia loci divini sunt, constat quod divinae quietis loci sunt, quia divini loci omnino esse non possent, nisi quietis et pacis loci essent, sicut eloquia aiunt: « In pace factus est locus ejus (Psal. LXXV). »

Sequitur: « Et quod monas est, et unitas tres substantialiter: et super coelestibus essentiis usque ad novissima terrae extendens bonitatem suam in omnia, quae sunt, providentiam tanquam omnis essentiae super principale principium, et causa, et omnium superessentialiter immensurabili continentia circumligans. » Hoc de sequentis expositione, quod de Isaia sumptum fuerat, adjungit. Ac si diceret: Sicut prima illa coelestis hierarchia clamans, 1070B« benedicta gloria Domini de loco suo, » Deum non solum in se, sed in sanctis etiam suis benedicendum et glorificandum esse docuit, ita quoque ter sanctum proclamando, et non dominos, sed Dominum Sabaoth subjungendo, tres personas in una Deitate, non tres deos, sed unum Deum esse significavit. Hoc est, quod dicit. Et quia monas est, et unitas tres substantialiter, quasi diceret: Non solum hoc, quod supradictum est de gloria Domini ex loco suo benedicenda ipsa prima hierarchia coelestis sequentibus se hierarchiis subintroduxit; sed etiam hoc, quod monas, et unitas, hoc est divinitas, quae vere una est, et simplex natura, tres personae est substantialiter, hoc est, quod tres personae una essentia vel substantia, et una essentia tres personae; 1070Cquia Deus in essentia unus est, et trinus in personis. Sane quod monas et unitas cum idem esse videatur, geminate positum est, pro Graeco factum est: in quo duo nomina sunt monas, et henas: quae quamvis unam habeant apud nos interpretationem (utrumque enim sonat unitas) haec tamen differentia esse videtur, quod monas illam magis unitatem significat, quae secundum discretionem dicitur henas vero illam, quae secundum simplicitatem notatur. Omne enim, quod simplex est, unum est. Non autem omne, quod unum est, simplex est; quoniam et unum collectione dicitur et unum compositione, et unum similitudine. Quae omnia, quia non totum, quod sunt unum sunt vere unum non sunt, et unitatis nomen similitudine tantum mutuantur, non proprietate. 1070DDivinae autem naturae, cui unum est et simplex esse, totum quod est, vere unum esse est et ideo recte non solum monas, sed henas quoque appellari debuit; quia unitas ejus in vera ejusdem atque indivisae substantiae semper simplicitate subsistit. Dicat ergo, quia in vera Deitate monas et unitas substantialiter sunt; quia, sicut trinitas personarum in Deo essentiae unitatem non dividit, ita unitas naturae trinitatem personarum non confundit. Sed tres unum substantialiter sunt, quibus tribus substantia est una.

Sequitur: « Et super coelestibus essentiis usque ad novissima terrae extendens bonitatem suam in omnia, quae sunt providentiam. » Et hoc, inquit, 1071Aprima hierarchia sequentibus post se insinuavit: quod vera unitas, et summa trinitas extendit, vel penetrare facit bonitatem suam a super coelestibus essentiis, usque ad novissima terrae, id est, a summis usque ad ima; bonitatem, dico existentem providentiam in omnia, quia omnibus providet et nihil a se alienum relinquit, ut pote quae est super principale, vel super essentiale principium omnis essentiae, et causa omnium; quia ab ipsa, et ad ipsam facta sunt omnia: et quae est omnium 1072Acircumligans, id est circumligatio, quia circumligat omnia, et complectitur, et continet superessentialiter cum immensurabili continentia, quae totum comprehendit, et in ipsa incomprehensibilis manet. Quia ergo principium est, a quo facta sunt omnia, et causa per quam facta sunt omnia, et circumligans continentia, in qua subsistunt universa, Idcirco plena est omnis terra gloria ejus, quoniam ab ipsa bonitate replentur, et nutriuntur omnia, ut subsistant in ipsa, quae facta sunt per ipsam.

BOOK SEVEN. Exposition of the remaining part of the seventh chapter of the divine Dionysius the Areopagite on the celestial hierarchy, the text of which has been set out above.

  • 1045

1045ALong leisures demand a new beginning. A little above we had entered upon the discourse concerning the surname of the angels, where the author shows why such surnames or appellations have been attributed to the several orders of the angels. And concerning the first, and highest, order indeed, which is surnamed Seraphim, we have pursued, according to our capacity, the account of that appellation which has been given by theology. Now it remains that we also consider the account which he renders of the surname of the following order. He had first said that the surname, or manifestation, of the Seraphim teaches « their mobile, and the unceasing, and the hot, and the keen, and the superfervent, » which were added after these: but now he brings in and says that the surname, 1045Bor manifestation, of the Cherubim teaches « their knowable, and the deiform, » etc. For he says: « But the Cherubim itself. » Two things are to be repeated from what precedes, "the surname" and "teaches." As if he should say: The very surname of the Cherubim teaches, that is, in that they are surnamed Cherubim, which is interpreted fullness of knowledge, there is taught and signified « their knowable, » that is, the knowledge or acquaintance and science which they have; and by this name there is signified also « their deiform, » that is, the vision of God which is in them, because through the light of wisdom implanted in them they clearly contemplate the majesty of their Creator. There is signified also « the receptive of the highest bestowal of lights: » that is, it is signified that they have received the lights divinely given most highly 1045Cand most perfectly. For in that they are signified, by their very surname, to have the fullness of knowledge, they are assuredly taught to have received the light of that same wisdom from elsewhere; because, according to the saying of the Apostle: « If they had not received it, they could not have had it at all (I Cor. IV). » But in that they have it, reception is noted; in that they have the fullness, advance is noted. And the order is this, that first they receive the light of wisdom divinely given, and afterward, illumined by that same light, they see and know God, the author of the light. Well, therefore, are they illumined, who are so illumined that they see and know him by whom they are illumined. Many are illumined that they may see other things, and see not him himself through whom they see. But it is no great thing to see a work, if you 1045Dknow not the craftsman. A thing made cannot beatify, if you do not reach to the beauty of the one who wrought it. Therefore the surname of the Cherubim teaches « their knowable, and the deiform, and the receptive of the highest streaming-in of light. » Note the unusual compositions in that he says "deiform," and "streaming-in of light." The surname of the Cherubim teaches 1046Aalso, namely, their contemplative in the first working power of the divine beauty, and their repleteness of wise handing-down, and their communicative of the copious wisdom given for the outpouring unto the second beings. Distinguish thus: The surname of the Cherubim teaches the contemplative of the divine beauty in the first working power. For in that they are called Cherubim, that is, full of knowledge, it is shown that through the light of the wisdom given they contemplate the divine beauty; since assuredly, whatever they knew, they would not be full of wisdom, if they did not know the divine beauty, from which, and in which, all things are beautifully and reasonably ordered. Because, therefore, they are full of wisdom, they assuredly contemplate the divine beauty. Nor do they contemplate it in any way whatever, 1046Bbut in the first working power, so that, namely, being first and principally illumined by God, they may illumine the rest that come after them. For the divine power works first, and principally, and of itself in those who are nearest; but afterward through them in the others who follow. This, therefore, the surname of the Cherubim teaches, namely that the contemplation of the divine beauty is in them through the first working power; because God works first in them, that afterward he may work through them. It teaches also the repleteness of the wise handing-down, that is, it teaches that they are replete with divine grace: which by the wise handing-down of the Creator is distributed in participation to some more, and to some less. A wondrous excellence of theirs, therefore, is shown, because of that good which the wisdom 1046Cof the Creator handed down unequally unto the beauty of the universe, they are proclaimed to have not a part but the fullness. It can also be distinguished otherwise, so that it be said that the surname of the Cherubim teaches their contemplative replete, that is, their contemplation replete with the divine beauty, and with the wise handing-down, in the first working power. And it can be understood, not unfittingly, by the divine beauty and the wise handing-down, that the divine wisdom effects a greater beauty in its works from this very thing, that it did not settle its gifts to be participated by all in one and the same mode. Of which beauty, indeed, and of which handing-down, those highest spirits are for this reason replete; because the gifts which were given in part to the lower and subject beings, they have merited 1046Dto possess according to the fullness.

There follows: « And the communicative of the wisdom given copiously for the outpouring unto the second beings. » Again it must be repeated from what precedes. The surname of the Cherubim teaches their communicative, that is, the communication, or participation, of the wisdom given copiously for the outpouring, 1047Athat is, that in communicating they participate not slightly, but copiously, in the wisdom given to them for the outpouring. Which outpouring, namely, was first made in them copiously, that through them it might afterward be made unto the second beings: inasmuch as the light of wisdom, which is first poured copiously into them from above, is afterward through them transfused unto the second, that is, the following orders, to be illumined. This fullness, therefore, and dignity, and excellence in the gift of wisdom, and in the light of truth, the surname of the Cherubim teaches.

There follows: « But it itself, of the highest and compacted seats, diligently to be exalted from all the ignominy of subjection, and bearing upward supramundanely unto the summit, and by every extremity ineffably unto the most sublime, and about the truly lofty placed with all its powers unchangeably 1047Band stably: and receptive of the divine coming-upon in all impassibility and immateriality, and God-bearing, and in a servile manner opened unto the divine receptions. » After the surname of the Seraphim, and of the Cherubim, he passes to explaining the surname of the Thrones. As if he should say: As the surname of the Seraphim signifies the ardor of love, and the surname of the Cherubim the brightness of knowledge, so also the surname of the Thrones signifies the loftiness of dignity, for the reason that the invisible Founder, sitting in them, through them disposes all subject things by judging. For on account of this dignity and excellence of the divine judgment, which is exercised through them, he named the Thrones themselves the highest and compacted seats; the highest, 1047Con account of their dignity; compacted, on account of their truth. For it is manifest that thrones are the seats of those who reign and judge. And to the one reigning belongs sublimity, but to the one judging belongs truth. And therefore he deservedly named the Thrones themselves the highest seats, because he who reigns in them has no superior; and compacted, because he who judges in them does not depart from the truth. What is "compacted"? Fitly and suitably joined together. See the joining of the seats of God. The joining of the seats of God is the fittingness of judgments. Every judgment infers one thing from another. From fault, punishment; from justice, glory; from merit, reward; from the quality of the work, the quality of the retribution. It finds fault, it adjudges punishment. It finds justice, it adjudges glory. Well is it joined, that seat is compacted. Well does it accord and 1047Dfitly cohere. Punishment to fault, glory to justice. If glory were joined to fault, and punishment to justice, they would not accord with one another, nor would the judgment have a compacted seat. The compaction, therefore, of the seats is the truth of the judgments. But it must be known that every lower judgment, when it comes into question or contradiction, is wont to take from a higher either testimony or confirmation. But the highest judgment, because it has not another above itself by which it may be confirmed; by right the seats of God are named not only compacted through truth, but also highest through dignity. But if we read not "compacted," but "raised up," which from the ambiguity of the Greek word can likewise be understood: this is signified, that those heavenly spirits, over whom God presides for judging, have merited to be singularly high 1048Ain glory, not through the loftiness of nature, but through the raising-up of grace. Let him say, therefore: « But it itself, of the highest and compacted seats, » that is, of the Thrones (again from what precedes "the surname" must be supplied) teaches this, namely that those same Thrones are exalted, or have been exalted, diligently, that is, perfectly, from all the ignominy of subjection, that is, from all ignominious subjection. For the more perfectly they are subject to the presiding God, the more truly they have merited to be raised above all other things through him, and in him. Because, therefore, thrones signify not subjection, but dominion, when the word of God names those heavenly spirits thrones, in that very thing he demonstrates them to be perfectly ruling, and free from all subjection. So, therefore, the surname of the Thrones teaches them to be exalted from all 1048Bthe ignominy of subjection; it teaches also their bearing upward, that is, their raising-up unto the summit: and this supramundanely, that is, spiritually or invisibly, namely by a spiritual and invisible exaltation, and one transcending all mundane and visible loftiness. The surname of the Thrones, therefore, not only teaches them to be preferred to the lower beings through dominion; but also, through sublimation, to be exalted unto the summit, so that, namely, between them and him who is the highest there be nothing in the middle.

There follows: « And by every extremity ineffably unto the most sublime: and about the truly lofty placed with all its powers unchangeably, and stably. 1048C" Namely, the surname of the Thrones teaches the placed, that is, their placing, or their establishment, made unchangeably, and stably, with all its powers, that is, with every kind of power, and unshaken strength. Made, I say, ineffably far from all extremity, that is, beyond every end, unto the most sublime, and about the truly lofty. For where would the seat of God be, except where God sits? Where God dwells, where he reigns, where he sits, where he rests, where his thrones are, and his seats. See how far they are from us. How far is the highest majesty from all subjection, the eternal unchangeableness from all corruption. Where majesty is, there is a throne; where unchangeableness is, there is a seat. A throne signifies unchangeableness. Therefore in that very eternity, in that very unchangeableness, the seats of God 1048Dhave been placed. And how far this is from all extremity, who can tell? What is extremity? An end: where an end is, there is extremity. An end at the top, an end at the bottom. In both the creature has an end. The end is at the bottom, where the falling-away ceases, lest that which is something go into nothing. The end is at the top, where the advancing sets a limit to itself, lest that which is great extend itself beyond measure. By how much, then, do those surpass the lowest things, who ineffably transcend the highest? We can still, not unfittingly, interpret those extremities in another mode. For all visible things are extremes; because, as to one ascending upward from the lowest there is a highest, than which nothing is higher, so to one coming forth outward from the inmost there is an extreme, than which nothing is more outward. The divine benches, therefore, as, in that they are called thrones, 1049Athey are shown to be excellently raised up, through dignity, in the summit, above the subjection of the lowest things, so also, in that they are called seats, they are demonstrated to be placed unchangeably, through stability, in the inmost, above all fluctuation of the extremes. And yet neither, raised up on high, can they be made equal to the ineffable loftiness under which they are; nor, gathered to the inner parts, can they be compared to the simple unity about which they are. On account of this, therefore, they are called seats, because they are both underneath, through the ineffable majesty, to him who presides above, and are in a circuit, through the unchangeable unity, to him who rests within. This, therefore, the surname of the Thrones teaches: and not only this, but it teaches also « the receptive of the divine coming-upon, » that is, that they receive the divinity coming upon them from above in all impassibility and 1049Bimmateriality, that is, incorruptly and purely. For because they receive it in purity, they receive it immaterially; and again, because they receive it flowing in sweetly, without labor and weariness, they receive it impassibly. Those who advance to the knowledge of the hidden divinity through study and labor, these receive the divine coming-upon passibly. Again, those to whom the hidden divinity presses itself in to be known through outward signs and corporeal figures, to these it comes in some manner as it were materially. Because, therefore, those highest spirits, in perceiving the knowledge of the divinity, neither advance by study, nor are taught by material figures: rightly are they declared to receive the divine coming-upon both impassibly and immaterially.

1049CThere follows: « And God-bearing, and in a servant's manner opened unto the divine receptions. » From what precedes it must again be supplied, "the surname of the Thrones teaches," namely their God-bearing, that is, that they bear God presiding over them; and "opened in a servant's manner unto the divine receptions," that is, that in a servant's manner, that is, obediently, they open themselves and voluntarily fit themselves, that they may receive into themselves God himself coming, inasmuch as the will subject to the divine operation may respond, and the sacred ministry may be proved to be not of constraint, but of love. A right order. First the benches of God are raised up through dignity; then they are placed on account of stability; afterward they receive God coming into themselves, and bear him. Lastly, because they are rational vehicles, that the work may be one of felicity, to the ministry they join desire, 1049Dand will.

There follows: « This indeed is the declaration of their names, as far as it concerns us. » He continues himself unto what follows. For, the surnames of the three orders having been told, he now passes to defining and setting forth their hierarchy, that is, their sacred power. « This indeed, » namely this which we have said above, « is the declaration of their names, » namely of the three orders. It is, I say, as far as it concerns us, that is, as far as it seems to us, or as far as it concerns us it is the declaration of their names, that is, for our sake, that they may be declared to us through names, not for their own sake, who can be known to themselves, and without names.

There follows: « But it must be told, what hierarchy 1050Aof theirs we deem it to be. » As if he should say: Thus far we have spoken concerning their surname; but now we ought to speak concerning their sacred power, of what sort we deem it to be. « For that the speculation of every hierarchy, depending ineffably upon a deiformity imitating God, is; and that every hierarchic action is divided into a sacred participation, and a handing-down of pure purgation, and of divine light, and of perfective knowledge: I think has already been sufficiently said by us. » The sense is this: I think it has already been sufficiently said by us, that the speculation of every hierarchy, that is, the general definition of the hierarchy, depends ineffably upon deiformity, that is, upon likeness to God: a likeness, I say, imitating God, that is, upon a likeness of the imitation of God. Enough, he says, 1050BI think has already been said, what the hierarchy is, defined generally, namely deiformity, that is, a conformation or likeness to God, which is in those who imitate God. For above, in the third chapter, he defines the hierarchy universally thus. The hierarchy is likeness and unity to God, as far as is possible. On account of this, therefore, I think it has now been sufficiently said what the hierarchy is, namely as far as pertains to the general definition. Likewise I think it has now been sufficiently said, that every hierarchic action is divided, that is, that every hierarchic action is divided into a sacred participation, and a handing-down of pure purgation, and of divine light, and of perfective knowledge. For the action of every sacred power consists either in this, 1050Cthat they participate from a higher; or in this, that they hand down to the lower purgation, and illumination, and perfection. Threefold is the grace, which they exercise in two modes, by receiving, and by imparting: first is purgation unto purity; then illumination unto truth; then perfection unto goodness. For this is the perfective knowledge, which perfects, and makes perfect, when from the habit of virtue truth is perceived. « But now let us worthily go on to tell of the most excellent intellects, how already according to them the hierarchy is manifested by the sacred words. » As if he should say: Since above the definition and the division of the hierarchy have been universally and sufficiently given by us; now let us go on worthily to tell of the most excellent intellects, that is, the highest spirits, 1050Dnamely the Seraphim, the Cherubim, and the Thrones, in whom the first angelic hierarchy is ordered. Let us go on, I say, to tell how the hierarchy according to them, that is, how their hierarchy is manifested by the sacred words. For this the order of reason demands, that after the general definition and division of the hierarchy, the discourse descend to the special treatment of it. First indeed, concerning the first hierarchy, which consists in those three highest orders, it must be asked of what sort the sacred words manifest it to be. And lest perhaps anyone should think their sacred power to be diverse for this reason, that their orders are found to be differing, he says that in all three there is one and altogether like hierarchy, 1051Ainasmuch, namely, as they are all in the first place united to the highest and principal hierarchy, and immediately obtain from it the dignity of their sacred power.

For this is what he subjoins, saying: « In the first essences, which, placed after their substantifying divinity, and ordered as it were in its vestibules, are made to be above all invisible and visible power, it must be deemed that there is a proper and altogether uniform hierarchy. » The first essences are those highest and principal three orders of angels, which among all creatures are first, and, after their substantifying divinity, that is, that which makes them subsist, are first constituted, and ordered as it were in its vestibules, that is 1051Bso near, that whatever is beyond, is only in it, and is itself the divinity. In those first essences, therefore, which, so placed and ordered, are next to the divinity, superexcellent, and transgressing every made power, invisible and visible, that is, the power of every making, or creature, invisible and visible; in those essences, I say, it must be deemed that there is a hierarchy, that is, a sacred power; proper, that is, distinct, and differing from others in itself, and altogether uniform, that is, like and equal among themselves. For in that sacred power which they have, as they are more excellent than all others, so among themselves they exist altogether equal, so that each in that which they receive immediately from the highest divinity have not others superior; and in that which to the lower beings 1051Cthey bestow out of the divine participation, all alike exist as first dispensers. In this, therefore, the hierarchy is one, and alike, in the three.

There follows: « They are therefore to be reckoned pure: not as freed from unclean stains and defilements, nor as receptive of material phantasms, but as clean of all diminution, and higher; and, above every over-established temple, set on high above all things according to the most exalted chastity, with all their most God-formed virtues; and by their own proper motion through themselves, and by that same motion, according to the unturnable [character] of the order that loves God, ineffably received; and altogether knowing no contumely in things subordinate, but holding the incapable-of-falling and also unchangeable 1051Dmost pure placement of their own God-formed specialty. » Above he said that in those three most excellent orders of angels there is one, and an altogether similar, hierarchy — that is, a sacred power; now, consequently, he adds that those things which pertain to hierarchical action — that is, to the operation of the sacred power — are perfectly present in them, namely purgation, illumination, perfection. These three every sacred power ordered under the supreme power exercises in two ways, namely by receiving from what is above and imparting to what is below. He says, therefore, that those first essences, in which the first hierarchy is ordered, have purgation, which they both receive from the divinity above, that they may be purged, and confer on those below, that they may purge. But they receive purgation not as though they were to be freed from some 1052Auncleanness or corruption, but as to be perfected from all imperfection and diminution — this is what he says: They are to be reckoned pure, namely those first essences; pure, I say, yet not as though freed from certain unclean stains and defilements, since they never had any uncleanness or defilement; nor pure as though receptive of material phantasms, since they do not at all receive material phantasms, and therefore do not need to be purged of them, since they do not have them at all; but rather pure as clean, and estranged from all diminution and imperfection. Indeed, by unclean stains and material phantasms he has expressed two kinds of spiritual defilement: one which is in depraved desires, the other 1052Bwhich is in vain thoughts. For depraved desires defile the cleanness of the heart like mud, while vain thoughts, like a certain dust sprinkled over it, becloud its brightness. Since therefore those most pure essences of the highest spirits take on no corruption either in depraved desires or in vain thoughts, they consequently do not require to be cleansed either from unclean stains or from material phantasms. They are therefore to be understood as pure, not as purified from corruption, but as clean from imperfection; and not only estranged from imperfection, but also, through the excellence of their perfection, higher than all the rest that are perfect, and set on high above them.

1052CFor this is what follows: « And higher » — supply: they are to be reckoned to be, those first essences — « and set on high above the over-established temple of all, » that is, above every rational creature in which God dwells, and which, through him dwelling within it, is confirmed toward the highest good. Above all these those first essences are set on high according to their most excellent chastity — that is, more excellent than the chastity of all the rest; a chastity, I say, existing in all their virtues, that is, in their virtues of every kind, the most God-formed, that is, drawing nearer to conformity with God than the virtues of others draw near. Thus, therefore, those first essences are to be reckoned both to be pure, and, through the excellence of their purity, higher than the rest, and set on high 1052Dabove them. And they are also to be reckoned to have been ineffably received, for the participating of that purity in God, by their own motion through themselves — that is, without a mediator; and by that same motion — that is, ever straining without deviation toward the selfsame thing; according to the unturnable — that is, according to the unturnableness of the order that loves God. For those who never grow lukewarm in love are never bent aside or turned away from their straining.

There follows: « And in things subordinate knowing no contumely at all — supply: they are to be reckoned. For just as they participate the purity of God from above without diminution, so they offer it to be participated below without elation; in this very thing imitating God, « who gives to all abundantly, and does not upbraid (Jac. I). » 1053AFor this reason, he says, « they are to be reckoned as knowing no contumely in things subordinate, but rather as holding the incapable-of-falling and also unchangeable placement of their own God-formed specialty. » By 'their own God-formed specialty' he understands the excellent and singular beauty of divine conformation, which is in those highest essences; in which they, most pure and most perfect, are so placed and grounded that they have a placement incapable of falling, over which a fall cannot hold sway; and rightly incapable of falling, inasmuch as it is unchangeable, or immutable. The sum, then, of this chapter is this: that those first and principal essences participate their purgation, or purity, without diminution, offer it to be participated without elation, and possess it uncorrupted without mutability. 1053BAnd these things, indeed, have been said concerning their purgation.

Afterward he adds concerning illumination, saying: « And again, contemplative of sensible symbols, or speculative of intellectual things, not as brought back into the divine by the variety of sacred-writing theory; but as filled with the higher light of every immaterial knowledge, and, as far as is lawful, replete with the contemplation of the form-making and principal beauty, both super-essential and thrice-shining; and likewise made worthy by the communion of Jesus: they do not figure the deiform likeness formatively in sacredly-fashioned images; but as truly drawing near to him himself in the first participation of the knowledge of his deiform lights; and because what is like to God has been substantially bestowed on them. And they communicate 1053Cin this manner, as is possible, in his pre-operative power, in his deiform and human virtues. » All this has been said concerning illumination. As if he said: Not only are those first essences to be reckoned to have purgation and to be pure; but again — that is, further — they are to be reckoned to have illumination, and to be contemplative of sensible symbols, and speculative of intellectual things. Sensible symbols are material signs — whether in creatures, or in the Scriptures, or in the divine sacraments — set forth for the demonstration of invisible things; whose mystical signification and invisible truth those highest angelic spirits recognize by contemplating through divine illumination. They also behold, through that same illumination, intellectual things 1053D— supply: symbols — that is, spiritual theophanies, that is, divine manifestations, through which the nature of the hidden and invisible divinity is manifested to them within. Or it can be read thus: They — namely the essences — are to be reckoned to be contemplative of sensible symbols, and speculative of intellectual things, and not (supply) of symbols. For outwardly, in sensible things, where there are material signs, there are symbols; but inwardly, in intellectual things, where there are no signs but truth, there are no symbols. Therefore in sensible sacred symbols they contemplate the signs of truth, but inwardly, in intellectual things, they behold the naked truth without signs. Therefore they are to be reckoned to be contemplative of sensible symbols, and likewise 1054Aspeculative of intellectual things; yet not as brought back into the divine — that is, into the divine cognition — by variety, that is, by the manifold teaching of theory, that is, of divine Scripture; theory, I say, of the sacred-writing [kind], because, namely, it writes and speaks about divine and sacred things. For, instructed by the simple illumination of divine contemplation, not by the varied and manifold teaching of the Scriptures, they contemplate all the sacred figurations and sensible signs which, whether in the Old or in the New Testament — such as the tabernacle of the covenant, and the ark of the testament, and other things of this kind, which Scripture sets forth for the demonstration of invisible things; the visible appearances of creatures too, through which invisible things are demonstrated; the mystical revelations also made through sensible formations — all these, namely, 1054Bsacred symbols they contemplate. And not only these things that are outward, but intellectual things too, which shine within through pure and naked truth, they behold. But to the beholding of all these things, and to the divine cognition, they are not to be reckoned to have been brought back by the variety of sacred-writing theory — that is, by the manifold teaching of the divine Scriptures, which is necessary only for this: that the minds of men, estranged from God, may be brought back to the knowledge of truth, and, scattered through diverse things, may be gathered into one. Therefore those highest essences are not to be reckoned to have the cognition of all these things as though instructed through the teaching of the Scriptures, but rather as filled with a higher light — that is, with a more excellent cognition of every immaterial, that is spiritual, knowledge. For higher and 1054Cmore worthy is the light of cognition that is poured in within through invisible inspiration than that which is possessed from without through the instruction of teaching. And so those highest essences are to be reckoned to have the cognition of things visible and invisible, inasmuch as they are filled with such a light; and also as replete with the contemplation of the form-making, principal, super-essential, and thrice-shining beauty. Replete, I say, as far as is lawful — that is, as is granted to the possibility of the creature. Now he signifies the divine beauty, which is form-making, because according to itself it formed all things made by itself; and is principal, because, though it is the form of all things, it itself received its form from no other; and is super-essential, because it not only goes before through 1054Dform, in that it is the exemplar of all things, but also transcends through essence, in that it is the creatress of all things.

There follows: « And of the thrice-shining » — namely beauty — « they are to be reckoned replete with the contemplation. » By 'thrice-shining beauty' he signifies that same divine beauty, which shines in three, though it itself is not triple, but one: Father, and Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons; but God is one, the Godhead one, the nature one, the essence one, the beauty one. You see the Father: you see that shining beauty in the Father; you see the Son: you see that shining beauty in the Son; you see the Holy Spirit: you see that shining beauty in the Holy Spirit. So it, as it were, shines thrice, because it shines in three, 1055Athough it itself is not triple; but it is one that shines. The Father is another in person: there it shines. The Son is another in person: there it shines. The Holy Spirit is another in person: there it shines. And yet, of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, as the Godhead is one and the nature one, so the beauty is one. Therefore, he says, « they are to be reckoned replete with the contemplation of the thrice-shining beauty. » What wonder, then, is it if those highest essences perfectly know the divine works, visible and invisible — they who are full of the contemplation of the Creator himself, as far, namely, as is possible for a creature.

There follows: « And likewise made worthy by the communion of Jesus, » — supply: they are to be reckoned. Note 1055Bthat there is a compound there, « made-worthy, » that is, made worthy. Not only, he says, did they merit to receive the contemplation and cognition of the divinity, but they were also made worthy — by the communion of that salvation which was accomplished in the humanity of Jesus, both by knowing and by participating. For they had communion with Jesus: the mystery of his incarnation — both by foretelling it before it came to pass, and by ministering when it came to pass, and, after it was accomplished, by rejoicing together with man, restored to eternity, in the same fellowship of blessedness. Afterward he adds, showing that they receive the divine contemplation without any figures, illumined immediately by the divinity itself. For just as above he demonstrated that they read and draw the cognition of all things visible and invisible not through outward teaching, 1055Cbut through the inner [teaching] in the very wisdom of God; so now he demonstrates that they receive that same divine contemplation not through any intervening forms or images, but from the divinity itself, in the first place, immediately, nakedly, and purely. « They do not, he says, figure the deiform likeness formatively in sacredly-fashioned images; but rather they figure it as truly drawing near to it, » namely to the deiform likeness, or to the divinity, « drawing near, » I say, in the first participation of the knowledge « of his deiform lights, » that is, of his deifying illuminations. The deiform likeness is the divine contemplation itself; because, while, illumined through it, they are shining, they in a certain manner receive the likeness of the illuminating light itself. But in this 1055Ddeiform likeness they do not figure themselves, nor do they acquire it for themselves through any sacred images formed and fashioned — that is, composed for the demonstration of spiritual things; as do men, who through visible and material demonstrations in the sacred discourse are instructed unto the cognition of invisible things. Therefore those highest essences are not illumined with the divine contemplation by means of such things. But, as truly drawing near to it — that is, drawing near to truth itself not through another, but through truth itself, since between them and truth there is nothing in between; and therefore they are drawing near in the first participation of knowledge, because in the first place they participate the knowledge of his deiform lights; because immediately they contemplate, and know, and recognize his deiform — that is, deifying — lights; 1056Abecause those illumined by them through the divine likeness they in a certain manner make gods.

There follows: « And because what is like to God has been substantially bestowed on them. » For this reason too, he says, they are truly, and in the first participation, drawing near to the Divinity itself; because what is like to God has been bestowed on them — that is, because the likeness of God has been substantially bestowed on them. For that they are like to God they have not from another, or through another; but because they receive the divinity itself substantially, nakedly, and purely. Or, what is like to God has been bestowed on them most subordinately, because in the nearest place they are subordinate, so that they receive the likeness of God itself by first participation.

There follows: « They communicate in this manner, as is possible, in his pre-operative power, in his deiform and 1056Bhuman virtues. » He concludes what was said above. For because they are replete in this manner — that is, those highest essences [are replete] with the contemplation of the principal beauty — therefore they communicate in the deiform virtues; and because they are made worthy by the communion of Jesus, therefore they communicate in the human virtues; and because they participate in the first and nearest place, therefore they communicate in the pre-operative power of God, which, namely, first operates in them, and afterward operates through them. Or he calls 'the human virtues of Jesus' his virtues [shown] from his humanity — that is, shown from clemency or kindness; so that the sense is: Since, just as they communicate in his virtues in the contemplation of his majesty, so also they communicate in the co-operation of his kindness. They communicate with him through contemplation in his majesty; they communicate 1056Cwith him through the ministry of co-operation in our redemption. Thus, therefore, they communicate in his deiform and human virtues; and this is as far as is possible for them, according to the measure of grace given. Thus far it has been said concerning their illumination. Now, in the third place, he adds concerning perfection.

There follows: « And likewise perfect, not as illumined unto analytic knowledge by the sacred variety, but as filled with the first and supereminent deification, according to the most excellent knowledge — as far as [is possible] in angels — of the divine works. » As if he said: Not only are they to be reckoned pure and illumined; but also perfect in the knowledge received from the habit of virtue, yet not as illumined, or instructed 1056D[in] analytic knowledge or discipline — that is, resolutory — by the sacred variety, that is, by the manifold sacred teaching of Scripture. For they are not, like men, instructed outwardly by the multiplicity of speech, so that for them, through disputations and distinctions, the things that are hidden and intricate are resolved in knowledge and discipline; but rather they receive to be illumined through simple contemplation within, so that from their cognition nothing of the things that can be known is hidden. Thus, therefore, they are to be reckoned to be perfect, not as illumined unto a resolutive and explicable knowledge through the variety of the sacred discourse; but as filled with the first and supereminent deification — that is, with the divine illumination by which they are illumined before all the other celestial essences, according to the knowledge of the divine works, 1057Aa most excellent knowledge, as far, namely, as it can be excellent in angels.

« For not through other holy essences, but sanctified by the Divinity itself, they are extended immediately into it; they are placed, with a virtue and order supereminent above all, unto an altogether most chaste fortitude, and are led into the contemplation of the immaterial and invisible beauty, as far as is lawful; and unto the knowable reasons of the divine works, as the first essences and [those] around God, they are bent, and by the very Prince of perfection are most exaltedly sanctified. » He proves in sum that those essences receive the divine illumination before all others, and above all other celestial essences; because, not through other holy essences, but sanctified by the Divinity itself, they are extended immediately into it through love and 1057Bexaltation, according to the virtue and order — that is, the grace and dignity — which they have supereminent above all. And so, thus immediately joined to the Divinity, they receive from it alone both purgation, and illumination, and perfection — this is what he says: they are placed, that is, established, unto an altogether most chaste fortitude, or inflexibility — that is, a strong and inflexible and incorruptible chastity. They are also led, through illumination, as far as is lawful — that is, as is permitted or granted — into contemplation, unto the contemplating of the immaterial and invisible beauty of the Creator. They are also bent, as into soft wax, or informed, or instructed, or even perfected unto the knowable reasons of the divine works, as the first essences 1057Cand [those] standing in the nearest place around God, and which are most exaltedly sanctified by the very Prince of perfection — namely the Divinity.

There follows: « This, therefore, the theologians also openly declare: that the subordinate dispositions of the celestial essences are indeed instructed in the deiform sciences by those set over them in an ordered way; but that those higher than all are illumined unto teaching by the Divinity itself, as far as is lawful. » By authority he proves what he had said: namely, that the supreme orders of angels are illumined by the Divinity alone; but that the lower are instructed by the higher. For this the theologians — that is, the prophets, and those holy men who spoke about celestial and divine things — openly declare: that the subordinate dispositions — that is, the lower orders of the celestial essences — 1057Dare instructed in an ordered way, that is, beautifully and fittingly, unto the deiform sciences, by those set over them, that is, by the orders placed above; but that those which are higher than all are illumined unto teaching by the Divinity itself, as far as is lawful — that is, as is possible for them.

There follows: « For some of them they introduce as sacredly instructed by those before them, that the Lord of the celestial powers, and the King of glory, has been received into the heavens according to his humanity. » He sets forth an example where the lower celestial essences were instructed by the higher: namely, where the theologians introduce some of them as instructed by those before them, or by the higher, so that they might know that God, the Lord of the celestial powers, and the King of glory, was received into the heavens according to his humanity. For thus 1058Ait is written that, when the Savior, according to the flesh he had taken, was ascending into heaven, some of the angels, still ignorant of the exaltation of his humanity, and therefore marveling, and saying: « Who is this King of glory? » it was said by others, more fully illumined: The Lord of powers, he himself is the King of glory. » (Psal. XXIII.) In which it is proved that at times some are instructed by others.

There follows: « But some [they introduce as] inquiring of Jesus himself, and learning the knowledge of his divine action [performed] for us; and [they introduce] Jesus himself as immediately teaching them, and, bestowing it beforehand upon them, manifesting his human kindness. For I, he says, dispute justice, and the judgment of salvation. » This example is taken from Isaiah, to prove that the supreme orders 1058Bof angels are illumined by God alone unto the knowledge of truth. But some celestial essences alone the theologians themselves introduce as inquiring — that is, making inquiry of Jesus himself; and learning, not from another, but from him who is God, the knowledge of his divine action displayed for us. By the divine action of Jesus himself he means the passion and death which he underwent for us. Which action is therefore called divine, because it was possible for God alone that, through death, he should destroy the power of death. The knowledge of this action, then, they introduce the celestial essences inquiring of Jesus himself, where, beholding the garment of the assumed flesh made bloody with the blood of the passion, they say: « Who is this that comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bosra? (Isai. LXIII.) » And thereafter: « Why 1058Cthen is thy garment red, and thy raiment like theirs that tread in the winepress? (ibid.) » Thus, therefore, they introduce them as inquiring and desiring to learn. They also introduce Jesus himself as teaching them immediately, and through his very self, and manifesting to them his human — that is, clement — kindness, which he displayed to us. Which manifestation he confers on them, bestowing it beforehand — that is, granting before all others the knowledge of his operation. « I, » he says, « dispute justice, and the judgment of salvation (ibid.). » Justice and the judgment of salvation — that is, of the Savior, or of salvation — signifies the redemption of the human race. In which there was both justice, inasmuch, namely, as the Maker called back his own creature from an alien domination; 1058Dand judgment, inasmuch as he powerfully cast out the devil, the invader of another's right, from the man whom he possessed. And he says that he disputes this justice and judgment for this reason: because that [work] which pertained to the sufferings of the assumed flesh he fulfilled with labor, and as it were with a certain struggle.

There follows: « But I marvel that even the first of the celestial essences, and [those] alone at once supereminent above all in the divine illuminations, seek questions reverently, as though mediated. » This looks back to what is said, that the highest essences are immediately illumined and instructed by God; for the contrary seems to be the case, that in this passage they are found inquiring not only of their superior, but also of one another, and as it were wishing to learn. But it must be known that this questioning is not 1059Aan inquiry after teaching, but a profession of ignorance. For they question, showing that they do not know, and that they have need to be taught. But where all question, they assuredly show that they ought to be taught from elsewhere. They question, therefore, among themselves, [being] to be taught from above themselves. Because so mutual a questioning seems to be an inquiry of teaching and knowledge from one another, whereas it is established that they are instructed by their superior alone, therefore he says: I marvel that those first and principal of the celestial essences — that is, among the celestial essences, and so far supereminent above all the other celestial essences at once in the divine illuminations — I marvel, I say, that they seek questions, that is, that they make questions seeking knowledge, reverently, that is, humbly like the humble and lower, and as though not attending to the excellence of their own illumination; and 1059Bthis is what he says, « as mediated, » that is, like those who have something in between themselves and God, and need to be instructed by others; or 'as mediated,' because they are not truly mediated, since they make no question to others; nor yet truly immediate, since they refer their question not to their own principle, but to one another.

There follows: « For indeed they do not thence ask: Why thy red garments? » He proves that they truly make their question 'as mediated,' because they direct their words not first to Jesus himself, but to one another, saying: « Who is this that comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bosra? » For they do not, he says, thence ask — that is, they do not begin their questioning from him — 'Why thy red garments?' where they would direct their speech immediately to Jesus himself; 1059Cbut first among themselves, as though mediately: « Who is this, » and the rest. Whence it is a marvel that those supreme essences, though they are first, and nearest to the Divinity, make their questions as though mediated.

There follows: « But among themselves they deliberate before asking, showing that they learn, and seek the deiform knowledge. » He now resolves the question, namely why those highest essences, though they are nearest to God, make their question among themselves; namely, because among themselves they deliberate about asking, lest perhaps by too eager a questioning they leap ahead of, or anticipate, that illumination which comes to be in them through the divine procession — that is, through the divine grace 1059Dproceeding to illumine them; showing also, by the very deliberation of their questioning, that they seek the deiform knowledge. For in that they ask, they signify that they seek knowledge; but in that they first confer among themselves, questioning and deliberating, they demonstrate that they do not dare to anticipate the divine procession into themselves.

For this is what follows: « But not leaping ahead of the illumination implanted through the divine procession. » For they seek knowledge, and therefore they ask, but not leaping ahead of the divine illumination, until it offers itself, proceeding of its own accord into them; therefore they deliberate among themselves, and do not first dare to question Jesus until he himself offers himself, saying: « I am he who speaks justice. » Then at last, 1060Ahaving taken confidence, they direct their question to him: « Why is thy raiment red, and thy garment like theirs that tread in the winepress? »

There follows: « Is not, then, the first hierarchy of the celestial intellects, sanctified by the very Prince of perfection in that it is extended immediately into it, purged, and illumined, and perfected — with a most holy purgation, with much light, with a fore-perfected consummation filling it proportionally? » The sense is this: Is not, then — 'num' for 'nonne' — the first hierarchy of the celestial intellects purged, and illumined, and perfected? Sanctified by the very Prince of perfection — that is, by the divinity itself, which is the prince and principle of all sanctification. Sanctified, I say, in that the divinity itself is extended immediately into it, 1060Billuminating, or irradiating, or filling it proportionally — that is, by a participation differing from the illumination of the rest — with a most holy purgation, and with much light, and with a fore-perfected — that is, super-excellent — consummation or perfection. « It is purged, » I say, and « illumined, and perfected, that it may be pure from all lessening or imperfection, and full of the first light, » that is, of the [light] shining into it first before the others; and that it may be « perfect, participating the perfect knowledge and cognition first given to it. » But when he says « sanctified » — or, as perhaps it is more fittingly, though less usually, translated, 'made pontiff' by the very Prince of purgation — he signifies, as we said, the divinity itself, which in Greek is called teletarchia, that is, the prince of purgation, or 1060Cof sanctification.

There follows: « But, comprehending, this too I would perhaps not undeservedly have said. » As though it were asked what this purgation is, he answers that the taking-up of the divine knowledge in the rational soul is both purgation, and illumination, and perfection. Purgation, because it purges ignorance; illumination, because it illumines with divine cognition; perfection, because, by illuminating, it consummates by the knowledge of perfect teachings, or disciplines, according to the illumined habit — this is what he says: « Comprehending, » that is, briefly gathering into one the things said above; this too I would perhaps not undeservedly have said, that the taking-up of the divine knowledge is both purgation, and illumination, and perfection. 1060DAnd he gives the reason why it is called purgation, and illumination, and perfection. « Purging, indeed, ignorance, inasmuch as the knowledge of perfect teachings is implanted according to order. » For this reason it is called purgation, inasmuch as it purges ignorance by implanted knowledge — that is, through the implanted knowledge of perfect teachings. Implanted, I say, according to order — that is, according to what the dignity and excellence of each order demands. « But illuminating by that very divine cognition, through which it also purges [the hierarchy] that does not contemplate beforehand. » For this reason it is called illumination, because it illumines each hierarchy with divine cognition, through which divine cognition, namely, it also purges that hierarchy. The hierarchy, I say, that does not contemplate before it is purged, as it is written: 1061A« Blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God (Matth. V). »

There follows: « Which it manifests through a higher illumination, and again perfecting, by that very light, according to habit, with the knowledge of the most lucid teachings. » Which hierarchy, namely, the very taking-up of the divine knowledge manifests through a higher illumination. For in this it declares it to be higher than all the rest: that it illuminates it with a higher and more excellent light of divine cognition.

There follows: « And again perfecting, by that very light, according to habit, with the knowledge of the most lucid teachings. » He does not distinguish illumination and perfection clearly enough, in that he seems to assign both to cognition and knowledge. Yet this 1061Bis the difference: that illumination properly pertains to that cognition which builds up knowledge; but perfection to that cognition which shows the form of good morals and the habit of the virtues. For there are certain things which are investigated only for the cognition of understanding; but certain things pertain especially to the understanding of doing. For the former, illumination is necessary; for the latter, perfection. For the cognition of truth does not make [a man] perfect, unless the habit of virtue follows. Therefore he calls 'most lucid teaching' that which consists in the habit of virtue, because experience is the mistress of understanding; and he knows virtue best who has learned it not by hearing alone, but also by tasting and by doing. In the experience and habit of virtue, the cognition of truth is perfected, which is begun in the illumination 1061Cof understanding alone. All of which, because it is acquired through the taking-up of the divine knowledge, is therefore fittingly called both purgation, and illumination, and perfection.

There follows: « This, therefore, as far as regards our knowledge, is the first disposition of the celestial essences, standing in the encircling of God, and around God, immediately, and simply, and incessantly encircling his eternal knowledge, according to a most excellent — as far as [is possible] in angels — ever-mobile placement. » He infers from what was said above. As if he said: Since that hierarchy of the highest spirits is first and principally both purged, and illumined, and perfected by the Divinity itself; therefore it is the first and principal 1061Ddisposition, or the principal order, of the celestial essences, standing immediately, both in the encircling of, and around, God. For it stands through the immutability of contemplation; but it encircles through the life-giving and unceasing desire of eternal love. Therefore incessantly, because it does not fail from love; therefore simply, because, encircling, it does not withdraw from unity. That unity in the midst is the simplicity of the Divinity, around which and in the encircling of which they are, inasmuch as they immediately draw near to it. In the encircling too, because to his ineffable and hidden incomprehensibility they too are in a certain manner outside, into which they do not at all penetrate. Yet they go about it and desire it; and they strive toward the inner things; and, drawing near by cognition and by love, they become nearest, according to the most excellent placement which 1062Athey have beside God; most excellent, I say, as far as [is possible] in angels — that is, in comparison with that [placement] which is found in all the other angels. And I call the placement 'ever-mobile,' because both by contemplation they do not withdraw, and by desire they ever draw near. For all these reasons, then, this disposition is principal among all the other celestial essences; principal, I say, as far as regards our knowledge — namely, as far as it can be comprehended through our knowledge. He further adds, in praise of this hierarchy, one thing after another, heaping up many lofty and sublime things worthy of divine wonder, and certain profound things, and [things] known only to the pure.
