Such, he says, is that disposition, or order, of the first hierarchy — nearest in placement, most ardent in desire and intention; 1062Bwhich, although it cannot penetrate to the whole of what belongs to God, [which is] incomprehensible, yet with eternal love does not cease to go about [it] as far as it can be grasped and comprehended by a creature. But lest perhaps it should seem a pursuit of toil, not of happiness, if it were always to go about [it] and never attain [it], always to seek and never to grasp, always to desire and never to taste, he adds the fruit of the inquiry and the effect of the desire, saying: « Seeing indeed many and blessed contemplations purely, and simple and immediate splendors, illumined, and filled with divine nourishment. [Filled] with many things, indeed, by the first given outpouring, and by the unity — sole, domestic, and unifying — of the divine refreshment; and made worthy by much communion with God, and co-operation with him, unto that [likeness], as is possible, by the likeness of good dispositions 1062Cand actions; and knowing many of the divine things super-positively, and made a partaker, according to what is lawful, of the divine knowledge and cognition. » He said, as best he could say it: Three stand about the Trinity — the Seraphim by love, the Cherubim by cognition, the Thrones by domination. Here is the whole Trinity. Domination in the Father, wisdom in the Son, love in the Holy Spirit. It seemed that he had set the Seraphim above, because charity is supereminent; but behold, we also see that the throne belongs to the Father, and the Thrones are joined with the Father, and love is given to the Holy Spirit. If you think the Thrones subordinate, because they are named after the Seraphim and Cherubim, then think them also set above, because they pertain to the Father, who is named before the Son and the Holy Spirit. But in 1062Dthe Trinity there is no degree. Father, and Son, and Holy Spirit is one God. Unity cannot be lower than itself. Therefore that hierarchy of the highest spirits, which is formed first and principally by the highest and supereminent domination of the Divinity, as far as concerns the most excellent likeness by which it imitates the simple unity, has no degree in domination — although, nevertheless, according to that measure of participation and distribution of grace (by which a creature cannot be made equal to the Creator) it has a difference. Therefore the domination of the three is one, by which they are universally set before all things subordinate — after the supreme and supereminent domination of the Deity — [but] are not subordinated to one another. Therefore they all together hold the first place, and they stand about [him], 1063Aeach in the nearest placement, so that one does not come between another by position, nor anticipate [another] by participation, nor surpass [another] by domination. Thus is this first disposition, standing in the encircling of God, and around God, immediately — thus properly. And what is the fruit of so great a familiarity?

Hear what follows: « Seeing indeed many and blessed contemplations purely, and simple and immediate splendors, illumined, and filled with divine nourishment. » Do not, then, marvel if they go about [it] thus, and do not suffer themselves to be drawn far off. There is something there that draws [them]; and what is this? You are waiting for it to be said what that is which so incites the affection of those who desire, and provokes their love. But how do you think it will be told by us, which is not penetrated by them? They themselves have not yet entered, but 1063Bstand in the encircling; and it is a great thing for them to draw near to it, that they may see, and touch, and taste, and experience what the sweetness of the good is — [the good] set forth to its lovers without obstacle; yet they neither enter nor penetrate so as to comprehend it, and to grasp even to the whole how great is the immensity of the hidden. How, then, do you think to set it forth outwardly, from which even those who are within remain outside? That good, then, cannot be told by us — [the good] which holds those blessed spirits immovable beside itself through the joy of eternal contemplation, that they may not flow away toward perishable things; and again, moving [them] by desire, draws them to itself, that they may seek it with unceasing love. But lest that be altogether passed over in silence which cannot be told at all, hear what it is that both holds them beside itself and draws them to itself. A certain good, and great above 1063Call those goods that you know, quite other — not only in difference, but in supereminence; yet, that it may be conveyed to you and made known according to these goods that you know, as far as can be, let us say: that good is light and sweetness. Why light? Because it makes the eyes grow bright. Why sweetness? Because it refreshes. These are two great goods among us, and no others are found greater than these, nor any that work more toward our joy or our happiness: light and sweetness. The one is for illumination, the other for refreshment. If you are illumined and not satisfied, it is a great good, but not a full one. If you are satisfied and not illumined, it is again a great good, but not a perfect one. Refreshment makes pleasant what is within; illumination 1063Dpresents as pleasant what is without; both are required for full joy. For if you are refreshed in the one and afflicted in the other, the gladness is not perfect, to which sadness is mixed. Seek, therefore, refreshment, that what is in you may be pleasant to you; seek also illumination, that what is outside you may be pleasant to you. Refreshment indeed would seem to be more necessary, just as the good which is in you is more properly your own than the good which is outside you. Nevertheless, how much pleasantness does the illumination of contemplation add? Sweet is the light, and delightful for the eyes to see the sun. Behold this world, which offers many spectacles of pleasantness. And all these things were made through the wisdom of God. All that you see went forth from there, where is the reason and cause of all things. If, then, it is so beautiful 1064Ato see the disposition and form of the work, how pleasant and delightful do you think it is to contemplate the wisdom of the craftsman? But do not think, because it is named one wisdom, [that it offers] a certain solitary and wearisome contemplation to those who see it: it is one, but not one in that way. For how do you think the wisdom of God is one? Perhaps as you call one essence, one species and one form, one place and one time: all these are one in number. What is [it] to be one in number? By distinction. What is [it] to be one in number? By smallness. What is [it] to be one in number? By imperfection. For thus you number this and that. For when you number, you say this and not that. What, therefore, is numbered by unity is separated by unity; and by that same unity it is proved to be diminished from all those from which it is shown, 1064Bby that very unity, to be distinct. Do you think the wisdom of God to be one in that way? Then you number it, and say, rightly, this and not that. If, then, it is [this] and not that, then it is not the whole; and there is something outside it which is not in it. If the whole is in it, it is the whole; how do you say [that] it is this and not that? Do not, then, number. Scripture tells you: « His wisdom is not number. All things that are from it were made in number, and weight, and measure. But it itself is not under number; » in which there is true unity without smallness, and universality without multiplicity; nor is it under weight, [being] inestimable; nor under measure, [being] incomprehensible. What, then, do you think it is to see the wisdom of God? When you see this world, how many things do you see in them? And all 1064Cthis comes from there; and the whole is there, where the wisdom of God is. And why do I say 'all this'? For it would be too little a thing, were there in the wisdom of God nothing else [but this]. If God understands his own work, and does not understand himself, what wisdom is that? For what God is is more than what is made by God. If, then, he knows what he made, and does not know what he himself who made [it] is, he is ignorant of what is greater, and there is not perfect wisdom in him. If your heart can grasp and comprehend the things that you do and that you unfold in work — you dispose all things by reason dictating within, and all that you are about to do you first conceive in reason; and when they go forth into work, they do not withdraw from reason — how can it be that in the eternal reason of the Founder there is not everything 1064Dthat has been made? Again, if it is a small thing for a rational soul to see and comprehend the things that are outside, unless it contemplate those things that are within — [things] far greater and more wonderful — and recognizes that what it itself is is greater than everything that is outside it: [then] the eternal craftsman cannot, in that wisdom by which he sees all that he himself made, be ignorant of what is greater than all things — which is he himself who made [them]. Consider, then, what that wisdom is, in which are all things that have been made, and — beyond all things and above all things — that which is greater than all things: he by whom all things were made. What kind of form do you think that is, in which there is such great beauty? When, therefore, you hear the wisdom of God named, think of all this: all this is in it; and to see it is to see all this. In it are seen all things that have been made; 1065Aand in it is seen he by whom all things were made. Therefore those highest spirits, who through the excellence of supereminent grace draw near immediately, are illumined by it to contemplate it, and in the contemplation of it they see both what was made through it, and what is in it, and him who through it made [all things], in whom it [itself] is. These, then, are the contemplations which the first hierarchy sees purely, immediately illumined unto the simple splendors — which contemplations are both many, inasmuch as all things are seen there; and blessed, because, with all things, he too who made all things is seen. For what is seen in him is not seen apart from him, because that which is seen is one, which is he himself; and in that one all things are seen, in which all things are one and one is all things. See how 1065Bmany are the contemplations, where nothing of all things is hidden; how blessed the contemplations, where in the highest good all things are seen; where to see and to have, to love and to taste the good, is the same; where nothing is seen but truth, nothing is loved but goodness. For there are two things: cognition and love. The one pertains to illumination; the other to refreshment. Cognition illumines, love satisfies. Cognition of truth, love of goodness: in these blessedness consists — to know and to love the good. « Taste, says Scripture, and see, for the Lord is sweet (Psal. XXXIII). » In « taste » is love; in « see » is cognition. These two he commends distinctly, namely cognition and love. « Seeing indeed many and blessed contemplations purely, and simple and immediate splendors, 1065Cillumined. » This has been said concerning illumination and cognition.

There follows: « Filled with divine nourishment. [Filled] with many things, indeed, by the first given outpouring, and by the unity — sole, domestic, and unifying — of the divine refreshment. » This has been said concerning love and refreshment. He commends both in many ways. First, cognition, in the many and blessed contemplations seen purely through the illumination of the simple splendors. What are the simple splendors? Pure illuminations. Through pure illuminations one comes to pure contemplations. Pure illumination is when the truth is conceived through itself; pure contemplation is when the truth is seen in itself. When the truth is learned through an underlying image or figure, 1065Dit is not pure illumination; when the truth is known in an underlying image or figure, it is not pure contemplation. For there can be neither simplicity except where there is [only] the one thing, nor purity except where there is the true. Simplicity in the one alone; purity in the true. Therefore those who contemplate immediately, and draw near to the truth through themselves, alone have simple illuminations and pure contemplations.

There follows: « Filled with divine nourishment. » What is the divine nourishment? The divine refreshment. And this refreshment, what is it but the love of God? Therefore, when he had said, « that surpassing angelic ordering filled with divine nourishment, » he added also, saying: « filled with the unity of the divine refreshment. » But what is the divine refreshment, if not the divine nourishment? 1066ATherefore the unity of refreshment and the unity of nourishment is one refreshment and one nourishment. Therefore at the table of God only one dish is set. But do not despise it. The satiety is great. « I shall be satisfied, » says the Psalmist, « when thy glory shall appear (Psal. XVI). » There are many things in this world, and all these cannot satisfy the heart of man. But there is one good with God, and when this alone is received, satiety is found. Therefore satiety is not in multitude, but in unity. When is there satiety? When the satiety is enough. Suppose now that of these many things which are in the world you have some few that you love, and you will see that it is not enough. Let more come: still you will not say, it is enough. Let all things be set before you; and you will find yourself still in need, and not yet having enough. In all these things, therefore, there 1066Bcan be no satiety, where there can be no enough. But that one good will come; and there will be satiety, because there will be enough. Do not wonder. All these are many, but they are not much. That is one, and it is much. Therefore that sinful woman, because she had many things to be forgiven, loved not many things but much. She let go many things, and chose much. She was wise; she did not regard the heap, but weighed the value. In many things, little; in one thing, much. Therefore do not atttendas to the number, but seek the fruit. There is one good, which God has prepared for you. Do not be afraid when you hear "one"; it is one good, but in that good is every good. He has prepared one refreshment, one food, one dish, one bread — but do not despise it. Hear what is written: « Having every taste, and 1066Cevery delight of sweetness (Sap. XV). » This is the divine nourishment, and the great outpouring, or abundant effusion, by which outpouring, namely, that blessed society, granted the first place, is filled. There is also the unity of the divine refreshment, by which unity alone — that is, singular and domestic and unifying — it has been made specially worthy. But this one and simple divine refreshment is called singular for this reason, that it is not received with any foreign delight or outside sweetness; domestic, because it is prepared only for friends and members of the household; unifying, because it makes one with itself all those to whom it grants itself to be taken and shared.

There follows: « And by much communion with God and cooperation: » — understood, the ordering is filled, or the 1066Dfirst hierarchy of the celestial essences. This, I say, has been made worthy of that communion and cooperation with God, as far as is possible for it; by the likeness of good dispositions, that is, of virtues and actions. For by good dispositions it has been made worthy of communion; by good actions, worthy of cooperation. And the order is right. First it is illumined by the brightness of knowledge; then it is refreshed by the sweetness of love, so that thus it may both commune with God in virtue and cooperate in action, as it is written: « If any one love me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him, and make our abode with him (Joan. XIV). »

There follows: « And knowing many divine things in a supereminent way, and made a partaker of divine knowledge and cognition, 1067Aaccording to what is lawful. » That is, this hierarchy knows many of the divine things, that is, many things concerning the divine, or concerning God, in a supereminent way, that is, more excellently than the other hierarchies « and it has been made in participation, » that is, it has been made a partaker of divine knowledge and of divine cognition, according to what is lawful for it, that is, granted to it.

There follows: « Therefore theology has handed down its praises also to those who are on earth, in which the eminence of its most exalted illumination is wondrously made manifest. » As if he said: Because so great is the excellence of the hierarchy of the first essences, therefore theology, that is Holy Scripture, has handed down to those who are on earth, that is, to men, its praises or laudations. In which laudations, namely, 1067Bthe eminence of its most exalted illumination is wondrously made manifest. As if he said: Because so great is its sublimity, therefore theology has made manifest to men its laudations, by which it praises God, so that through the excellence of the laudation the eminence of the illumination might be made manifest.

There follows: « For some of it, speaking perceptibly, resound like the voice of waters: Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place. » As if he said: Truly excellent are the laudations of this hierarchy, which are made manifest by Holy Scripture, because some of it, that is certain of them, sounding perceptibly resound, or re-echo, or cry out like the voice of waters: Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place. Or it can be read thus. Theology has handed down its praises perceptibly, that is, 1067Cby the likeness of sensible and corporeal things, speaking of spiritual things, namely that « some of it. » That is, of its number « resound like the voice of waters. Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place. » This testimony is taken from Ezekiel, where the prophet records a voice of great commotion made behind him. Which voice, although it is not said there by whom it was uttered, yet this author testifies without ambiguity that it was made by the highest spirits of the celestial orders.

There follows: « But others cry back that most laudable and most holy theology: Holy, holy, holy: the Lord God of Sabaoth. All the earth is full of his glory (Isa. VI). » This testimony is taken from Isaiah, where two seraphim, flying, are recorded to have proclaimed this theology, that is, this divine address or laudation, one to 1067Danother, back and forth.

There follows: « But these most exalted hymnologies of the celestial minds we have already, indeed, opened up as far as possible in those things which concern the divine praises. And it has been said of these, in those places, sufficiently as far as we are concerned. » These aforesaid hymnologies, that is, the divine laudations of the celestial minds, that is, of the celestial spirits, he says that he has opened up, or expounded, as far as was possible for him, in other writings, which were made by him concerning the divine praises; and concerning these hymnologies, namely, he testifies that it has been said sufficiently in those (understood) writings, as far as pertained to him, that is, to his capacity. But this 1068Awriting, which he asserts that he made concerning the divine praises, is nowhere found among these his writings which are with us. Yet from this statement we can know that he wrote concerning the divine praises, since in the book On the Divine Names he introduced certain things from the amatory hymns of Saint Hierotheus, in which something of the aforesaid praises is treated.

There follows: « Of which it suffices, for a reminder, to say only this much according to the present occasion: that this first ordering has been illumined in theological knowledge, as far as is lawful, by the divine goodness, through which, as a deiform hierarchy, it then handed itself down to others also. » As if he said: Of which, namely of the divine praises sufficiently 1068Bexpounded in the aforementioned book, now, according to the present occasion, it suffices to say only this much for a reminder or admonition, namely that this first ordering, that is, the first hierarchy of angels, has been illumined in theological, that is divine, knowledge by the divine goodness itself. Note the construction in that he says, "illumined knowledge." For it is said thus: But I am instructed, I am taught a discipline. He says, therefore, that the first ordering has been illumined unto knowledge by the divine goodness alone; through which knowledge, namely, this ordering handed down itself; then, that is, consequently, to the other hierarchies following after it. « It handed down, » I say, « itself as a deiform hierarchy, » that is, having conformity and likeness to God, and imitating God in this, that, being illumined by him, 1068Cit illumines others, and sets forth itself, as it were, as a form and exemplar of divine conformity. This, therefore, now suffices to say concerning the aforesaid praises: that in them the first ordering of angels, praising its Creator, handed down itself as a form of praising to the other hierarchies following after, « introducing, » that is, suggesting to them, or insinuating, « that by speaking briefly. » For it introduced, or suggested, as it were something hidden, and manifest to few. And it suggested by speaking briefly the other thing which it suggested. And rightly was that suggested only in a hidden way which was invisible, and that spoken only briefly which was ineffable. For however much it were expounded unto knowledge, that would remain hidden which was impenetrable; 1068Dand however much it were extended through speech, it would be brief in relation to it, which was without end. Yet it suggested, and insinuated, and expounded, so that through it there might come to the knowledge of others that which it itself had perceived with no intermediary. What did it suggest?

Hear: « That most holy, and supremely blessed, and altogether blessed divinity, it is lawful that it be blessed by those receiving God, as far as it is possible for it to be known and praised by the intellects. For they are, as it were, deiform divine places, of the divine repose, as the oracles say. » He expounds the aforementioned testimony taken from Ezekiel. « Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place. » This first hierarchy, he says, crying out, « Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his 1069Aplace, » teaches that it is lawful — that is, just, or due, or worthy — that this most holy and supremely blessed and altogether blessed divinity be blessed by the intellects that receive God, and blessed to just such a degree as it is possible for it to be known and praised. It is just, he says, that this divinity, which is in itself ever most holy — ready, namely, to bestow, and not needing to receive — and which is supremely blessed, and altogether, or most strongly, blessed, that is, whose glory in itself is so great that it can neither be increased by another's benefit nor be further commended by another's praise. It is lawful, he says, that although it be in itself so perfect that it needs not to be blessed or praised, yet that the intellects — that is, rational hearts — should bless and praise it, as far, namely, as they can know it 1069Band praise it according to the knowledge received. For although his glory be perfect of itself, yet we ought not to cease from blessing and praising him: we who, even if by blessing and praising we add no perfection to him, are nevertheless perfected by him. Or what he says can be understood otherwise: that it is just that the divinity, which is in itself supremely blessed, be blessed by the intellects that receive God. As if he said: Although the praise of God be in itself supremely perfect, yet this is by right assigned to his praise, that through grace he deigns to inhabit the hearts made by him. Thus, then, it is just that the divinity, in itself supremely blessed, be blessed also for this, and be blessed, that it offers itself to be received by the minds to be beatified, and deigns to inhabit them as its own 1069Cplace. For it does not so dwell in them as though seeking a support, and as though about to fall if it had no prop. For God does not seek a place for himself, as though he could not exist unless he were contained; but he seeks, as it were, a receptacle into which to pour himself: which certainly could not be blessed, unless it were filled by him. Therefore it is added, above all his praise, that he who is supremely blessed in himself makes others blessed from himself. Let him be blessed by them, let him be blessed also for them. Let him be blessed by them, in so far as he is revealed to them to be known and praised; let him be blessed for them, in so far as he is made manifest in them.

There follows: « For they are, as it were, deiform divine places, of the divine repose, as the oracles say. » He gives the reason why, from that which has been said, « Blessed be the 1069Dglory of the Lord from his place, » he understands it to be signified that the glory ought to be blessed by the intellects that receive God: because, he says, these intellects that receive God, they themselves are the divine places. For "Theodocos" is said in Greek, that is, "receiver of God." By which name every pure mind, whether human or angelic, can be signified. For in these two God dwells and rests. They, then, are as it were deiform divine places. He gives, as it were, the reason why they are called divine places. For the cause is the same why they are places and why they are deiform. For from the fact that they receive light, they become a place of light. And again from the very fact that they receive light, they become shining, and exist conformed to the light. They are, then, divine places, inasmuch as 1070Athey are deiform, and have the likeness of God from the God who dwells within. Again, because they are divine places, it is clear that they are places of the divine repose, because they could not be divine places at all unless they were places of repose and peace, as the oracles say: « In peace is his place made (Psal. LXXV). »

There follows: « And that it is a monad, and a unity three substantially: and, over the celestial essences down to the uttermost parts of the earth, extending its goodness into all things that are — a providence, as the super-principal principle of all essence, and the cause, and binding all things about, superessentially, with an immeasurable containment. » This he adds concerning the exposition of what follows, which had been taken from Isaiah. As if he said: Just as that first celestial hierarchy, crying out, 1070B« Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place, » taught that God is to be blessed and glorified not only in himself, but also in his saints, so too, by proclaiming him thrice holy, and by adding not "lords" but "the Lord of Sabaoth," it signified that there are three persons in one Godhead — not three gods, but one God. This is what he says. And because it is a monad, and a unity three substantially, as if he said: Not only this, which was said above concerning the glory of the Lord to be blessed from his place, did this first celestial hierarchy introduce to the hierarchies following after it; but also this, that the monad and unity — that is, the divinity, which is truly one and a simple nature — is three persons substantially, that is, that the three persons are one essence or substance, and the one essence is three persons; 1070Cbecause God is one in essence, and three in persons. Truly, that "monad" and "unity," though they seem to be the same, are set down doubled, is done on account of the Greek: in which there are two names, "monas" and "henas": which, although they have one interpretation with us (for both sound "unity"), yet this difference seems to exist, that "monas" signifies rather that unity which is spoken of according to distinction, while "henas" signifies that which is marked according to simplicity. For everything that is simple is one. But not everything that is one is simple; since a thing is called one by collection, and one by composition, and one by likeness. All of which, because it is not the whole of what they are that is one, are not truly one, and borrow the name of unity by likeness only, not by property. 1070DBut to the divine nature, for which to be one and to be simple is the same, its whole being is truly to be one; and therefore rightly it had to be called not only "monas," but "henas" also; because its unity subsists ever in the true simplicity of the same and undivided substance. Let him say, then, that in the true Godhead the monad and unity are substantially; because, as the trinity of persons in God does not divide the unity of essence, so the unity of nature does not confound the trinity of persons. But the three are substantially one, of which three the substance is one.

There follows: « And, over the celestial essences down to the uttermost parts of the earth, extending its goodness into all things that are — a providence. » And this too, he says, 1071Athe first hierarchy insinuated to those following after it: that the true unity and supreme trinity extends, or makes to penetrate, its goodness from the supercelestial essences down to the uttermost parts of the earth, that is, from the highest things to the lowest; its goodness, I say, being a providence into all things, because it provides for all and leaves nothing foreign to itself, inasmuch as it is above the principal, or super-essential, principle of all essence, and the cause of all; because from it and unto it all things were made: and which is the binding-about of all things 1072A— that is, the encirclement, because it binds about all things, and embraces, and contains them superessentially with an immeasurable containment, which comprehends the whole, and in it itself remains incomprehensible. Because, then, it is the principle from which all things were made, and the cause through which all things were made, and the binding-about containment in which all things subsist, therefore all the earth is full of his glory, since from that goodness all things are filled and nourished, that they may subsist in it, which were made through it.

LIBER OCTAVUS.

  • 1071

BOOK EIGHT.

  • 1071

TITULUS CAPITULI VIII: De dominationibus, et potestatibus, et de media eorum hierarchia.

TITLE OF CHAPTER VIII: On the dominations, and the powers, and on their middle hierarchy.

LITTERA.

  • 1071B

Transeundum autem nunc nobis in mediam coelestium intellectuum dispositionem, dominationes illas supermundanis oculis, quantum possibile est, explorantibus, et vere potentia speculamina divinarum potestatum, et virtutum. Etenim unaquaeque supra nos essentiarum cognominatio Dei imitatorias earum significat deiformes proprietates. Igitur sanctarum dominationum manifestativam nominationem existimo declarare absolutam quamdam, et omni pedestri minoratione liberam anagogen, nullaque tyrannicarum dissimilitudinum ullo modo universaliter eam inclinatam, liberaliter severam dominationem, omni minutivae servituti superpositam, superiorem subjectioni omni, et remotam 1071Cab universa dissimilitudine, et dominationis incessanter appetentem, et ad illius ipsius naturaliter subsistentis virtutis similitudinem, quantum possibile est, et seipsam, et quae post eam sunt, optime, et speciose conformantem, ad nullum una videntium, sed ad proprie ὄν universale conversam, et Dominicae semper deiformitatis in participatione, secundum quod possibile est, ipsi factam. Ipsam vero sanctarum virtutum fortem quamdam, et incommutabilem virilitatem in omnes secundum earum deiformitatem operationes, ad nullam susceptionem inditarum ei divinarum illuminationum imbecilliter infirmatam, potenter in imitationem Dei reductam, non relinquentem suimet imbecillitate deiformem motum, sed firmiter ferentem in superessentialem, 1071Det potentificam virtutem, et ipsius imaginem virtuti similem, juxta quod licet, factam, et ad ipsam quidem ut principalem virtutem potenter conversam: ad secunda vero virtutem dando [dans et] deiformiter provenientem. Ipsam autem sanctarum potestatem aequipotentem divinarum dominationum, et virtutum bene ornatam, et inconfusam circa divinas susceptiones ordinationem, et ordinatum supermundanae et intellectualis potestatis, non tyrannice 1072Bin ea, quae inferiora sunt, potestativis virtutibus praecipitatae, sed potenter in divina post bene ordinatas reductae, et quae post eam deiformiter reducentis, et ad potentificam causalem potentiam, quantum fas est, assimilatae, et eam, ut possibile, angelis revelantis in bene ornatis per ipsam ordinibus potestativa virtute. Has habens deiformes proprietates media coelestium animorum dispositio purgatur quidem, et illuminatur, et perficitur, quemadmodum dictum est, a divinis illuminationibus inditis sibi secundo per primam hierarchiam dispositionem, et per mediam illam secunda manifestatione delatis. Itaque per alium dictum venientem in alium angelum auditum, symbolum faciemus a longe super perfectae, et per processionem 1072Coccultae in sequentia perfectionis. Nam sapientes circa sacras nostras immolationes aiunt, per seipsas lucentes divinorum plenitudines per alias contemplativarum participationum esse perfectiores. Sic existimo et angelicorum ordinum immediatam participationem primo in Deum extentorum perfectorem esse per medietatem perfectorum. Propter quod et a nostra sacerdotali traditione perfectivae, lucificae, et purgativae virtutes primi intellectus nominantur inferiorum, tanquam per eos in omnium superessentiale principium reductorum, et mysticarum purgationum, et illuminationum et perfectionum in participatione, secundum quod eis fas, factorum. Poc enim est omnino divina ordinatione divinitus promulgatum, per prima secunda divinis participare 1072Dilluminationibus. Invenies autem hoc et multoties a theologis expressum. Quando enim divina, et paterna humanitas Israel nutritive pro sacra ejus salute corripiens, et ulciscentibus, et immanibus nationibus in correptionem tradens, omnigena provisorum in melius traductione, et captivitatem dimisit, et ad priorem clementer reduxit beneficentiam, vidit theologorum unus Zacharias unum primorum, ut existimo, et circa Deum angelorum (communis 1073Aenim, ut dixi, est omnibus haec angelica cognominatio) ab ipso Deo discentem de hoc consolatoria, ut dictum est, verba. Alterum vero subjectorum angelorum in occursum primi provenientem, tanquam ad illuminationis susceptionem et perceptionem, deinde ab ipso divinum consilium tanquam a summo sacerdote eruditum, et hoc docere theologum conversum, quoniam fructuose habitabitur Hierusalem a multitudine hominum (Zach. I). Alter autem theologorum Ezechiel (Ezech. VIII), et ab ipsa, inquit, hoc sacratissime promulgatum esse cherubim superfirmata gloriosissima divinitate. Ipsum enim Israel, ut dictum est, dux exercitus humanitas per disciplinas in melius traducens justitia divina corrigentibus respondetur, correctos justificavit. Hoc 1073Bdocetur, primus post cherubim lumbos sapphiro praecinctus, qui podera juxta symbolum hierarchicum induebatur. Reliquos autem angelos, qui secures habebant, divina ordinatio imperat a priori doceri de hoc divinum judicium (Ezech. X). Ei quidem enim dixit mediam pertransire Hierusalem, et dare signum in frontes correctorum virorum; aliis: Exite in civitatem post eum, et percutite, et nolite parcere oculis vestris; ad omnes autem, super quos est signum, ne appropinquetis (Ezech. IX). Quid fortassis quis dixerit de dicente angelo ad Danielem: Exiit sermo; aut de ipso primo ignem ex medio cherubim recipiente (Dan. IX). Aut illud ejusdem quod abundantius in ordinis angelici ostensionem, quoniam 1073Cet cherubin immittit ignem in manus sanctam stolam induti (Ezech. X); aut de vocante divinissimum Gabrielem, et dicente ei: « Fac illum intelligere visionem (Zach. I); » aut quaecunque alia a sacris theologis dicta sunt de coelestium hierarchiarum deiformi ornatu. Ad quem nostrae hierarchiae ordinatio, secundum quod possibile est, assimilata, angelicam pulchritudinem, quantum in characteribus habebit formata per eum, et reducta ad superessentialem simul omnis hierachiae.

THE TEXT.

  • 1071B

But now we must pass over into the middle ordering of the celestial intellects, exploring those dominations, as far as is possible, with supermundane eyes, and the truly powerful contemplations of the divine powers and virtues. For each appellation, among the essences above us, signifies their deiform properties, imitative of God. Therefore I judge that the manifesting naming of the holy dominations declares a certain absolute anagogy, free from all pedestrian diminishment, and in no way whatsoever universally inclined by any of the tyrannical dissimilitudes, a dominion liberally severe, set above all diminishing servitude, superior to every subjection, and remote 1071Cfrom every dissimilitude, and unceasingly desirous of dominion, and conforming, as far as is possible, both itself and the things that are after it, in the best and most beautiful way, to the likeness of that very virtue subsisting naturally, turned toward none of the things seen as one, but toward the properly ὄν universal, and made, as far as is possible for it, ever in participation of the Lordly deiformity. But that certain strong and unchangeable manliness of the holy virtues, in all their operations according to their deiformity, in no way feebly weakened toward any reception of the divine illuminations imparted to it, powerfully led back into the imitation of God, not abandoning by its own feebleness the deiform motion, but firmly bearing itself into the superessential 1071Dand power-making virtue, and made its image like to the virtue, according to what is permitted, and powerfully turned toward it indeed as toward the principal virtue: but toward the second things, giving [dans et] virtue, coming forth deiformly. But that ordination of the holy powers, equal in power to the divine dominations and virtues, well-ordered and unconfused about the divine receptions, and the ordered rank of the supermundane and intellectual power, not tyrannically 1072Bhurled down by its power-wielding virtues into the things that are lower, but powerfully led back into the divine things after the well-ordered ones, and leading back deiformly the things that are after it, and assimilated, as far as is lawful, to the power-making causal power, and revealing it, as is possible, to the angels in the ranks well-ordered through it by its power-wielding virtue. Having these deiform properties, the middle ordering of the celestial minds is indeed purged, and illumined, and perfected, as has been said, by the divine illuminations imparted to it in the second place through the first hierarchical ordering, and conveyed through that middle one by a second manifestation. And so, by the utterance passing from one angel [and] heard in another angel, we shall make a symbol of the perfection which is from afar above [all], and 1072Chidden through the procession into the things that follow. For those wise concerning our sacred immolations say that the plenitudes of the divine things, shining through themselves, are more perfect than [those] through other contemplative participations. So too I judge that the immediate participation of the angelic orders first extended into God is more perfect through the mediation of the perfected. On which account, by our priestly tradition, the first intellects are named the perfective, light-bringing, and purgative virtues of the lower ones, as of those led back through them into the superessential principle of all, and made partakers of the mystical purgations, and illuminations, and perfections, according to what is lawful for them. For Poc has been divinely promulgated altogether by the divine ordination: that the second things participate in the divine 1072Dilluminations through the first. And you will find this too expressed many times by the theologians. For when the divine and paternal humanity, correcting Israel nurturingly for its sacred salvation, and handing it over into correction to avenging and monstrous nations, by an all-kinds conveyance of things provided for unto the better, both dismissed the captivity and clemently led it back to its former beneficence, one of the theologians, Zachariah, saw one of the first — as I judge — and of the angels about God (for this angelic appellation is common 1073Ato all, as I said) learning from God himself concerning this the consoling, as has been said, words. But another of the subject angels coming forth to meet the first, as to the reception and perception of illumination, then instructed by him in the divine counsel as by a high priest, and turned to teach this to the theologian, namely that Jerusalem shall be fruitfully inhabited by a multitude of men (Zach. I). But another of the theologians, Ezekiel (Ezech. VIII), [says] that this too, he says, was most sacredly promulgated by the most glorious divinity established above the cherubim. For Israel itself, as has been said — the leader of the host, the humanity, conveying it unto the better through disciplines, divine justice being rendered to those who correct — justified the corrected. This 1073Bis taught: the first after the cherubim, girt about the loins with sapphire, who was clothed in the podere according to the hierarchic symbol. But the rest of the angels, who had axes, the divine ordination commands to be taught by the prior one concerning this divine judgment (Ezech. X). For to him indeed it said to pass through the midst of Jerusalem, and to give a sign on the foreheads of the corrected men; to the others: Go out into the city after him, and strike, and spare not your eyes; but to all, upon whom the sign is, do not draw near (Ezech. IX). What, perhaps, would one say of the angel saying to Daniel: The word went forth; or of that first one receiving fire from the midst of the cherubim (Dan. IX). Or that [saying] of the same, which [is] more abundantly toward the showing of the angelic order, namely that 1073Cthe cherub also puts fire into the hands of the one clothed in the holy stole (Ezech. X); or of the one calling the most divine Gabriel, and saying to him: « Make him understand the vision (Zach. I); » or whatever other things have been said by the sacred theologians concerning the deiform adornment of the celestial hierarchies. To which the ordination of our hierarchy, assimilated as far as is possible, will have the angelic beauty, in so far as it is formed in characters through it, and led back to the superessential of the whole hierarchy at once.

EXPOSITIO.

Octavum caput est de dominationibus, et virtutibus, et potestatibus, et de media, quae eorum est hierachia. In praecedenti siquidem capite tractavit 1073Dde tribus primis ordinibus, seraphim, et cherubim, et thronis, et de hierarchia, id est sacra potestate eorum, quae in coelesti dispositione prima est et principalis, et post Deum immediate ordinata. Nunc ergo consequenter ingreditur tractare de tribus sequentibus ordinibus, id est dominationibus, virtutibus et potestatibus; et de hierarchia, id est sacra potestate eorum, quae in coelesti dispositione secunda, vel media est constituta, id est, post primam, et ante ultimam. De hac ergo hierarchia, eodem, quo et de superiori ordine tractat, primum ostendendo causam vel rationem cognominationis, quae ipsis ordinibus hujus hierarchiae attributa est, deinde virtutem ipsius sacrae potestatis latius exponendo.

1074A« Transeundum, inquit, nunc nobis est in mediam coelestium intellectuum dispositionem: dominationes, illas super mundanis oculis, quantum possibile est, explorantibus, et vere potentia speculamina divinarum potestatum, et virtutum. » Continua: seipsum ad sequentem dictionem, ac si diceret. Post expositionem supremae hierarchiae, ordo expostulat ut transeamus ad mediam, id est ad expositionem mediae hierarchiae coelestium intellectuum, id est angelicorum spirituum. Postea exponit nominatim qui sunt illi ordines angelorum, in quibus media illa potestas sacra constat: ad cujus expositionem se transire debere dicit, addens: « Dominationes: illas supermundanis oculis, quantum possibile est, explorantibus, et vere potentia 1074Bspeculamina divinarum potestatum et virtutum. Transeundum, inquit, est nobis, » dicit, « explorantibus in illa, » scilicet hierarchia dominationes, « et vere potentia speculamina potestatum et virtutum, » id est et potestates, et virtutes. Isti enim sunt tres ordines secundae hierarchiae, quorum virtutem et officia diligenter explorare oportet eum, qui eorum sacram potestatem exponere desiderat. Ideo, inquit, « supermundanis oculis, » id est spiritualibus explorandum. Non enim ista corporalibus oculis videntur. « Explorantibus » itaque « nobis illas, » scilicet dominationes coelestes, et « explorantibus speculamina, » id est speculationes, vel contemplationes « potestatum, et virtutum. » Quod dicit exploraturum se speculationes vel contemplationes 1074Cpotestatum et virtutum; vel ita intelligendum est, ac si diceret, per speculationem vel contemplationem de illis habitam se illorum dignitatem exploraturum, vel ipsam eorum contemplationem, qua Deum contemplantur, et divina percipiunt exploraturum, et investigaturum se testatur. Vere potentia speculamina, vel potentes speculationes vocat propterea, quod ipsos vere potentes explorant. Potentem enim speculationem potentium speculationem intelligit. Vere potentes idcirco nominat, quia in bonitate potentes et in veritate. Malum siquidem posse, vere posse non est, sed non posse, sicut scriptum est: « Quid gloriaris in malitia, qui potens es in iniquitate (Psal. LI): » Quapropter et ipsas 1074Dpotestates divinas vocat, quia ex Deo et in Deo possunt omne quod possunt.

Sequitur: « Etenim unaquaeque supra nos essentiarum cognominatio Dei imitatorias earum significat deiformes proprietates. Ac si diceret: Recte potestates, et virtutes divinas nominavi, quia et hoc ipsa earum cognominatio docet. Sicut unaquaeque cognominatio essentiarum, quae supra nos sunt, id est coelestium, significat deiformes proprietates earum: et ideo deiformes, quia Dei imitatorias. Quod enim formitatem habent coelestes illae essentiae, non ex qualitate habent, sed ex imitatione, quia similitudinem Dei illis non natura confert, sed gratia.

Sequitur: « Igitur sanctarum dominationum manifestativam nominationem existimo declarare, absolutam 1075Aquamdam, et omni pedestri minoratione liberam anagogem; nullaque tyrannicarum dissimilitudinum ullo modo eam inclinatam universaliter, liberaliter severam dominationem, omni minutivae servituti superpositam: superiorem subjectione, omni et remotam ab universa dissimulatione, et dominationis incessanter appetentem; et ad illius ipsius naturaliter subsistentis virtutis similitudinem, quantum possibile, et seipsam, et quae post eam sunt, optime, et speciose conformantem; ad nullum vana videntium, sed ad proprie ὄν on universale conversam, et Dominicae semper deiformitatis in participatione, secundum quod possibile est ipsi factam. » Haec omnia nominatio dominationum docet; in eo enim, quod dominationes appellantur, haec 1075Bomnia, quae de seipsis dicta sunt, habere et facere significantur. Hoc est quod dicit: « Existimo manifestativam nominationem sanctarum dominationum, » id est nominationem, qua manifestatur et declaratur earum virtus, et excellentia, et dignitas: existimo, inquit, illam nominationem declarare haec omnia. Quae omnia? Audi. « Multa enim sunt. » Ideo dixi haec omnia: quia multa sunt ad nos, sed pauca ad ipsas. « Existimo, inquit, sanctarum dominationum nominationem declarare absolutam quamdam, » id est liberam, et ab omni depressione alienam « anagogem, » id est excellentiam, sive sublimitatem, vel sursum ductionem earum, qua ad summum elevantur, ut nulli infra summum subjiciantur. Et existimo ipsam nominationem etiam 1075Cdeclarare, eam scilicet anagogen, sive excellentiam ipsarum non esse inclinatam universaliter ullo modo, id est nullo modo omnino esse inclinatam ulla tyrannicarum dissimilitudinem, id est per ullam, sive secundum ullam tyrannicam dissimilitudinem, id est secundum aliquam tyrannidem, quae omnino ab earum dominatione dissimilis est. Ac si diceret: Sicut per excellentiam universalem supra omnem subjectionem elevantur, ita ad oppressionem subjectorum per nullam tyrannidem inclinantur.

Sequitur: « Liberaliter severam dominationem; omni minutivae servituti superpositam. » A superioribus (subaudiendum est) existimo declarare nominationem dominationum, dominationem earum liberaliter severam, id est benigne severam. Severitatem 1075Dhabentem in potestate, liberalitatem in benignitate. Severam, quia a superiori potestas exercetur, inferiori libertas non tollitur. Ideo liberaliter severam dominationem, omni minutivae servituti superpositam, id est non subjectam alicui ad servitutem, quae libertatem imminuat, sed superiorem omni subjectione, et remotam ab universa dissimilitudine, id est ab omni minoritate, sive imperfectione, quae eam dissimilem Creatori suo efficiat, et incessanter appetentem dominationis, id est per similitudinem dominationis, et conformitatem Creatoris respicientem, sive tendentem, vel inhaerentem, et conformantem se, et ea, quae post eam sunt, ut singula, quantum sibi possibile est. divinam virtutem 1076Aoptime et speciose imitentur. Propterea inquit, « existimo declarare nominationem earum dominationem conformantem se, et ea quae post eam sunt, divinae virtuti; et ad nullum vana videntium, sed ad proprie on universale conversam. » Videntium ponit pro eo, quod dicere debuerat visorum, usitatissimo Graecorum more; quoniam a verbo δοκοῦμαι, hoc est, video vel videor, quoniam commune est, derivatur: ut sit sensus: Existimo declarare conversam non ad aliquid eorum quae vana videntur, id est quae per se considerata ima apparent, et transitoria. Sed conversam potius ad proprie on universale, id est conversam ad id, quod est proprie, et universale; ad Deum, scilicet cui et proprium esse est, quia per se subsistit, et universale, 1076Bquia omnibus esse tribuit. Sciendum vero quod ὄν on apud Graecos quando per ὄντῶν μικρὸν per omicron, id est o breve seu parvum scribitur, neutrale est, et interpretatur quod est. Quando vero ὤν per ω τὸν μέγα, id est ω longum vel magnum scribitur, masculinum est, et interpretatur qui est. On ergo, ipse est Creator omnium, et principium, qui est, et quod est proprie in se, et universale ad omnia: ad quod principium dominationem hanc conversam dicit, et factam in participatione, id est participem effectam Dominicae deiformitatis, id est divinae similitudinis, quam semper, id est incommutaibiliter retinet: factam dico, secundum quod possibile est ipsi. Hactenus demonstravit quid significet nominatio dominationum; nunc transit ut demonstret quid significet 1076Cnominatio virtutum.

Sequitur: « Ipsam vero sanctarum virtutum fortem quamdam et incommutabilem virilitatem in omnes, secundum earum deiformitatem, operationes, ad nullam susceptionem inditarum eis divinarum illuminationem imbecilliter infirmatam, potenter in imitationem Dei reductam: non relinquentem suimet imbecillitate deiformem motum, sed firmiter ferentem in superessentialem, et potentificam virtutem, et ipsius imaginem virtuti similem, juxta quod licet, factam, et ad ipsam quidem ut principalem virtutem potenter conversam. Ad secundam vero virtutem dans et deiformiter provenientem. » Ipsam, inquit, sanctarum virtutum (subauditur 1076Dcognominationem) existimo declarare quamdam virilitatem fortem et incommutabilem in omnes operationes: virilitatem dico, inditam eis secundum deiformitatem earum, quia in hoc similes, vel conformes Deo sunt, quod ad omnia agenda fortem et incommutabilem virilitatem, sive virtutem accipere meruerunt. Divina siquidem virtus et fortis est agendum ut non frangatur in difficultate alicujus operis, et incommutabilis est ad perseverandum ut non langueat, aut infirmetur spatio diuturnitatis. In hoc ergo virtutes deiformes sunt, et ideo consimiles sunt quod ad omnia agenda robur forte habent; et incommutabile. Nec solum virilitatem habent fortem, et incommutabilem ad omnia agenda sub se, sed habent etiam virilitatem sive virtutem non infirmatam 1077Aimbecilliter, ad illam susceptionem inditarum ei divinarum illuminationum. Fortes enim sunt in exsecutione operum, fortes etiam sunt in perceptione donorum, quia virtutes eorum, et si infirmetur ad divinam virtutem comparata, non tamen infirmatur ad divinam conformata. Infirmatur conditione ad capiendum totum, quod Creatori proprium est; sed non infirmatur corruptione ad percipiendum totum, quod creaturae debitum est. Non ergo imbecilliter infirmatur: quae etsi virtutem non habeat Creatori aequalem, habet tamen fortitudinem creaturae sufficientem. Propterea virilitatem habet fortem, et incommutabilem ad exsecutionem faciendorum, et non infirmatam ad perceptionem munerum; et reductam potenter, hoc est, conversam sive 1077Breformatam in imitatione Dei, hoc est, ut Deum imitetur; reductam quidem per illuminationes, in imitationem per operationes. Et habent virilitatem non relinquentem deiformem motum aliqua imbecillitate suimet. Deiformem motum vocat, quod ipsae virtutes coelestes incessabiliter moventur, ut Deum imitentur; vel desuper scilicet appetendo accipere, quod ille habet, ut idem sint cum ipso; aut deorsum, faciendo quod facit, ut non recedant ab ipso. Sic itaque habent virilitatem non relinquentem deiformem motum; sed per illum deiformem motum firmiter ferentem se, vel extollentem in superessentialem, et potentificam virtutem Creatoris: ac per hoc factam imaginem similem virtuti ipsius Creatoris, juxta quod licet, hoc est, secundum quod 1077Cconcessum est ipsis, vel possibile. In hoc enim quod virilitas illorum per deiformem motum in superessentialem, et potentificam virtutem Creatoris sustollitur, ejusdem divinae virtutis imago et similitudo fieri comprobatur. Propterea, inquit, existimo virilitatem illorum imaginem effectam similem divinae virtuti, et conversam ad illam divinam virtutem, utpote ad principalem virtutem; ad secunda vero virtutem dans, et deiformiter provenientem. Sic, inquit, cognominatio virtutum docet virilitatem eorum conversam ad superiorem virtutem Dei, ut ab illa quasi a prima deiformitatem accipiat; et docet etiam eam provenientem vel procedentem ad secunda, id est, ad subsequentes ordines, ut illis deiformiter proveniat, dans eis virtutem, et in ipsa virtute 1077DDei conformitatem, ut ipsam deiformitatem, et a superiori accipiat, et inferioribus tribuat: accipiat per donum, tribuat per exemplum.

Sequitur: « Ipsam autem sanctarum potestatum aequipotentem divinarum dominationum, et virtutum bene ornatam, et inconfusam circa divinas susceptiones ordinatione, et ordinatum supermundanae, et intellectualis potestatis, non tyrannice in ea, quae inferiora sunt, potestativis virtutibus praecipitatae, sed potenter in divina post bene ordinatas reductae: et post eam deiformiter reducentis, et ad potentificam causalem potentiam, quantum fas est, assimilatae: et eam, ut possibile, angelis revelantis in bene ornatis per ipsam ordinibus potestativa 1078Avirtute. » Post cognominationem virtutum transit ad cognominationem potestatum. Ipsam autem sanctarum potestatum (subauditur nominationem) existimo declarare ordinationem quamdam illarum, aequipotentem divinarum dominationum, et virtutum, id est aequalis potentiae cum dominationibus et virtutibus ordinationem, dico, bene ornatam et inconfusam circa divinas susceptiones, id est circa dona divina suscipienda, quia dona Dei, quae ad ornatum pulchritudinis spiritualis suscipit, in suo gradu, et ordine humiliter persistens sine confusione custodit. Existimo etiam ipsam nominationem potestatum declarare ordinatum, id est ordinationem potestatis supermundanae, et intellectualis: potestatis, dico, non praecipitatae tyrannice in ea, 1078Bquae inferiora sunt, cum potestativis virtutibus, id est violenta fortitudine. Sed potius reductae, sive conversae potenter in divina post bene ordinatis, id est post virtutes, quae ante eam ordinatae sunt: et potestatis, dico, reducentis deiformiter, id est secundum similitudinem divinam, quae post eam sunt, id est, illos ordines angelorum, qui post eam subsequuntur. Sicut enim ipsa meditantibus superioribus ad similitudinem Dei convertitur, ita mediante ipsa quae inferiora sunt ad eamdem Dei similitudinem revocantur. Adhuc sequitur: Potestates assimilatae, quantum fas est, id est, vel licitum, vel concessum ad potentificam, causalem potentiam; quia omnia potest, et causa est omnium. Et potestatis, dico, revelantis, eam scilicet divinam 1078Cpotentiam, quantum possibile est, angelis eam revelare. Quomodo revelantis? potestativa virtute. Ubi revelantis? In ordinibus per ipsam bene ornatis, hoc est, in subsequentibus ordinibus, quos ornat, divinam eis potentiam exemplo sui revelando.

Sequitur: « Has habens deiformes proprietates media coelestium animorum dispositio, purgatur quidem, et illuminatur, et perficitur, quemadmodum dictum est, a divinis illuminationibus inditis sibi secundo per primam hierarchiam dispositionem, et per mediam illam secunda manifestatione delatis. » Media, inquit, dispositio coelestium animorum, de qua scilicet hactenus tractatum est quae constat dominationibus et virtutibus, et potestatibus: ipsa habens deiformes proprietates, has 1078Dscilicet quas supra diximus, purgatur et illuminatur, et perficitur, quemadmodum superius dictum est de prima hierarchia; purgatur dico, a divinis illuminationibus inditis sibi secundo (subauditur loco) per primam hierarchicam dispositionem. Prima hierarchica dispositio in tribus primis ordinibus constat, id est seraphim, cherubim, et thronis: quae primo loco ab ipsa divinitate divinas suscipit illuminationes: quibus illuminationibus postea secunda manifestatione per mediam illam ad secundam hierarchiam delatis, ipsa secunda hierarchia per easdem divinas illuminationes secundo loco purgatur, et illuminatur, et perficitur.

Sequitur: « Itaque per alium dictum venientem 1079Ain alium angelum auditum, symbolum faciemus a longe super perfectae, et per processionem occultae in sequentia perfectionis. » Exemplo et auctoritate probat quod dixerat, scilicet mediam dispositionem angelorum illuminari a prima, sive per primam, hoc est, quod dicit: Symbolum faciemus, hoc est exemplum, sive demonstrationem perfectionis, scilicet divinae a longe super omnia perfectae: et occultae per processionem in sequentia; quia, cum in se occulta sit et invisibilis, per processionem tamen exit, et manifestatur in sequentia, id est, in eos qui post ipsam primo loco sunt immediate, sive in eos qui post illos sequuntur. Hujusmodi, inquam, perfectionis divinae in se perfectae et occultae, et tamen per largitionem gratiae in sequentia procedentis 1079Bsymbolum faciemus, dictum, id est dictionem, sive sermonem per alium angelum prolatum et postea venientem in alium angelum, et ab eo auditum. In eo enim quod alius angelus dixit, alius audivit, alius doctrinam protulit, alius suscepit: symbolum factum est, hoc est demonstratio, sive argumentum, quod divina perfectio per priores et superiores ad sequentes et inferiores participanda procedit. « Nam sapientes circa nostras sacras immolationes aiunt per seipsas lucentes divinorum plenitudines, per alias contemplativarum participationum esse perfectiores. » Ac si diceret: Non est mirum, si in angelis, alius docuit, alius docebatur, quando alius alio doctior est. Nam qui sapientes sunt circa sacras nostras immolationes, 1079Cid est circa nostra sacrificia sive sacramenta, ipsi aiunt divinorum plenitudines, id est illos angelos, qui pleni sunt divinis donis, sive illuminationibus et per seipsos lucent, perfectiores esse participationum contemplativarum per alios, hoc est, participationibus contemplativis per alios. Genitivum enim posuit pro ablativo. Qui, inquit, sapientes sunt, vel periti in nostris sacramentis, testantur, quod illi angelici spiritus qui per semetipsos divinam immediate contemplationem suscipiunt, perfectiores sunt quam caeteri, qui mediantibus superioribus eamdem participant contemplationem.

Sequitur: « Sic existimo et angelicorum ordinum immediatam participationem primo in Deum 1079Dextentorum perfectiorem esse per medietatem perfectorum. » Quia, inquit, sapientes hoc testantur, propterea et ego existimo immediatam participationem angelicorum ordinum, primo in Deum extentorum, hoc est, illos angelicos ordines, qui primo loco, et principaliter in Deum extenti immediate ipsum participant, perfectiorem esse, id est, perfectiores participatione esse perfectorum per medietatem, hoc est, perfectis participantibus per medietatem, hoc est, perfectiores esse quam iis, qui perfecti sunt aliis mediantibus.

Sequitur: « Propter quod a nostra sacerdotali traditione perfectivae, lucificae, et purgativae virtutes primi intellectus nominantur inferiorum; tanquam per se in omnium superessentiale principium 1080Areductorum; et mysticarum purgationum, et illuminationum, et perfectionum in participatione, secundum quod eis fas factorum. » Ac si diceret: Quia superiores spiritus perfectiores sunt inferioribus et consequentibus, propterea a nostra sacerdotali traditione primi intellectus, id est, supremi ordines angelorum vocantur perfectivae, et lucificae, et purgativae virtutes inferiorum, quia per eos inferiores perficiuntur et purgantur, et illuminantur: virtutes nominantur inferiorum, utpote reductorum per se, hoc est, per seipsos in superessentiale principium omnium, id est Deum, et inferiorum, dico, factorum in participatione, quia participes facti sunt, quantum eis fas est, mysticarum purgationum, et illuminationum, et perfectionum. 1080BPer ipsos itaque superiores, per quos purgantur, et illuminantur, et perficiuntur.

Sequitur: « Hoc enim est omnino divina ordinatione divinitus promulgatum: per prima secunda divinis participare illuminationibus: hoc, inquit, est divinitus promulgatum, » vel manifestatum « omnino, » id est, universaliter de divina ordinatione, quod secunda ubique per prima participant divinis illuminationibus.

Sequitur: « Invenies autem hoc et multoties a theologis expressum: » hoc, inquit, quod dico secunda per prima participare divinis illuminationibus, invenies tu expressum, id est, manifeste magnificatum, et notatum in Scripturis scilicet sacris: a theologis, id est, iis qui de divinis ratiocinati 1080Csunt, et scripserunt.

Sequitur: « Quando enim divina et paterna humanitas Israel nutritive pro sacra ejus salute corripiens et ulciscentibus, et immanibus nationibus in correptionem tradens omnigena provisorum in melius traductione: et captivitatem dimisit, et ad priorem clementer reduxit beneficentiam: Vidit theologorum unus Zacharias unum primorum, ut existimo, et circa Deum angelorum (communis enim, ut dixi, est omnibus haec angelica cognominatio) ab ipso Deo discentem de hoc consolatoria, ut dictum est, verba. Alterum vero subjectorum angelorum in occursum primi provenientem, tanquam ad illuminationis susceptionem, et perceptionem; 1080Ddeinde ab ipso divinum consilium tanquam a summo sacerdote eruditum: Et hoc docere theologum conversum, quoniam fructuose habitatur Hierusalem a multitudine hominum. » Probat exemplum, quod dixerat. In Zacharia propheta legitur angelum mandato accepto a Deo exisse, et angelo alteri sibi occurrenti mandatum dedisse ut curreret, et prophetae nuntiaret, quod adhuc absque muris habitaretur Hierusalem. Hoc est enim quod dicit: « Quando divina, et paterna humanitas, » id est pietas Dei paterna, « nutritive corripiens, » id est, more nutritii qui parvulum filium ad hoc flagellat, ut castiget, corripiens Israel flagello Babylonicae captivitatis pro sacra ejus salute, ut scilicet dum corporaliter eum ad tempus exterius disperderet, interius 1081Aad sanctitatem reparando salvaret. Sic itaque pietas Dei paterne corripiens Israel et tradens eum in correptionem, ad hoc scilicet ut corrigeretur tradens eum nationibus, Chaldaeis videlicet: nationibus dico, et ulciscentibus, et immanibus; quia et injuriam Dei ultae sunt, et tamen hoc non zelo justitiae sed crudelitatis furore fecerunt. Tradens dico traductione; ut scilicet traducerentur de patria in exsilium, de terra sua in terram alienam, de Hierusalem in Babylonem, de visione pacis in captivitatem confusionis: traductione dico omnigena, id est universali, sive generali omnium provisorum in melius, hoc est, ad salutem praedestinatorum. Per hanc siquidem captivitatem et reductionem, quae in uno populo corporaliter facta est 1081Bomnium electorum, et a captivitate peccati liberandorum forma demonstrata est. Quando igitur divina pietas paterne tradens Israel tali traductione; postea et captivitatem dimisit, et ipsum Israel ad priorem beneficentiam clementer reduxit. Tunc « vidit unus theologorum Zacharias scilicet, unum primorum angelorum, » id est, unum de primis angelis, hoc est unum de excellentibus et superioribus, et circa Deum positis angelis. Dicit, « unum de primis, ut ego existimo: » nam theologia hoc non dicit, quod ille unus de primis fuerit. Sed ego existimo, quod ille unus de primis fuit, quia praeceptum ab alio priore non accepit, sed mandatum ad secundum dedit. Ideo, inquit, « existimo ego, » quod ille unus fuit primorum angelorum. Quomodo 1081Cprimorum angelorum, cum angeli primi non sint, quoniam qui ultimi sunt et infimi tantum angeli nominantur? Non inquit, sic angelum dico. Sed secundum hoc, quod communis est aliquando omnibus, sicut supra dictum est, haec angelica cognominatio nunc supremos ordines angelos voco. Sic itaque unus theologorum Zacharias vidit unum primorum angelorum ab ipso Deo discentem consolatoria verba, de hoc scilicet negotio captivitatis, et reductionis Israel, ut dictum est in prophetia, scilicet ipsius Zachariae. Vidit etiam alterum subjectorum angelorum in occursum primi angeli provenientem id est exeuntum, vel praevenientem, id est, praecurrentem antequam vocetur, tanquam paratum, et 1081Ddevotum per se ad susceptionem, et perceptionem illuminationis suae, quam accepturus erat ab illo. Deinde vidit ipse Zacharias illum secundum angelum eruditum consilium ab ipso primo angelo tanquam a summo sacerdote, utpote scilicet a superiori, et sacra dante: et vidit etiam eumdem secundum angelum postea conversum, hoc docere theologum, hoc est conversum a primo angelo, cui intendebat; ad theologum, hoc est ad ipsum Zachariam, ut eum doceret, hoc scilicet consilium divinum, quod ipse didicerat a primo angelo: primus autem angelus a Deo, hoc est autem consilium, quod ipse annuntiavit « quoniam fructuose, » id est, copiose « habitabitur » Hierusalem a multitudine hominum. Alia translatio dicit: « Absque muris 1082Ahabitabitur Hierusalem. » Sub eodem utique sensu, pro eo quod post interniciem captivitatis divina gratia populus ille in tantum multiplicandus foret, ut ambitu murorum Hierusalem habitantium multitudo includi non posset.

Sequitur: « Alter autem theologorum Ezechiel: et ab ipsa, inquit, hoc sacratissime promulgatum esse cherubim superfirmata gloriosissima divinitate. » Alterius theologi testimonio probat, quod dixit, scilicet quod divina consilia a primis angelis immediate suscepta; deinde per inferiores angelos usque ad theologorum animos deferuntur, hoc est, quod ait: « Alter theologorum Ezechiel, » scilicet hoc consilium divinum etiam ab ipsa gloriosissima divinitate, et superfirmata sacratissime promulgatum 1082Besse cherubim: hoc, inquit. Ezechiel dicit, quod divinitas ipsa gloriosissima in majestate superfirmata in aeternitate, consilium suum cherubim sacratissime promulgavit vel revelavit, a quibus postea consequentibus est ordinibus manifestatum amplius? « Ipsum enim Israel, ut dictum est, dux exercitus humanitas, per disciplinas in melius traducens, Justitia divina corrigentibus respondetur, correctos justificavit. » Humanitas, inquit, id est, pietas, dux exercitus sive magistra exercitationis, traducens ipsum Israel in melius per disciplinas, noxios condemnavit, correctos justificavit, et hoc, scilicet judicium ex divina justitia respondetur corrigentibus angelis, qui missi erant ad puniendum: quod idcirco divina pietas flagella induceret, ut 1082Creprobos condemnaret, correctos justificaret. Vel ipsa divina justitia respondetur corrigentibus quod justum est, ut reprobi condemnentur, correcti justificentur. Vel corrigentibus Chaldaeis, id est, persequentibus per quos Deus populum suum flagellavit et correxit, ex divina justitia respondetur, ut recipiant sicut meruerunt; Israelitas autem correctos divina pietas justificavit. « Hoc docetur primus post cherubim lumbos sapphiro praecinctus, qui podere juxta symbolum hierarchicum induebatur: » hoc, inquit, divinum consilium condemnationis et justificationis « docetur, primus post cherubim constitutus qui induebatur podere juxta symbolum hierarchicum. » Quod enim post cherubim quidam 1082Dapparuit lumbos sapphiro praecinctus, et podere indutus, symbolum erat hierarchicum, id est figura hierarchica, quia hierarchia visibilibus figuris utitur ad invisibilium demonstrationem. Et non solum ille, qui post cherubim primus erat, docetur divinum consilium, sed etiam reliqui, qui sequuntur. Hoc est enim quod subjungit: Reliquos autem angelos, qui secures habebant, divina ordinatio imperat a priori doceri de hoc divinum judicium. De hoc scilicet consilio, sive de hoc opere divina ordinatio imperat ipsi cherubim « reliquos angelos doceri ab eo, » qui primus erat post cherubim, ut eo ordine praeceptum divinum primum in cherubim descenderet, deinde per cherubim ad eum qui proximus erat podere indutus, per quem tandem ad consequentes 1083Aangelos, qui cum securibus parati erant veniret.

Sequitur: « Ei quidem enim dixit mediam pertransire Hierusalem, et dare signum in frontes correctorum virorum: » vel ei, hoc est, cherubim dixit divina ordinatio, ut ille praeciperet sequentem se pertransire mediam Hierusalem, etc. Vel ei, hoc est, sequenti post cherubim, per ipsum cherubim « dixit mediam pertransire Hierusalem, » etc. Et non solum illi per cherubim praeceptum dedit, sed aliis etiam post ipsum sequentibus hoc est, quod subdiditur: « Aliis exite in civitatem post eum, et percutite; et nolite parcere oculis vestris. Ad omnes autem super quos est signum, ne appropinquetis. » Haec autem omnia, quae de visionibus propheticis 1083Bassumpta sunt, ad hoc valent, ut ostendatur, quod primi et summi angeli ab ipso Deo erudiuntur, secundi a primis, tertii a secundis.

Sequitur: « Quid fortassis quis dixerit de dicente angelo ad Danielem: Exiit sermo; aut de ipso primo ignem ex medio cherubim recipiente? aut illud ejusdem, quod abundantius in ordinis angelici ostensionem; quoniam et cherubim immittit ignem in manus sanctam stolam induti; aut de vocante divinissimum Gabrielem, et dicente ei: Fac illum intelligere visionem. Aut quaecunque alia a sacris theologis dicta sunt de coelestium hierarchiarum deiformi ornatu, ad quem nostrae hierarchiae ordinatio, secundum quod possibile est, assimilata, angelicam pulchritudinem, quantum in characteribus 1083Chabebit formata per eum et reducta ad superessentialem simul omnis hierarchiae. » In his testimoniis propheticis, sicut supra diximus, hoc solum probare intendit, quod in angelis alii alios docent, et inferiores a superioribus praeceptum, et doctrinam suscipiunt; sive etiam cum homines ab angelis erudiuntur, et inferiores a superioribus cognitionem accipiunt. Quid enim dixerit quis, hoc est, aliquis, de angelo dicente ad Danielem, nisi, quod inferior a superiore eruditur, et doctrinam suscipit? Aut etiam quid dixerit aliquis de illo primo superius post cherubim commemorato podere induto, et ignem, ex medio cherubim recipiente, nisi hoc similiter, quod alius ab alio accipere ostenditur, quod 1083Dper se habere non potest? Aut quid aliud est etiam illud ejusdem, scilicet visionis, sive exempli, quod abundantius est sive copiosius in ostensionem angelici ordinis, id est ad ostendendum, quod in angelis aliis alii superiores ordines ordinati sunt, sicut dico, quod cherubim immittit ignem in manus sanctam stolam induti, nisi manifeste dispensatio per 1084Aalium in alium fieri demonstratur? Illud quidem in visione Ezechielis, de qua hoc sumptum est, testimonium conjicitur magis, quam exponit; quoniam ex eo quod primus ille post cherubim sanctam stolam, sive podere indutus de medio cherubim ignem accipere jubetur, eumdem ignem ab ipso cherubim non inconvenienter accepisse creditur. De hoc itaque quid dicere poterit aliquis, nisi quod manifeste ostenditur divinam largitionem per alios ad alios transire? Aut etiam de angelo vocante divinissimum Gabrielem, et dicente ei: Fac illum intelligere sermonem [visionem]: quid dicere poterit aliquis, nisi quod secundum ejusdem dispositionis ordinationem divinum praeceptum per alios ad alios descendit; et qui superiores sunt, inferioribus 1084Bimperant facienda, quemadmodum cognoscenda insinuant? De his itaque aut etiam de aliis omnibus, quaecunque alia a sacris theologis dicta sunt de coelestium hierarchiarum deiformi ornatu, quid aliquis dicere poterit, nisi quod supradictum est? Ad quem scilicet ornatum coelestium hierarchiarum nostrae, id est humanae, sive Ecclesiasticae hierarchiae ordinatio assimilata, quantum ei possibile (scilicet assimilari) ex ipsa similitudine habebit angelicam pulchritudinem quantum in characteribus, hoc est, figuris, et similitudinibus. Quantum enim modo habet in figura similitudinis, tantum postmodum habebit in celsitudine glorificationis. Modo quidem characterem et signum habet in figura; tunc rem et veritatem habitura in gloria. Quidam characteres 1084Cistos extranee interpretari conati sunt; in illa futura gloria beatitudinis supernae phantasias quasdam et imagines errorum pro Deo in contemplatione speculantibus opponentes, Deum in sua substantia nulli unquam visibilem asserentes. Sed nos beatitudinem non exspectamus in contemplatione figurarum, quibus veritas ipsa promissa est. Nostrae igitur hierarchiae dispositio ad angelicum ornatum formata, quantum modo in characteribus et figura habet similitudinis, tantum postmodum habebit in gloria pulchritudinis. Modo quidem formata per eum: hoc est, et secundum eum angelicum scilicet ornatum, et mediante eodem ornatu angelico, reducta ad superessentialem simul omnis hierarchiae, hoc est, 1084Dreparata ad similitudinem Dei, qui est superessentialis omnis hierarchiae; quia ab eo omnis hierarchia non solum formam, sed etiam substantiam habet; quia omnem hierarchiam ipse non solum instituit, sed etiam creavit, ut post ipsum esset similitudine, sub ipso conditione.

THE EXPOSITION.

The eighth chapter is on the dominations, and the virtues, and the powers, and on the middle hierarchy, which is theirs. For in the preceding chapter he treated 1073Dof the three first orders — the seraphim, and the cherubim, and the thrones — and of the hierarchy, that is, their sacred power, which in the celestial ordering is first and principal, and ordered immediately after God. Now, therefore, he proceeds consequently to treat of the three following orders, that is, the dominations, virtues, and powers; and of the hierarchy, that is, their sacred power, which in the celestial ordering is constituted second, or middle, that is, after the first and before the last. Of this hierarchy, then, he treats in the same manner as he does of the higher order: first by showing the cause or reason of the appellation which is attributed to the orders themselves of this hierarchy, then by expounding more fully the power of that sacred authority.

1074A« We must now, he says, pass over into the middle ordering of the celestial intellects: exploring those dominations, as far as is possible, with supermundane eyes, and the truly powerful contemplations of the divine powers and virtues. » Join it together: himself to the following statement, as if he said. After the exposition of the supreme hierarchy, the order demands that we pass over to the middle, that is, to the exposition of the middle hierarchy of the celestial intellects, that is, of the angelic spirits. Afterward he sets forth by name which are those orders of angels in which that middle sacred power consists: to whose exposition he says he ought to pass over, adding: « The dominations: exploring those, as far as is possible, with supermundane eyes, and the truly powerful 1074Bcontemplations of the divine powers and virtues. We must pass over, he says, » he says, « as we explore in that » — namely hierarchy — « the dominations, and the truly powerful contemplations of the powers and virtues, » that is, both the powers and the virtues. For these are the three orders of the second hierarchy, whose power and offices he must diligently explore who desires to expound their sacred power. Therefore, he says, « with supermundane eyes, » that is, with spiritual ones, it must be explored. For these things are not seen with bodily eyes. « As we explore, » therefore, « those, » namely the celestial dominations, and « as we explore the contemplations, » that is, the speculations or contemplations « of the powers and virtues. » As to his saying that he will explore the speculations or contemplations 1074Cof the powers and virtues; either it is to be understood thus, as if he said, that through the speculation or contemplation had concerning them he will explore their dignity, or he testifies that he will explore and investigate their very contemplation, by which they contemplate God and perceive divine things. He calls them "truly powerful contemplations," or "powerful speculations," for this reason, that they explore those who are truly powerful. For by "powerful speculation" he understands "speculation of the powerful." He names them "truly powerful" for this reason, that they are powerful in goodness and in truth. For to be able to do evil is not truly to be able, but to be unable, as it is written: « Why dost thou glory in malice, thou that art mighty in iniquity (Psal. LI): » Wherefore he also calls those 1074Dpowers divine, because from God and in God they can do all that they can.

There follows: « For each appellation of the essences which are above us signifies their deiform properties, imitative of God. As if he said: Rightly have I named the powers and virtues divine, because their very appellation also teaches this. Just as each appellation of the essences which are above us, that is, the celestial ones, signifies their deiform properties: and they are deiform for this reason, that they are imitative of God. For that those celestial essences have conformity, they have it not from quality, but from imitation, because it is not nature that confers on them the likeness of God, but grace.
