There follows: « Therefore I judge that the manifesting naming of the holy dominations declares a certain absolute 1075Aanagogy, free from all pedestrian diminishment; and in no way whatsoever universally inclined by any of the tyrannical dissimilitudes, a dominion liberally severe, set above all diminishing servitude: superior to every subjection, and remote from every dissimulation, and unceasingly desirous of dominion; and conforming, as far as is possible, both itself and the things that are after it, in the best and most beautiful way, to the likeness of that very virtue subsisting naturally; turned toward none of the things seen as vain, but toward the properly ὄν on universal, and made, according to what is possible for it, ever in participation of the Lordly deiformity. » All these things the naming of the dominations teaches; for in that they are called dominations, they are signified to have and to do all these things 1075Bwhich have been said of them. This is what he says: « I judge the manifesting naming of the holy dominations, » that is, the naming by which their power and excellence and dignity is manifested and declared: I judge, he says, that that naming declares all these things. All what things? Hear. « For they are many. » Therefore I said "all these things": because they are many with respect to us, but few with respect to them. « I judge, he says, that the naming of the holy dominations declares a certain absolute, » that is, free, and estranged from all depression, « anagogy, » that is, their excellence, or sublimity, or upward leading, by which they are raised to the highest, so that they are subjected to none below the highest. And I judge that this naming also 1075Cdeclares that this anagogy, or their excellence, is not universally inclined in any way — that is, that it is in no way at all inclined by any of the tyrannical dissimilitudes, that is, through any, or according to any, tyrannical dissimilitude, that is, according to any tyranny, which is wholly dissimilar from their dominion. As if he said: Just as by their universal excellence they are raised above all subjection, so toward the oppression of their subjects they are inclined by no tyranny.

There follows: « A dominion liberally severe; set above all diminishing servitude. » From what precedes (it is to be understood) "I judge the naming of the dominations to declare" their dominion "liberally severe," that is, kindly severe. Having severity 1075Din power, liberality in kindness. Severe, because power is exercised from the superior; yet liberty is not taken away from the inferior. Therefore he calls it a dominion liberally severe, set above all diminishing servitude, that is, not subject to anyone unto a servitude which would diminish liberty, but superior to every subjection, and remote from every dissimilitude, that is, from all inferiority or imperfection which would make it dissimilar to its Creator, and unceasingly desirous of dominion, that is, looking toward — or tending toward, or clinging to — the Creator through likeness of dominion and conformity, and conforming both itself and the things that are after it, so that each, as far as is possible for it, may 1076Aimitate the divine virtue in the best and most beautiful way. Therefore he says, « I judge their naming to declare their dominion conforming itself, and the things that are after it, to the divine virtue; and turned toward none of the things seen as vain, but toward the properly on universal. » He puts "of those seeing" (videntium) for what he ought to have said, "of things seen" (visorum), by the most usual manner of the Greeks; since it is derived from the verb δοκοῦμαι, that is, "I see" or "I am seen," because it is common: so that the sense is: I judge it to declare her turned not toward any of those things which seem vain, that is, which, considered in themselves, appear lowly and transitory. But rather turned toward the properly on universal, that is, turned toward that which is properly and universally; namely toward God, to whom being is both proper, because he subsists through himself, and universal, 1076Bbecause he grants being to all. But it must be known that ὄν on among the Greeks, when it is written with ὄντῶν μικρὸν, through omicron — that is, a short or small "o" — is neuter, and is interpreted that which is. But when ὤν is written with ω τὸν μέγα, that is, a long or great "ω," it is masculine, and is interpreted who is. "On," therefore, is the Creator of all himself, and the principle, who is, and that which is properly in himself, and universal toward all: toward which principle he says this dominion is turned, and made in participation, that is, made a partaker of the Lordly deiformity, that is, of the divine likeness, which it retains always, that is, unchangeably: made, I say, according to what is possible for it. Thus far he has shown what the naming of the dominations signifies; now he passes on to show what the naming 1076Cof the virtues signifies.

There follows: « But that certain strong and unchangeable manliness of the holy virtues, in all their operations according to their deiformity, in no way feebly weakened toward any reception of the divine illuminations imparted to them, powerfully led back into the imitation of God: not abandoning by its own feebleness the deiform motion, but firmly bearing itself into the superessential and power-making virtue, and made its image like to the virtue, according to what is permitted, and powerfully turned toward it indeed as toward the principal virtue. But toward the second virtue giving and coming forth deiformly. » That, he says, of the holy virtues (understood: the appellation) 1076DI judge to declare a certain strong and unchangeable manliness in all their operations: a manliness, I say, imparted to them according to their deiformity, because in this they are like, or conformed, to God, that they have merited to receive a strong and unchangeable manliness, or virtue, for the doing of all things. For the divine virtue is both strong for acting, so that it is not broken by the difficulty of any work, and unchangeable for persevering, so that it does not grow faint or be weakened by the length of duration. In this, therefore, the virtues are deiform, and therefore they are alike in that for the doing of all things they have a strong and unchangeable vigor. Nor do they only have a manliness strong and unchangeable for doing all things beneath them, but they have also a manliness or virtue not feebly weakened 1077Atoward that reception of the divine illuminations imparted to it. For they are strong in the execution of works, and strong also in the reception of gifts, because their virtue, even if it be weak when compared to the divine virtue, is nevertheless not weak when conformed to the divine. It is weak by its condition for grasping the whole that is proper to the Creator; but it is not weak by corruption for receiving the whole that is owed to a creature. It is not, therefore, feebly weakened: for even if it does not have a virtue equal to the Creator, it nevertheless has a strength sufficient for a creature. Therefore it has a manliness strong and unchangeable for the execution of things to be done, and not weakened for the reception of gifts; and powerfully led back, that is, turned or 1077Breformed in the imitation of God, that is, that it may imitate God; led back indeed through illuminations, into imitation through operations. And they have a manliness not abandoning the deiform motion by any feebleness of their own. He calls it "deiform motion," that these celestial virtues are moved unceasingly, that they may imitate God; either from above, namely by desiring to receive what he has, that they may be the same with him; or downward, by doing what he does, that they may not depart from him. And so they have a manliness not abandoning the deiform motion; but through that deiform motion firmly bearing or exalting itself into the superessential and power-making virtue of the Creator: and through this made an image like to the virtue of the Creator himself, according to what is permitted, that is, according to what 1077Cis granted to them, or possible. For in this, that their manliness is raised through the deiform motion into the superessential and power-making virtue of the Creator, it is proven to become the image and likeness of that same divine virtue. Therefore, he says, I judge their manliness to be made an image like to the divine virtue, and turned toward that divine virtue, inasmuch as toward the principal virtue; but toward the second things giving virtue, and coming forth deiformly. Thus, he says, the appellation of the virtues teaches that their manliness is turned toward the higher virtue of God, that from it, as from the first, it may receive deiformity; and it teaches also that it comes forth or proceeds toward the second things, that is, toward the subsequent orders, that it may come forth to them deiformly, giving them virtue, and in that virtue 1077Dconformity to God, so that it both receives that deiformity from the superior and bestows it on the inferiors: receiving through gift, bestowing through example.

There follows: « But that of the holy powers, equal in power to the divine dominations and virtues, well-ordered and unconfused about the divine receptions by its ordination, and the ordered rank of the supermundane and intellectual power, not tyrannically hurled down by power-wielding virtues into the things that are lower, but powerfully led back into the divine things after the well-ordered ones: and leading back deiformly the things after it, and assimilated, as far as is lawful, to the power-making causal power: and revealing it, as is possible, to the angels in the ranks well-ordered through it by its power-wielding 1078Avirtue. » After the appellation of the virtues he passes on to the appellation of the powers. But that of the holy powers (understood: the naming) I judge to declare a certain ordination of theirs, equal in power to the divine dominations and virtues, that is, an ordination — I say — of equal power with the dominations and virtues, well-ordered and unconfused about the divine receptions, that is, about the divine gifts to be received, because the gifts of God, which it receives for the adornment of spiritual beauty, it guards without confusion, humbly persisting in its own degree and order. I judge also that this naming of the powers declares the ordered rank, that is, the ordination of the supermundane and intellectual power: a power, I say, not tyrannically hurled down into the things 1078Bthat are lower, with power-wielding virtues, that is, with violent force. But rather a power led back, or powerfully turned, into the divine things after the well-ordered ones, that is, after the virtues, which are ordered before it: and a power, I say, leading back deiformly, that is, according to the divine likeness, the things that are after it, that is, those orders of angels which follow after it. For just as it itself is turned to the likeness of God by the superiors meditating, so, with it mediating, the things that are lower are called back to the same likeness of God. There follows further: The powers assimilated, as far as is lawful, that is, either permitted or granted, to the power-making, causal power; because it can do all things, and is the cause of all. And a power, I say, revealing, namely that divine 1078Cpower, as far as it is possible to reveal it to the angels. Revealing how? By its power-wielding virtue. Where revealing? In the ranks well-ordered through it, that is, in the subsequent orders, which it adorns, by revealing to them the divine power by its own example.

There follows: « Having these deiform properties, the middle ordering of the celestial minds is indeed purged, and illumined, and perfected, as has been said, by the divine illuminations imparted to it in the second place through the first hierarchical ordering, and conveyed through that middle one by a second manifestation. » The middle ordering of the celestial minds, he says — of which, namely, treatment has thus far been made, which consists of dominations and virtues and powers: this, having the deiform properties, namely those 1078Dwhich we said above, is purged and illumined and perfected, just as was said above concerning the first hierarchy; purged, I say, by the divine illuminations imparted to it in the second (understood: place) through the first hierarchical ordering. The first hierarchical ordering consists of the three first orders, that is, seraphim, cherubim, and thrones: which in the first place receives the divine illuminations from the divinity itself: which illuminations afterward being conveyed by a second manifestation, through that middle one, to the second hierarchy, this second hierarchy is in the second place purged, and illumined, and perfected, through those same divine illuminations.

There follows: « And so, by the utterance passing 1079Afrom one angel [and] heard in another angel, we shall make a symbol of the perfection which is from afar above [all] perfect, and hidden through the procession into the things that follow. » By example and authority he proves what he had said, namely that the middle ordering of angels is illumined by the first, or through the first, that is, what he says: We shall make a symbol, that is an example, or a demonstration, of the perfection, namely the divine perfection perfect from afar above all things: and hidden, through the procession, into the things that follow; because, although in itself it is hidden and invisible, yet through the procession it goes forth and is made manifest in the things that follow, that is, in those who are immediately after it in the first place, or in those who follow after them. Of this kind of divine perfection, I say — perfect in itself and hidden, and yet, through the bestowal of grace, proceeding into the things that follow 1079B— we shall make a symbol: the utterance, that is, the saying or word brought forth by one angel, and afterward passing into another angel, and heard by him. For in this, that one angel spoke, another heard, one brought forth the teaching, another received it: a symbol has been made, that is a demonstration or argument, that the divine perfection proceeds, to be participated, through the prior and superior ones to the following and inferior ones. « For those wise concerning our sacred immolations say that the plenitudes of the divine things, shining through themselves, are more perfect than [those] through other contemplative participations. » As if he said: It is no wonder if among the angels one taught and another was taught, since one is more learned than another. For those who are wise concerning our sacred immolations, 1079Cthat is, concerning our sacrifices or sacraments, they say that the plenitudes of the divine things, that is, those angels who are full of divine gifts, or illuminations, and shine through themselves, are more perfect than the contemplative participations through others, that is, than those participating by contemplative participations through others. For he put the genitive for the ablative. Those who are wise, he says, or skilled in our sacraments, testify that those angelic spirits who receive the divine contemplation immediately through themselves are more perfect than the rest, who, with the superiors mediating, participate in the same contemplation.

There follows: « So too I judge that the immediate participation of the angelic orders first extended 1079Dinto God is more perfect through the mediation of the perfected. » Because, he says, the wise testify this, therefore I too judge that the immediate participation of the angelic orders first extended into God — that is, those angelic orders which, in the first place and principally extended into God, participate in him immediately — is more perfect, that is, that they are more perfect in participation than the perfected who participate through mediation, that is, than the perfected participating through mediation, that is, that they are more perfect than those who are made perfect by others mediating.

There follows: « On which account, by our priestly tradition, the first intellects are named the perfective, light-bringing, and purgative virtues of the lower ones; as of those led back through themselves into the superessential principle of all, 1080Aand made partakers of the mystical purgations, and illuminations, and perfections, according to what is lawful for them. » As if he said: Because the superior spirits are more perfect than the inferior and following ones, therefore by our priestly tradition the first intellects, that is, the supreme orders of angels, are called the perfective, and light-bringing, and purgative virtues of the inferiors, because through them the inferiors are perfected and purged and illumined: they are named the virtues of the inferiors, inasmuch as these are led back through themselves, that is, through their own selves, into the superessential principle of all, that is, God; and the inferiors, I say, made in participation, because they have been made partakers, as far as is lawful for them, of the mystical purgations, and illuminations, and perfections. 1080BThrough those superiors, therefore, by whom they are purged, and illumined, and perfected.

There follows: « For this has been divinely promulgated altogether by the divine ordination: that the second things participate through the first in the divine illuminations: this, he says, has been divinely promulgated, » or made manifest, « altogether, » that is, universally, concerning the divine ordination — that the second things everywhere participate in the divine illuminations through the first.

There follows: « But you will find this too expressed many times by the theologians: » this, he says — that I say the second things participate in the divine illuminations through the first — you will find expressed, that is, manifestly magnified and marked in the Scriptures, namely the sacred ones: by the theologians, that is, those who have reasoned 1080Cconcerning divine things and written.

There follows: « For when the divine and paternal humanity, in a nurturing way correcting Israel for the sake of its holy salvation, and handing it over for correction to avenging and savage nations, by a universal translation of the things provided-for unto the better: both dismissed the captivity, and mercifully led it back to its former beneficence: one of the theologians, Zechariah, saw one of the first angels, as I suppose, and of those about God (for this angelic surname is, as I have said, common to all), learning from God himself, concerning this matter, consoling words, as has been said. But another of the subject angels coming to meet the first, as if unto the reception and perception of illumination; 1080Dthen instructed by him in the divine counsel as by a high priest: and this angel, being turned, teaches the theologian, that Jerusalem is fruitfully inhabited by a multitude of men. » He proves by an example what he had said. In the prophet Zechariah it is read that an angel, having received a command from God, went forth, and gave a command to another angel meeting him, that he should run and announce to the prophet that Jerusalem was as yet inhabited without walls. For this is what he says: « When the divine and paternal humanity, » that is, the paternal mercy of God, « in a nurturing way correcting, » that is, in the manner of a foster-father who scourges his little son for this end, that he may chastise him, correcting Israel with the scourge of the Babylonian captivity for the sake of its holy salvation, namely so that, while for a time he outwardly dispersed it in bodily fashion, he might inwardly 1081Asave it by restoring it unto holiness. And so thus the mercy of God, in a fatherly way correcting Israel and handing it over unto correction — that is, handing it over to the nations that it might be corrected, namely to the Chaldeans: nations, I say, both avenging and savage; because they both avenged the injury done to God, and yet did this not out of zeal for justice but out of the fury of cruelty. Handing over, I say, by a translation; namely that they might be carried over from their homeland into exile, from their own land into a foreign land, from Jerusalem into Babylon, from the vision of peace into the captivity of confusion: by a translation, I say, that is universal, that is, general, of all the things provided-for unto the better — that is, unto the salvation of the predestined. For indeed through this captivity and leading-back, which was done bodily in one people, 1081Bthere was shown forth a figure of all the elect, and of those to be freed from the captivity of sin. When therefore the divine mercy, in a fatherly way handing over Israel by such a translation, afterward both dismissed the captivity, and mercifully led Israel itself back to its former beneficence. Then « one of the theologians, namely Zechariah, saw one of the first angels, » that is, one of the first angels, that is, one of the excellent and superior angels, and of those set about God. He says, « one of the first, as I suppose: » for theology does not say this, that that one was of the first. But I suppose that that one was of the first, because he did not receive a command from another prior to him, but gave a command to the second. Therefore, he says, « I suppose » that that one was of the first angels. How 1081Cof the first angels, since the angels are not first, seeing that only those who are last and lowest are named angels? Not so, he says, do I mean 'angel.' But according to this, that this angelic surname is sometimes common to all, as was said above, I now call the supreme orders angels. And so thus one of the theologians, Zechariah, saw one of the first angels learning from God himself consoling words, namely concerning this matter of the captivity and the leading-back of Israel, as was said in the prophecy, namely of Zechariah himself. He saw also another of the subject angels coming forth to meet the first angel, that is, going out, or coming before, that is, running on ahead before he is called, as one ready and 1081Ddevoted of himself unto the reception and perception of his illumination, which he was about to receive from him. Then Zechariah himself saw that second angel instructed in the counsel by the first angel himself as by a high priest, namely as by a superior, and one giving holy things: and he saw also that same second angel afterward turned, teaching the theologian this — that is, turned away from the first angel, to whom he was attending, toward the theologian, that is, toward Zechariah himself, that he might teach him this, namely the divine counsel which he himself had learned from the first angel: but the first angel from God — and this is the counsel which he himself announced, « that fruitfully, » that is, abundantly, « Jerusalem shall be inhabited » by a multitude of men. Another translation says: « Without walls 1082Ashall Jerusalem be inhabited. » Under the same sense assuredly, in that after the slaughter of the captivity that people would, by divine grace, be multiplied to such a degree that the multitude of those dwelling in Jerusalem could not be enclosed within the circuit of its walls.

There follows: « But the other of the theologians, Ezekiel: and, he says, this was most sacredly promulgated to the cherubim by that same most glorious divinity, established firmly above. » By the testimony of the other theologian he proves what he said, namely that the divine counsels, immediately received by the first angels, are then carried through the lower angels even unto the minds of the theologians — that is, what he says: « The other of the theologians, Ezekiel, » namely that this divine counsel was most sacredly promulgated to the cherubim by the most glorious divinity itself, established firmly above 1082B: this, he says. Ezekiel says that the most glorious divinity itself, established firmly above in majesty, in eternity, most sacredly promulgated or revealed its counsel to the cherubim, from whom it was afterward manifested more fully to the following orders. « For humanity itself — as has been said, the leader of the army — translating Israel unto the better through chastisements, is answered by divine Justice to those who correct, [and] justified the corrected. » Humanity, he says, that is, mercy, the leader of the army, or the mistress of the exercise, translating Israel itself unto the better through disciplines, condemned the guilty, justified the corrected; and this, namely the judgment, is answered out of divine justice to the correcting angels, who had been sent to punish: because for this reason the divine mercy brought in the scourges, that 1082Cit might condemn the reprobate, and justify the corrected. Or the divine justice itself is answered to those who correct, in that which is just, that the reprobate be condemned, and the corrected be justified. Or, to the correcting Chaldeans, that is, the persecutors through whom God scourged and corrected his people, it is answered out of divine justice, that they may receive as they have deserved; but the divine mercy justified the corrected Israelites. « This is taught to the first after the cherubim, girded about the loins with sapphire, who was clothed with the podere according to the hierarchical symbol: » this, he says, divine counsel of condemnation and justification « is taught to the one set first after the cherubim, who was clothed with the podere according to the hierarchical symbol. » For the fact that after the cherubim a certain one 1082Dappeared girded about the loins with sapphire, and clothed with the podere, was a hierarchical symbol, that is, a hierarchical figure, because the hierarchy uses visible figures for the demonstration of invisible things. And not only is he who was first after the cherubim taught the divine counsel, but also the rest who follow. For this is what he subjoins: But the divine ordinance commands that the rest of the angels, who had axes, be taught concerning this the divine judgment by the one prior to them. Namely concerning this counsel, or concerning this work, the divine ordinance commands the cherubim themselves « that the rest of the angels be taught by him » who was first after the cherubim, so that in that order the divine precept might first descend into the cherubim, then through the cherubim to him who was next, clothed with the podere, through whom it might at last come to the following 1083Aangels, who were made ready with axes.

There follows: « For to him indeed he said to pass through the midst of Jerusalem, and to give a sign upon the foreheads of the corrected men: » — either 'to him,' that is, the divine ordinance said to the cherubim, that he should command the one following him to pass through the midst of Jerusalem, etc. Or 'to him,' that is, to the one following after the cherubim, through the cherubim itself he « said to pass through the midst of Jerusalem, » etc. And not only did he give the precept to that one through the cherubim, but also to the others following after him — this is what is added: « To the others: Go forth into the city after him, and strike; and do not spare your eyes. But to all upon whom is the sign, draw not near. » But all these things, which have been taken from the prophetic visions, 1083Bavail for this, that it may be shown that the first and highest angels are instructed by God himself, the second by the first, the third by the second.

There follows: « What perhaps might someone say of the angel saying to Daniel: The word went forth; or of that first one himself receiving fire from the midst of the cherubim? or that saying of the same, which is more abundantly for the showing of the angelic order; namely that the cherubim also sends fire into the hands of the one clothed with the holy stole; or of the one calling the most divine Gabriel, and saying to him: Make him understand the vision. Or whatsoever other things have been said by the sacred theologians concerning the deiform adornment of the celestial hierarchies, unto which the ordination of our hierarchy, assimilated according to what is possible, will have the angelic beauty, as far as in figures, 1083Cbeing formed through it and led back to the superessential at once of every hierarchy. » In these prophetic testimonies, as we said above, he intends to prove this alone: that among the angels some teach others, and the lower receive precept and doctrine from the higher; or also when men are instructed by the angels, and the lower receive knowledge from the higher. For what might one — that is, someone — say of the angel speaking to Daniel, except that the lower is instructed by the higher, and receives doctrine? Or again, what might someone say of that first one, mentioned above after the cherubim, clothed with the podere, and receiving fire from the midst of the cherubim, except this likewise, that one is shown to receive from another that which 1083Dhe cannot have of himself? Or what else also is that saying of the same — namely of the vision, or of the example — which is more abundantly, or more copiously, for the showing of the angelic order, that is, for showing that among the angels some superior orders are set over others, as I say, that the cherubim sends fire into the hands of the one clothed with the holy stole, except that manifestly a dispensation is demonstrated to be made through 1084Aone into another? That testimony, indeed, in the vision of Ezekiel, from which this is taken, is rather conjectured than expounded; because from the fact that that first one after the cherubim, clothed with the holy stole, or podere, is bidden to receive fire from the midst of the cherubim, he is believed, not unfittingly, to have received that same fire from the cherubim itself. Concerning this, therefore, what will anyone be able to say, except that it is manifestly shown that the divine bounty passes through some unto others? Or again, of the angel calling the most divine Gabriel, and saying to him: Make him understand the word [visionem]: what will anyone be able to say, except that, according to the ordination of the same disposition, the divine precept descends through some unto others; and those who are superior 1084Bcommand to the inferior the things to be done, even as they insinuate the things to be known? Concerning these things therefore, or also concerning all the others, whatsoever other things have been said by the sacred theologians concerning the deiform adornment of the celestial hierarchies, what will anyone be able to say, except what has been said above? Unto which adornment of the celestial hierarchies, namely, the ordination of our — that is, of the human, or Ecclesiastical — hierarchy being assimilated, as far as is possible for it (namely, to be assimilated), will have from that very likeness the angelic beauty, as far as in figures, that is, in figures and likenesses. For as much as it now has in the figure of likeness, so much will it afterward have in the loftiness of glorification. Now indeed it has the character and the sign in figure; then it will have the reality and the truth in glory. Certain men have tried to interpret these characters 1084Cin a strange way; setting before those who contemplate, in that future glory of the supernal blessedness, certain phantasms and images of errors in place of God, asserting that God is never visible to anyone in his own substance. But we do not await blessedness in the contemplation of figures, to whom the very truth has been promised. Therefore the disposition of our hierarchy, formed unto the angelic adornment, as much as it now has of likeness in characters and figure, so much will it afterward have in the glory of beauty. Now indeed it is formed through it: that is, both according to it, namely the angelic adornment, and by the mediation of that same angelic adornment, led back to the superessential at once of every hierarchy — that is, 1084Drestored unto the likeness of God, who is the superessential of every hierarchy; because from him every hierarchy has not only form, but also substance; because he himself not only instituted every hierarchy, but also created it, so that it might be after him in likeness, under him in condition.

LIBER NONUS.

  • 1083

BOOK NINE.

  • 1083

TITULUS CAPITULI IX: De principatibus, archangelis et angelis, et de ultima eorum hierarchia.

TITLE OF CHAPTER IX: On the principalities, archangels, and angels, and on their last hierarchy.

LITTERA.

  • 1083D

Reliquus nobis in contemplationem ornatus angelicas 1084Dconcludens hierarchias a deiformibus principibus, archangelis, et angelis dispositas. Et primo quidem 1085Adicere necessarium existimo, secundum quod mihi impossibile, sacrarum earum cognominationum manifestationes. Manifestat enim ipsa quidem coelestium principum illud deiformiter principale eductivum cum ordine sacro, et principalibus decentissimis virtutibus, et ad superprincipale principium eas universaliter converti, et alias hierarchice ducere, et ad illud ipsum, quantum possibile, formari princificum principium, manifestareque superessentialem ejus ordinationem ornatumque principalium virtutum. Ipsa autem sanctorum archangelorum aequipotens quidem est coelestibus principatibus. Est enim, et eorum, et angelorum, ut dixi, hierarchia una, et dispositio. Verumtamen quoniam quidem non est hierarchia non et primas, et medias, et ultimas virtutes habens, archangelorum 1085Bsanctus ordo communicativae hierarchicae medietati extremorum recipitur. Etenim sacratissimis principatibus communicat, et sanctis angelis. Ipsis quidem quoniam ad superessentiale principium principaliter convertitur, et ad ipsum, ut possibile, reformatur, et angelos unificat secundum bene ornatos ejus, et ordinatos, et invisibiles ducatus. Istis vero, quod et eis prophetico est ordini, divinas illuminationes hierarchice per primas virtutes suscipiens, et angelis eas deformiter annuntians, et per angelos nobis manifestans secundum sacram uniuscujusque divinitus illuminatorum analogiam. Ipsi enim angeli, sicut praediximus, completive consummant omnes coelestium animorum dispositiones, secundum quod consummandum est: quippe in coelestibus essentiis 1085Chabentes angelicam proprietatem et magis apud nos angeli, quam priores aptius nominati, quantum circa id, quod manifestius est, ipsis est hierarchia, et magis circumornatus. Excellentissimam quidem enim, ut dictum est, dispositionem tanquam ipsi occulto primitus ordinate proximantem, clam, formans [formantem] existimandum ordinare secundam. Secundam vero, quae completur a sanctis dominationibus, et virtutibus, et potestatibus, ei, quae est principibus, et archangelis, et angelis, hierarchiae praeesse. Primam quidem hierarchiam manifestius; eam vero, quae est post eam, occultius. Principatuum autem, archangelorum, et angelorum manifestativam dispositionem, humanis hierarchiis per consequentia praecipere, ut si per ordinem ad Deum ascensus, et conversio, 1085Det communicatio, et unitas. Et quidem necnon a Deo omnibus hierarchicis optime indita, et communicative superveniens, et cum ornatu sacratissimo processio. Inde theologia nostram hierarchiam angelis distribuit, principem Judaeorum populi Michaelem nominans (Dan. X), et alios gentium diversos. Statuit enim Excelsus terminos gentium, secundum numerum angelorum Dei (Deut. XXXII). Si autem quis dixerit, et quomodo Hebraeorum populus reductus est solus in divinas illuminationes, respondendum quod non angelorum rectas dominationes accusari oportet aliarum gentium in non existentes deos errore, sed illos ipsos propriis inflexionibus ex ea quae est in divinum recta reductione recidentes amore proprio, et superbia 1086Aipsis visorum divinitus, et corrationaliter cultui. Hoc perhibetur et ipse Hebraeorum populus perpessus esse. Cognitionem enim Dei repulisti, ait, et post cor tuum existi (Ose. IV; Jer. II). Neque enim coactam habemus vitam; neque per providentium propriam potestatem, divina lumina providae illuminationis revelantur, sed intellectualium visionum dissimilitudo superplena paterna bonitate lucis donationem, aut omnino non participatam facit, ad earum reformationem non distributam, aut participationes facit differentes, parvas aut magnas, obscuras aut claras, unius et simplicis, et semper eodem se modo habentis, et superexpensi fontalis radii. Deinde quia et aliis gentibus, ex quibus et nos respeximus in illud, omnibus paratum in traditionem et apertum divini luminis, et magnum, 1086Bet copiosum pelagus, non alienigenae quidam imperabant dii: unum autem omnium principium, et ad ipsum reduxerunt sequentes, secundum unamquamque gentem sacerdotio fungentes angeli. Melchisedech intelligendum summum sacerdotem existentem Domino amicissimum existentium, non existentium, sed vere existentis excelsi Dei. Etenim sic simpliciter Melchisedech ipsi theosophi non amicum Dei tantum, sed et sacerdotem vocaverunt (Gen. XIV). An ut sapientibus aperte significarent, quod non solum ex eis in ipsum, qui vere est, Deum convertit. Adhuc autem et aliis ut summus sacerdos educet ea, quae est ad veram, et solam divinitatem reductione. Et hoc autem tuam summe sacerdotalem intelligentiam admonebimus, quod et Pharaoni apud ipsos Aegyptios imperante 1086Cangelo (Gen. XLI), et Babyloniorum principi praeside proprio, omni providentia, et dominationis providum, et potestativum secundum divisiones distributum, et gentibus illis veri Dei ministri duces statuti sunt formationum ab angelis visionis manifestatione, angelis continuo sacris viris Joseph, et Danieli ex Deo per angelos revelatae (Dan. II). Unum enim est omnium principium, et providentia. Et nullo modo existimandum Judaeos quidem pleniter dixisse divinitatem; angelos autem specialiter, aut aeque honorabiliter, aut oppositis, aut Deos quosdam altero imperare aliis gentibus. Sed et eloquium illud secundum ipsam sacram intelligentiam accipiendum non ut patiente Deo cum alteris diis, aut angelis nostrum ducatum, in Israel principatum, et gentis ducatum Israel contento. 1086DSed ut ipsa quidem una simul, et excelsa providentia omnes homines salutariter propriorum angelorum restitutoriis manuductionibus distribuente, solo fere ultra omnes Israel in viri Dei illuminationem, et cognitionem converso. Unde theologia quidem ipsum possedisse Israel in veri Dei famulatum significans, facta est portio Domini, ait (Psal. CXXXIV; Deut. XXXII; Isa. XIX). Ostendens autem et eum viritim caeteris gentibus distribuisse cuidam sanctorum angelorum in cognoscendum per eum unum omnium principium Michaelem, dixit Judaicum duxisse populum (Dan. X). aperte nos edocens unam esse omnium providentiam, simul omnibus invisibilibus et visibilibus virtutibus superessentialiter supercollocatam. Omnes 1087Aautem per singulas gentes imperantes angelos in ipsum, ut proprium principium sequentes, voluntate essentiali quasque virtutes extendere

THE TEXT.

  • 1083D

The adornment remaining to us for contemplation, 1084Dconcluding the angelic hierarchies disposed by the deiform principalities, archangels, and angels. And first indeed 1085AI judge it necessary to speak, according to what is impossible for me, the manifestations of their sacred surnames. For it manifests, indeed, that deiform principal eductive of the celestial principalities, together with the sacred order and the most becoming principal powers, and that they are universally converted unto the superprincipal principle, and lead others hierarchically, and are, as far as possible, formed unto that very principial principle, and that it manifests his superessential ordination and the adornment of the principal powers. But that of the holy archangels is indeed of equal power with the celestial principalities. For there is, both of them and of the angels, as I have said, one hierarchy and disposition. Nevertheless, since indeed there is no hierarchy not having also first, and middle, and last powers, the 1085Bholy order of the archangels is received into the communicative hierarchical middle of the extremes. For it communicates with the most sacred principalities, and with the holy angels. With the former indeed, because it is principally converted unto the superessential principle, and is, as far as possible, reformed unto it, and unifies the angels according to its well-adorned, and ordered, and invisible leadings. But with the latter, because it is to them also a prophetic order, receiving the divine illuminations hierarchically through the first powers, and announcing them deiformly to the angels, and manifesting them through the angels to us according to the sacred analogy of each of those divinely illumined. For the angels themselves, as we have said before, completively consummate all the dispositions of the celestial minds, according to what is to be consummated: inasmuch as, in the celestial essences, 1085Chaving the angelic property, and more fittingly named angels among us than the prior ones, in so far as, concerning that which is more manifest, there is to them a hierarchy, and more of the circum-adornment. For it is to be judged that the most excellent disposition, as itself firstly and orderly approaching the hidden one, secretly, forming [formantem], ordains the second. But the second, which is completed by the holy dominations, and virtues, and powers, presides over that hierarchy which is of the principalities, and archangels, and angels. The first hierarchy indeed more manifestly; but that which is after it, more hiddenly. But the manifestative disposition of the principalities, archangels, and angels commands the human hierarchies through the consequent things, so that there be through order an ascent unto God, and conversion, 1085Dand communication, and unity. And indeed also, from God, best imparted to all the hierarchical ones, and communicatively supervening, and a procession with most sacred adornment. Thence theology distributes our hierarchy to the angels, naming Michael the prince of the people of the Jews (Dan. X), and others, diverse, of the nations. For the Most High established the bounds of the nations according to the number of the angels of God (Deut. XXXII). But if anyone should say, and how was the people of the Hebrews alone led back into the divine illuminations? it must be answered that the right dominations of the angels are not to be accused of the error of the other nations unto non-existent gods, but those very ones, by their own inflexions, falling away from that right leading-back which is unto the divine, by their own love, and by pride 1086Aof the things divinely seen by them, and, in a co-rational manner, unto worship. This is reported that the people of the Hebrews itself also suffered. For thou hast repelled the knowledge of God, he says, and hast gone forth after thy own heart (Ose. IV; Jer. II). For neither do we have a coerced life; nor are the divine lights of provident illumination revealed through the proper power of those who provide, but the dissimilarity of the intellectual visions makes the donation of light, out of the superfull paternal goodness, either wholly not participated, not distributed unto their reformation, or makes the participations differing — small or great, obscure or clear — of the one and simple, and ever holding itself in the same mode, and superexpended fontal ray. Then, because also to the other nations, out of which we also have looked back unto that, [there is] prepared unto tradition and open the [ray] of divine light, and the great, 1086Band copious sea, no alien gods indeed ruled: but the one principle of all, and unto it the angels, exercising the priesthood according to each several nation, led back their followers. Melchizedek is to be understood as a high priest, existing most friendly to the Lord — not of the non-existent, but of the truly existent, most high God. For thus simply the theosophists themselves called Melchizedek not only the friend of God, but also priest (Gen. XIV). Or, that to the wise they might openly signify, that he converted not only out of them unto that God who truly is. But still also to others, as a high priest, he brings forth those things which are of the leading-back unto the true and sole divinity. And this, moreover, we shall admonish thy most-priestly understanding: that both with the angel ruling over Pharaoh among the Egyptians themselves 1086C(Gen. XLI), and with the prince of the Babylonians having his own presiding one — with all providence, both provident and empowered of domination, distributed according to the divisions — and for those nations there were established leaders, ministers of the true God, by the manifestation of the vision of the formations from the angels; the [visions] revealed continually by the angels, from God through the angels, to the holy men Joseph and Daniel (Dan. II). For there is one principle and providence of all. And in no way is it to be judged that the Jews indeed spoke of the divinity fully; but that the angels specially, or equally honorably, or oppositely, or that certain gods, one over another, rule the other nations. But that saying also is to be received according to the sacred understanding itself, not as though God, together with other gods, or angels, contending, suffered our leadership — the principate in Israel, and the leadership of the nation Israel. 1086DBut as, that same one and lofty providence at once salutarily distributing all men by the restorative hand-leadings of their proper angels, Israel almost alone beyond all being converted unto the illumination and knowledge of the man of God. Whence theology, signifying that he possessed Israel unto the service of the true God, said, He became the portion of the Lord (Psal. CXXXIV; Deut. XXXII; Isa. XIX). But showing that he also distributed, man by man, to the rest of the nations, [and] to a certain one of the holy angels, Michael, for the knowing through him of the one principle of all, said that he led the Jewish people (Dan. X). openly teaching us that there is one providence of all, superessentially set above at once all the invisible and visible powers. 1087AAnd all the angels ruling throughout the several nations extend their several powers unto him, as unto their proper principle, following him by an essential will

EXPOSITIO.

« Reliquus nobis in contemplationem ornatus, angelicas concludens hierarchias a deiformibus principibus archangelis, et angelis dispositas. » Plana sunt verba. Ornatus, inquit, concludens angelicas hierarchias, dispositas a deiformibus principibus archangelis, et angelis, est nobis reliquus, id est reliquum nobis est nunc hoc, ut contemplemur sive consideremus ornatum, id est pulchram dispositionem angelicae hierarchiae, quae quasi conclusio est duarum praecedentium, et finis, in qua dispositi sunt tres ordines, id est principatus, angeli et archangeli.

1087BSequitur: « Et primo quidem dicere necessarium existimo secundum quod mihi possibile, sanctarum earum cognominationum manifestationes. » Ego, inquit, existimo necessarium esse, ut primum dicam manifestationes cognominationum earum, ut per interpretationem cognominationum manifestentur proprietates earum. Hoc igitur primum existimat exponendum, quare in hac ultima hierarchia alii principes, alii archangeli, alii angeli nominantur, quia ex ipsa discreta cognominatione proprietates singulorum manifestantur. Hoc est, quod subdit: « Manifestat enim ipsa quidem coelestium principum illud deiformiter principale eductivum cum ordine sacro et principalibus decentissimis virtutibus 1087Cet ad super principale principium eas universaliter converti, et alias hierarchice ducere; et ad illud ipsum, quantum possibile formari princificum principium, manifestareque superessentialem ejus ordinationem, ornatumque principalium virtutum. » Exponit quid singulares cognominationes in hac hierarchia ultima significent: et primum de cognominatione principatuum tractat, ostendens quod ipsa scilicet cognominatio manifestat illud principale eductivum, hoc est, illum principalem ducatum, quem habent, deiformiter, hoc est similitudinem Dei; quia sicut Deus unus, et summus princeps est omnium, ita ipsi principes, et duces sunt subjectorum angelorum et hominum. Hunc 1087Ditaque ducatum ipsa cognominatio manifestat cum ordine sacro, et principalibus decentissimis virtutibus, quia ipsum ducatum et ex ordine sacro, habent, et ex principalibus virtutibus. Quia quod duces et principes aliorum sunt, et ex eo habent, quod ad hoc ex officio ordinati sunt, et ex hoc, quod principalibus virtutibus caeteris excellentiores existunt.

Sequitur: « Et ad super principale principium eas universaliter converti; » hoc, inquit, etiam manifestat cognominatio principum, eas scilicet virtutes, quas ipsi habent: universaliter converti ad superprincipale principium, hoc est, Deum. Et significat etiam ipsa eorum cognominatio, alias scilicet virtutes, vel aliorum virtutes ducere ad illud ipsum 1088Aprincificum principium, quantum possibile est, eas scilicet virtutes formari ad illud, vel conformari illi: ducere, dico, hierarchice, id est secundum modum et mensuram praelationis suae. Suae enim virtutes ad principium suum ducunt, universaliter convertendo; aliorum virtutes ad principium suum ducunt hierarchice praecedendo; quia in tantum ducere habent, in quantum praecedere, vel praeesse debent. Ideo hierarchice ducunt, quia in eo, in quo praelati non sunt, recte duces esse non possunt. Hoc itaque manifestat eorum cognominatio, quod scilicet principatum habent ad similitudinem Dei ex officio, et virtute: et quod ad principium suum et suas virtutes convertunt, et aliorum virtutes ducunt. Manifestat etiam eorum cognominatio ornatum 1088Bipsarum principalium virtutum, hoc est ipsorum principatuum dispositionem, manifestare superessentialem ordinationem ejus principii primi. Ex ipsa quippe cognominatione principatuum innuitur, quod in eorum praelatione primus principatus manifestatur, quia ipsum principando et imitantur, et manifestant.

Sequitur: « Ipsa autem sanctorum archangelorum aequipotens quidem est coelestibus principatibus. Est enim et eorum, et angelorum, ut dixi, hierarchia una et dispositio. » Ipsa (subauditur) cognominatio « sanctorum archangelorum, aequipotens est, » id est aequam potentiam, vel aequalem potentiam, significat, « coelestibus principatibus; » quia una hierarchia est, et una dispositio trium ordinum, 1088Choc est, et angelorum, et eorum scilicet archangelorum, et principatuum. Et licet ex eo, quod una est hierarchia, una est et aequalis potestas trium: tamen quia nulla hierarchia est, quae non habeat et primos, et medios, et ultimos ordines, ideo archangeli inter principatus, qui primi sunt, et angelos qui ultimi sunt, medio loco constituti, utrorumque participant proprietatem. Hoc est, quod dicit: « Verumtamen quoniam quidem non est hierarchia, non et primas, et medias et ultimas virtutes habens, archangelorum sanctus ordo communicative hierarchiae medietati extremorum recipitur. » Quoniam, inquit, non est hierarchia aliqua quae non habeat et primas, et medias, et ultimas virtutes: 1088Dideo « sanctus ordo archangelorum recipitur communicative medietati hierarchiae extremorum: » hoc est, recipitur ut in medietate sit extremorum communicans hierarchiae, id est sacrae potestati illorum, vel hierarchicae medietati recipitur, hoc est ad possidendam hierarchicam medietatem, quae communicativa est extremorum, hoc est, quod sequitur: « Et enim sacratissimis principatibus communicat, et sanctis angelis. » In quo autem utriusque communicet, subsequenter ostendit, dicens: « Ipsis quidem, quia ad superessentiale principium principaliter convertitur, et ad ipsum, ut possibile, reformatur; et angelos unificat secundum bene ornatos, ejus, et ordinatos, et invisibiles ducatus. » In hoc, inquit, participat archangelorum ordo cum 1089Aprincipatibus in eadem virtute, quia « convertitur ad superessentiale principium suum, et reformatur ad ipsum, » quantum possibile est sibi: et quia etiam unificat, hoc est, ad unitatem ejusdem principii colligit, angelos post se ducendo secundum ducatus invisibiles, et ordinatos, quibus illos subjectos et sequentes ducere habet. In hoc ergo archangelorum ordo virtuti principatuum communicat, quod ad similitudinem, sive imitationem illorum ad primum principium suum et se convertit, et sequentes se colligit. Et non solum principatibus supra positis, sed etiam angelis infra constitutis communicat ipse ordo archangelorum. Hoc est, quod subdit: « Istis vero, quod et eis prophetico est ordini divinas illuminationes hierarchice per primas 1089Bvirtutes suscipiens: et eas angelis deiformiter annuntians: et per angelos nobis manifestans secundum sacram uniuscujusque divinitus illuminatorum analogiam. » Illis, inquit, id est principatibus communicat, sicut supra diximus, ordo archangelorum. Istis vero, id est, angelis in hoc communicat, quod eis et prophetico est ordini, id est, ordo propheticus, et ad prophetandum ordinatus, prophetans eis utpote inferioribus divina secreta, divinas quidem illuminationes suscipiens per primas virtutes, hoc est, per principatus, qui priores, et superiores sunt: ipse suscipiens, dico, « hierarchice, » hoc est, secundum quod ordo, et dispositio hierarchica exposcit, ut scilicet inferiores a superioribus suas illuminationes suscipiant. « Suscipiens, » 1089Cdico, « et annuntians eas, » scilicet illuminationes, quas a superioribus suscipit, angelis inferioribus: annuntians autem deiformiter, ut in hoc, quod a superioribus suscipit, hierarchicam dispositionem custodiat; in hoc vero, quod inferioribus tribuit, a Dei conformitate non recedat, qui summus omnium universis subjectis sua dona participanda largitur. Illuminationem quippe a superiori suscipere hierarchicum est, inferiori autem dare divinum. Ac per hoc ordo archangelicus medio constitutus secundum dispositionem hierarchiae et superioribus et inferioribus participat, divinas illuminationes a superioribus suscipiens principatibus, et angelis inferioribus eas annuntians: et per angelos 1089Dnobis quasi postremis et infimis easdem divinas illuminationes annuntians secundum sacram uniuscujusque divinitus illuminatorum analogiam, hoc est secundum modum et mensuram capacitatis uniuscujusque nostrum ad eamdem divinam illuminationem percipiendam; vel annuntians nobis per angelos secundum sacram analogiam uniuscujusque illorum, scilicet angelorum, divinitus illuminatorum, id est in tantum per unumquemque divinam illuminationem annuntiant, in quantum unusquisque aptus est ad eam capiendam in se, et annuntiandam aliis per se.

Sequitur: « Ipsi enim angeli, sicut praediximus, completive consummant omnes coelestium animorum dispositiones, secundum quod consummandum 1090Aest. » Ac si diceret: Congrue nobis ordo archangelicus per angelos divinas illuminationes annuntiat, quia ipsi angeli in coelesti dispositione ultimi sunt, et hominibus proximi, et in eis complentur, sive terminantur et consummantur omnes dispositiones sive ordines coelestium animorum, hoc est, angelorum. Ita ergo angeli omnes coelestes ordines consummant, secundum quod consummandum est, ut subaudiatur de eis; vel, ut expressius dicatur, secundum quod consummandi sunt ipsi scilicet ordines angelorum. Quomodo autem perficiant, aut consumment ipsi angeli coelestes ordines, subjungit, dicens: « Quippe in coelestibus essentiis habentes angelicam proprietatem, et magis apud nos angeli quam priores aptius nominati, quantum 1090Bcirca id quod manifestius est ipsis est hierarchia, et magis circumornatus. » Non, inquit, mirum est si in eis coelestes ordines terminantur, quia inter omnes coelestes essentias eorum proprium est nobis divina secreta nuntiare; et in hoc habent angelicam proprietatem, quod eorum proprium est nuntios esse nobis; et idcirco apud non aptius angeli nominati sunt magis quam priores sive superiores, in quantum videlicet ipsis est hierarchia, id est potestas, vel officium circa id quod manifestius est nobis, et in quantum etiam ipsorum ornatus, sive dispositio, vel ordo magis circum, id est, circumscriptibilis est, et intelligibilis nobis propter ministerium visibilibus appropinquans. Ideo eis magis est circumornatus, hoc est, cognoscibilis vel comprehensibilis 1090Cordo, quia nobis proximus.

Sequitur: « Excellentissimam quidem enim, ut dictum est, dispositionem tanquam ipsi occulto primitus ordinare proximantem clam formans [forma] existimandum ordinare secundam. Secundam vero, quae completur a sanctis dominationibus, et virtutibus, et potestatibus, ei quae est principibus et archangelis, et angelis, hierarchiae praeesse. Primam quidam hierarchiam manifestius, eam vero quae post eam, occultius. Principatuum autem, et archangelorum, et angelorum manifestativam dispositionem, humanis hierarchiis, per consequentia praecipere, ut sit per ordinem ad Deum ascensus, et conversio, et communicatio, et unitas. » Existimandum 1090Dest, inquit, excellentissimam dispositionem, hoc est, supremam hierarchiam tanquam primitus, id est, principaliter approximantem ipsi occulto, id est Deo, ordinare secundam, clam, id est, occulte, vel incomprehensibiliter formans eam. Secundam vero hierarchiam, quae completur a sanctis dominationibus, et virtutibus, et potestatibus, existimandum est praeesse ei, scilicet hierarchiae, quae ex principatibus, et archangelis, et angelis, et existimandum est primam quidem hierarchiam, hoc est, supremam, percipere manifestius divinas illuminationes, vel manifestius praeesse tertiae; eam vero, quae post eam est, hoc est, secundam, occultius scilicet praeesse. Dispositionem autem, id est, hierarchiam principatuum, et archangelorum, et angelorum, 1091Amanifestativam, id est, notam, et notificantem existimandum est praecipere humanis hierarchiis per consequentia, hoc est, consequenter postquam ei a superioribus praeceptum fuerit: ut sic sit per ordinem ad Deum ascensus, et conversio, et communicatio, et unitas, id est, ut humanae mentes per inferiorem hierarchiam ad mediam, et de media ad supremam conversae, ascendant ad illum unum communicandum quod Deus est.

Sequitur: « Et quidem necnon a Deo omnibus hierarchicis optime indita, et communicative superveniens, et cum ornatu sacratissimo processio. » Tali, inquit, ordine unum bonum ab omnibus communicatur, a Deo procedens in omnes hierarchicos ordines, ut eos ornet superveniens eis et inditum 1091Bper communicationem. Hoc est, quod ait: Et quidem necnon, id est, etiam, processio fit a Deo illius summi videlicet boni, omnibus hierarchicis, subauditur, ordinibus, optime indita: eis « superveniens communicative, » hoc est, ad communicandum, et cum ornatu sacratissimo. In hoc enim magnum est ornatus divinae dispositionis, quod cum unum bonum omnes participent, non uno tamen modo communicandum provenit, sed per alios alii illud percipiunt, et rursum aliis post se communicandum praebent. Quemadmodum in illis spiritibus prima hierarchia secundae, secunda tertiae, tertia nostrae, id est, humanae, divinas illuminationes communicandas praebet. Hoc est, quod subsequenter adjungit, dicens: « Inde theologia nostram hierarchiam 1091Cangelis distribuit, principem populi Judaeorum Michaelem nominans, et alios gentium diversos. » Inde, ait, hoc est, propterea, quia inferiores a superioribus reguntur, theologia, id est, divina Scriptura, distribuit nostram hierarchiam angelis regendam, nominans Michaelem principem populi Judaeorum, et alios angelos diversos principes gentium scilicet nominans: sicut in Daniele principem Persarum, et principem Graecorum nominatum legimus. Et non solum in illis testimoniis probatur angelos principari hominibus, sed etiam alibi testatur Scriptura, dicens: « Statuit excelsus terminos gentium secundum numerum angelorum Dei (Dan. X). » Terminos, hoc est, divisiones, sive distributiones gentium statuit Altissimus juxta numerum 1091Dangelorum Dei: quia numero angelorum numerum gentium aptavit, ut singulis gentibus singuli angeli praeessent; quamvis quia secundum aliam translationem ibi non angeli, sed filii Dei, nominantur, aliud aliquid significatum videatur.

Sequitur: « Si autem quis dixerit: Et quomodo Hebraeorum populus reductus est solus in divinas illuminationes? Respondendum quod non angelorum rectas dominationes accusari oportet, aliarum gentium in non existentes deos errore, sed illos ipsos propriis inflexionibus ex ea quae est in divinum recta reductione recidentes amore proprio, et superbia, ipsis visorum divinitus et corrationabiliter cultui. » Ac si diceret Mirum quidem videtur. Si 1092Aquis, ait, miratur cur boni angeli illas gentes quibus praefuerunt a cognitione veri Dei recidere passi sunt, respondendum hoc culpa angelorum factum non esse, et quod non oportet accusari rectas dominationes angelorum pro errore gentium aliarum, quae non fuerunt ex Israel, in deos non existentes, id est, quia errando illos coluerunt qui non erant dii; sed illos ipsos propriis inflectionibus, id est, propria voluntate, recidentes a recta reductione, id est, cognitione, per quam homo reducitur in divinum, ut crederent deos, qui non erant dii; illos, inquam, ipsos accusandos, qui propria voluntate, in quantum liberi arbitrii erant, a veritate in errorem lapsi sunt, et hoc ex amore proprio, quia seipsos amaverunt plusquam Deum, et suam gloriam 1092Bquaerebant, et ideo superbi erant; et ex superbia visorum ipsis divinitus, id est, eorum quae ipsis revelata sunt divinitus, et quae revelata sunt eis etiam corrationabiliter cultui scilicet divino, id est, ex quibus rationabiliter vel probabiliter intellexisse potuissent quemadmodum Deum colere deberent. Quia sicut dicit Apostolus: « Cum cognovissent Deum, non sicut Deum glorificaverunt; sed evanuerunt in cogitationibus suis. Dicentes enim se esse sapientes [ecce superbia] stulti facti sunt, et obscuratum est insipiens cor eorum [ecce error in non existentes deos], quia servierunt potius creaturae quam Creatori, qui est benedictus in saecula (Rom. I). » Vel divinitus et corrationabiliter retribuente, subauditur eis, Deo: hoc est, sapienter et condigne 1092Ccultui; hoc est, sicut decebat cultores falsorum, scilicet deorum, visorum ipsis, hoc est, qui ipsis videbantur dii, et non erant. In hoc enim sapienter et rationabiliter retribuit eis Deus, quod, sicut dicit Apostolus, quia Deum non probaverunt habere in notitia, tradidit eos Deus in reprobum sensum, ut faciant quae non oportet in semetipsis. In semetipsis enim puniendi fuerant, qui in semetipsis peccaverant.

Sequitur: « Hoc perhibetur et ipse Hebraeorum populus perpessus esse, hoc scilicet, quod a cultu Dei recessit, sicut et aliae nationes recesserant in culturam idolorum; vel hoc, id est, vindictam divinam consimilem, quia similiter a cultu Dei recessit, et cognitionem Dei abjecit. Ait enim divina vox ipsi 1092DIsrael. « Cognitionem Dei repulisti: et post cor tuum existi. » Relicto scilicet Deo, qui intus pura mente colitur. Existi foras per amorem visibilium, quo te cor tuum, id est, desiderium et voluntas prava distrahebat. In quibus omnibus liberi arbitrii potestas apparet, quia sine coactione homo, sive ad bonum adjutus, sive ad malum permissus, propria voluntate inclinatur. Hoc est quod sequitur: « Neque enim coactam habemus vitam. » Voluntas enim rationali creaturae dari potest libera, sed cogi omnino non potest. Et sicut in nostra potestate non est ut divinae illuminationis donum nobis offeratur, ita nonnisi in nostra potestate est ut oblatum suscipiatur. Nam aliquando et cum nolumus offertur. 1093Ased nunquam suscipitur, nisi cum volumus. Et cum volumus, quidem a Deo volumus, quia donum Dei est voluntas bona. Cum autem nolumus, a nobis nolumus, quia nolle nihil aliud est quam non velle: quod desertio boni est ad non esse, et nihil, quod sine ipso factum est. Itaque « divina lumina providae illuminationis, » quia per ea Deus provide illuminat, illa quidem non « revelantur per propriam potestatem providentiam: » id est, eorum qui ex eis acceptis providentes fiunt; vel provisorum, id est, eorum qui provisi sunt, vel praedestinati a Deo ad illa accipienda. Notandum, quod ubi nos revelantur habemus, alia littera habet obcaecantur; quae licet diversa sint, ad eamdem tamen veritatem astruendam pertinent: ut scilicet ostendatur 1093Bquod utrum divina lumina revelentur, id est, manifestentur, an obcaecentur, id est, abscondantur et occultentur, non in potestate accipientium, sed in arbitrio dantis constat. Sed tamen quamvis ipsa manifestatio vel occultatio in eorum potestate non sit, susceptio tamen nunquam fit, nisi cum eorum voluntate, quia rationale bonum est quod non potest nisi a cognoscente et volente percipi. Igitur aut prava voluntate fit ut omnino repellantur, aut differentia bonae voluntatis, ut dissimiliter participentur. Hoc est quod dicit: « Sed intellectualium visionum, » hoc est, spiritualium oculorum, rationalium scilicet mentium, « dissimilitudo facit donationem lucis, » venientem scilicet « de superplena, » hoc est, de valde plena et excellenter plena paterna 1093Cbonitate; illam, inquam, donationem facit ipsa dissimilitudo, aut omnino non participantem, et non distributam ad earum scilicet visionum reformationem: « aut facit participationes differentes, hoc est, parvas aut magnas, obscuras aut claras, unius fontalis radii, et simplicis, et semper eodem modo se habentis, et superexpansi. » Radius enim divinae illuminationis a fonte boni descendens in se unus et simplex, et semper eodem modo se habens, cunctis rationalibus mentibus superexpanditur, et ab eis non secundum suam simplicitatem, sed secundum illarum diversitatem differenter participatur. Aut enim pravae sunt, et omnino illam repellunt, et faciunt ut nullo modo participetur, neque 1093Ddistribuatur ad earum reformationem; aut dissimiliter bonae sunt, et differenter eum suscipiunt.

Sequitur: « Deinde quia et aliis gentibus, ex quibus et nos respeximus in illud, omnibus paratum in traditionem et apertum divini luminis, et magnum, et copiosum pelagus; non alienigenae quidem imperabant dii, unum autem omnium principium; et ad ipsum reduxerunt sequentes secundum unamquamque gentem sacerdotio fungentes angeli. » Ac si diceret: Quod gentibus boni angeli praelati fuerint, non solum ex eo probari potest, quod Altissimus terminos populorum constituisse dicitur juxta numerum angelorum Dei, sed ex eo etiam, quod ipsis gentibus non alienigenae dii ab initio imperabant, sed unus Deus. Probabile enim est omnino 1094Aquod bonus Dominus in republica sua bonos sub se ministros constituerit: quorum ministerio et hoc postea factum est, quod nos, qui ex gentibus credidimus, respeximus per fidem ad Deum, et ad plenitudinem illuminationis ejus, reducti per eos: quod utique non fecissent, si boni non fuissent. Hoc est quod dicit. Deinde etiam ex hoc probari potest, quod boni angeli praelati fuerunt gentibus, quia scilicet ipsis aliis gentibus, quae non fuerunt ex Israel, ex quibus gentibus et nos, qui postea credimus, respeximus, conversi per fidem in id magnum et copiosum pelagus divini luminis, quod paratum est et apertum omnibus in traditionem, sive largitionem, quia largitur se et tradit omnibus volentibus et desiderantibus illud accipere. Illis videlicet gentibus 1094Bnon imperabant alienigenae quidam dii, quamvis hoc videri posset, quia idola coluerunt, et falsos deos adoraverunt. Sed unus Deus illis imperabat, et dominabatur, quia sicut est unum principium omnium, a quo sunt omnia, ita est unus Dominus, et rector, sub cujus potestate constituta sunt universa. Qui sicut in seipso bonus est, ita ministros bonos sub se rectores et duces angelos constituit, et illi angeli reduxerunt nos sequentes per fidem ad ipsum principium nostrum. Reduxerunt, dico, secundum quod erant sacerdotio, id est sacra praelatione, fungentes secundum unamquamque gentem, hoc est, unusquisque ex ea gente in qua sacerdotio, id est sacra potestate, fungebatur, ad fidem convertit eos, qui crediderunt, et ad principium suum respexerunt.

1094CSequitur: « Melchisedech, intelligendum, summum sacerdotem existentem Domino amicissimum existentium, non existentium, sed vere existentis excelsi Dei. » De angelorum ministerio et officio tractans, subito de Melchisedech narrationem inducit: non quia, ut quidam putaverunt, angelum ipsum fuisse, aut per hoc ejus sacerdotium inter ministeria angelorum commemorandum existimet, sed ut ostendat quod non solum angelorum, sed etiam sanctorum et Deo placentium hominum, aliisque hominibus in iis quae divina fuerunt praepositorum, opere et ministerio factum sit quod increduli ex gentibus ad fidem et cultum veri Dei conversi sunt. Secundum 1094Dhunc itaque modum, quo angeli ex officio praelationis suae sacerdotio functi sunt in gentibus, ad fidem veri Dei convertentes, intelligendum est Melchisedech summum sacerdotem fuisse existentem Domino amicissimum omnium existentium, imo potius non existentium, sed vere existentis excelsi Dei. Littera perplexa est. Sensus autem hic est. Quia dixerat Melchisedech Domino fuisse amicissimum omnium existentium, quasi corrigens dictum suum, quia eos qui vere non sunt existentes dixerat, subjungit, non existentium, secundum quod scriptum est: « Omnes gentes quasi non sint, sic sunt coram eo (Isa. XL). » Et quasi quaereretur quis ergo existat, subjungit: « Solus excelsus Deus, qui veram habet existentiam. » Quod autem non ait vere existens excelsus 1095ADeus, « sed vere existentis excelsi Dei, propter similitudinem praecedentis vocis factum est, ut per eumdem casum responderet non existentium, « si vere existentis excelsi Dei. » Vel sic legi potest. Melchisedech existentem Domino amicissimum omnium existentium intelligendum est fuisse sacerdotem non quorumlibet existentium, sed excelsi Dei vere existentis, sicut scriptum est: « Erat enim sacerdos Dei altissimi (Gen. XIV). »

Et sequitur: « Etenim sic simpliciter Melchisedech ipsi theosophi non amicum Dei, sed et sacerdotem vocaverunt. » Bene, inquit, dixi Melchisedech sacerdotem intelligendum quia theosophi, id est divina scribentes non sic simpliciter amicum tantummodo Dei. sed etiam sacerdotem vocaverunt. Et quare 1095Bsacerdotem vocaverunt subjungit, dicens: « An ut sapientibus significarent aperte quod non solum ex eis in ipsum qui vere est Deum convertit? Adhuc autem et aliis ut summus sacerdos educet ea quae est ad veram et solam divinitatem reductione. » Quod, inquit, Melchisedech, qui de Judaeis non erat, non solum amicum Dei, sed etiam sacerdotem Dei vocaverunt; an ideo hoc fecerunt? utique sic ideo hoc fecerunt, ut sapientibus aperte significarent quod non solum ex eis, id est ex Israel, qui soli tunc ad cognitionem divinam reducti et conversi videbantur, convertit in ipsum Deum, hoc est, ad fidem et cognitionem ipsius Dei, qui vere est, sed etiam ex aliis gentibus multos educet de tenebris ignorantiae, videlicet ea reductione quae est ad veram 1095Cet solam divinitatem, hoc est, ad cognitionem Dei. Non quod ipse Melchisedech aliquos ex Israel convertisse legatur, qui necdum populus erat: nisi forte Israel in patribus superioribus accipiamus, ex quibus aliqui fortassis per ipsum Melchisedech tempore ipsius ad notitiam Dei ducti sunt. Vel ut sic legatur, quod scilicet idcirco non solum amicus Dei, sed et sacerdos vocatus sit, quia convertit, subauditur, ignaros et nescios, ad ipsum Deum, cui vere est credendum. Et quasi aliquis objiceret, quod ipse Melchisedech, qui de Israel non erat, sed alienigena, nullum ad fidem Dei convertit, quia solus Israel Deum cognovit, respondet quod non solum ex Israel ad fidem Dei conversi sunt, sed etiam ex aliis gentibus: quae scilicet conversio aliorum per ipsum Melchisedech facta est. Qui tunc quidem, id est quando Abraham benedixit, sacerdos Dei altissimi vocatus est, cum non esset ex Israel, ut ostenderetur quod educturus esset ad Deum multos, et quod Deus non solum in Israel, sed etiam in gentibus et sacerdotem haberet et populum. Propterea non ait eduxit, sed « educet, » inquid. Ad illud quidem tempus, quando haec dicta sunt, futurum significans, quando vel ipse Melchisedech postea per se ex gentibus ad Deum convertit: vel Christus, cujus ille typus erat, non solum ex Israel. sed etiam ex omnibus gentibus per fidem multos ad Ecclesiam suam de tenebris infidelitatis eduxit.

Sequitur: « Et hoc autem, tuam, summe sacerdotalem 1096Aintelligentiam admonebimus quod et Pharaoni apud ipsos Aegyptios imperante angelo et Babyloniorum principi praeside proprio, omni providentia, et dominationis providum, et potestativum secundum divisiones distributum: et gentibus illis veri Dei ministri duces statuti sunt formationum ab angelis visionis manifestatione, angelis continuo sacris viris Joseph et Danieli ex Deo per angelos revelatae. » Adhuc aliam subjungit auctoritatem, ex qua probare vult gentibus bonis angelos a Deo praelatos, quod videlicet apud Aegyptios Pharaoni angelus visionem demonstrat, et per eam illi de futura sterilitate cautelam imperat: manifestata deinde eadem visione per Joseph, et similiter Babyloniorum principi, scilicet Nabuchodonosor, proprius praeses, id est proprius 1096Bpraepositus suus, videlicet proprius angelus visionem format, eademque postea per Danielem reserando manifestat. In quibus omnibus apparet quod Deus omnium rerum et providentiam habet, et dominationem, et potestatem, secundum quod per illas visiones discretum, vel distinctum, vel distributum est: quae visiones primum angelis revelatae sunt a Deo, et deinde continuo per angelos sacris viris Joseph et Danieli, hoc est quod dicit: O Timothee, non solum superiora, sed etiam hoc admonebimus tuam, summe, sacerdotalem intelligentiam, id est intelligentiam tuam, qui summus sacerdos es, admonebimus hoc, quod angelo imperante Pharaoni apud Aegyptios, et Babyloniorum principi imperante praeside proprio, id est, angelo, qui ei praelatus 1096Cerat; per hoc, inquam, quod angeli illis imperasse leguntur, distributum est providum et potestativum divinae providentiae et dominationis secundum illas, scilicet visiones, id est ostensum est quod Deus providentiam suam et potestatem singulis gentibus gubernandis distribuit; et ostensum est etiam quod gentibus illis veri Dei ministri duces statuti sunt; et quomodo ostensum sit, hoc subjungit: manifestatione, scilicet visionis formationum ab angelis, hoc est, visionis in qua demonstratae sunt formationes, sive figurae ab angelis factae in mentibus prophetarum, ad significanda futura, quales fuerunt vaccae, et spicae, quas vidit Pharao (Gen. XLI), et arbor, et statua, quam vidit Nabuchodonosor (Dan. II). Talis itaque visionis manifestatione demonstrata est divina providentia et potestas, per angelos gentes disponens; visionis, dico, primum revelatae angelis a Deo, et deinde continuo per angelos revelatae sacris viris, Joseph scilicet et Danieli ex Deo.

Sequitur: « Unum enim est omnium principium et providentia: et nullo modo existimandum Judaeos quidem pleniter duxisse divinitatem: angelos autem specialiter, aut aeque honorabiliter, aut oppositis, aut deos quosdam alteros imperare aliis gentibus. » Repetitio probat, quod supra dixit, quod unum est principium et providentia omnium, id est, unus Deus, a quo sunt omnia, et per quem reguntur universa; et idcirco nullo modo 1097Aexistimandum est divinitatem duxisse Judaeos, hoc est, ducatum praebuisse Judaeis pleniter, vel absolute, hoc est, per semetipsam, scilicet sine mediante angelorum ministerio: aliis autem gentibus imperare angelos specialiter, hoc est, particulariter, sive minus excellenti potestate, aut aeque honorabiliter, hoc est potestate aequali et consimili divinae dominationi, aut oppositis (subauditur imperiis), quemadmodum apostata angelus dixisse legitur sedem se ad aquilonem positurum et Altissimo potestate futurum consimilem (Isa. XIV). Aut etiam non est existimandum alteros quosdam deos imperare aliis gentibus, quasi unius et veri Dei potestati et dominationi omnia subjecta non sint. Non est, inquit, ita existimandum quasi in solis Judaeis verus Deus 1097Bpotestatem habeat, et aliis gentibus sive angeli, sive alteri quidam dii, sive aequali, sive inaequali, contraria tamen et extranea divinae dominationi imperent potestate. Vel sic legatur: Nullo modo existimandum Divinitatem per se ipsam sine interposita subjecta potestate angelica, Judaeis ducatum praebuisse: angelos autem aliis gentibus imperasse specialiter, hoc est, particulariter, scilicet in gentibus potestate et dignitate inferioribus quam ipsi Judaei fuerunt; aut aeque honorabiliter, hoc est, in gentibus scilicet aeque potentibus et honorabilibus: aut etiam in oppositis gentibus, quae ipsis scilicet Judaeis oppositae et contrariae fuerunt, oppugnantes et opprimentes eos. Non est, inquit, ita existimandum, quod scilicet Deus idcirco Judaeos per semetipsum 1097Cduxerit, quasi ipsi caeteris gentibus omnibus honorabiliores fuerint, alias autem gentes quasi inferiores et viliores dominationi angelicae reliquerit, cum in aliis nationibus plures non solum aeque honorabiles, sed etiam fortiores et potentiores, ipsosque Judaeos, sua potentia et fortitudine opprimentes fuisse non dubitentur. Nam quod dictum est: « Quando dividebat Altissimus gentes, statuit terminos populorum juxta numerum angelorum Dei: pars autem Domini populus ejus, Jacob funiculus haereditatis ejus; » non ita intelligendum est, quasi caeteras gentes angelis regendas dederit, solo Israel sibi, hoc est, suae providentiae et gubernationi retento: ut videlicet vel ipse Israel sine angelis vel angeli reliquas gentes 1097Dsine ipso disponerent, quia et Israel Michael praelatus legitur, et Deus omnes gentes in sacro eloquio possidere et gubernare memoratur. Non itaque sic intelligendum est quod scriptum est: « Sed eloquium illud, » in quod videlicet hoc dicitur accipiendum: « est secundum ipsam sacram intelligentiam, » hoc est, secundum talem intelligentiam, quae a sacro, hoc est a veritate, non discordet. Haec autem est sacra intelligentia, ut intelligamus hoc dictum non ita ut, hoc est, quasi, partiente Deo ducatum nostrum, id est humani generis cum alteris quibusdam diis aut angelis: partiente, dico, in principatum Israel, et in ducatum gentis, contento scilicet Deo Israel, id est, principatu in Israel, aut retento sibi, ita ut 1098Ailli soli princeps et dux esset. Non, inquam, ita intelligendum est. Sed ita ut, hoc est, quasi, ipsa quidem excelsa, vel Excelsi providentia, quae est una simul omnium, quia omnibus providet; illa, inquam, providentia salutariter distribuente omnes homines restitutoriis manuductionibus propriorum angelorum, id est ducatibus, quibus quasi caeci in tenebris ignorantiae manuducerentur, et ad lumen veritatis restituerentur, et solo Israel converso in illuminationem et cognitionem veri Dei fere ultra omnes gentes. Propterea enim solus Israel a Deo in portionem aceeptus, et ductus legitur; quia solus tunc ex omnibus gentibus ad cognitionem Dei revocatus est, et ad cultum divinum institutus. « Unde, inquit, theologia significans 1098Bipsum, » hoc est Deum, « possedisse Israel in veri Dei famulatum, » ait: « Facta est portio Domini, » ipse scilicet Israel. Sic itaque portio ejus fuit Israel, qui sic ab ipso possidebatur, ut ipsum possideret et haberet.
