Sequitur: « Ostendens autem et eum viritim caeteris gentibus distribuisse, cuidam sanctorum angelorum in cognoscendum per eum unum omnium principium Michaelem dixit Judaicum duxisse populum. » In hoc, inquit, quod sacra Scriptura dixit Michaelem duxisse Judaicum populum, ostendit plane eum, id est Deum distribuisse etiam in caeteris gentibus scilicet ducatum viritim, hoc est sigillatim, cuidam, hoc est, alicui sanctorum angelorum, vel, ut expressius dicatur, unam uni, vel unamquamque 1098Cunicuique vel singula singulis: distribuisse, dico, in cognoscendum per eum scilicet angelum, hoc est, ut unaquaeque gens per suum angelum cognosceret unum omnium principium, a quo sunt omnia, et sub quo reguntur universi, ut hoc, inquit, ostenderet sacra Scriptura, dixit Michaelem ducem Judaici populi, quem specialiter Deus sua sub providentia, et gubernatione tuendum susceperat. Nam, hoc dicens, aperte nos edocuit unam esse providentiam, quae omnibus gubernando praesidet. sub qua per singulas gentes imperantes angeli easdem gentes sequentes ipsos voluntate essentiali, hoc est, libero arbitrio naturaliter insito, extendunt vel promovent 1098Din ipsum proprium principium, scilicet suggerendo et adjuvando, Scriptura, inquit, dixit Michaelem Judaicum duxisse populum, cujus ducem ipsum Dei alibi commemoraverat. In hoc « aperte nos edocens unam esse omnium providentiam superessentialiter supercollocatam, » hoc est, non solum potentialiter, sed etiam naturaliter praesidentem simul omnibus invisibilibus et visibilibus virtutibus, angelorum scilicet et hominum. Hoc est enim, quod in utrisque bonum constat. Ostendens etiam « omnes angelos sub illa providentia per singulas gentes imperantes extendere quasque, » sive singulas virtutes illarum videlicet gentium in ipsum subauditur Deum, « ut in proprium principium: » virtutes, dico, « sequentes 1099Avoluntate essentiali, » hoc est arbitrio libero naturali. Angeli enim humanas mentes ad Deum amandum 1100Avirtutes suggerendo excitant, non coactas necessitate, sed « sequentes voluntate. »

EXPOSITION.

« The adornment remaining to us for contemplation, concluding the angelic hierarchies disposed by the deiform principalities, archangels, and angels. » The words are plain. The adornment, he says, concluding the angelic hierarchies, disposed by the deiform principalities, archangels, and angels, is remaining to us — that is, it now remains for us to contemplate or consider the adornment, that is, the beautiful disposition of the angelic hierarchy, which is, as it were, the conclusion of the two preceding, and the end, in which three orders are disposed, that is, principalities, angels, and archangels.

1087BThere follows: « And first indeed I judge it necessary to speak, according to what is possible for me, the manifestations of their holy surnames. » I, he says, judge it to be necessary that I first speak the manifestations of their surnames, so that through the interpretation of the surnames their properties may be manifested. This therefore he judges must first be expounded: why in this last hierarchy some are named principalities, others archangels, others angels, because from the very distinct surname the properties of each are manifested. This is what he adds: « For it manifests, indeed, that deiform principal eductive of the celestial principalities, together with the sacred order and the most becoming principal powers, 1087Cand that they are universally converted unto the superprincipal principle, and lead others hierarchically; and that they are, as far as possible, formed unto that very principial principle, and that it manifests his superessential ordination, and the adornment of the principal powers. » He expounds what the several surnames in this last hierarchy signify: and first he treats of the surname of the principalities, showing that this very surname manifests that principal eductive, that is, that principal leadership which they have, deiformly, that is, [in] the likeness of God; because just as God is the one and highest prince of all, so they themselves are the princes and leaders of the subject angels and men. This 1087Dleadership, therefore, the surname itself manifests together with the sacred order and the most becoming principal powers, because they have that leadership both from the sacred order and from the principal powers. For that they are leaders and princes of others, they have both from this, that they have been ordained to this by office, and from this, that by their principal powers they are more excellent than the rest.

There follows: « And that they are universally converted unto the superprincipal principle; » this also, he says, the surname of the principalities manifests, namely those powers which they themselves have: that they are universally converted unto the superprincipal principle, that is, God. And their surname also signifies that they lead other powers, or the powers of others, unto that very 1088Aprincipial principle, [and], as far as is possible, that those powers are formed unto it, or conformed to it: to lead, I say, hierarchically, that is, according to the manner and measure of their own precedence. For their own powers they lead unto their principle by universally converting; the powers of others they lead unto their principle by hierarchically preceding; because they have to lead only in so far as they ought to precede or preside. Therefore they lead hierarchically, because in that in which they are not set above, they cannot rightly be leaders. This therefore their surname manifests: namely that they have a principate in the likeness of God, from office and from power; and that they convert both their own powers unto their principle, and lead the powers of others. Their surname also manifests the adornment 1088Bof the principal powers themselves — that is, the disposition of the principalities themselves manifests the superessential ordination of that first principle. For from the very surname of the principalities it is intimated that in their precedence the first Principate is manifested, because by ruling they both imitate it and manifest it.

There follows: « But that of the holy archangels is indeed of equal power with the celestial principalities. For there is, both of them and of the angels, as I have said, one hierarchy and disposition. » That surname (it is understood) « of the holy archangels is of equal power, » that is, signifies an equal power, or an equal potency, « with the celestial principalities; » because there is one hierarchy and one disposition of the three orders, 1088Cthat is, of the angels, and of them, namely the archangels, and of the principalities. And although from this — that the hierarchy is one — there is also one and equal power of the three: nevertheless, because there is no hierarchy which does not have first, and middle, and last orders, therefore the archangels, set in the middle place between the principalities, who are first, and the angels, who are last, participate in the property of both. This is what he says: « Nevertheless, since indeed there is no hierarchy not having also first, and middle, and last powers, the holy order of the archangels is received communicatively into the middle of the extremes of the hierarchy. » Since, he says, there is no hierarchy which does not have first, and middle, and last powers: 1088Dtherefore « the holy order of the archangels is received communicatively into the middle of the extremes of the hierarchy: » that is, it is received so as to be in the middle of the extremes, communicating with the hierarchy, that is, with their sacred power; or it is received into the hierarchical middle, that is, for the possessing of the hierarchical middle, which is communicative of the extremes — this is what follows: « For it communicates both with the most sacred principalities, and with the holy angels. » But in what it communicates with each, he shows subsequently, saying: « With the former indeed, because it is principally converted unto the superessential principle, and is, as far as possible, reformed unto it; and it unifies the angels according to its well-adorned, and ordered, and invisible leadings. » In this, he says, the order of the archangels participates with 1089Athe principalities in the same power, because « it is converted unto its superessential principle, and is reformed unto it, » as far as is possible for it: and because it also unifies — that is, gathers unto the unity of that same principle — by leading the angels after itself according to invisible and ordered leadings, by which it has to lead those subject and following ones. In this, therefore, the order of the archangels communicates with the power of the principalities: that in the likeness, or imitation, of them it both converts itself unto its first principle, and gathers those following it. And not only with the principalities set above, but also with the angels established below, does the order of the archangels itself communicate. This is what he adds: « But with the latter, because it is to them also a prophetic order, receiving the divine illuminations hierarchically through the first 1089Bpowers: and announcing them deiformly to the angels: and manifesting them through the angels to us according to the sacred analogy of each of those divinely illumined. » With the former, he says, that is, with the principalities, the order of the archangels communicates, as we said above. But with the latter, that is, with the angels, it communicates in this: that it is to them also a prophetic order — that is, an order prophetic, and ordained for prophesying — prophesying to them, as to inferiors, the divine secrets, receiving indeed the divine illuminations through the first powers, that is, through the principalities, who are prior and superior: itself receiving, I say, « hierarchically, » that is, according to what the hierarchical order and disposition requires, namely that the inferior receive their illuminations from the superior. « Receiving, » 1089CI say, « and announcing them, » namely the illuminations which it receives from the superiors, to the inferior angels: but announcing deiformly, so that in this — that it receives from the superiors — it may keep the hierarchical disposition; but in this — that it imparts to the inferiors — it may not depart from conformity to God, who, the highest of all, bestows his gifts upon all subject things to be participated. For to receive illumination from a superior is a hierarchical thing, but to give to an inferior is a divine thing. And through this the archangelic order, established in the middle according to the disposition of the hierarchy, participates both with the superiors and with the inferiors — receiving the divine illuminations from the superior principalities, and announcing them to the inferior angels: and through the angels 1089Dannouncing to us, as though to the last and lowest, those same divine illuminations according to the sacred analogy of each of those divinely illumined, that is, according to the manner and measure of the capacity of each of us for perceiving that same divine illumination; or, announcing to us through the angels according to the sacred analogy of each of them, namely of the angels divinely illumined — that is, they announce the divine illumination through each one only in so far as each is fit to receive it in himself, and to announce it to others through himself.

There follows: « For the angels themselves, as we have said before, completively consummate all the dispositions of the celestial minds, according to what is to be 1090Aconsummated. » As if he should say: Fittingly does the archangelic order announce the divine illuminations to us through the angels, because the angels themselves are last in the celestial disposition, and nearest to men, and in them are completed, or terminated and consummated, all the dispositions or orders of the celestial minds, that is, of the angels. Thus therefore the angels consummate all the celestial orders, according to what is to be consummated, so that it may be understood concerning them; or, that it may be said more expressly, according as they themselves, namely the orders of the angels, are to be consummated. But in what way the angels themselves perfect, or consummate, the celestial orders, he subjoins, saying: « Inasmuch as, in the celestial essences, having the angelic property, and more fittingly named angels among us than the prior ones, in so far as, 1090Bconcerning that which is more manifest, there is to them a hierarchy, and more of the circum-adornment. » It is not, he says, wondrous if the celestial orders are terminated in them, because among all the celestial essences it is their property to announce the divine secrets to us; and in this they have the angelic property, that it is their property to be messengers to us; and therefore they are named angels more fittingly among not than the prior or superior ones, namely in so far as there is to them a hierarchy, that is, a power or office concerning that which is more manifest to us, and in so far also as their adornment, or disposition, or order is more 'circum-,' that is, is more circumscribable and intelligible to us, approaching visible things because of their ministry. Therefore to them belongs more the circum-adornment — that is, a knowable or comprehensible 1090Corder — because it is nearest to us.

There follows: « For it is to be judged that the most excellent disposition, as itself firstly approaching to order the hidden one, secretly forming [forma], ordains the second. But the second, which is completed by the holy dominations, and virtues, and powers, presides over that hierarchy which is of the principalities, and archangels, and angels. The first hierarchy indeed more manifestly, but that which is after it, more hiddenly. But the manifestative disposition of the principalities, and archangels, and angels commands the human hierarchies through the consequent things, so that there be through order an ascent unto God, and conversion, and communication, and unity. » It is to be judged, 1090Dhe says, that the most excellent disposition — that is, the supreme hierarchy, as firstly, that is, principally, approaching the hidden one, that is, God — ordains the second, secretly, that is, hiddenly, or incomprehensibly forming it. But the second hierarchy, which is completed by the holy dominations, and virtues, and powers, is to be judged to preside over that — namely the hierarchy which is of the principalities, and archangels, and angels; and the first hierarchy, that is, the supreme, is to be judged to perceive the divine illuminations more manifestly, or to preside more manifestly over the third; but that which is after it, that is, the second, to preside, namely, more hiddenly. But the disposition — that is, the hierarchy of the principalities, and archangels, and angels — 1091Athe manifestative, that is, the known and notifying one, is to be judged to command the human hierarchies through the consequent things, that is, consequently, after a precept has been given to it by the superiors: so that thus there may be through order an ascent unto God, and conversion, and communication, and unity — that is, so that human minds, turned through the lower hierarchy unto the middle, and from the middle unto the supreme, may ascend unto that one thing to be communicated which God is.

There follows: « And indeed also, from God, best imparted to all the hierarchical ones, and communicatively supervening, and a procession with most sacred adornment. » By such an order, he says, the one good is communicated by all, proceeding from God into all the hierarchical orders, so that it may adorn them, supervening upon them and imparted 1091Bthrough communication. This is what he says: And indeed also, that is, even so, there comes to be from God a procession of that highest good, namely, best imparted to all the hierarchical — it is understood, orders: upon them « supervening communicatively, » that is, unto communicating, and with most sacred adornment. For in this is the great adornment of the divine disposition: that, although all participate in the one good, yet it comes forth to be communicated not in one mode, but some perceive it through others, and in turn offer it to be communicated to others after them. Just as, among those spirits, the first hierarchy offers the divine illuminations to be communicated to the second, the second to the third, the third to ours, that is, to the human. This is what he subsequently adds, saying: « Thence theology distributes our hierarchy 1091Cto the angels, naming Michael the prince of the people of the Jews, and others, diverse, of the nations. » Thence, he says, that is, for this reason — because the inferior are ruled by the superior — theology, that is, Holy Scripture, distributes our hierarchy to the angels to be ruled, naming Michael the prince of the people of the Jews, and naming other diverse angels as princes of the nations, namely: as in Daniel we read the prince of the Persians, and the prince of the Greeks named. And not only in those testimonies is it proved that the angels have rule over men, but Scripture also testifies elsewhere, saying: « The Most High established the bounds of the nations according to the number of the angels of God (Dan. X). » The bounds — that is, the divisions, or distributions, of the nations — the Most High established according to the number 1091Dof the angels of God: because he fitted the number of the nations to the number of the angels, so that individual angels might preside over individual nations; although, because according to another translation there not 'angels' but 'sons of God' are named, something else seems to be signified.

There follows: « But if anyone should say: And how was the people of the Hebrews alone led back into the divine illuminations? It must be answered that the right dominations of the angels are not to be accused of the error of the other nations unto non-existent gods, but those very ones, by their own inflexions, falling away from that right leading-back which is unto the divine, by their own love, and by pride — [pride] of the things divinely seen by them, and, in a co-rational manner, unto worship. » As if he should say: It seems indeed wondrous. If 1092Aanyone, he says, wonders why the good angels suffered those nations over which they presided to fall away from the knowledge of the true God, it must be answered that this was not done by the fault of the angels, and that the right dominations of the angels ought not to be accused for the error of the other nations, which were not of Israel, unto non-existent gods — that is, because by erring they worshipped those who were not gods; but that those very ones, by their own inflexions, that is, by their own will, falling away from the right leading-back, that is, from the knowledge by which man is led back unto the divine, so that they believed [to be] gods those who were not gods; those very ones, I say, are to be accused, who by their own will, in so far as they were of free choice, slipped from the truth into error, and this out of their own love, because they loved themselves more than God, and sought their own glory, 1092Band were therefore proud; and out of the pride of the things divinely seen by them, that is, of those things which were divinely revealed to them, and which were revealed to them also in a co-rational manner unto worship, namely the divine — that is, from which they might reasonably or probably have understood in what manner they ought to worship God. For as the Apostle says: « When they had known God, they glorified him not as God; but they became vain in their thoughts. For saying themselves to be wise [behold, pride], they were made fools, and their senseless heart was darkened [behold, the error unto non-existent gods], because they served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever (Rom. I). » Or, 'divinely and co-rationally' [means] with God recompensing — it is understood, to them: that is, wisely and worthily 1092Cunto worship; that is, as was fitting for the worshippers of false [gods], namely gods seen by them — that is, who seemed to them gods, and were not. For in this God recompensed them wisely and reasonably: that, as the Apostle says, because they approved not to have God in [their] knowledge, God delivered them up unto a reprobate sense, that they should do the things which are not fitting, in their very selves. For they were to be punished in their very selves, who had sinned in their very selves.

There follows: « This is reported that the people of the Hebrews itself also suffered — namely this, that it withdrew from the worship of God, just as the other nations also had withdrawn unto the cult of idols; or this, that is, a like divine vengeance, because it likewise withdrew from the worship of God, and cast off the knowledge of God. For the divine voice says to Israel itself 1092D: « Thou hast repelled the knowledge of God: and hast gone forth after thy own heart. » Namely, God being forsaken, who is worshipped within by a pure mind. Thou hast gone forth outward through the love of visible things, whither thy own heart — that is, thy desire and depraved will — was drawing thee. In all which the power of free choice appears, because without coercion man — whether aided unto good, or permitted unto evil — is inclined by his own will. This is what follows: « For neither do we have a coerced life. » For the will can be given free to a rational creature, but it cannot be coerced at all. And just as it is not in our power that the gift of divine illumination be offered to us, so it is only in our power that, once offered, it be received. For sometimes it is offered even when we are unwilling, 1093Abut it is never received except when we are willing. And when we are willing, we are willing indeed from God, because a good will is the gift of God. But when we are unwilling, we are unwilling from ourselves, because to be unwilling is nothing other than not to will: which is a desertion of the good unto non-being, and nothing, which was made without it. And so « the divine lights of provident illumination, » because through them God providently illumines, are indeed not « revealed through the proper power of providence: » that is, of those who, having received them, become provident; or 'of the things provided-for,' that is, of those who have been provided for, or predestined by God to receive them. It is to be noted that where we have revelantur ('are revealed'), another text has obcaecantur ('are blinded'); which, although they are different, yet pertain to establishing the same truth: namely that it may be shown 1093Bthat whether the divine lights be revealed, that is, manifested, or blinded, that is, hidden and concealed, this stands not in the power of those receiving, but in the choice of the giver. But nevertheless, although the manifestation or concealment itself is not in their power, yet the reception never comes to be except with their will, because a rational good is that which cannot be perceived except by one who knows and wills. Therefore either it comes about, by a depraved will, that they are wholly repelled, or, by a difference of good will, that they are participated dissimilarly. This is what he says: « But of the intellectual visions, » that is, of the spiritual eyes, namely of the rational minds, « the dissimilarity makes the donation of light, » coming namely « out of the superfull, » that is, out of the exceedingly full and eminently full paternal 1093Cgoodness; that donation, I say, the dissimilarity itself makes either wholly non-participating, and not distributed unto the reformation of those visions: « or it makes the participations differing, that is, small or great, obscure or clear, of the one fontal ray, and simple, and ever holding itself in the same mode, and superexpanded. » For the ray of divine illumination, descending from the fount of the good, in itself one and simple, and ever holding itself in the same mode, is superexpanded upon all rational minds, and is participated by them differently, not according to its own simplicity, but according to their diversity. For either they are depraved, and wholly repel it, and cause that it be in no way participated, nor 1093Ddistributed unto their reformation; or they are dissimilarly good, and receive it differently.

There follows: « Then, because also to the other nations — out of which we also have looked back unto that — [there was], prepared unto tradition and open to all, the great and copious sea of the divine light; no alien gods indeed ruled, but the one principle of all; and unto it the angels, exercising the priesthood according to each several nation, led back their followers. » As if he should say: That good angels were set over the nations can be proved not only from this, that the Most High is said to have established the bounds of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God, but also from this, that over those nations no alien gods ruled from the beginning, but one God. For it is altogether probable 1094Athat the good Lord established in his commonwealth good ministers under himself: by whose ministry this too was afterward done, that we, who have believed out of the nations, looked back through faith unto God, and unto the fullness of his illumination, being led back through them: which assuredly they would not have done, if they had not been good. This is what he says. Then also from this it can be proved that good angels were set over the nations: namely because to those other nations, which were not of Israel — out of which nations we also, who afterward believed, looked back, turned through faith unto that great and copious sea of the divine light, which is prepared and open to all unto tradition, or bestowal, because it bestows itself and hands itself over to all who will and desire to receive it. Over those nations, namely, 1094Bno alien gods ruled, although this might seem [so], because they worshipped idols, and adored false gods. But one God ruled over them, and had dominion, because just as there is one principle of all, from whom are all things, so there is one Lord and ruler, under whose power all things are established. Who, as he is good in himself, so established good ministers under himself, as rulers and leaders, [namely] angels, and those angels led us back, following through faith, unto that very principle of ours. They led back, I say, according as they were exercising the priesthood — that is, the sacred precedence — according to each several nation; that is, each one, out of that nation in which he exercised the priesthood, that is, the sacred power, converted unto the faith those who believed, and looked back unto their principle.

1094CThere follows: « Melchizedek, it is to be understood, being the highest priest, most beloved by the Lord of those that exist — nay, not of those that exist, but of the truly existing most high God. » Treating of the ministry and office of the angels, he suddenly introduces a narrative about Melchizedek: not because, as certain men have supposed, he holds that Melchizedek himself was an angel, or that on this account his priesthood is to be commemorated among the ministries of the angels, but that he may show that it was not only by the work and ministry of angels, but also of the saints and of men pleasing to God, and set over other men in the things that were divine, that unbelievers from among the Gentiles were converted to the faith and worship of the true God. According to this manner, then, 1094Dby which the angels, from the office of their prelacy, exercised the priesthood among the Gentiles, converting them to the faith of the true God, it is to be understood that Melchizedek was the highest priest, being most beloved by the Lord of all that exist — nay rather, of those that do not exist, but of the truly existing most high God. The letter is intricate. But the sense is this. Since he had said that Melchizedek was most beloved by the Lord of all that exist, as though correcting his own statement — because he had called those who truly are not "existing" — he adds "of those not existing," according to what is written: « All the nations are before him as though they were not (Isa. XL). » And, as though it were asked who then exists, he adds: « The most high God alone, who has true existence. » But that he does not say "the truly existing most high 1095AGod," « but of the truly existing most high God, this was done because of the likeness of the preceding word, so that by the same case it might answer to "of those not existing," « if of the truly existing most high God. » Or it may be read thus. It is to be understood that Melchizedek, being most beloved by the Lord of all that exist, was a priest not of any existing things whatsoever, but of the most high God who truly exists, as it is written: « For he was a priest of the most high God (Gen. XIV). »

And there follows: « For indeed thus simply the theosophers themselves called Melchizedek not a friend of God, but also a priest. » Rightly, he says, did I say that Melchizedek is to be understood a priest, since the theosophers, that is, those who write of divine things, called him not thus simply a friend of God only, but also a priest. And why 1095Bthey called him a priest he adds, saying: « Was it that they might signify openly to the wise that he converted not only from among them into him who truly is God? But moreover also others, that as highest priest he may lead them forth by that leading-back which is unto the true and sole divinity. » That Melchizedek, he says, who was not of the Jews, they called not only a friend of God, but also a priest of God — did they do this for this reason? Assuredly they did this for this reason: that they might openly signify to the wise that he converted not only from among them, that is, from Israel, who alone then seemed to be led back and converted to divine knowledge, into God himself, that is, to the faith and knowledge of that same God who truly is, but that he would also lead forth many from other nations out of the darkness of ignorance, namely by that leading-back which is unto the true 1095Cand sole divinity, that is, unto the knowledge of God. Not that Melchizedek himself is read to have converted any from Israel, which was not yet a people: unless perhaps we take Israel in the earlier fathers, of whom some perhaps through Melchizedek himself, in his own time, were led to the knowledge of God. Or so that it be read thus, namely that for this reason he was called not only a friend of God, but also a priest, because he converted — understand: the ignorant and those who knew not — unto God himself, in whom truly one must believe. And as though someone should object that Melchizedek himself, who was not of Israel but a foreigner, converted no one to the faith of God, since Israel alone knew God, he answers that not only from Israel were men converted to the faith of God, but also from other nations: which conversion of the others, namely, was accomplished through Melchizedek himself. Who then indeed, that is, when he blessed Abraham, was called a priest of the most high God, though he was not of Israel, that it might be shown that he was to lead forth many unto God, and that God had both a priest and a people not only in Israel, but also among the Gentiles. Therefore he does not say "he led forth," but « he shall lead forth, » he says. Signifying indeed something future to that time when these things were said — when either Melchizedek himself afterward by himself converted men from the Gentiles unto God, or Christ, of whom he was a type, led forth many, not only from Israel but also from all nations, through faith, unto his Church out of the darkness of unbelief.

There follows: « And this also we shall bring to the notice of thy highest 1096Apriestly understanding: that — the angel ruling over Pharaoh among the Egyptians themselves, and its own president presiding over the prince of the Babylonians, by all providence both provident of dominion and endowed with power, distributed according to the divisions — for those nations also the ministers of the true God were established as leaders of the formations by the manifestation of the vision from the angels, the angels forthwith revealing to the holy men Joseph and Daniel from God through the angels. » He adds yet another authority, from which he wishes to prove that good angels were set by God over the Gentiles: namely, that among the Egyptians the angel shows a vision to Pharaoh, and through it enjoins upon him a precaution concerning the coming barrenness; the same vision being then made manifest through Joseph; and likewise upon the prince of the Babylonians, namely Nebuchadnezzar, his own president, that is, his own 1096Bappointed one, namely his own angel, forms a vision, and afterward makes it manifest by unlocking it through Daniel. In all which it appears that God has both providence, and dominion, and power over all things, according to which, through those visions, it was discerned, or distinguished, or distributed: which visions were first revealed to the angels by God, and then forthwith through the angels to the holy men Joseph and Daniel. This is what he says: O Timothy, not only the higher things, but this also shall we bring to the notice of thy highest priestly understanding, that is, thy understanding — thou who art the highest priest — we shall bring this to thy notice, that, the angel ruling over Pharaoh among the Egyptians, and its own president ruling over the prince of the Babylonians, that is, the angel who was set over 1096Chim; by this, I say, that the angels are read to have ruled over them, there was distributed the provident and powerful quality of the divine providence and dominion according to those, namely, visions — that is, it was shown that God distributes his providence and power for the governing of the several nations; and it was also shown that for those nations the ministers of the true God were established as leaders; and how it was shown, this he adds: by the manifestation, namely, of the vision of the formations by the angels, that is, of the vision in which were displayed the formations, or figures, made by the angels in the minds of the prophets, to signify things to come — such as were the cows and the ears of grain which Pharaoh saw (Gen. XLI), and the tree and the statue which Nebuchadnezzar saw (Dan. II). By the manifestation, therefore, of such a vision was displayed the divine providence and power, disposing the nations through the angels; the vision, I say, first revealed to the angels by God, and then forthwith revealed through the angels to the holy men, namely Joseph and Daniel, from God.

There follows: « For one is the principle and providence of all; and by no means is it to be supposed that the Jews indeed led the divinity fully, but that the angels, either specially, or equally honorably, or as opposites, or certain other gods, ruled over the other nations. » The repetition proves what he said above, that one is the principle and providence of all, that is, one God, from whom are all things, and by whom all things are ruled; and therefore by no means 1097Ais it to be supposed that the divinity led the Jews, that is, that it furnished leadership to the Jews fully, or absolutely, that is, through itself, namely without the intervening ministry of angels; but that over the other nations the angels ruled specially, that is, particularly, or with a less excellent power; or equally honorably, that is, with a power equal and like to the divine dominion; or as opposites (understand: with opposing sovereignties), just as the apostate angel is read to have said that he would set his seat toward the north and would be like to the Most High in power (Isa. XIV). Or, again, it is not to be supposed that certain other gods ruled over the other nations, as though all things were not subject to the power and dominion of the one and true God. It is not, he says, so to be supposed, as though the true God had power 1097Bover the Jews alone, and over the other nations either angels, or certain other gods, ruled with a power either equal or unequal, yet contrary and foreign to the divine dominion. Or let it be read thus: By no means is it to be supposed that the Divinity, through itself, without an interposed subject angelic power, furnished leadership to the Jews; but that the angels ruled over the other nations specially, that is, particularly, namely among nations of a power and dignity inferior to that of the Jews themselves; or equally honorably, that is, among nations, namely, equally powerful and honorable; or even among opposing nations, which, namely, were opposed and contrary to the Jews themselves, assailing and oppressing them. It is not, he says, so to be supposed — namely that God for this reason led the Jews through himself 1097Cas though they were more honorable than all the other nations, and left the other nations, as inferior and baser, to the angelic dominion — since in other peoples many are not doubted to have been not only equally honorable, but even stronger and more powerful, oppressing the Jews themselves by their power and strength. For what has been said: « When the Most High divided the nations, he set the bounds of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God; but the Lord's portion is his people, Jacob the cord of his inheritance; » is not to be so understood, as though he had given the other nations to be ruled by angels, retaining Israel alone to himself, that is, to his own providence and governance — as if either Israel itself, without angels, or the angels, without him, 1097Ddisposed the remaining nations; since both Michael is read to be set over Israel, and God is recorded in the sacred eloquence to possess and govern all nations. Not thus, therefore, is what is written to be understood: « But that eloquence, » in which, namely, this is said to be taken, « is according to the sacred understanding itself, » that is, according to such an understanding as does not disagree with the sacred, that is, with the truth. And this is the sacred understanding: that we understand this saying not as if, that is, as though, God dividing our leadership, that is, the leadership of the human race, with certain other gods or angels — dividing it, I say, into the principate of Israel and into the leadership of the nation, God being content, namely, with the principate over Israel, that is, retaining it to himself, so that 1098Ahe alone should be to that people prince and leader. Not, I say, is it so to be understood. But so as, that is, as though, the exalted providence itself, or the providence of the Exalted One, which is one and at once of all, because it provides for all — that providence, I say, salutarily distributing all men by the restorative hand-leadings of their own angels, that is, by leaderships, by which as blind men in the darkness of ignorance they were led by the hand, and restored to the light of truth; and Israel alone being converted to the illumination and knowledge of the true God almost beyond all nations. For on this account Israel alone is read to have been received by God into a portion, and led; because it alone then, out of all nations, was called back to the knowledge of God, and established in the divine worship. « Whence, he says, theology, signifying that he, 1098Bthat is God, » « possessed Israel unto the service of the true God, » says: « It became the portion of the Lord, » namely Israel itself. Thus, therefore, Israel was his portion, which was so possessed by him that it possessed and had him.

There follows: « But showing that he distributed even it, man by man, to the other nations, he said that Michael led the Jewish people, unto a certain one of the holy angels, that through him the one principle of all might be known. » In this, he says, that Holy Scripture said Michael led the Jewish people, it plainly shows that he, that is God, distributed also among the other nations, namely, leadership man by man, that is, one by one, to a certain one, that is, to some one of the holy angels — or, to say it more expressly, one nation to one, or each nation 1098Cto each, or the several to the several: distributed it, I say, that through him, namely the angel, that is, that each nation, through its own angel, might know the one principle of all, from whom are all things, and under whom all are ruled; so that, in order that Holy Scripture might show this, he says, it said that Michael was the leader of the Jewish people, whom God had specially taken up to be guarded under his own providence and governance. For, in saying this, it plainly taught us that there is one providence which presides over all in governing, under which the angels ruling over the several nations extend, or promote, those same nations that follow them by essential will, that is, by free choice naturally implanted, 1098Dinto their own proper principle, namely by suggesting and helping; Scripture, he says, said that Michael led the Jewish people, whose leader it had elsewhere recorded him to be from God. In this « plainly teaching us that there is one providence of all, superessentially set above, » that is, presiding not only potentially, but even naturally, over all invisible and visible virtues at once, namely of angels and of men. For this is what stands as good in both. Showing also « that all the angels under that providence, ruling over the several nations, extend each, » or the several virtues of those nations, namely, into (understand: God) himself, « as into their own proper principle: » the virtues, I say, « following 1099Aby essential will, » that is, by free natural choice. For the angels arouse human minds to love God 1100Aby suggesting virtues, not compelled by necessity, but « following by will. »

TITULUS CAPITULI X. Synagogae angelicae ordinationis repetitio.

TITLE OF CHAPTER X. A recapitulation of the ordering of the angelic synagogue.

LITTERA.

  • 1099A

Connexa est itaque sic ipsa quidem honorabilissima circa Deum animorum dispositio ex perfectiva illuminatione ordinata, in eam immediate ascendendo occultior: et manifestior divinitatis illuminatione purgatur, et illuminatur, et perficitur. Occultior quidem 1099Btanquam invisibilior, et magis simplificata et unificata. Manifestior vero ut ante data, et primo lucet, et universalior, et magis in eam, ut oportet, forma effusa. Ab ipsa autem iterum proportionaliter secunda, et a secunda tertia, et ex tertia secundum nos hierarchia, secundum ipsam bene ornantis ordinationis legem in harmonia divina, et analogia ad simul omnis boni ornatus super principale principium et consummationem hierarchiae reducitur. Manifestatores autem omnes sunt et angeli eorum, qui ante ipsos sunt. Ipsi quidem honorabilissimi Dei moventis, proportionaliter autem caeteri ex Deo motorum. Tantum enim omnium superessentialis harmonia unicuique rationalium, et intellectualium sacro ornatu, 1099Cet ordinata ductione praevidit, quantum ipse hierarchiarum unusquisque ordo sacre, et decenter positus est. Et omnem hierarchiam videmus in primas, et medias, et ultimas virtutes divisam. Sed et ipsam, per singulas specialiter dicendum, dispositionem ipsis divinis harmoniis discrevit. Propter quod et ipsos divinissimos seraphim theologi aiunt alterum ad alterum clamare (Isai. IV), aperte hoc, ut existimo, declarantes, quod theologicas sententias ipsi primi secundis tradunt. Addiderim autem fortassis, et hoc non incongrue, quod et secundum seipsum unusquisque et coelestis, et humanus animus speciales habet et primas, et medias, et ultimas ordinationes, et virtutes, ad jam dictas per unumquemque hierarchicarum illuminationum proprias anagogas proportionaliter manifestatas: 1099Dper quas unumquodque in participatione fit, sicut idipsum et fas est, et possibile, superincognitissimae purgationis plenissimi luminis, anteperfectae perfectionis. Etenim nihil per se perfectum indigens universalis perfectionis, nisi vere perfectissimum et ante perfectum.

THE TEXT.

  • 1099A

Thus, therefore, is the most honorable disposition of the minds about God connected, ordered from the perfective illumination, immediately ascending into it, more hidden: and by the more manifest illumination of the divinity it is purged, and illuminated, and perfected. More hidden indeed 1099Bas being more invisible, and more simplified and unified. But more manifest as given before, and shining first, and more universal, and having form more poured out into it, as is fitting. But from it again proportionally the second, and from the second the third, and from the third the hierarchy according to us, according to that same law of the well-adorning ordination, in the divine harmony and analogy unto the whole adornment of all good at once, is led back to the sovereign principle and consummation of the hierarchy. And all are manifesters, even the angels of those who are before them. They themselves indeed the most honorable of God who moves them, but proportionally the rest of those moved by God. For the superessential harmony of all foresaw for each of the rational and intellectual ones, with sacred adornment 1099Cand ordered leading, as much as each order of the hierarchies itself is sacredly and becomingly placed. And we see every hierarchy divided into first, and middle, and last virtues. But it also distinguished the very disposition — speaking specially, through each one — by those divine harmonies themselves. For which reason the theologians say that the most divine seraphim themselves cry one to another (Isai. IV), openly declaring this, as I suppose: that the first themselves hand on the theological utterances to the second. But I would add perhaps, and this not incongruously, that each celestial and human mind, according to itself also, has special first, and middle, and last ordinations and virtues, manifested proportionally through each of the hierarchic illuminations, unto the aforesaid proper anagogies: 1099Dthrough which each is made, insofar as this itself is both lawful and possible, in participation of the most superunknown purgation, of the fullest light, of the fore-perfected perfection. For nothing is perfect through itself, needing the universal perfection, save only the truly most perfect and fore-perfect.

EXPOSITIO.

Decimi capitis titulus est: Synagogae angelicae ordinationis repetitio. Hic enim breviter repetitur, quod supra dictum est, scilicet, ordinata Synagoga, id est congregatio, vel multitudo angelica in omnibus suis primis, et secundis, et tertiis. Caput autem sic incipit:

« Connexa est itaque sic ipsa quidem honorabilissima circa Deum animorum dispositio, ex perfectiva illuminatione ordinata, in eam immediate ascendendo, 1100Aoccultior et manifestior divinitatis illuminatione purgatur, et illuminatur, et perficitur. » De prima hierarchia dicit, quae in tribus constat ordinibus, seraphim, cherubim et thronis. Haec itaque dispositio, sive ordinatio animorum, hoc est spirituum honorabilissima vel excellentissima omnium: 1100Bconnexa est circa Deum, hoc est, et inter se concorditer juncta, et Deo immediate sociata; sic ordinata ex perfectiva illuminatione, id est divina, quae sola perfecte lucet et illuminat. Quicunque enim ab ipsa illuminantur, lucendo quidem ei assimilantur, et illuminando alios eam imitantur. Sed tamen nec in eo quod lucent, ei coaequantur, nec in eo quod illuminant, comparantur. Propterea hierarchia ista, quae sola ab ipsa illuminatur immediate, singulariter ex perfectiva illuminatione ordinatur. Alii quippe, qui inferiores illuminationes mediate suscipiunt, convenienter etiam inferius dispositi et ordinati sunt. Ista vero hierarchia, quae ex perfectiva, sive teletarchica, et divina illuminatione, quae princeps 1100Cest sanctificationis, id est prima, et maxima, ac singularis causa sanctificationis ordinatur, vel, ut expressius dicatur, pontificatur, hoc est in pontificalem ordinem, sive dignitatem sublimatur: convenienter cunctis dignitate superponitur, in eam videlicet illuminationem immediate ascendendo, occultior existens, et manifestior ex eadem divinitatis illuminatione purgatur, et illuminatur, et perficitur. Quomodo autem prima hierarchia, ex eo quod divinam illuminationem immediate suscipit, et occultior, et manifestior sit, verbis subsequentibus exponit, dicens: « Occultior quidem tanquam invisibilior, et magis simplificata et vivificata. Manifestior vero ut quae ante data lucet, et primo lucet, et universalior est, et magis in eam ut oportet, forma 1100Deffusa. » Occultior, inquit, est in eo quod invisibilior est, et magis simplificata, et unificata. In eo occultior est quod magis invisibilis est, et propinquior simplicitati, et unitati Deitatis. Manifestior autem est, utpote quae lucens ex luce data sibi ante, id est priusquam aliis: ideo primo lucet, et excellentius. Manifestior est etiam, quia universalior est, in qua una similitudo in pluribus constat, quia magis notum est quod magis commune est, et pluribus convenit. Unde autem universalior sit et magis consimilis, adinvicem consequenter ostendit, quia scilicet forma, id est divina illuminatio, ex qua formatur ut luceat, magis, id est expressius, vel abundantius effusa est in eam, quam in alias hierarchias subditas. Sensus autem hic est: Quia scilicet divina illuminatio in istam hierarchiam primo effunditur, idcirco 1101Aipsa perfectius illuminatur. Quanto autem perfectius ii, qui in ea sunt, spiritus unam illuminationem suscipiunt, tanto perfectius et clarius lucentes in ipsa una forma unius luminis unum fiunt: et quod in ipsis diversum ex natura multipliciter distinguitur, una claritatis forma superveniente cunctis dissimile non videtur. Ita ergo ista hierarchia, quia prius lucet, perfectius lucet; et quia perfectius lucet, universalius, vel similius, vel expressius lucet, quia expressius lucet, manifestius lucet. Quae ergo essentialiter occultior est, formaliter est manifestior; et quae subtilior est ex natura, clarior est ex gratia.

Sequitur: « Ab ipsa autem iterum proportionaliter secunda, et a secunda tertia, et ex tertia secundum 1101Bnos hierarchia, secundum ipsam bene ornantis ordinationis legem in harmonia divina, et analogia ad simul omnis boni ornatus super principale principium et consummationem hierarchice reducitur. » Ab ipsa, inquit, hierarchia prima reducitur vel convertitur a secunda et a secunda tertia convertitur, et a tertia convertitur illa scilicet hierarchia, quae est secundum nos. Prima enim hierarchia angelica convertit secundam, secunda tertiam, tertia angelica convertit humanam. Quomodo autem convertat ostendit, dicens: Ad super principale principium, et consummationem simul omnis bonus ornatus, id est ad Deum, qui principium est et perfectio omnis bonae et pulchrae dispositionis. Reducit autem hierarchice, hoc est secundum officium, vel 1101Cordinationem, sive legem hierarchiarum in quibus ordinatum est, ut superiores secundum modum et virtutem suam inferiores illuminando et suggerendo ad principium suum convertant. Convertunt autem secundum ipsam legem bene ornantis ordinationis, id est divinae ordinationis, quae ornat omnia: cujus lex est et institutio, ut alii ab aliis illuminentur, et convertantur in harmonia et analogia divina, hoc est, in concordia et proportione a Deo universitati collata. In eo enim quod boni participatio per alios aliis proportionaliter transfunditur, concordia in universitate perficitur et consummatur. Quod autem ait, iterum reducitur, sic intelligendum est quasi secunda reductione. Prima enim reductio est, quando 1101Dprimi ab ipso Deo illuminati in ipsum Deum convertuntur. Secunda quando a primis secundi, vel a secundis tertii. « Manifestatores autem sunt omnes, et angeli eorum, qui ante ipsos sunt. » Omnes, inquit, spiritus coelestes manifestatores sunt, et angeli, hoc est, nuntii eorum qui sunt ante ipsos. Quod enim a praecedentibus accipiunt sequentibus post se nuntiant et manifestant.

Sequitur: « Ipsi quidem honorabilissimi Dei moventis, proportionaliter autem caeteri ex Deo motorum. » Dixerat omnes nuntios esse praecedentium ad sequentes: nunc subdistinguit, quod ipsi quidem honorabilissimi, id est, excellentissimi spiritus, qui solum Deum ante se habent, nuntii sunt ipsius Dei moventis eos per inspirationem, ut per eos secreta 1102Asua sequentibus revelet. Caeteri eidem, qui post ipsos sequuntur, nuntii sunt ipsorum motorum ex Deo. Nuntii, inquam, sunt proportionaliter, id est, secundi primorum, et Dei per primos; tertii secundorum, et primorum per secundos; Dei autem per secundos et primos; atque in hunc modum caeteri post hoc sequentes. Quomodo autem proportionaliter singuli divina secreta revelent, subsequentibus verbis exponit, ostendens quod unicuique tantum posse datum est, quantum competit ordini et loco in quo positus est. Hoc est, quod dicit: « Tantum enim omnium superessentialis harmonia unicuique rationalium et intellectualium sacro ornatu et ordinata ductione praevidit, quantum ipse hierarchiarum unusquisque ordo sacre et decenter positus est. » 1102BSuperessentialis, inquit, harmonia, id est, divina providentia, quae omnia concorditer disposuit tantum praevidit, scilicet virtutis vel potentiae, unicuique rationalium vel intellectualium, cum sacro ornatu, et ordinata ductione, scilicet sacre ornans, et ordinate ducens; tantum, inquam, praevidit, quantum est sacre et decenter positus unusquisque ordo hierarchiarum, hoc, quantum decet sanctitatem et decentiam ordinis uniuscujusque. De quo ordine in unaquaque hierarchia distinctiones subjungit, dicens: « Et omnem hierarchiam videmus in primas, et medias, et ultimas virtutes sive ordines divisam. » Et non solum unamquamque hierarchiam, sed etiam unumquemque ordinem per singulas hierarchias. Hoc est, quod sequitur: « Sed et ipsam, per singulas 1102Cspecialiter dicendum, dispositionem ipsis divinis harmoniis discrevit. » Ipsa, inquit, divina providentia discrevit, vel distinxit, ipsam scilicet unamquamque dispositionem, hoc est ordinem, divinis harmoniis, ut scilicet distinctio esset, et discrepantia non esset. Et hoc dicendum est specialiter per singulas hierarchias: singuli ordines speciales habent discretiones.

Sequitur: « Propter quod et ipsos divinissimos seraphim ipsi theologi aiunt alterum ad alterum clamare: aperte, ut aperte existimo, declarantes quod theologicas sententias ipsi primi secundis tradunt. » Propter quod, quia scilicet singuli ordines in semet discreti sunt, idcirco ipsi theologi aiunt ipsos seraphim, 1102Dqui divinissimi sunt, id est, divinitatis propinquissimi, clamare alterum ad alterum, sicut in Isaia legitur (Isai. VI). In hoc scilicet quod alterum ad alterum clamare dicunt, aperte declarantes quod theologicas, id est divinas sententias, ipsi qui primi sunt in illo ordine tradunt iis qui secundi in eodem ordine constituti sunt. In quo claret unum eumdemque ordinem primos et secundos habere. Quod si de primo et de supremo ordine veraciter accipitur, de sequentibus nullo modo dubitari potest.

Sequitur: « Addiderim autem fortassis et hoc non incongrue, quod et secundum seipsum unusquisque et coelestis et humanus animus speciales habet et primas, et medias, et ultimas ordinationes et virtutes, addictas per unumquemque hierarchicarum 1103Ailluminationum proprias anagogas proportionaliter manifestatas: per quas unumquodque in participatione fit, sicut idipsum et fas est, et possibile, superincognitissimae purgationis, et plenissimi luminis, et ante perfectae perfectionis. » Sensus hic est: quod non solum universalis hierarchia in primam, et mediam, et ultimam hierarchiam, et singulae hierarchiae in primos, et medios, et ultimos ordines, et singuli ordines in primos, et medios, et ultimos spiritus dividuntur; sed etiam ipsi singuli spiritus angelici, si humani in semetipsis virtualiter discreti sunt; primas, et medias, et ultimas virtutes continentes: per quas propriis anagogis, id est, sursum ductionibus, sive ascensionibus, ab infimis ad medias, et a mediis ad supremas, secundum hierarchicas 1103Billuminationes proportionaliter ascendentes, participes fiunt, quantum eis possibile, divinae purgationis, quae est incognitissima, vel occultissima, quia intime purgat, et divini luminis, quod est plenissimum, quia omnes tenebras fugat, et divinae perfectionis, quae est anteperfecta, quia cunctis et prior est aeternitate, et superior dignitate, et plenior veritate. Hierarchicas autem illuminationes idcirco proportionales dicit, quia in sacris potestatibus, ubi alii superiores, alii inferiores constituti sunt, divinas illuminationes non omnes uno modo percipiunt. Superioribus enim et capacioribus in donis gratiae amplius tribuitur, inferioribus secundum modum capacitatis suae minus participandum praebetur. Secundum hunc itaque modum, quo vel in singulis 1103Chierarchiis diversis ordinibus et diversis animis differenter divinae illuminationes tribuuntur, unusquisque etiam animus in semetipso in eisdem illuminationibus rationabili differentia a minoribus ad majora excrescens provehitur. Hoc est quod dicit: « Addiderim autem et hoc non incongrue, » ac si diceret: Non solum de singulis hierarchiis sive ordinibus congrue dicere possum quod habeant et primos, et medios, et ultimos ordines, vel spiritus; sed etiam hoc fortassis non incongrue supradictis addere possum, quod unusquisque et coelestis et humanus animus secundum seipsum, vel in seipso, habet speciales, hoc est, proprias et primas, et medias, et ultimas ordinationes et virtutes, hoc est, virtutes in ipso primo, et medio, et ultimo loco ordinatas. Ad 1103Dquid autem virtutes habeat differentes, subjungit, 1104Ascilicet ad proprias anagogas, ut habeat videlicet ascensiones suas unusquisque proprias, et promotiones in melius, sicut scriptum est: « Ascensiones in corde suo disposuit (Psal. LXXXIII); » et iterum: « Ascendunt de virtute in virtutem: et videbitur Deus deorum in Sion. » Ad has autem anagogas, id est ascensiones, dispositae sunt virtutes aliae inferiores, aliae superiores, ut ab inferioribus ad superiora ascendendo participes tandem fiant summi boni, quod est Deus deorum in Sion. Habet, inquit, unusquisque spiritus proprias virtutes, primas, et medias, et ultimas, ad proprias anagogas, id est, ascensiones faciendas. Anagogas dico, dictas jam, id est, quas supra jam diximus, per unumquemque scilicet ordinem hierarchicarum illuminationum: 1104Bquia cum ostendimus qualiter in distributione hierarchiarum distincti ordines differentes illuminationes percipiunt, demonstravimus etiam quemadmodum in eis inferiores proportionaliter, id est, rationabili differentia promotionis per superiores ad suprema ascendunt. Propterea dixit anagogas hierarchicarum illuminationum proportionaliter manifestatas, sive in proportionibus manifestatas, sive ex praecedenti tractatione, in qua hoc demonstratum est quod ascensiones istae proportionaliter fiunt vel in hoc proportionaliter manifestatas, quia quanto magis crescit ascensio, tanto magis crescit cognitio. Propter has igitur ascensiones gradus virtutum dispositi sunt, per quas videlicet ascensiones unumquodque, id est, unusquisque animus ascendens 1104Cper eas fit in participatione, id est, fit particeps superincognitissimae purgationis, et plenissimi luminis, et anteperfectae perfectionis. Particeps, dico, fit sicut idipsum, id est ut particeps fiat, fas est et possibile: fas, quantum ad participandi boni dignitatem; possibile, quantum ad suam capacitatem.

Sequitur: « Etenim nihil per se perfectum indigens universalis perfectionis, nisi vere perfectissimum, et ante perfectum. » Bene, inquit, dixi divinam perfectionem anteperfectam; quia omnia, quae perfecta sunt, ex ipsa perfecta sunt; quia nihil est per se perfectum, et nihil quod non sit per se imperfectum, et quod non sit indigens per se invisibilis, vel omnis perfectionis, nisi illud bonum summum: 1104Dquod est et vere perfectissimum quia nihil ei deest; et anteperfectum, quia ejus plenitudo aeterna est.

EXPOSITION.

The title of the tenth chapter is: A recapitulation of the ordering of the angelic synagogue. For here is briefly repeated what was said above, namely, the ordered synagogue, that is, the congregation, or angelic multitude, in all its first, and second, and third members. And the chapter thus begins:

« Thus, therefore, is the most honorable disposition of the minds about God connected, ordered from the perfective illumination, immediately ascending into it, 1100Amore hidden and more manifest; and by the illumination of the divinity it is purged, and illuminated, and perfected. » He speaks of the first hierarchy, which consists of three orders — seraphim, cherubim, and thrones. This disposition, then, or ordination, of the minds, that is, of the spirits, the most honorable or most excellent of all, 1100Bis connected about God, that is, both joined among themselves in concord, and immediately associated to God; thus ordered from the perfective illumination, that is, the divine, which alone perfectly shines and illuminates. For whosoever are illuminated by it are indeed, in shining, made like to it, and in illuminating others, imitate it. Yet neither in that they shine are they made equal to it, nor in that they illuminate are they compared to it. Therefore this hierarchy, which alone is illuminated by it immediately, is singularly ordered from the perfective illumination. Others, indeed, who receive the lower illuminations mediately, are also fittingly disposed and ordered lower down. But this hierarchy, which is ordered from the perfective, or teletarchic, and divine illumination, which is the sovereign 1100Cof sanctification, that is, the first and greatest and singular cause of sanctification — or, to say it more expressly, is made pontiff, that is, is raised into the pontifical order, or dignity — is fittingly set above all in dignity, namely by immediately ascending into that illumination, being more hidden, and more manifest, and by that same illumination of the divinity being purged, and illuminated, and perfected. But how the first hierarchy, from the fact that it receives the divine illumination immediately, is both more hidden and more manifest, he sets forth in the following words, saying: « More hidden indeed as being more invisible, and more simplified and vivified. But more manifest as that which, given before, shines, and shines first, and is more universal, and has form 1100Dmore poured out into it, as is fitting. » It is more hidden, he says, in that it is more invisible, and more simplified, and unified. In this it is more hidden, that it is more invisible, and nearer to the simplicity and unity of the Godhead. But it is more manifest, inasmuch as it shines from the light given to it before, that is, before it was given to others: therefore it shines first, and more excellently. It is also more manifest because it is more universal, in which one likeness stands in many, since that is more known which is more common and suits more. And whence it is more universal and more alike, he consequently shows in turn, namely, because the form, that is, the divine illumination, from which it is formed so as to shine, is more, that is, more expressly, or more abundantly, poured out into it than into the other hierarchies below it. But the sense is this: because, namely, the divine illumination is poured first into this hierarchy, therefore 1101Ait is itself more perfectly illuminated. And by how much the more perfectly they who are in it, the spirits, receive the one illumination, by so much the more perfectly and clearly do they, shining in that one form of one light, become one; and what in them is diverse by nature and manifoldly distinguished, when the one form of clarity comes upon all, does not appear unlike. Thus, therefore, this hierarchy, because it shines first, shines more perfectly; and because it shines more perfectly, it shines more universally, or more alike, or more expressly; because it shines more expressly, it shines more manifestly. That, then, which is essentially more hidden, is formally more manifest; and that which is subtler by nature is clearer by grace.

There follows: « But from it again proportionally the second, and from the second the third, and from the third the hierarchy according to 1101Bus, according to that same law of the well-adorning ordination, in the divine harmony and analogy, unto the whole adornment of all good at once, is led back to the sovereign principle and consummation of the hierarchy. » From it, he says, the first hierarchy, is led back or converted the second, and by the second the third is converted, and by the third is converted that hierarchy, namely, which is according to us. For the first angelic hierarchy converts the second, the second the third, the third angelic converts the human. But how it converts he shows, saying: Unto the sovereign principle, and the consummation of the whole good adornment at once, that is, unto God, who is the principle and perfection of every good and beautiful disposition. And it leads back hierarchically, that is, according to the office, or 1101Cordination, or law of the hierarchies, in which it is ordained that the higher, according to their manner and virtue, by illuminating and suggesting to the lower, convert them to their principle. And they convert according to that same law of the well-adorning ordination, that is, of the divine ordination, which adorns all things: whose law and institution it is, that some be illuminated by others, and converted in divine harmony and analogy, that is, in the concord and proportion conferred by God upon the universe. For in this, that the participation of the good is transfused through some to others proportionally, the concord in the universe is perfected and consummated. But that he says, "is again led back," is to be so understood as by a second leading-back. For the first leading-back is when 1101Dthe first, illuminated by God himself, are converted unto God himself. The second, when the second are converted by the first, or the third by the second. « And all are manifesters, even the angels of those who are before them. » All the celestial spirits, he says, are manifesters, and angels, that is, messengers, of those who are before them. For what they receive from those preceding, they announce and manifest to those following after them.

There follows: « They themselves indeed the most honorable of God who moves them, but proportionally the rest of those moved by God. » He had said that all are messengers of those preceding to those following: now he subdistinguishes, that they themselves indeed, the most honorable, that is, the most excellent spirits, who have God alone before them, are messengers of God himself moving them by inspiration, that through them his secrets 1102Ahe may reveal to those following. The rest, who follow after them, are messengers of those same, who are moved by God. Messengers, I say, they are proportionally, that is: the second, of the first, and of God through the first; the third, of the second, and of the first through the second; but of God, through the second and the first; and in this manner the rest that follow after this. But how the several proportionally reveal the divine secrets, he sets forth in the following words, showing that to each is given only so much power as befits the order and place in which it is set. This is what he says: « For the superessential harmony of all foresaw for each of the rational and intellectual ones, with sacred adornment and ordered leading, as much as each order of the hierarchies itself is sacredly and becomingly placed. » 1102BThe superessential harmony, he says, that is, the divine providence, which disposed all things concordantly, foresaw only so much, namely of virtue or power, for each of the rational or intellectual ones, with sacred adornment and ordered leading, namely sacredly adorning and orderly leading; foresaw only so much, I say, as each order of the hierarchies is sacredly and becomingly placed — this, as much as befits the holiness and becomingness of the order of each. Concerning which order in each hierarchy he adds distinctions, saying: « And we see every hierarchy divided into first, and middle, and last virtues, or orders. » And not only each hierarchy, but also each order through the several hierarchies. This is what follows: « But it also distinguished the very 1102Cdisposition — speaking specially through each one — by those divine harmonies themselves. » The divine providence itself, he says, distinguished, or distinguished apart, the very disposition, namely each one, that is, the order, by the divine harmonies, so that, namely, there might be distinction, and there might be no discrepancy. And this is to be said specially through the several hierarchies: the several orders have special distinctions.

There follows: « For which reason the theologians themselves say that the most divine seraphim themselves cry one to another: openly, as I openly suppose, declaring that the first themselves hand on the theological utterances to the second. » For which reason — namely, because the several orders are distinct within themselves — therefore the theologians themselves say that the seraphim themselves, 1102Dwho are most divine, that is, nearest to the divinity, cry one to another, as is read in Isaiah (Isai. VI). In this, namely, that they say they cry one to another, openly declaring that the theological, that is, divine utterances, they who are first in that order hand on to those who are constituted second in the same order. In which it is clear that one and the same order has first and second. But if this is truly taken of the first and highest order, of those following it can by no means be doubted.

There follows: « But I would add perhaps, and this not incongruously, that each celestial and human mind, according to itself also, has special first, and middle, and last ordinations and virtues, assigned through each of the hierarchic 1103Ailluminations, manifested proportionally unto its proper anagogies: through which each is made, insofar as this itself is both lawful and possible, in participation of the most superunknown purgation, and of the fullest light, and of the fore-perfected perfection. » The sense is this: that not only is the universal hierarchy divided into a first, and a middle, and a last hierarchy, and the several hierarchies into first, and middle, and last orders, and the several orders into first, and middle, and last spirits; but even the several angelic, or human, spirits themselves are, within themselves, virtually distinct, containing first, and middle, and last virtues: through which, by their own anagogies, that is, upward-leadings, or ascensions, from the lowest to the middle, and from the middle to the highest, ascending proportionally according to the hierarchic 1103Billuminations, they are made partakers, as far as is possible for them, of the divine purgation, which is most unknown, or most hidden, because it purges inwardly; and of the divine light, which is fullest, because it puts all darkness to flight; and of the divine perfection, which is fore-perfected, because it is prior to all in eternity, and higher in dignity, and fuller in truth. But he calls the hierarchic illuminations proportional for this reason, because in the sacred powers, where some are constituted higher, others lower, they do not all perceive the divine illuminations in one manner. For to the higher and more capacious, more is bestowed in the gifts of grace; to the lower, according to the measure of their capacity, less is granted to be participated. According to this manner, then, by which, whether in the several 1103Chierarchies to the diverse orders, and to the diverse minds, the divine illuminations are differently bestowed, each mind also within itself, in those same illuminations, growing by a reasonable difference from lesser to greater, is advanced. This is what he says: « But I would add this also, not incongruously, » as if he should say: Not only concerning the several hierarchies or orders can I fittingly say that they have first, and middle, and last orders, or spirits; but this also perhaps I can, not incongruously, add to what has been said above, namely, that each celestial and human mind, according to itself, or in itself, has special, that is, proper, first, and middle, and last ordinations and virtues, that is, virtues ordained in the first, and middle, and last place within it. To 1103Dwhat end it has differing virtues, he adds, 1104Anamely, unto its proper anagogies — that each, namely, may have its own proper ascensions, and advancements unto the better, as it is written: « He hath disposed ascensions in his heart (Psal. LXXXIII); » and again: « They go from virtue to virtue: and the God of gods shall be seen in Sion. » And unto these anagogies, that is, ascensions, are disposed the virtues, some lower, some higher, so that, by ascending from the lower to the higher, they may at length be made partakers of the highest good, which is the God of gods in Sion. Each spirit, he says, has its own proper virtues, first, and middle, and last, unto its proper anagogies, that is, ascensions, to be made. Anagogies, I say, already spoken of, that is, which we have already spoken of above, namely, through each order of the hierarchic illuminations: 1104Bbecause, when we showed how, in the distribution of the hierarchies, the distinct orders perceive differing illuminations, we also demonstrated in what manner among them the lower ascend proportionally, that is, by a reasonable difference of advancement, through the higher unto the highest. Therefore he said the anagogies of the hierarchic illuminations manifested proportionally, or manifested in proportions, or from the preceding treatment, in which this was demonstrated, that those ascensions are made proportionally; or manifested proportionally in this, because by how much the more the ascension grows, by so much the more the knowledge grows. On account of these ascensions, therefore, the grades of virtues are disposed, by which ascensions, namely, each thing, that is, each mind ascending 1104Cthrough them, is made in participation, that is, is made partaker of the most superunknown purgation, and of the fullest light, and of the fore-perfected perfection. Partaker, I say, it is made "as this itself," that is, that it may be made partaker, is both lawful and possible: lawful, as to the dignity of the good to be participated; possible, as to its own capacity.

There follows: « For nothing is perfect through itself, needing the universal perfection, save the truly most perfect, and fore-perfect. » Rightly, he says, did I call the divine perfection fore-perfected; because all things that are perfect are perfect from it; because nothing is perfect through itself, and there is nothing which is not through itself imperfect, and which is not through itself needy of the invisible, or of every perfection, save that highest good: 1104Dwhich is both truly most perfect, because nothing is lacking to it; and fore-perfect, because its fullness is eternal.

TITULUS CAPITULI XI. Quare omnes coelestes essentiae communiter virtutes coelestes nominantur.

TITLE OF CHAPTER XI. Why all the celestial essences are commonly named celestial virtues.

LITTERA.

  • 1103D

His autem definitis, illud dignum intelligere oportet, ob quam causam omnes similiter angelicas essentias, virtutes coelestes vocare consuevimus. Non enim est dicendum ut in angelis, quod omnium novissima est dispositio ipsa sanctarum virtutum. Et quidem novissimarum sanctam, et decoram illuminationem superpositarum essentiarum dispositiones participant; 1104Dultimae vero primarum nullo modo. Et cujus gratia coelestes quidem virtutes omnes divini intellectus nominantur; seraphim autem, et throni, et dominationes nullo modo. Participatae enim extremae ab excellentissimis sunt universalibus proprietatibus. Ipsi namque angeli, et ante angelos archangeli, et principatus, et potestates post virtutes ab ipsa theologia ordinati communiter saepe a nobis similiter cum aliis 1105Asanctis essentiis coelestes virtutes vocantur. Dicimus autem quod communiter in omnibus utentes coelestium nominatione virtutum, non confusionem quamdam uniuscujusque dispositionis proprietatum introducimus; sed, quia in tria dividuntur secundum se supermundana ratione omnes divini intellectus, in essentiam, et virtutem, et operationem, cum simul omnes, aut eorum quosdam inobservate coelestes essentias, aut coelestes vocamus virtutes, periphrasticos, de quibus sermo est, significare nos existimandum, ex ea, quae per singulos eorum est, essentia vel virtute. Neque enim superpositam proprietatem facile est jam a nobis discretarum sanctarum virtutum minoribus omnino annectere essentiis in conversione inconfusae angelicorum ornatuum ordinationis. Juxta enim saepe a 1105Bnobis recte redditam rationem ipsae quidem superfirmatae dispositiones abundanter habent minorum etiam sacras proprietates; ultimae vero majorum superpositas universitates non habent, particulariter in eas primo apparentibus illuminationibus per primas proportionaliter eis distributis.

THE TEXT.

  • 1103D

But these things being defined, it behooves to understand that which is worthy: for what cause we are wont to call all the angelic essences alike celestial virtues. For it is not to be said, as in the angels, that the very disposition of the holy virtues is the last of all. And indeed the dispositions of the superposed essences partake the holy and comely illumination of the last; 1104Dbut the last in no wise the illumination of the first. And for whose sake are all the divine intellects indeed named celestial virtues; but the seraphim, and thrones, and dominations in no wise. For the extremes are partaken of by the most excellent, in the universal properties. For the angels themselves, and before the angels the archangels, and the principalities, and the powers, ordered after the virtues by theology itself, are often commonly called by us, together with the other 1105Aholy essences, celestial virtues. But we say that, using commonly in all the naming of celestial virtues, we do not introduce a certain confusion of the properties of each disposition; but, because they are divided into three according to themselves by a supermundane reason — all the divine intellects — into essence, and virtue, and operation, when we call all of them at once, or certain of them unobservantly, either celestial essences, or celestial virtues, it is to be supposed that we signify periphrastically those of whom the discourse is, from that essence or virtue which is through each of them. For neither is it easy for us now to annex the superposed property of the holy virtues, already distinguished by us, altogether to the lesser essences, in a turning-about of the unconfused ordination of the angelic adornments. For according to the reason often rightly 1105Brendered by us, the superfirmed dispositions indeed have abundantly the sacred properties even of the lesser; but the last do not have the superposed universalities of the greater, the illuminations first appearing particularly into them, distributed to them proportionally through the first.

EXPOSITIO.

Undecimi capitis titulus est: Quare omnes coelestes essentiae communiter virtutes vocantur. Haec est quaestio: Cum unus tantum ordo in coelestibus spiritibus virtutes vocetur, quare hoc vocabulum omnibus communiter tribuatur. Dicit autem:
