Et hoc est quod sequitur: « Mirantur eos principium esse omnis sacrae et divinae scientiae et divinae imitationis: » quae scilicet ad subjecta per ipsos manant tanquam divina illuminatione distributa per illos in omnes alias coelestes virtutes, et non solum in eas, sed etiam in nos; videlicet homines, qui divinas illuminationes illis mediantibus accipimus. Et quia omnes reliquae essentiae 1122Ccoelestes primis mediantibus illuminantur, idcirco quidquid sacrum operari possunt, et Deo simile, hoc quidem primum Deo attribuunt, qui causa est omnium; deinde ipsis primis spiritibus, quibus operantibus et mediantibus gratiam divinam percipiunt. Hoc est, quod dicit: « Propter quod, » scilicet, quia per illos a Deo illuminatos reliqui illuminantur, ideo ipsi reliqui « omnem sacram et Deo similem operationem suam in Deum quidem quasi causalem referunt » quia ipse est prima causa omnium; « deinde referunt in primos intellectus. » id est, supremos spiritus, qui deiformes sunt, vel Deo, conformes, in hoc quod dona spiritalia tribuunt: non tamen ut Deus, qui prima causa est a quo sunt, sed 1122Dtanquam primi effectus, per quos sunt. Ideo ad eos referunt bonum suum, per quos est « tanquam per primos operatores, et magistros divinorum, » scilicet donorum. Operatores quidem in eo quod movent efficiendo, magistri vero in eo quod praesident dirigendo.

Sequitur: « Num ergo prima, » etc. Num pro nonne. « Nonne ergo, inquit, prima dispositio sanctorum angelorum, » quae tantopere caeteris omnibus sublimior est, « magis omnibus habet, » summam et « igneam proprietatem, » hoc est, charitatem, sicut in seraphim; « et effusam, » id est, abundantem « traditionem divinae sapientiae, et mysticum excelsissimae divinarum illuminationum scientiae, » id est mysticam, vel occultam sive profundam excelsissimam 1123Ascientiam, quam ex divinis illuminationibus percipit, sicut in cherubim, et sessivam proprietatem, sicut in thronis, gestantem, Deum scilicet, et « significantem divinam susceptionem: » quia in eo, quod throni dicti sunt, aperte significatur quod Deum in se sedentem et quiescentem suscipiunt. Sensus est: Nonne prima hierarchia excellentius et abundantius caeteris omnibus habet et ignem charitatis, et lumen cognitionis, et judicium discretionis? Habet utique haec omnia amplius caeteris omnibus. « Ipsae vero » dispositiones « suppositarum essentiarum, » id est, subjectorum ordinum, participant quidem et ipsae « igneam virtutem, » id est charitatem, sicut seraphim, sapientem, atque scientem « virtutem, » id est, cognitionem, sicut 1123Bcherubim, et virtutem susceptoriam Dei, sicut throni: « participant, » dico; sed « infra, » id est, imperfectius quam primae: « et aspicientes ad primas, » id est, imitantes primas, « et per eas, » scilicet primas, reductae in id deiformitatis quod possibile ipsis est, hoc est, reductae ad tantam deiformitatem quantam eis possibile est; per eas scilicet primas, dico, « digne factas » hoc est, dignas factas, « divina imitatione, » id est, ut Deum imitentur « praeoperatrices, » id est, prius et excellentius omnibus aliis ab ipso et secundum ipsum operantes.

Sequitur: « Dictas ergo sanctas proprietates, » etc. Quandoquidem, inquit, per primas subsequentes dona gratiarum accipiunt, ergo sanctas proprietates jam superius dictas, quale fuit prophetae labia carbone 1123Cincendere, quod proprium videtur esse seraphim, et scientiam docere, quod proprium videtur cherubim. Ejusmodi ergo proprietates, « quarum participatio fit per primas essentias, » aliae essentiae « subsistentes post eas, » has, inquam, proprietates, « reponunt in ipsis, » id est, attribuunt ipsis illis primis, scilicet per quas eas participant: « tanquam in hierarchis, » id est in principibus, et superioribus, ut eas ad illos referant, a quibus acceperunt. « Reponunt » dico « in illis post Deum: » quia primo eas Deo attribuunt, deinde illis qui proximi sunt post Deum. Quod autem ait, quod subsequentes essentiae participatio fiunt proprietatum primarum, modus loquendi talis est ac si diceret: Participes 1123Dfiunt proprietatum primarum, quia quod primi possident per proprietatem, secundi communicant per participationem.

Sequitur: « Ait ergo haec, dicens, » etc. Ille, inquit, de quo superius dixi, qui mihi non inconvenientem praestitit apologiam. Ille dicens haec, quae hactenus dicta sunt de divina illuminatione per alios ad alios descendente, ait visionem supradictam, de qua quaestio orta est de purificatione labiorum prophetae « susceptam fuisse ab ipso theologo, » Isaia scilicet, « per unum sanctorum, et beatorum, » angelorum « imperantium nobis, » hominibus, « descendentem ab illa, » subauditur, prima hierarchia. Hoc enim ait ille, quod visio illa, quam vidit Isaias prima hierarchia descendit, et allata est ipsi prophetae 1124Aper unum angelum de novissimo ordine eorum, qui in angelis extremi sunt et nobis tantum praesunt: et ideo ait illum angelum « ante illuminativam ipsius manuductionem, » id est revelationem illam, qua ipse manuduxit, et erudivit prophetam, et qua ipse ante illuminatus erat a prima hierarchia: « reposuisse in, » id est, retulisse ad « illam sanctam contemplationem, » hoc est, in ipsam primam hierarchiam, a qua contemplabatur se habuisse quod habuit, et fecisse quod fecit. « Videt etiam » ipse Isaias « supersedere, » id est in alto et sublimi sedere, « excelsissimas essentias, collocatas post Deum, et circa Deum, et cum Deo, quantum in symbolis, » id est, figuris et similitudinibus est « dicendum. » Hoc enim totum symbolicum est et figurativum, 1124Bquod Deus secundum corporalem similitudinem in solio excelso sedere dicitur; et seraphim circa eum et juxta stare perhibentur. Et videt etiam ipse Isaias summitatem sublimiorem « omnibus ipsis, » scilicet excelsissimis spirituum beatorum essentiis; « etiam superarcane, » id est, excellentissimo modo: « summitatem, » dico, « super principalem, » id est Deum, qui summus et principalis omnium est, supercollocatam « in medio superfirmatarum virtutum. » In medio enim virtutum, id est sanctorum spirituum, qui firmati sunt et stabiliti aeterna collocatione circa Deum super omnia, ipse Deus summus, et principalis sedens videtur in solio excelso et elevato. « In his ergo visionibus didicit ipse theologus, » Isaias hoc scilicet, « quod divinum, » id est divinitas, 1124C« supercollocata est incomparabiliter supra omnem superessentialem superexcellentiam omni invisibili, et visibili virtuti, » hoc est, quod divinitas incomparabiliter, transcendit secundum omnem excellendi modum, omnem virtutem, visibilem et invisibilem. Et non mirum, si transcendit omnia ipsum divinum: « atqui, » id est certe, « quia ab omnibus est remotum, » per excellentiam scilicet, utpote illud, quod universale est ab iis, quae ex parte sunt omnia, et intantum remotum et excellens, ut « nec primis essentiis eorum, » quae sunt, « simile sit, » sed longe distans et transcendens. Quod autem ait « primis essentiis eorum, quae sunt, » tale est ac si diceret, essentiis eorum qui sunt primi, vel essentiis quae 1124Dsunt primae, id est, supremis spiritibus angelorum. Nec solum didicit divinum ab omnibus remotum, et nulli simile esse. « Sed adhuc, » sive insuper etiam hoc didicit ipsum « esse omnium principium, » quia ab eo sunt omnia; et causam sanctificam, quia per eum subsistunt universa; et immutabile fundamentum eorum, quae sunt, secreta singularitate, quia in eo subsistentia perseverant universa: qui secreta et occulta divinitate sua omnia continens unitas universitatem colligit, et singularitas multiplicitatem constringit. Ex quo et esse, et bene esse est etiam ipsis summe munitis virtutibus, id est illis spiritibus, qui in summa virtute et felicitate firmati sunt et stabiliti: qui ab illo habent non solum ut sint, sed etiam ut beati sint. Hoc ergo totum didicit in 1125Avisione illa de divinitatis excellentia. « Deinde, » etiam didicit, et « edoctus est, easdem sanctissimorum seraphim, » vel, ut expressius dicatur, eorumdem sanctissimorum seraphim, « deiformes virtutes, » vel easdem virtutes, quas in Deo esse didicerat, didicit etiam esse in seraphim ex conformitate Dei; quia, quod Deus habet per naturam, ipsi habent per gratiam, conformati Deo. Quas autem, et quales virtutes, sive etiam ex quo didicerit virtutes esse in seraphim subjungit, dicens: « Ex sacra quidem cognominatione ipsorum, quod, » id est, quae cognominatio, « est ignitum. » Quia seraphim ardens, vel succedens interpretatur, et significat ignitum: « de quo » ignito, inquit, nos « paulo post dicemus, quantum possibile nobis erit, subintroducere anagogas, » 1125Bid est, sursum ductiones « virtutis ignitae, » scilicet charitatis ipsorum seraphim, « in deiforme: » hoc est, in rem tam dignam et Deo consimilem. Vel sic: Ex hac, inquam sacra cognominatione, didicit ipse propheta: anagogas, id est, sursum ductiones, sive ascensus, vel provectus ignitae virtutis, id est, charitatis ipsorum seraphim. « In expansa autem sacra formatione alarum, » id est in sacra formatione expansarum alarum, didicit ipse propheta « absolutam, et altissimam in divinum extensionem, » quae est « in primis, et in mediis, et in ultimis intellectibus. » Per cognominationem igitur, quae ignitum sonat, didicit igneam virtutem; id est, charitatem desiderio ad alta ascendentem; per expansionem vero alarum, didicit cognitionem subtilitate 1125Cin longinqua se porrigentem, et usque in divina capienda se extendentem, in primis, et mediis, et ultimis intellectibus, id est, spiritibus in illo ordine primis, et mediis, et ultimis: vel primis intellectibus quibus divina capiunt supra se, mediis quibus divina capiunt in se, ultimis quibus divina capiunt sub se. Extensio vero ipsa, sive porrectio cognitionis et absoluta est, quia nulla ignorantiae caligine ad immensitatem se diffundens circumvolvitur; et altissima, quia ad summa pergens nulla infirmitate praegravatur. Et non solum ex iis, quae dicta sunt, virtutem dilectionis et cognitionis ipsorum cognovit, « sed etiam multificum, et multiforme eorum videns ipse intellectualis theologus » 1125DIsaias, « et videns etiam eam visionem distingui alis subtus pedes, et distingui eam alis subtus facies: et videns etiam eum semper motum, » id est, qui semper est, in mediis alis: per haec omnia « reductus est, » et eruditus « ad invisibilem scientiam eorum, quae visa sunt. » Per hoc enim, quod distinctionem vidit alarum, quae subtus pedes deorsum; et alarum, quae subtus facies sedentis sursum porrigebantur; et alarum, quae in medio semper movebantur: per hoc scilicet vidit ipse multiplicem virtutem illorum, quae et multificata est in opere, signata per motionem, et multiformis in cognitione et dilectione, significata per porrectionem. Et in his omnibus reductus est ille et admonitus, ut invisibiliter cognosceret, quod secundum speciem visibilium 1126Avidit: « manifestata ei per haec omnia multivia, et multivida virtute istorum altissimorum intellectuum. » Quae scilicet, virtus et multivia est, inquantum multipliciter movetur appetendo; et multivida, inquantum multipliciter beatificatur possidendo. Multivia in eo, qua pergit scrutando; multivida in eo, quod invenit penetrando. Multae sunt viae, quibus itur ad bonum unum: ideo recte multivia. Sed quare multivida, cum unum sit, quod videtur, nisi quia in uno cuncta videntur? Sic ergo reductus est propheta ad scientiam veritatis, monstrata, ei per sacras imagines multivia, et multivida virtute altissimorum intellectuum. Monstrata etiam « ei sacra formidine eorum, » sive reverentia, « quam habent supermundane, » id est, impassibiliter et 1126Bpure, « in superbam et audacem et inpossibilem scrutationem altiorum et inferiorum, » id est, ne superbe, et audacter, et impossibiliter scrutentur, ultra mensuram possibilitatis suae secreta Dei, quae altiora ipsis sunt per majestatem, et inferiora per profunditatem. Ideo quippe velant caput, ut altiora tecta sibi profiteantur: ideo velant pedes, ut inferiora et profundiora impenetrabilia esse testentur. Propter ea superbi, et audaces esse formidant ad id, quod impossibile est scrutandum. Superbi ad alta, audaces ad profunda; superbi ne nimis eleventur, audaces, ne praecipitentur. In hoc ergo sacram formidinem habent, quia sacrum est timere, quod praesumptum noceret, et supermundane habent, quia sine passione et afflictione formidant. Timent enim, 1126Cet non afficiuntur; contremiscunt, et non concutiuntur. Pavent securi, et sine ulla molestia, vel corruptione suae quietis verentur ad incomprehensibilem majestatem mensuram transire suae possibilitatis. Ad horum omnium scientiam reductus est propheta, supradicta videns, in extensione alarum. Et videns etiam incessabile, et altivolum semper, scilicet perseverantis motionis in commotione alarum: quae commotio in commensuratione constat actionum Deum imitantium, id est in actionibus ipsorum, quibus imitantur Deum, commensurantes se possibilitati suae, ut nihil praeter rationem et mensuram agere praesumant.

Sequitur: « Sed et illam divinam, et multum 1126Dpretiosam hymnodiam eruditus est. » Ac si diceret: Non solum in habitu seraphim virtutem eorum cognovit; sed etiam in voce eorum hymnodiam, id est laudem divinam, didicit « formante angelo visionem ipsi theologo secundum virtutem » capacitatis ipsius, « et tradente propriam sacram scientiam: » quia quod ipse angelus scivit, per hanc sacram visionem theologum scire fecit. « Docuit ergo » ipse angelus « eum, » scilicet theologum, in hoc quod labia ejus, qui jam justus videbatur, purgavit carbone sumpto de altari, « quia ipsa participatio incognitae divinae claritatis accepta, quantum possibile est, purgatio est quantumcunque perfectis. » Quia quantumcunque quis purgatus sit, purgatior fit illa percepta.

1127ASequitur: « Haec autem, » etc. Dixit, quod perceptio claritatis divinae purgatio est: nunc consequenter ostendit quod haec claritas, ex occulto summae divinitatis procedens, ad perficiendos et illuminandos omnes sacros intellectus, primum se manifestat altissimis virtutibus apertius circa se positis: et ostendit quomodo est in proprio, et vero esse suo; deinde post primas ostendit se secundis; et postea novissimis; ad postremum etiam, nostris humanis intellectibus, et ita descendens conducit illuminationem suam ad unamquamque virtutem, secundum quod unaquaeque deiformis facta est ab ea, hoc est, quod ait: « Haec, » scilicet « claritas procedens ex remotis causis divinitatis, a qua divinitate exiens, perficit omnes sacros intellectus, » id 1127Best rationales mentes, illustrando eos « superessentiali occultatione, » id est valde occulta et secreta aspiratione: ex illis, inquam, remotis causis procedens ad manifestationem, primum manifestior fit quomodo est, id est secundum verum esse suum, altissimis virtutibus circa se positis: et manifestat, « et distribuit semetipsam illis magis, » quam aliis; « et deinde » post illas « manifestat secundis » se, « deinde novissimis, » postremo etiam « nostris intellectualibus virtutibus, » id est rationalibus mentibus; « et sic » a primis usque ad ultima descendens, « conducit illuminationem suam per singulas virtutes: sic » hoc est, intantum manifestam in singulis, quantum unaquaeque virtus existit ab ipsa scilicet claritate secundum deiforme, hoc est secundum 1127Cconformitatem Dei. Tanto magis enim unamquamque virtutem illuminat, quanto magis eam ad deiformitatem coaptat. Quare autem claritas ista procedat ad manifestationem subjungit: « Ad propriae occultationis laudandum ignotum. » Idcirco enim aliquid de ipsa percipimus, ut in illo, et per illud quod occultum, et ignotum, et incomprehensibile omnino in ipsa est, laudemus.

Sequitur: « Lucet autem per singula secundis per prima. » Ubique enim secundis lucet per prima, sive per primos, « Et si oportet breviter dicere, » hoc in summa dici potest, quod « primum ex occulto ad manifestum ducitur per primas virtutes. » Quod enim in seipsa est omnino occulta est; et tunc 1127Dprimum incipit videri quando primum incipit haberi. Neque enim ab aliquo unquam videtur, nisi a quo habetur. « Hoc ergo theologus didicit ex lucem ducente angelo. » Ex ductore claritatis angelo didicit hoc. Nova compositio, lucem ducente, ac si diceret luciductore. Ab illo igitur didicit hoc theologus. Quid hoc? hoc est scilicet quod didicit: « Purgationem, et omnes divinas operationes relucentes per primas essentias per eas in omnes reliquas distribui, secundum uniuscujusque reliquorum analogiam, » id est modum et mensuram, « ad deificas participationes. Propter quod et ignite purgativam proprietatem reposuit » ille angelus, id est attribuit, « ipsis seraphim consequenter post Deum: » et ideo « nihil inordinatum » dicitur « si seraphim dicitur purgare 1128Atheologum. Sic enim et Deus purgat omnes, quorum totius purgationis, » vel quorum omnium purgationis « est causa; » et non solum Deus, sed magis in hoc exemplo videri potest quomodo facere aliquid dicitur, non per quem fit solum, sed etiam a quo fit. Quia « magis proxime utemur exemplo. » Sic seraphim dicitur purgare illum, quem purgat inferior angelus, accepta virtute et mandato a seraphim: « Sicut secundum nos summus sacerdos per suos ministros, aut sacerdotes purgans, aut illuminans, ipse dicitur purgare, et illuminare ordinibus per ipsum purgatis, proprias suas sacras operationes reponentibus in ipsum, » id est attribuentibus ei per se. Quod enim per illas operatur, per illas ei attribuitur. « Sic et propriam purgativam scientiam, 1128Bet virtutem, ipse purgationem theologi perficiens, angelus, in Deum quidem veluti causalem, deinde in ipsum seraphim tanquam primo agentem summum sacerdotem reponit. » Ita ergo angelus quod fecit, primum Deo, deinde seraphim attribuit, per quos fecit. « Veluti fortassis quis dixerit, » id est ut verbi gratia: « Si quis cum angelica reverentia, » id est sub persona angeli, quae est reverenda: « edocens, » prophetam « purgatum » esse a se, « diceret » ei: O Isaia, « purgationis perficiendae in te, » scilicet per me, « non ego sum principium, sed ante me principium est excelsum quidem, » id est Deus, qui est et « essentia, et Creator, et causalis » omnium et adducens adesse primas essentias; « et continens eas circa se collocatione, » id 1128Cest stabili firmitate; « et conservans eas inconversibiles, et casu carentes, » id est ne simul a se vertantur, et cadant; « et seipsum movens in primas participationis propriarum providarum operationum, » id est operationum, quas secundum providentiam facit; quia omne quod temporaliter facit, in aeterna providentia disposuit. Propria operatio Dei est, quando per semetipsum operatur sine mediante creatura, ex qua nimirum prima participatio venit; quia illi eum sine medio suscipiunt, qui ejus operationis primi effectus fiunt. Prima siquidem Dei operatio est, quando se movet a se; prima participatio, quando sese praebet per se. Et illa quidem altissima creatura est, ad quam est prima operatio, 1128Det in qua est prima participatio per illam, deinde ad subsequentia descendens. Ad hunc modum subjectus angelus hoc quod fecit, superiori seraphim attribuit, a quo, ut hoc facere posset, accepit. « Hoc enim, » quod ab alio illud facere acceperit, ait « docens me haec manifestare, » vel significare « missionem ipsius seraphim. » Ille inquit, qui supradicta haec omnia apologiam praestans me docuit, ipse ait missionem seraphim significare hoc, quod scilicet illud, quod fecit ab illo utique facere acceperat, a quo venit. Idcirco convenienter ipse angelus prophetae dicere potest. « Ego purgationis, quam in te facio, principium non sum. Sed excelsum, et primum principium ante me est » Deus, qui est Creator et causa omnium. Deinde autem ipse « ornatus 1129Apraestantium essentiarum, » id est ordo summorum spirituum, qui est « post Deum sacerdos, et dux » divina tribuens, et ad Deum reducens: « a quo » ordine et « ego eruditus sum deiformiter purgare, » quemadmodum nunc in te facio. « Ipse » scilicet ordo « est purgans te per me, » propter hoc quia me purgare docuit: « per quem, » scilicet ordinem, ipsa causa et opifex totius purgationis (subauditur divinitas) « providas suas actiones producit ex occulto etiam in nos » extremos, scilicet angelos. Haec et his similia verba si angelus purgationem faciens ad prophetam diceret, inconveniens non esset: unde patet quod cum seraphim ad prophetam volare dicitur, et prophetam purgare dicitur, non inconvenienter intelligi potest quod haec operatio 1129Bper subjectum quidem angelum administrata est, sed superiori, a quo erat, attributa.

Sequitur: « Haec ille quidem docuit me: » verba sunt auctoris ad propositum redeuntis. Ille, inquit, qui apologiam mihi praestitit, docuit me haec supradicta omnia. « Ego autem, » o Timothee! « tibi trado » omnia a me sive dicta, sive approbata, sed ad utramque partem habentia. « Tuae autem intellectuali et discretivae scientiae, » id est discretioni: « concesserim alteram partem dictarum causarum absolvi » scilicet per te « dubitatione, » id est pro rata et indubitata haberi: « et eamdem honorari ante alteram tanquam habentem consequens, et rationabile, et aeque verum. » Hoc et tuae voluntati concedo, et discretioni, et scientiae, ut alteram partem sententiarum istarum, remota dubitatione, eligas, 1130Aet honores plusquam alteram tanquam veram et rationabilem. « Aut » si hoc non placet, concedo tibi « a teipso invenire, quod vere vero vicinius sit. Aut, » si adhuc illud non placet, concedo tibi « ab altero discere, Deo videlicet dante, » sive hoc, sive ullo alio modo agnoscas: « prius » tamen ipsam scientiam veritatis « recipientibus angelis » a Deo, et postea per angelos angelorum amicis sanctis viris nobis revelare, id est ad hoc recipientibus, ut nobis eam revelent. Aut sic. Et concedo tibi revelare nobis « per ejus magis amabilem contemplationem, » angelis, et angelorum amicis recipientibus prius scilicet ipsam scientiam veritatis. Verbum mirabile. Angeli a Deo accipiunt, et homines ab angelis; et ipsi rursum homines ab 1130Bangelis docti alios homines docent; et venit doctrina veritatis per alios in alios, et videntur multi esse magistri et doctores veritatis; et nemo tamen docetur, quia ab ejus contemplatione non illuminatur. Alii magistri adhibent ministerium; unus magister est, qui solus praestat sensum. Ille sine aliis docere potest; alii sine ipso non possunt. Tu mihi das verbum. Quid autem est verbum sine intelligentia? Per verbum quidem intelligentia venit. Sed ille intelligentiam in corde ponit, qui intus illuminat, non qui foris sonat. Unctio ejus docet nos de omnibus. Tu foris loqueris; sed intus non ungis. Propterea amabilis mihi quidem est tua eruditio. Sed magis amabilis est ejus contemplatio; quia et hoc, quod in tua eruditione amabile est, nonnisi ex ejus contemplatione est.

EXPOSITION.

« Come, let us consider this also according to virtue. » Come now, he says, O Timothy, after the other things which have been said, 1114Dlet us consider this also according to our virtue and possibility, « for what reason, namely, it is said by the theologians that one of the seraphim was sent » — in Isaiah, namely, when, the coal having been taken up from the altar with the tongs, he purged the lips of the prophet (Isa. VII). And it is necessary that we inspect this question, and discuss it, because it can become doubtful whether by 'seraph' here some one of the higher order is to be understood, on account of the property of the name; or one of the lower, on account of the property of administration, because it is proper to the weak and the lowest to administer our hierarchy. Therefore the question is to be inspected, that the ambiguity of the estimation may be taken away. For perhaps « someone may answer that it is not one of the subordinate ones, » that is, some one of the Angels, « that purges the priest, » 1115Anamely Isaiah; « but a certain one of the innermost and greatest essences, » that is, the supreme spirits. But this again can be doubtful to someone, for the reason that the supreme orders are not sent to dispense, or administer, exterior things.

Therefore « certain ones say that, according to the definition of the society of all the intellects already rendered before » by us, that is, according to that which we defined above — they say that all spirits have among themselves a certain society of properties and names — that the oracle « does not name, » that is, « does not » say « that some one of the first minds came unto the purgation of the theologian, » that is, of the first spirits about God, understand: established. But they say « that a certain one rather of those excelling us, » who 1115Bare set only over us men, « performing the sacrifice of the prophet's purgation, » that is, making it holy, and offering as it were a sacrifice pleasing to God, « was called seraph, by equivocation, » that is, of the name, not by the excellence of the property. But by what likeness an angel of the lowest order was called seraph, he subjoins: « On account of the fiery and celestial washing away, » or cleansing, « of the » sins « aforesaid » already above, of the prophet himself, and on account of the « raising up » also, or vivification, of that same one « purged into the divine obedience; » because just as it belongs to fire to purge rust by burning, and to vivify dead and extinguished things by heating, so by that divine fire he was both purged from sins, and inflamed 1115Cto the love of God. And because this was done by the ministry of an angel, certain ones « say » that the sacred « oracle » « said 'one of the seraphim' simply, not one » of the virtues « set about God, » but rather one « of the purgative virtues excelling us, » that is, one of the angels set over us, that is, over men — yet him called 'seraph' on account of the likeness of the action.

There follows: « But another furnished me a certain not too unfitting apology concerning this kind of state. » Certain ones, he says, hold that the angel who purged the prophet was of the supreme spirits, on account of this, that he was called seraph. But others say that he was of the lower ones, and called seraph only on account of the likeness of the action: 1115Dthus each one defining probably according to his own opinion. But a certain « other, » agreeing wholly neither with those nor with these, « furnished me a certain apology, » that is, an excuse, or satisfaction, or defense, « not too unfitting, » concerning this kind of state, that is, definition, by which the state of the matter is described; or concerning this kind of instance, that is, question, which in some manner presses, and is importunate until it is resolved. But what satisfaction or defense he himself furnished concerning this question, he subjoins: « For he says (understand: he who furnishes the apology) that that great angel, who then was forming the vision for teaching the theologian divine things, » that is, in the mind of the theologian, whom that angel was bound to teach divine things through that vision 1116A— namely, his own purgative sacrifice, that is, the operation by which he then properly and singularly purged the lips of the prophet, and made them holy, that operation of his he referred back « unto God, » that is, attributed to God, « and after God referred it back unto the pre-operative hierarchy, » that is, unto the hierarchy in which and through which God first, that is, before all the others, operates. But he attributed his action to that hierarchy for this reason, that from it, after God, he principally received that he should do this. And this is the reason why the seraph is said to be the highest, namely because the angel who did this, just as he principally received it, after God, from the seraph, so also, after God, attributed it to the seraph itself. This reason therefore he rendered concerning this kind of question. « And is not this reason then 1116Btruthful? » These are the words of the author, who seems to accommodate his own estimation to this opinion.

This reason seems to be truthful because that man, « who said this, » says, showing « how the divine virtue, coming into all things, fills all » — and not only comes, but also penetrates, and passes through all, immeasurably crossing over them, « and is invisible to all. » And again this is invisible, thus transcending all without end, as it is invisible to all, subsisting before all without beginning. Or « again it is invisible » through immensity, as it is invisible through eternity, because just as temporal intelligence does not grasp eternity, so a circumscribable nature does not comprehend immensity. Or again « it is invisible, » that is, not only in itself, according as 1116Cit is essentially and ineffably remote from all, but also to us, according as it is incomprehensibly hidden from all. In itself therefore it is invisible, and in us it is invisible, and in both ways it remains incomprehensible. This is what he says: « Because it is not only invisible in itself, as being superessentially remote from all, but » it is also invisible in us, « as secretly letting, » or causing to penetrate, « into all things its provident operations. » Thus therefore the divine virtue is both invisible in itself as remote, and invisible in us as hidden, through operation, because according to its providence it operates in us. « But nevertheless, » although it is thus invisible, it shines above, pouring itself out 1116Dunto manifestation « to all the intellectual beings, » that is, to the rational minds. « It shines above, » I say, « proportionally, » that is, to some more, to others less, namely according to the measure and capacity of each one. And though it shines above commonly to all, yet excellently « bringing its own illumination into the most precious essences, » that is, into the subtlest and most excellent spirits: « through those » essences, namely, « as the first ones » it afterward distributes itself in well-adorned fashion « into others, » namely essences, « established » « under those » first ones, that is, made firm, or collocated, or disposed. « It distributes, » I say, « according to the contemplative commensuration of each disposition, » that is, according as each disposition, or order, is capable of that contemplation according to its proper 1117Ameasure: « which, » understand: distribution of the divine illumination, arriving thus differently according to the measure of the receivers, « that I may say it more openly, also through examples proper; » proper, I say, « though » that is, although, yet « deficient in relation to God, remote from all; » that is, deficient in comparison with God, who is remote from all things, and can properly be demonstrated by no likeness. Therefore deficient, and not proper. « Nevertheless » proper, because « more manifest to us. » Not proper to the divine majesty, proper to human possibility; not proper as it is in him, proper as it can be shown to us. That therefore I may show, through examples not proper to God but proper to us, the distribution of the divine illumination to be dispensed, 1117BI set forth this likeness. « The distributions of the solar ray, well distributed into the first matter, fill it, the most lucid of all, and through it it more manifestly declares its own splendors. » The distributions, he says, or outpourings of the solar ray, well distributed into the first matter, that is, coming into that matter which is first, that is, best and purest, and most apt for illumination; coming, I say, to such a matter, they fill it, finding in no part any obstacle to the light, and by filling they make it more lucid, most lucid of all; and thus through it the ray itself more manifestly declares its own splendors, because the more perfectly it radiates, the more perfectly it will be illuminated; and the more perfectly it is poured into it, the more brightly 1117Cit is poured back from it. « But approaching grosser matters, » that is, the grosser matters, and those which are less apt for illumination, there « it has a dimmer distributive over-appearance. » For just as, when it pours itself into them, it is received imperfectly, so also, when it pours itself out through them, over this it appears dimly from without: which comes from « the inopportuneness of the matters to be illuminated; » the inopportuneness harms, and is a hindrance to « the distributive habit of illumination, » that is, to this, that the illumination itself be either distributed, or possessed. Thus therefore in pure and polished bodies it shines more perfectly, in the grosser and coarser ones it is lessened; and a little afterward, descending to others still less apt, from this defect, 1117Dthat is, after this defect, it is contracted almost to the perfectly undistributed, that is, to this, that it be in no way distributed. For from the subtlest matters, by which it is perfectly comprehended, descending to the less apt, by which it is imperfectly received, it comes at last to others so dreggy, and gross, and dull, that they almost wholly repel the light, and can receive nothing of the illumination. In this manner the spiritual light, coming to the rational minds, perfectly illuminates those which it finds pure and purified, but those which it finds less apt it illumines with a lesser brightness, and, so to speak, with a dimmer light. But those which it meets as wholly contrary and dreggy, it leaves altogether free from its participation and communion. Thus through the likeness of visible things the truth of invisible things is demonstrated. 1118ANot only in light, but also in material heat, is there an image of the invisible truth. For heat itself more kindles those bodies which it finds more apt for its reception, but others less, until at last, meeting things wholly contrary and dissimilar, it shows in them no effect of its operation.

This is what he says: « Again the heat of fire, » as if he said: Not only in the splendor of light, but also in the heat of fire, can the aforesaid likeness be seen. « For the heat of fire distributes itself more into the more capacious ones » — understand: bodies — and into those which are well suited to its likeness, so that, namely, they may be heated by the heat, because between the hot and heat there stands a likeness, as between the white and whiteness, and the good and goodness, and, in short, of every 1118Bproperty to its own affection. But coming, namely the heat, « to the essences contrary to its re-formings, » because, namely, they resist by a contrary quality the heating through which they ought to have been re-formed unto the likeness of heat, in them the heat itself « manifests no trace, » or at least « hidden, » or obscure, « of its primal operation; » that is, it shows there no effect, in which it could even faintly be recognized that it has there at least some beginning of operation. In this manner the rational substances either receive the fire of celestial love, if they have been apt, and dwelling-places prepared and suited to its reception, or they wholly repel it, if they disagree by a contrary quality, or cannot 1118Cbe kindled. I desire that my soul repel not, by any dregginess of earthly filth, the light of the inner brightness, that it shut not out, by any coldness of malice, the heat of holy devotion, but that it grow bright and grow warm, re-formed from heaven unto the divine likeness. O what an essence, joined to the superessential good! A blessed nature, full of the supernatural good! Happily has it been made, which merits thus to be refreshed. If this be granted to me, I have nothing further to complain of concerning all these things which have passed before. The creature shows the craftsman, and the form of wonderful works commends the beauty of the author. There is one good and one beauty, and the good itself is the very beauty. The highest good and the highest beauty, and in the highest good every good, one good, and in the highest beauty every beauty, 1118Done beauty. But the visible nature could not contain all things in that one; and by God many good things were made, that they might show forth one highest good, and likewise many beautiful things, that they might demonstrate the image of one highest beauty. But many lives too were established in those whose condition merited to have something more, beyond those which were made indeed good and beautiful, and yet cannot receive this good which is life. And all these lives emulate one highest life: each in its own kind, in that which it is, and inasmuch as it is from her, and according to her who alone is true. But of every corporeal life there are two principles, heat and moisture: the one, namely moisture, furnishes the nourishment of life; the other, that is, heat, makes life to feel. Without heat 1119Athat which subsists does not live; without moisture that which lives does not subsist. Therefore these two, by a rational tempering, pour themselves into all things to be vivified, so that from them each life may receive the measure of its own capacity, as much as is fitting, to the end that the lower lives may advance, through the steps of their increments, unto the image of the highest life. For the first step of corporeal life is sense-making; the second, entering through sense, imagination; the third, through the imagination of the things conceived, memory; the fourth, according to the passible application of sense, a certain foresight without the discernment of understanding. In which there is indeed as it were an image of reason, but there is no reason. According to this, certain brute animals too seem craftier than others of their kind, and, by a certain readiness as it were of sense, imitating the foresight of a rational 1119Bmind. Which nevertheless is proved to be rather a passion of sense than an operation of the understanding. But in all these the corporeal life imitates the spiritual life. First, namely, in that it feels; secondly, in that it conceives sense; thirdly, in that it retains the things conceived; fourthly, in that, whether in things imagined or in things felt, through the passion of sense, according to a certain likeness of reason, it bends itself either to seeking or to fleeing. And so in all these the corporeal lives hold the image of the spiritual lives, and through them as intermediaries emulate, as far as they can, the highest life. For the spiritual lives themselves too all receive from the highest life that they are lives, partaking the spiritual heat and moisture descending thence, whereby they may be nourished and vivified that they may live. 1119CThese two, spiritually conceived, perfect the spiritual life: the spiritual moisture nourishing through joy; and there stands no life which has not its own heat and moisture nourishing and making to feel, that it may be able to subsist in that which is life; and that which has these more is deservedly called more a life. As there are many lives, so there are many participations, and every participation is from one, and every life from one; and so the highest good, diffusing itself into all things, constitutes every life, and by forming leads back every life unto the highest life.

There follows: « And this the more. » As if he said: Not only is this an argument of the invisible truth, that some bodies receive corporeal light and material heat, while some 1119Dwholly repel them, but this also, that through those which are more warm the other less warm ones are kindled: this, he says, is a still further argument. Further after the first, not further above the first: this is an argument of the invisible truth. Because the heat itself of material fire is admitted, and poured into those bodies, namely, « which are not cognate » to it, that is, apt to receive it: poured, I say, into them « through others having what is opportune, » that is, which stand opportunely toward it. « First, » they receive it, « inasmuch as it makes things easily movable ignited from the fiery ones. » For the heat itself, from the fiery things which, more warm, are ignited, makes others, which are secondarily and less heated, which yet themselves become ignited from the fiery ones for this reason, that they are easily movable 1120Aand apt for the reception of heat. And so from the fiery things first and principally warm it makes things ignited, and through these ignited things, namely afterward, it heats still colder and more remote ones, that is, either water, or something else, that is, « something other of the things not easily catching fire, » that is, of those which do not easily catch fire. « It heats, » I say, « proportionally, » that is, each thing according to its manner, and its measure, and its capacity for receiving heat.

There follows: « According to this then, » etc. He adapts the likeness. « According to this, he says, reason, » that is, likeness « of natural ordination, » that is, of the ordination of natural and visible things, « the supernatur alis ordination itself also, » that is, the 1120Bdistribution of divine grace, which is « the ordination of every good adornment, » that is, of every order well and comelily disposed, whether « visible » as in men, or « invisible » as in angels; that, I say, supernatural ordination fittingly manifests first « the brightness of illumination, » that is, of manifestation, or revelation, « to the most exalted essences, » that is, to the supreme spirits: that « brightness, » I say, « first appearing » in them, inasmuch as « in the most copious outpourings, » that is, as it befits it to appear when it copiously pours itself out, or to those into whom it has most copiously poured itself. « And through those, » namely the most exalted essences, those essences « which are after » them « partake the divine ray, » that is, the divine brightness. « For these, » 1120Cnamely the most exalted essences, « are the first knowing God, and supereminently desiring the divine virtue. » And because they principally know and love, they have been made worthy « to become pre-operative, as far as is possible, with virtue and action like to God; » that is, that before all the others, first after God, they may operate into all subject things, by bestowing the divine virtue; and in that very thing become like to God, because the virtue which they receive from above they expend upon their subjects. For they « extend the essences which are after them, or subject to them, unto a like virtue, » namely to their own virtue, inasmuch as it is a virtue holding itself deiformly, because in that they do this, by their virtue they imitate God, « copiously delivering to them, » namely to the subject essences, « from the brightness supervening upon them. And those, » 1120Dnamely the subject essences, « again » deliver « to their own subjects; » « and » thus « through each one, » the outpouring of the divine gift running on, « the first delivers to that which is after it, » and so onward unto the end.

There follows: « The water itself, » etc. After the likeness which he set forth concerning fire according to brightness and heat, he sets forth again another likeness concerning water. « The water itself, he says, does it not proportionally reach into all? » The moisture itself of water, which diffuses itself through all the parts of earthly bodies, proportionally fills all, moistening some more, some less, according to this, namely, that each one is more or less capable of moistening. In this example therefore is fittingly demonstrated, likewise, the distribution of divine grace, coming forth to all in no equal 1121Amanner.

There follows: « It is therefore, » etc. Since, he says, just as one visible light illuminates many things, and from that light many shining things shine, so the invisible light illumines all things invisibly shining. « Therefore God is the principle of illuminating, » or of illumination, « at once to all the illuminated. » Nor is it a wonder: since he too is light, and not light in any manner whatsoever, but by nature, that is, naturally, and truly, and properly. Naturally, because from himself; and truly, because in himself; and properly, because through himself. Naturally, because from that which he is he is light; and truly, because that very thing which he is is light; and properly, because through that which he is he is light. For that is natural which is not taken from elsewhere, 1121Bthat is truly which is essentially possessed, that is properly which is not conferred through another. And so thus God is light: and I say too little when I say that he is light, inasmuch as he is the essence of the light itself. For the rest, who shine, are not the essence of light, but its effect. They therefore, in that they are lights, are from light; but he is light from that which he is. « And it is also causal of being and seeing, that is, of the essence and vision of the light itself; » as if it were said thus: God is the essence of light, and is also the cause of that essence, because that which is light, is essentially; and that which is essentially, is from itself. Thus therefore he is the cause of the essence of light: and not only of the essence of light, but also of the vision itself, or manifestation, of the light, because he has from himself not only that he is essentially light 1121Cshining by nature, but this also, that he temporally shines, illuminating by grace.

There follows: « Then, deiformly and God-likely remaining superposed, » etc. In God, he says, the light itself is nothing other than the essence itself, to him for whom to be and to be light are the same, who from his very self is the principle of illuminating, because those who first shine he illuminates from his very self. But then, that is, thereafter, after him, namely God, each thing « remaining superposed deiformly and God-likely, » that is, according to the conformation and likeness of God — understand: it becomes the principle of illuminating after itself, « transferring through itself the divine lights into that, » namely into what is constituted after itself. The sense is this: That God, who is superposed to all, illuminates through himself those who are nearest; 1121Dand thus he becomes the principle of illumination, illuminating the first shining ones; then each one of those first shining ones, superposed to all the other subjects according to the conformity and likeness of God, becomes the principle of illumination to each one of the subjects, transferring through himself the divine lights into that, namely the subject. But that he put 'superposed' in the neuter, in place of what he should have said, 'superposed' in the masculine, namely order, or angel, was done after the manner of Scripture, especially when unknown and wonderful things are treated of, when it is said 'that,' as if it were said, 'whatever that is.' But that he subjoined 'to each one after itself,' this seems said as though that superposed thing, whatever it is, being one, is the principle of illumination to the several 1122Asubjects, so that it may furnish a light not as many to many, but as one to many. But in that which after this he again added, « transferring the divine lights into that, » it seems to minister illumination not as one to many, but as one to one. Whence it is plain that, according to the manner of Scripture, whether number be put alternately for number, or gender for gender, the truth of the same understanding is not changed.

There follows: « Therefore the most exalted disposition of the celestial minds. » He infers from the aforesaid, as if he said: Since the first disposition has received the divine things, and furnishes illumination to all its subjects; « therefore the essences of all the remaining ones marvel at the disposition, » that is, the spirits of all the remaining orders 1122Bcontemplate with admiration and astonishment « that most exalted disposition of the celestial minds itself, the principle after God, according to what is consequent. » For thus it is consequent, that they should know God as the first principle; then also should venerate those who are first after God, as in their own manner a principle unto the things that follow, through whom the divine grace descends to those who are subject. And this is what follows: « They marvel that these are the principle of all sacred and divine knowledge and of divine imitation: » which, namely, flow to the subjects through them, as the divine illumination distributed through them into all the other celestial virtues, and not only into them, but also into us; namely men, who receive the divine illuminations by their mediation. And because all the remaining celestial 1122Cessences are illuminated by the mediation of the first ones, therefore whatever sacred thing they can perform, and like to God, this indeed they first attribute to God, who is the cause of all; then to those first spirits, by whose operating and mediation they receive the divine grace. This is what he says: « Wherefore, » namely, because through those illuminated by God the rest are illuminated, therefore the rest themselves « refer every sacred and God-like operation of theirs unto God as the causal one, » because he is the first cause of all; « then they refer it unto the first intellects, » that is, the supreme spirits, who are deiform, or conformable to God, in this, that they bestow the spiritual gifts: not however as God, who is the first cause from whom they are, but 1122Das the first effects, through whom they are. Therefore they refer their good to those, through whom it is, « as through the first operators, and masters of divine things, » namely of gifts. Operators indeed in that they move by effecting, but masters in that they preside by directing.

There follows: « Does not then the first, » etc. Num stands for nonne. « Does not then, he says, the first disposition of the holy angels, » which is so greatly more sublime than all the rest, « have more than all » the highest and « fiery property, » that is, charity, as in the seraphim; « and the poured-out, » that is, abundant « tradition of the divine wisdom, and the mystical of the most exalted knowledge of the divine illuminations, » that is, the mystical, or hidden, or profound, most exalted 1123Aknowledge, which it perceives from the divine illuminations, as in the cherubim; and the sedent property, as in the thrones, bearing, namely, God, and « signifying the divine reception: » because in that they are called thrones, it is openly signified that they receive God sitting and resting in them. The sense is: Does not the first hierarchy, more excellently and more abundantly than all the rest, have both the fire of charity, and the light of knowledge, and the judgment of discernment? It has assuredly all these more than all the rest. « But the » dispositions themselves « of the subordinate essences, » that is, of the subject orders, do indeed themselves also partake the « fiery virtue, » that is, charity, as the seraphim; the wise and knowing « virtue, » that is, knowledge, as the 1123Bcherubim; and the virtue receptive of God, as the thrones: « they partake, » I say; but « below, » that is, more imperfectly than the first ones: « and looking to the first ones, » that is, imitating the first ones, « and through them, » namely the first ones, brought back into that of deiformity which is possible for them, that is, brought back to as much deiformity as is possible for them; through them, namely the first ones, I say, « made worthily, » that is, made worthy, « by divine imitation, » that is, that they may imitate God, « pre-operative, » that is, operating, before and more excellently than all the others, from him and according to him.

There follows: « The said holy properties therefore, » etc. Since, he says, through the first ones the subsequent ones receive the gifts of graces, therefore the holy properties already said above — such as was to set the prophet's lips on fire with a coal, 1123Cwhich seems to be proper to the seraphim, and to teach knowledge, which seems proper to the cherubim. Such properties therefore, « of which the participation comes about through the first essences, » the other essences « subsisting after them, » these properties, I say, « place back in them, » that is, attribute to those first ones, namely through whom they partake them: « as in hierarchs, » that is, in princes, and superiors, so that they may refer them to those from whom they received them. « They place back, » I say, « in them after God: » because they first attribute them to God, then to those who are nearest after God. But that he says that the subsequent essences become the participation of the properties of the first ones, the manner of speaking is such as if he said: They become partakers 1123Dof the properties of the first ones, because that which the first possess through property, the second share through participation.

There follows: « He says therefore these things, saying, » etc. He, he says, of whom I spoke above, who furnished me a not unfitting apology. He, saying these things which have thus far been said concerning the divine illumination descending through some to others, says that the aforesaid vision — about which the question arose concerning the purification of the prophet's lips — « was received by the theologian himself, » namely Isaiah, « through one of the holy and blessed » angels « ruling over us, » that is, over men, « descending from that, » understand: the first hierarchy. For he says this, that that vision which Isaiah saw descended from the first hierarchy, and was brought to the prophet himself 1124Athrough one angel of the last order of them, who are the lowest among the angels and preside over us alone: and therefore he says that that angel « before its own illuminative hand-leading, » that is, that revelation by which he himself led the prophet by the hand and instructed him, and by which he himself had before been illuminated by the first hierarchy: « had reposed in, » that is, had referred to « that holy contemplation, » that is, to the first hierarchy itself, from which he contemplated that he had had what he had, and had done what he did. « He sees also, » Isaiah himself, « sitting above, » that is, sitting on high and aloft, « the most exalted essences, placed after God, and about God, and with God, as far as, in symbols, » that is, in figures and likenesses, it « is to be said. » For all this is symbolic and figurative, 1124Bthat God, according to a corporeal likeness, is said to sit upon a lofty throne; and the seraphim are reported to stand about him and beside him. And Isaiah himself sees also a summit more sublime than « all these, » namely than the most exalted essences of the blessed spirits; « even super-secretly, » that is, in a most excellent manner: « the summit, » I say, « above the principal, » that is, God, who is the highest and principal of all, superplaced « in the midst of the superfirmed virtues. » For in the midst of the virtues, that is, of the holy spirits, who are firmed and established by an eternal placing about God above all things, God himself, the highest and principal, is seen sitting upon a throne lofty and elevated. « In these visions therefore the theologian himself learned, » namely Isaiah this, « that the divine, » that is, the divinity, 1124C« is superplaced incomparably above every superessential superexcellence, above every invisible and visible virtue, » that is, that the divinity incomparably transcends, according to every mode of excelling, every virtue, visible and invisible. And no wonder, if the divine itself transcends all things: « and yet, » that is, assuredly, « because it is removed from all, » namely by excellence, inasmuch as that which is universal is removed from those things which are all in part, and so far removed and excelling that « it is not like » « even to the first essences of those » which are, but far distant and transcending. But that he says « to the first essences of those which are, » it is as if he should say, to the essences of those who are first, or to the essences which 1124Dare first, that is, to the supreme spirits of the angels. Nor did he learn only that the divine is removed from all, and like to none. « But still, » or moreover, he learned this also, that it « is the principle of all, » because from it are all things; and the sanctifying cause, because through it all things subsist; and the immutable foundation of those things which are, by a secret singularity, because all things persevere subsisting in it: which, containing all things by its secret and hidden divinity, as a unity gathers together the universe, and as a singularity binds together multiplicity. From which both being and well-being belongs even to those most highly fortified virtues, that is, to those spirits who are firmed and established in the highest virtue and felicity: who have from it not only that they are, but also that they are blessed. All this therefore he learned in 1125Athat vision concerning the excellence of the divinity. « Then, » he also learned, and « was taught, the same deiform virtues of the most holy seraphim, » or, to speak more expressly, of the same most holy seraphim, « the deiform virtues, » or the same virtues which he had learned to be in God, he learned also to be in the seraphim out of conformity to God; because, what God has by nature, they have by grace, being conformed to God. But which and what sort of virtues, or also from what he learned the virtues to be in the seraphim, he subjoins, saying: « From their sacred surname indeed, which, » that is, which surname, « is fiery. » Because seraphim is interpreted burning, or succeeding, and signifies fiery: « concerning which » fiery thing, he says, we « shall a little later, as far as it will be possible for us, introduce the anagogies, » 1125Bthat is, the upward-leadings « of the fiery virtue, » namely of the charity of the seraphim themselves, « into the deiform: » that is, into a thing so worthy and altogether like to God. Or thus: From this sacred surname, I say, the prophet himself learned the anagogies, that is, the upward-leadings, or ascents, or advancements of the fiery virtue, that is, of the charity of the seraphim themselves. « But in the expanded sacred formation of the wings, » that is, in the sacred formation of the expanded wings, the prophet himself learned « an absolute and most lofty extension into the divine, » which is « in the first, and in the middle, and in the last intellects. » Through the surname therefore, which sounds "fiery," he learned the fiery virtue; that is, charity ascending to the heights by desire; but through the expansion of the wings, he learned knowledge stretching itself by subtlety 1125Cinto far-off things, and extending itself even unto the divine to be grasped, in the first, and middle, and last intellects, that is, in the spirits first, and middle, and last in that order: or in the first intellects by which they grasp the divine above themselves, the middle by which they grasp the divine in themselves, the last by which they grasp the divine below themselves. But the extension itself, or the stretching-forth of knowledge, is both absolute, because, diffusing itself unto immensity, it is enwrapped by no darkness of ignorance; and most lofty, because, pressing on to the highest things, it is weighed down by no infirmity. And not only from these things which have been said did he recognize the virtue of their love and knowledge, « but also, seeing their manifold and multiform character, the intellectual theologian himself » 1125DIsaiah, « and seeing also that vision distinguished by wings beneath the feet, and it distinguished by wings beneath the faces: and seeing also the ever-moved, » that is, that which ever is, in the middle wings: through all these things « was led back, » and instructed « to the invisible knowledge of the things which were seen. » For through this, that he saw the distinction of the wings which downward beneath the feet; and of the wings which beneath the faces of the one sitting were stretched upward; and of the wings which in the middle were ever moved: through this, namely, he himself saw the manifold virtue of them, which is both multiplied in operation, signified through the motion, and multiform in knowledge and love, signified through the stretching-forth. And in all these things he was led back and admonished, that he might invisibly recognize what he saw according to the appearance of visible things: 1126A« the manifold-wayed and manifold-seeing virtue of those most lofty intellects being manifested to him through all these things. » Which virtue, namely, is both manifold-wayed, inasmuch as it is moved in manifold ways by desiring; and manifold-seeing, inasmuch as it is beatified in manifold ways by possessing. Manifold-wayed in that by which it presses on by searching; manifold-seeing in that which it finds by penetrating. Many are the ways by which one goes to the one good: therefore rightly manifold-wayed. But why manifold-seeing, since it is one that is seen, unless because in the one all things are seen? Thus therefore the prophet was led back to the knowledge of truth, the manifold-wayed and manifold-seeing virtue of the most lofty intellects being shown to him through sacred images. There being shown to him also « their sacred dread, » or reverence, « which they have supermundanely, » that is, impassibly and 1126Bpurely, « against a proud and audacious and impossible searching-out of higher and lower things, » that is, lest they should proudly, and audaciously, and impossibly search out, beyond the measure of their possibility, the secrets of God, which are higher than they by majesty, and lower by profundity. For this reason indeed they veil the head, that they may profess the higher things to be covered from them: for this reason they veil the feet, that they may testify the lower and deeper things to be impenetrable. On this account they dread to be proud and audacious toward that which is impossible to be searched out. Proud toward the heights, audacious toward the depths; proud, lest they be too much lifted up; audacious, lest they be cast down headlong. In this therefore they have a sacred dread, because it is a sacred thing to fear that which, if presumed, would do harm; and they have it supermundanely, because they dread without passion and affliction. For they fear, 1126Cand are not affected; they tremble, and are not shaken. They are afraid, yet secure, and without any trouble, or corruption of their rest, they are wary of passing, toward the incomprehensible majesty, beyond the measure of their possibility. To the knowledge of all these things the prophet was led back, seeing the aforesaid things, in the extension of the wings. And seeing also the unceasing and ever-high-flying character, namely of the persevering motion in the commotion of the wings: which commotion consists in the commensuration of actions imitating God, that is, in their actions by which they imitate God, commensurating themselves to their possibility, so that they presume to do nothing beyond reason and measure.

There follows: « But he was instructed also in that divine and much 1126Dprecious hymnody. » As if he should say: Not only in the habit of the seraphim did he recognize their virtue; but also in their voice he learned the hymnody, that is, the divine praise, « the angel forming the vision for the theologian himself according to the virtue » of his capacity, « and handing on his own sacred knowledge: » because what the angel himself knew, through this sacred vision he made the theologian to know. « He taught therefore » the angel himself « him, » namely the theologian, in this, that he purged his lips — of him who already seemed just — with a coal taken from the altar, « because the very participation of the unknown divine brightness, received as far as is possible, is a purgation to however perfect ones. » Because however much anyone has been purged, he becomes more purged when that is received.

1127AThere follows: « But these things, » etc. He said that the perception of the divine brightness is a purgation: now consequently he shows that this brightness, proceeding from the hidden depth of the highest divinity, unto the perfecting and illuminating of all the sacred intellects, first manifests itself to the most lofty virtues placed more openly about it: and he shows how it is in its own and true being; then after the first ones it shows itself to the second; and afterward to the last; and at the very last also to our human intellects, and so, descending, it conducts its illumination to each virtue, according as each has been made deiform by it, this is what he says: « This, » namely « brightness proceeding from the remote causes of the divinity, going forth from which divinity it perfects all the sacred intellects, » that 1127Bis, the rational minds, illuminating them « by a superessential hiddenness, » that is, by a very hidden and secret inspiration: proceeding, I say, from those remote causes unto manifestation, it first becomes more manifest as it is, that is, according to its true being, to the most lofty virtues placed about it: and it manifests, « and distributes itself to those more » than to others; « and then » after those « it manifests itself to the second, » « then to the last, » lastly also « to our intellectual virtues, » that is, to the rational minds; « and so, » descending from the first even to the last, « it conducts its illumination through the several virtues: so, » that is, manifest in the several ones to just so great a degree as each virtue exists from that same brightness according to the deiform, that is, according to 1127Cconformity to God. For it illuminates each virtue the more, the more it fits it to deiformity. But why this brightness proceeds to manifestation he subjoins: « Unto the praising of the unknown thing of its own hiddenness. » For we perceive something of it for this reason, that in that, and through that which is hidden, and unknown, and altogether incomprehensible in it, we may praise it.

There follows: « But it shines through the several ones, to the second through the first. » For everywhere it shines to the second through the first, or through the first ones. « And if it behooves to say it briefly, » this can be said in sum, that « the first is led from the hidden to the manifest through the first virtues. » For that which is in itself is altogether hidden; and it then 1127Dfirst begins to be seen when it first begins to be had. For neither is it ever seen by anyone, except by him by whom it is had. « This therefore the theologian learned from the light-leading angel. » From the angel that is leader of the brightness he learned this. A new composition, "light-leading," as if he should say "light-leader." From him therefore the theologian learned this. What is this? this, namely, is what he learned: « That the purgation, and all the divine operations shining back through the first essences, are distributed through them into all the rest, according to the analogy of each of the rest, » that is, the mode and measure, « unto the deifying participations. Wherefore also he reposed the fierily-purgative property » — that angel, that is, attributed it — « to the seraphim themselves consequently after God: » and therefore « nothing inordinate » is said « if the seraphim is said to purge 1128Athe theologian. For so also God purges all, of whose whole purgation, » or of whose purgation of all, « he is the cause; » and not only God, but rather in this example it can be seen how not only he through whom something is done, but also he from whom it is done, is said to do it. Because « we shall use an example more nearly at hand. » Thus the seraphim is said to purge him whom the inferior angel purges, the virtue and mandate having been received from the seraphim: « Just as, according to us, the highest priest, purging or illuminating through his ministers, or priests, is himself said to purge and to illuminate, the orders purged through him reposing their own sacred operations upon him, » that is, attributing them to him of themselves. For what he works through them, is through them attributed to him. « So also his own purgative knowledge 1128Band virtue, the angel himself perfecting the purgation of the theologian, reposes upon God indeed as upon the causal one, then upon the seraphim itself as upon the highest priest that first acts. » So therefore the angel attributed what he did, first to God, then to the seraphim, through whom he did it. « As perhaps someone would say, » that is, for example: « If anyone with angelic reverence, » that is, under the person of an angel, which is to be revered: « teaching » the prophet « to be purged » by him, « should say » to him: O Isaiah, « of the purgation to be perfected in thee, » namely through me, « I am not the principle, but before me the principle is exalted indeed, » that is, God, who is both « essence, and Creator, and causal » of all and bringing the first essences to be present; « and containing them about himself by a placing, » that 1128Cis, by stable firmness; « and preserving them unchangeable, and lacking a fall, » that is, lest they be together turned from themselves, and fall; « and moving himself into the first ones of the participation of his own provident operations, » that is, of the operations which he does according to providence; because everything that he does in time, he disposed in eternal providence. The proper operation of God is when he works through his very self without a mediating creature, from which, doubtless, the first participation comes; because they receive him without a medium who become the first effects of his operation. For the first operation of God is when he moves himself from himself; the first participation, when he presents himself through himself. And that indeed is the most lofty creature, unto which the first operation is, 1128Dand in which is the first participation through it, then descending to the things that follow. In this manner the subject angel attributed what he did to the superior seraphim, from whom he received the power to be able to do this. « For this, » that he received from another the power to do it, he says, « teaching me to manifest these things, » or to signify « the mission of the seraphim itself. » He, he says, who, furnishing an apology for all these aforesaid things, taught me, himself says that the mission of the seraphim signifies this, namely that what he did he had assuredly received to do from him from whom he came. Therefore fittingly the angel himself can say to the prophet: « I am not the principle of the purgation which I work in thee. But the exalted and first principle before me is » God, who is Creator and cause of all. Then, moreover, that « adornment 1129Aof the excelling essences, » that is, the order of the highest spirits, which is « after God the priest, and leader » bestowing divine things, and leading back to God: « from which » order « I also was instructed to purge deiformly, » even as now I do in thee. « It, » namely the order, « is that which purges thee through me, » on this account, because it taught me to purge: « through which, » namely order, the very cause and worker of the whole purgation (understand: the divinity) « brings forth its provident actions from the hidden even into us » lowest ones, namely the angels. If the angel working the purgation should say these and words like these to the prophet, it would not be unfitting: whence it is plain that when the seraphim is said to fly to the prophet, and is said to purge the prophet, it can be understood not unfittingly that this operation 1129Bwas indeed administered through the subject angel, but attributed to the superior one, from whom it was.

There follows: « These things indeed he taught me: » they are the words of the author returning to his subject. He, he says, who furnished me the apology, taught me all these aforesaid things. « But I, » O Timothy! « hand on to thee » all things either said by me, or approved, but holding to either side. « But to thy intellectual and discretive knowledge, » that is, to thy discretion: « I would grant that the one part of the said causes be released, » namely by thee, « from doubt, » that is, to be held as ratified and undoubted: « and that the same be honored before the other as having what is consequent, and reasonable, and equally true. » This I grant both to thy will, and to thy discretion, and to thy knowledge, that thou choose the one part of these opinions, doubt being removed, 1130Aand honor it more than the other as true and reasonable. « Or, » if this pleases not, I grant thee « to find from thyself what is truly nearer to the true. Or, » if that still pleases not, I grant thee « to learn from another, God, namely, giving it, » whether thou recognize it in this or in any other way: « yet the angels first » receiving the very knowledge of truth « from God, » and afterward, through the angels, revealing it to us holy men, the friends of the angels — that is, receiving it for this, that they may reveal it to us. Or thus. And I grant thee to reveal to us « through its more lovable contemplation, » the angels, and the friends of the angels, first receiving, namely, the very knowledge of truth. A wonderful word. The angels receive from God, and men from the angels; and men themselves in turn, 1130Btaught by the angels, teach other men; and the doctrine of truth comes through some into others, and many seem to be masters and teachers of truth; and yet no one is taught, because he is not illuminated from the contemplation of it. Other masters apply the ministry; there is one master, who alone furnishes the understanding. He can teach without the others; the others cannot without him. Thou givest me the word. But what is a word without intelligence? Through the word indeed intelligence comes. But he places intelligence in the heart who illuminates within, not he who sounds without. His unction teaches us concerning all things. Thou speakest without; but within thou dost not anoint. Therefore thy erudition is indeed lovable to me. But more lovable is the contemplation of him; because even this, which in thy erudition is lovable, is nothing except from the contemplation of him.

TITULUS CAPITULI XIV. Quid significat traditus angelicus numerus.

TITLE OF CHAPTER XIV. What the handed-down angelic number signifies.

LITTERA.

  • 1129C

Quid significat angelicus numerus traditus. Et hoc autem dignum, ut existimo, intellectuali cognitione, quia eloquiorum de angelis traditio, « millies millia » esse ait, et « decem millia decies millies (Dan. VII), secundum nos sublimissimos numerorum in seipsam revolvens, et multiplicans, et per hoc aperte significans innumerabiles coelestium essentiarum ordinationes. Multae enim sunt beatae militiae supermundalium intellectuum, infirmam et coarctatam superantes materialium secundum nos numerorum commensurationem, et a sola gnostica definitae supermundana, et coelesti intelligentia, et scientia, secundum ipsam ditissime eis donatam sanitatem divinae multae scientiae sapientifica omnium simul quae sunt superessentialiter 1129Dsubsistentis principii, et causae substantificae, et continentis virtutis, et ambientis consummationis.

THE TEXT.

  • 1129C

What the handed-down angelic number signifies. And this too is worthy, as I judge, of intellectual cognition, because the tradition of the oracles concerning the angels says there to be « a thousand times a thousand, » and « ten thousand ten thousand times (Dan. VII), according to us the most sublime of numbers, revolving them into itself, and multiplying them, and through this openly signifying the innumerable ordinations of the celestial essences. For many are the blessed hosts of the supermundane intellects, surpassing the weak and constricted commensuration of material numbers according to us, and defined by the gnostic supermundane and celestial intelligence and knowledge alone, according to the very health most richly bestowed on them of the divine and manifold knowledge, sapiential of all things at once which are — of the principle superessentially 1129Dsubsisting, and of the substance-making cause, and of the containing virtue, and of the environing consummation.

EXPOSITIO.

« Quid significat angelicus numerus traditus, » id est datus, vel definitus a Scripturis sanctis? Non solum, inquit, supradicta; sed et « hoc intellectuali cognitione dignum est, » quare scilicet certus et definitus numerus angelicis spiritibus attribuatur: 1130C« quia traditio » divinorum « eloquiorum de angelis ait esse millies millia, et decies millies decem millia » angelorum, « revolvens sublimissimos numerorum secundum nos, » id est numeros qui secundum nos sublimissimi sunt. Revolvens dico in seipsam, hoc est, in pronuntiatione verborum, quae in ipsa continentur verba, revolvens in verba, et alia per alia multiplicans, sicut millia in millies et decem millia in decies millies per multiplicationem revolvuntur. Quod apertius dixisset revolvens numeros in seipsos, quamvis tamen hoc expressius dictum sit, quia non numeri, sed nomina numerorum per multiplicationem in se collocata revolvuntur. Si itaque traditio eloquiorum multitudinem coelestium spirituum signans, ait millies millia, et decies 1130Dmillies decem millia esse angelorum, sublimissimos secundum nos numeros in se revolvens, vel inter se conferens, et alios per alios multiplicans. « Et per hoc aperte significans innumerabiles esse ordinationes coelestium essentiarum. » In eo enim quod maximos numeros posuit, patenter innuit, quod adhuc dicere debuisset, si amplius dicere potuisset. Sane sciendum quod hoc, quod ait millies millia, et decies millies decem millia, nostra translatio hoc modo 1131Anon continet; sed millia millium, et decies millies centena millia, quod tamen ad eamdem veritatem spectat. Ideo ergo infinitos significare volens, maximos numeros finitos posuit, quia « multae sunt beatae militiae, » id est beatae multitudines Deo militantes, « supermundalium intellectuum, superantes infirmam et coarctatam commensurationem materialium numerorum secundum nos, et definitae a sola gnostica, id est cognitiva scientia; vel cognitione scilicet divina, quae omnia cognoscit, et sola novit numerum illarum supernarum virtutum, et sola discernit eas, et plene cognoscit secundum ipsam sanitatem, id est puritatem, vel integritatem simplicis et incorruptibilis naturae earum, donatam eis ditissime et abundantissime supermundana, et 1131Bcoelesti sapientifica intelligentia et scientia divinae, et multae scientiae principii omnium quae sunt superessentialiter et existentis, et causae substantificae omnium et virtutis continentis omnia, et consummationis ambientis omnia. » Sensus talis est, quia sola Dei sapientia, quae est gnostica, id est cognitiva omnium, definite et perfecte cognoscit numerum 1132Aillarum essentiarum coelestium in illa puritate et integritate, in qua eas creavit et formavit. Quae scilicet scientia et coelestis est, et divina, et multa. Coelestis, per puritatem; divina, per veritatem; multa, per incomprehensibilitatem. Et cum talis sit in se, sapientifica etiam est in opere suo, sapienter faciens omnia, nihilque reprehensione dignum constituens. Et ista talis sapientia, per quam omnia creata sunt, et omnia cognoscuntur, ipsa est illius, qui est principium omnium, quae sunt (quia ab ipso sunt omnia) superessentialiter subsistens per se, videlicet perfectus, et nullo indigens; et qui est causa substantifica omnium, quia omnia subsistere facit, ut sint; et est virtus continens omnia, ut maneant in eo quod sunt; et est consummatio 1132Bambiens omnia ne diffluant, aut decidant ab eo, quod sic sint.
